summary: Leopold Takawira, known as the Lion of Chirumanzi, was a Midlands-born teacher who rose to headmaster in Highfield before giving up the classroom for full-time nationalist politics in 1957. He helped found the NDP, served as its interim president and as its representative in London, then became a founding member of ZAPU and, from 1963, Vice-President of ZANU. Detained from 1964, he collapsed and died in prison on 15 June 1970, and his remains were moved from his home area to the National Heroes Acre in 1982.

timeline.text: Born in Gambiza Village, Chirumanzu District, as the only child of Samuel and Theresa Hapazari Takawira.
Began school at Holy Cross Mission in Chirumanzu, later moving on to Chishawasha Mission and then Kutama Mission, where he did his secondary schooling.
Studied for a Diploma in Education at Marianhill College in Natal, South Africa.
Went to Roma University College in Basutoland (now Lesotho) to study for a BA, but left without completing it and returned to Southern Rhodesia in 1954.
Began teaching at Mhofu Primary School in Highfield and later became headmaster at Chipembere Primary School, where Highfield's nationalist climate drew him into organised political activism.
Gave up teaching to devote himself full time to nationalist politics, and entered the Capricorn Africa Society, later becoming its Executive Officer.
Became associated with the Bantu Voice newspaper, an influential platform for nationalist ideas and mobilisation.

timeline.date: after the 1959 ban of the SRANC
timeline.text: After the SRANC was banned, played a key part in setting up the National Democratic Party and quickly became chairman of its Harare Branch and a Central Executive Committee member.

Was arrested on allegations of political agitation; although later acquitted, the prosecution caused widespread anger among nationalists and a large solidarity march in Salisbury (now Harare), marking an escalation of the anti-colonial struggle.
Was elected Interim President of the NDP during a reshuffle of its leadership.
Was appointed the NDP's Director of International Relations in London, and from there cabled home to reject the 1961 constitutional proposals that gave Africans only 15 seats in a 65-seat Parliament.

timeline.date: after the ban of the NDP
timeline.text: After the NDP was banned, became a founding member of ZAPU and was later appointed its Secretary for External Affairs.
Joined ZANU and was appointed its Vice-President.
Was arrested in Harare and detained at Wha Wha and Sikombela prisons.

Following the 1965 Unilateral Declaration of Independence he was moved to Salisbury Central Prison, where he became acquainted with fellow nationalists such as Enos Nkala and Robert Mugabe and went on encouraging resistance despite failing health.
Collapsed while in detention, fell into a coma and died; he was first buried in his home area in Chirumanzu.
His body was exhumed and laid to rest again at the National Heroes Acre in honour of his role in the liberation struggle.

summary: Herbert Chitepo was a Manicaland-born, mission-educated lawyer who became the first black Zimbabwean admitted to the English Bar in 1953 and the first African advocate in Southern Rhodesia in 1954. He defended nationalists as legal adviser to the ANC, NDP and ZAPU, briefly served as Tanzania's Director of Public Prosecutions, then became founding chairman of ZANU and a central figure in the armed struggle. He was killed by a car bomb in Lusaka on 18 March 1975 and reburied at the National Heroes Acre in 1981; a law school and a school of ideology carry his name.

timeline.text: Born at Bonda Mission Hospital in Nyanga District, the third of three children of Hubert Tiyane and Isabel Chitepo.
His father died when he was three and his mother a year later, leaving him in the care of an uncle named Halward Dzwingwe and local Anglican clergy.
Started primary school at St David's Mission.
Attended St Augustine's School in Penhalonga until 1941, becoming one of the first three Zimbabweans to complete secondary school.
Studied at Adams College in Natal, South Africa, and in 1945 began teacher training at the same college.
Entered Fort Hare University in South Africa to study for a BA in English and History.

Taught briefly at St Augustine's Mission in Penhalonga, where Anglican priests had him give Shona lessons to incoming missionaries, an assignment that led to a post as Research Assistant in Shona at London's School of Oriental and African Studies.
Began studying English law at King's College and the Inns of Court in London, becoming roommate and close friend of Julius Nyerere.
Was called to the Bar at the Temple, the first black Zimbabwean admitted to the English Bar.
Came back to Southern Rhodesia and was enrolled by its High Court, the first African to practise there as an advocate.
Married Victoria Fikile Mahamba Sithole.

timeline.date: ANC 12 September 1957 to 1959; NDP 1 January 1960 to 9 December 1961; ZAPU 17 December 1961 to 1963
timeline.text: Served as legal adviser to the ANC, NDP and ZAPU in turn as each was founded and banned, using the law to defend nationalists and challenge colonial legislation.
As a founding member and legal adviser of the NDP, delivered a paper on the impact of legislation on the community at its national convention, condemning the exclusion of Africans from lawmaking.
Was invited by Julius Nyerere to be Tanzania's first Director of Public Prosecutions at independence, but gave up the post to concentrate on the liberation struggle at home.
Became the founding chairman of ZANU, playing a key role in building the armed struggle through ZANLA and in winning international support.
Was killed in a car bomb attack blamed on Rhodesian forces as he left his house in Chilenje, Lusaka, Zambia.
Was reburied at the National Heroes Acre in Harare.

notes: born.date: year read as 1923 from OCR '4923'; the printed age at death (52) would be 51 for a 15 June 1923 birth.
ZANU chairmanship: start read as December 1963; the end date and surrounding sentence are garbled.
Burial: 'reburied at the National [Heroes Acre] ... Harare on the 11th of August 1981' is partly garbled but consistent.
Location of the Chitepo Law School is garbled ('Mas...') and not recorded.

summary: Josiah Magama Tongogara, affectionately called Tongo, was born in Shurugwi in 1940, trained as an accountant in Zambia, then joined ZANU and received military training in Tanzania and China. He rose to command ZANLA and serve as ZANU's Secretary for Defence, building bases and routes, opening the North-Eastern front and coordinating operations with FRELIMO in Mozambique. A delegate at the Geneva and Lancaster House talks, he was valued as a moderating voice for ZANU-ZAPU unity and is described as Zimbabwe's first African General. He died in a car accident in Mozambique in December 1979 aged 39 and was reburied at the National Heroes Acre in 1981.

timeline.text: Born at Shurugwi Hospital, the third of eight children of Magama and Sukai Tongogara.
Went to Rockford Primary School and then Jovo Lingo Primary School, pursued private accounting studies in Northern Rhodesia (Zambia) and worked there as an accountant for golf and theatre clubs.
Became politically active in Zambia through UNIP and then ZAPU, and joined ZANU in 1963, holding several leadership posts for the Lusaka District.
Underwent military training in Tanzania.
Went on to further training in China, with courses on rallying the masses, military intelligence, political theory and guerrilla tactics.
Rose to command ZANLA, ZANU's military wing, and became known for his military expertise, discipline and ability to unify diverse factions within the liberation movement.
Served as ZANLA Chief of Defence and as a member of the Dare reChimurenga war council and High Command, linking political leaders and fighters at the front.
Organised and equipped ZANU guerrilla groups, set up forward bases across the Zambezi and negotiated joint operations with FRELIMO, fighting the Portuguese alongside it in Tete Province.
Launched the North-Eastern front in 1971-72, setting up routes and camps that ran from Zambia across Mozambique to the Mount Darwin district of Mashonaland Central.
Is credited in the book with planning the Chinhoyi battle and the sabotage of petrol tanks in Harare, which it says changed the course of the war.
Took part as a delegate in the Geneva Constitutional conference.
Took the post of Secretary for Defence on ZANU's Central Committee.
Was the military member of the ZANU-PF team at the Lancaster House talks that paved the way to independence, and was viewed as a moderating influence favouring ZANU-ZAPU unity.
Died in a car accident at Magacai Village, Massinga District, in Mozambique's Inhambane Province, aged 39.
His remains were reinterred at the National Heroes Acre in Harare; the Josiah Magama Tongogara Barracks in the city carry his name.
Received, after his death, the Great Commander of Zimbabwe Order of Merit in recognition of his ZANLA service.

summary: Jason Moyo, known as JZ, was a Plumtree-born builder who became a trade unionist and then a nationalist leader, chairing the Bulawayo branch of the ANC and serving on the NDP executive before becoming ZAPU's National Treasurer. Based in Lusaka, he led the ZAPU faction from 1971, helped build ZIPRA and the Patriotic Front, and became ZAPU's second Vice-President in 1976. He was killed by a parcel bomb on 22 January 1977 and reburied in Zimbabwe on 11 August 1981.

timeline.text: Born in Plumtree, one of six children.
Began primary school at Dongwedongwe School in Matobo District, studying up to Standard 6.

Gained a Building and Carpentry diploma at Mzingwane Vocational Training School, moved to Bulawayo as a builder, built a strong reputation in the construction trade and later put up a classroom block for his former primary school.
Early in 1950 was drawn into trade unionism by Benjamin Burombo, who then led the African Workers Voice Association, and was later elected General Secretary of the African Artisans' Union.
Became a member of the ANC's Bulawayo Branch and was soon its Chairman; his success in rallying people against the settler government brought persecution on his relatives.
Was imprisoned at Marandellas (today Marondera) and freed in 1960.
Was elected to the National Executive of the NDP at its congress.

timeline.date: after the NDP ban in December 1961
timeline.text: Joined ZAPU and was nominated its National Treasurer.
Remained with ZAPU when it split from ZANU.
Following the successive bans, went to Lusaka with ZAPU's external wing to oversee the opening phase of the armed struggle.
When FROLIZI was created to bridge the ZAPU-ZANU divide, refused to take part and instead assumed leadership of the ZAPU faction in Lusaka.
Remained in Lusaka when the nationalist parties merged under the ANC banner.
Served as one of the ANC's consultants during the Victoria Falls talks.
Became ZAPU's second Vice-President with responsibility for External Affairs.
Was chosen as a delegate for the Geneva Conference.

During his years in exile he developed the ZIPRA forces, rallied international backing for Zimbabwean freedom, argued for closer ties between ZANLA and ZIPRA and helped bring about the Patriotic Front of ZANU and ZAPU.

Opened a parcel sent from Botswana shortly after coming back from the Geneva Conference; it exploded, killing him on the spot and wounding several officials, among them Dumiso Dabengwa and Jane Ngwenya.
Was reburied in Zimbabwe.

notes: Plumtree is printed under 'Matabeleland North Province' (Plumtree is normally in Matabeleland South); kept as printed.
Reburial site is not named beyond 'in Zimbabwe'; heroStatus 'national hero' inferred from the Heroes Acre guide context, not printed in the biography.

summary: George Silundika, known as TG, was born in 1929 in Bulilima-Mangwe, schooled at Empandeni Mission and in Natal, and politicised at Fort Hare before being expelled from South Africa in 1951. After teaching at Empandeni he joined the SRANC, NDP and then ZAPU, helping to write ZAPU's constitution and later serving as its Secretary for Information and Publicity, scholarship organiser and diplomat in Lusaka and abroad. He was appointed Minister of Roads, Posts and Telecommunications at independence and died in April 1981 after collapsing in his office.

timeline.text: Born in the Plumtree area of Bulilima-Mangwe District, the only child of his parents; he was baptised a Catholic and later adopted the English form of his father's name, George.
Excelled at Empandeni Mission, the first Catholic mission school in southern Africa, and its missionaries gave him a scholarship to complete his primary education.
Went with his Empandeni friend James Chikerema to Marian Hill High School in Natal, South Africa, where both earned first-class matric passes.
Enrolled at Fort Hare University, joined the militant ANC Youth League and campaigned against apartheid.
Was detained and ordered to leave South Africa, then went to Roma University in Lesotho to finish his studies, where the authorities refused demands to expel him.
Returned to Rhodesia because his safety was at risk and took a teaching post at Empandeni Mission School, whose pupils included future figures such as Sydney Malunga and Callistus Ndlovu.
Joined the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress founded by Joshua Nkomo and, after it was banned, immediately joined the National Democratic Party.

Moved to the Harare (Salisbury) area and bought a house in the New Canaan section of Highfield, a hub of African nationalist politics, gaining a reputation as a shrewd politician whose writings were presented to continental and international bodies.

Travelled to China to ask for supplies and diplomatic backing for NDP cadres, and afterwards coordinated scholarships offered by socialist states (including Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, the USSR and Hungary) alongside his work as party strategist.
Was part of the NDP delegation led by Joshua Nkomo, alongside Herbert Chitepo, Enock Dumbutshena and Ndabaningi Sithole, at a constitutional conference.
Was detained when the Rhodesian regime outlawed the NDP, being held at Salisbury, Gweru (then Gwelo) and finally Marandellas (Marondera) prisons.
After the leaders' release ZAPU was born, and he was responsible for crafting its constitution together with a few other national leaders.
When ZAPU was also banned, its leaders defied the ban and agreed to begin military action, sending the first cadres, among them future president E. D. Mnangagwa, to China for guerrilla training.
Was dispatched to Lusaka to run the early phase of the armed struggle, strengthening the party there and working to bring ZANU and ZAPU cadres together.
Working as ZAPU's Secretary for Information and Publicity, rallied people in Zambia behind the struggle and started the party's official newspaper, edited at the outset by Saul Gwakuba Ndlovu.

Was posted to ZAPU's Foreign Affairs Department as part of a drive to revive the party, placing seasoned diplomats abroad to seek military training, weapons, study places and money, which brought new ZAPU missions in Libya, Nigeria, East Germany, Poland, the UK, Mozambique, Angola, Iraq, Mali, Botswana and the USA.
After serving ZAPU until independence, was appointed Minister of Roads, Posts and Telecommunications.
Collapsed in his office and later died at Andrew Fleming Hospital (now Parirenyatwa) aged 52.

summary: Senator Chief Rekayi Tangwena was a Nyanga-born traditional leader, former railway worker, waiter and boxer who became chief of the Tangwena people in 1966. He led his community's defiance of settler attempts to evict them from their ancestral lands, a confrontation remembered as the Tangwena Struggle, and used his base near the Mozambique border to help liberation fighters cross and to feed and shelter thousands of them. After campaigning for ZANU-PF he served as a Senator from 1980 for four years and was re-installed as chief in 1982; he died on 10 June 1984 aged 74.

timeline.text: Born at Tsatse Village in Nyanga, the eldest of six children.
Began primary school in Bulawayo, where his parents were working.
Pursued secondary studies in Bulawayo through private night classes, then worked for the Rhodesian Railways and later as a hotel waiter.
Took up boxing, earning the nickname Magodo for the force with which he overpowered opponents.
Returned to Nyanga from Bulawayo.

Took office as Chief of the Tangwena; white settlers resisted his appointment and mocked him with labels such as Miscellaneous Chief and Chief without style, which only hardened his opposition to the settler regime.

Resisted a settler-led eviction of his people from their ancestral territory between Troutbeck and Gaerezi Ranch, when Charles Hanmer sent in armed men, tractors and bulldozers; the community withdrew into the nearby mountains and he appealed to Herbert Chitepo for support, a standoff later called the Tangwena Struggle.
Endured repeated arrests, torture and intimidation without giving up his insistence that the land was sacred ancestral heritage.

Because he lived close to the Mozambican frontier and got on well with FRELIMO commanders, he guided guerrillas over the border, including Robert Mugabe and Edgar Tekere, whom he met at Nyafaru Primary School in Nyanga, and he also recruited fighters.
Campaigned prominently for ZANU-PF in Manicaland, raising political awareness alongside Simba Makoni and another comrade.
Was appointed Senator, a post he held for four years.
Was installed as Chief again at Tsatse Village, earning the title Senator Chief Tangwena, and championed cooperatives such as Tangenhamo in Tsatse and Bongozozo in Nyafaru.
Died after a short illness, aged 74.

A comrade named 'Mahachi' who campaigned with him has an illegible given name; not recorded.

summary: Sergeant Masotsha Ndlovu was born around 1890 near Plumtree and, despite leaving school at Standard Four, worked his way to Cape Town where he kept studying and absorbed trade-union ideas. Back in Rhodesia he organised workers, became General Secretary of the Reformed Industrial Commercial Union in 1929 and was repeatedly jailed, later joining the ANC and ZAPU. He spent long periods in detention and restriction camps between 1959 and 1971 and served in ZAPU's National Assembly from 1977; schools and streets were named after him, and he died on 2 July 1982.

timeline.text: Born at Thekwani Village near Plumtree, the first of six children; his father called him Masotsha, inspired by the armed soldiers then arriving in the country.
White settlers invaded Matabeleland, seizing livestock and land, and his family relocated to arid south-eastern Plumtree.
Attended Zimnyama Primary School only up to Standard Four because colonial restrictions discouraged African schooling.
Left Plumtree to live with his mother's brothers outside Bulawayo and took a job as a post boy with Thomas Meikles, whose owner gave him the second name Sergeant as a rendering of Masotsha from Zulu.
Applied to join the King's African Rifles when the First World War broke out, but was turned away.
Was transferred to the Thomas Meikles branch at Shabanie (now Zvishavane).
Tried to reach Mahikeng to continue his education by hiding in a train, but was discovered while passing Botswana and sent back to Nyathini in Plumtree.

Having saved one hundred pounds, travelled by train to Cape Town, where a white woman arranged through his church put him up in exchange for housework while he studied in the evenings; he later worked as a packer for B. Rohlers and then Jagger's Wholesalers.

Passed Standard Six and then followed a matric-level English course by correspondence; contact with the South African Communist Party and the trade union movement strengthened his resolve against discrimination.
Came back to Rhodesia and worked to put the Southern Rhodesia Industrial and Commercial Workers Union on a proper footing.

Became General Secretary of the Reformed Industrial Commercial Union, created when several workers' unions merged, and toured rural areas voicing African grievances and attacking racial discrimination, which led to frequent clashes with whites and spells in Grey Prison.

Was sent away to Buhera by the authorities because his influence among African workers was growing, and there he joined the Southern Rhodesia ANC, recruiting members and winning over traditional leaders.
After the State of Emergency was declared, was detained at Khami Prison and then sent to the Mafungabusi Forest Restriction Area in Gokwe District, from which he was released in 1961.
Was soon re-arrested and held at Marandellas Prison, then moved to Wha Wha Restriction Camp near Gweru, where he met Ruth and Josiah Chinamano.
Was sent to the isolated Gonakudzingwa Restriction Camp, where many leading nationalists were held, stayed until his release in 1971, and then went back to Buhera.
With his property and livestock destroyed by the regime, relocated to Bulawayo and joined ZAPU's National Assembly, helping to keep up morale until the end of the struggle.
Died of natural causes.

notes: 'Sergeant' is explained in the text as a second name given by his employer (not a military rank); kept as part of the name, with 'Cde' as the honorific.

summary: Robson Manyika, born at Goromonzi in 1934, entered politics through the Youth League in 1957 and rose through the ANC and NDP before being arrested after the NDP ban. After military training in the Soviet Union he became ZAPU's Chief of Staff and later joined ZANU, where he served as a military commissar in the ZANLA High Command and helped launch the north-eastern offensive. A military adviser at the Geneva, Malta and Lancaster House talks, he became Deputy Minister of Labour, Manpower Planning and Social Welfare after independence and died of heart failure at Chinhoyi on 24 June 1985 aged 51.

timeline.text: Born at Goromonzi near Harare.
Attended several primary schools and completed secondary education by correspondence, and began revolutionary activity while still at primary school.
Began his political life in the Youth League.
Joined the ANC as a committee member.
Was the NDP's publicity and organising secretary and was arrested once the party was outlawed.
Was held at Hartley Prison until 1963 (details of the detention are partly garbled) and on release left the country for military training in the Soviet Union.
On his return was made ZAPU's Chief of Staff and tasked with building up the ZIPRA guerrilla army, including training in weapons and their use.
Later joined ZANU, in circumstances that are partly illegible in the OCR.
As a field commander, helped Josiah Tongogara and others launch the north-eastern offensive.
Was appointed Chief Military Commissar and put in charge of training personnel in the newly established ZANLA High Command, covering all ZANLA camps in Zambia, Tanzania and Mozambique.
Went to the Geneva Conference as the party's military expert.

Won a seat on the ZANU Central Committee at Chimoio and became Deputy Secretary for Manpower Planning and Labour, a job that covered finding study places abroad for Zimbabwean refugees and examining workers' complaints at home.
Attended the Malta I and II conferences as a defence expert.
Served as one of ZANU's military advisers at the Lancaster House Conference.
Heart failure took his life at Chinhoyi while he was Deputy Minister of Labour, Manpower Planning and Social Welfare and standing for the Kariba Constituency; he was buried on June 27.

title: Dr

Obstetrician and gynaecologist, Andrew Fleming (now Parirenyatwa) Hospital, Salisbury

Founding member, ZANU

summary: Dr Simon Mazorodze, born in Mhondoro in 1933 and nicknamed Gutsa as a pupil, trained in medicine at the University of Natal and became an obstetrician-gynaecologist in the Rhodesian health service. A ZANU founding member, he secretly supported the struggle, and after resigning from government service in 1974 he treated wounded guerrillas, hid medicines and raised funds, which brought repeated arrests. Elected for ZANU-PF in 1980, he served as Deputy Minister and then Minister of Health and died of heart failure on 2 November 1981; many schools and facilities carry his name.

timeline.text: Born at Nyamweda Village in Mhondoro District, the first of five children of Charles and Mareetekwa Mazorodze.
Started school at Mufuka Primary School in Mhondoro and next went to Marshal Hartley School in Msengezi.
Transferred to Sandringham Primary School and then to Waddilove Mission, where he finished Standard Six in 1950 and earned the nickname Gutsa (log of wood) for studying while leaning against a log.
Entered Goromonzi High School, where he excelled, became Head Boy and took part in the non-racial Capricorn Africa Society and the Boys' Scout Movement.
Went to the University of Natal in South Africa to read medicine, became politically aware through student politics and met his future wife, Alice Madinga.

After gaining his medical and surgical degrees, came back to Rhodesia and entered the public health sector, working at Mpilo Hospital and then Andrew Fleming Hospital in Salisbury, where he specialised in obstetrics and gynaecology.
Became a founding member of ZANU while quietly supporting the underground movement with funds, help for refugees and treatment for wounded fighters.
Was transferred to Ndanga Hospital in Zaka as District Medical Officer, overseeing satellite clinics and drawing patients from far afield.

Resigned from government service for private practice while stepping up support for the liberation struggle, treating wounded guerrillas at night, hiding medical supplies in caves and raising funds from business leaders in several towns for medicines for ZANLA forces.
While mobilising structures ahead of the 1980 elections, was arrested for allegedly treating a wounded freedom fighter, then subjected to repeated arrests and charged as an accomplice.
Took a Senior House Officer post at Harare Hospital and served there until December 1979.

Stood for ZANU-PF in the general election and was elected Member of Parliament for Fort Victoria (Masvingo), then became Deputy Minister and later Minister of Health, helping to restructure and modernise the health sector.
Died of heart failure at Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals.

Was honoured through institutions named after him, including a classroom block at Capota School for the Blind, Mazorodze Maternity Home in Masvingo, a trust, Mazorodze Secondary School in Mhondoro and a science laboratory at Mashoko Mission.

Age at death and burial are not printed; heroStatus 'national hero' inferred from the Heroes Acre guide context, not printed in the biography.

summary: Josiah Chinamano, who used the nom de guerre Nkumo, was an educationist from Mashonaland East who taught, headed schools and supervised Methodist schools before turning to full-time nationalist politics in the early 1960s. He served on ZAPU's Executive Committee and later as its Vice-President, ran a Highfield shop that doubled as an NDP base, and founded Highfield Community School. He was among the first detainees at Gonakudzingwa in 1964, spent most of the next decade in detention or restriction with his wife Ruth, and after his release became the African National Council's first treasurer and a vice president. He served briefly as Minister of Transport in 1981-82 and died on 1 October 1984.

timeline.text: Born at Epworth Mission, the eldest of four children of Chinyani and Dekete Chinamano; his nom de guerre was Nkumo.
Began primary school at Tjipange Primary School in Manicaland, where his parents worked.
Went to Kutama Mission for secondary schooling, then trained as a teacher at Waddilove Mission, qualifying in 1942.
Began teaching at a Methodist primary school in Salisbury and later served at Waddilove Mission as supervisor of student teachers for three years.
Went to Fort Hare University to study for a BA in History and African Administration, and met his future wife, Ruth Nyombolo.
Married Ruth Nyombolo and soon moved to Rhodesia, where he worked in the Social Welfare Department of the City of Bulawayo.
Became headmaster at Marshall Hartley Boarding School.
Moved to Marandellas (now Marondera) as supervisor of 26 Methodist schools across Mashonaland.
Went to England as a guest lecturer at Selly Oak Colleges in Birmingham and also studied for a Diploma in Education at Birmingham University.
After returning, worked in Marondera until the end of 1957 and then taught at Waddilove Mission, where meetings addressed by Joshua Nkomo drew him from education into active nationalist politics.

Was appointed an instructor at the Government Teachers' Training College in Umtali, later serving as General Secretary of the African Teachers' Association; he resigned that post after a dispute over a salary memorandum but was elected its Vice President.

Became Programme Officer in the political section of the US Consulate General in Harare, left the post in February 1961, and in mid-1961 attended a UNESCO conference in Boston, where he received a State Department Leadership Grant.
Quit teaching and moved to Highfield, running a small shop whose back rooms served as an NDP base; after the NDP was banned he joined ZAPU and was appointed to its Executive Committee.

Testified before the United Nations Committee on Colonialism in New York about conditions in Southern Rhodesia, and the same year founded Highfield Community School to ease the shortage of school places for African pupils.
Was arrested with his wife Ruth, Joseph Msika and Joshua Nkomo and detained as one of the first four prisoners at Gonakudzingwa Restriction Camp.
Was later moved with his wife to Wha Wha Prison, where they stayed until their release in 1970, after which they were confined to an eight-kilometre radius in Highfield.
Was arrested again after widespread resistance to the Smith regime's constitutional proposals and held at Marondera Prison until 1974.
Was freed after British and South African pressure and became the first Treasurer of the African National Council (Zimbabwe) under Nkomo, then its vice president from late 1974.
ZAPU put him forward for a vacant parliamentary seat as he took up the Transport portfolio, which he held until February 1982.
Died of a heart attack at Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals, aged 61.

summary: Maurice Nyagumbo (born 12 December 1924 near Rusape) became politically aware while working in South Africa, was deported home, helped found the Youth League in 1955 and was first detained in 1959. A ZANU central committee member from the party's 1964 founding congress, he linked detained leaders with the exile structures and spent roughly 21 years in prison or detention before his final release in 1979. After independence he held cabinet office, notably Mines and later Senior Minister of Political Affairs, sat on the ZANU (PF) Central Committee and Politburo, and was tasked in 1987 with overseeing the merger of ZANU (PF) and PF-ZAPU. He quit his posts in April 1989 after the Sandura Commission report, died in Harare on 20 April 1989 and was buried at the National Heroes Acre three days later.

timeline.text: Born in Makoni district near Rusape.
Did his primary schooling at St. Faith's Anglican Mission in Makoni and at St. Augustine's, Penhalonga.
Worked in South Africa, where he took up politics and joined the Communist Party, and was eventually deported for his activism.
Back in Rhodesia, became a founder member of the Youth League.
Joined the African National Congress and was detained later that year, the start of a long record of imprisonment.
Released from detention and joined ZANU.
Elected to the ZANU central committee at the party's inaugural congress; when ZANU was banned later that year he was among the leaders who avoided arrest.

Acted as a go-between linking detained leaders with central committee members in Zambia and Tanzania, and later the Revolutionary Council in Lusaka with guerrillas who had entered the country after the Chinhoyi Battle.
Held at Salisbury Prison and Que Que until 1973.
Helped recruit cadres for the armed struggle, was rearrested and sentenced to 15 years in prison.
Freed from prison, having spent about 21 years in prison or detention for the liberation struggle.
Wrote most of his book 'With the People' while detained, with the book appearing soon after independence (passage garbled).
Took up cabinet office, serving as Minister of Mines and later as Senior Minister of Political Affairs (details partly illegible).
Sat on the ZANU (PF) Central Committee and Politburo, where he served as Secretary for Administration.
After the Unity Accord between Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo, was tasked with overseeing the reintegration of ZANU (PF) and PF-ZAPU.
Resigned from his cabinet and party posts after the Sandura Commission report, which concerned vehicle sales by Willowvale Motor Industries.
Died in Harare and was buried at the National Heroes Acre on April 23.

summary: William Ndangana (born 2 January 1932 in Chipinge) trained as a carpenter and briefly taught before leaving for Zambia in 1962, joining ZANU the next year and in 1964 leading the Crocodile Gang, whose sabotage raids in eastern Rhodesia ended with three members sentenced to death. After escaping to Zambia he trained in Ghana and China and rose through ZANLA to the General Staff, High Command and Chief of Operations, earning the nickname 'Military Encyclopedia', and survived kidnapping and detention in Zambia around Chitepo's assassination. At independence he won the Chipinge seat, became Deputy Minister of State for Paramilitary Training and was appointed Senator for Manicaland in 1985. He died in an accident near Nyazura on 27 June 1989 and was buried at the National Heroes Acre on 30 June.

timeline.text: Born in Bangira Village, Chipinge District, the fourth of five children.

Began primary school at Bangira and moved to Chikore Mission for secondary schooling, finishing it by private study, then trained in carpentry and building and taught building and sports at Musirizwi Primary School.
Left teaching, unhappy under colonial rule, and went to Zambia, where he lodged with his brother Hyena in Lusaka and found work as a carpenter.
Joined ZANU and rose to a chairmanship in the party, using it to mobilise and organise young people for the struggle.
Recruited four comrades in Lusaka (Mlambo, Kademaunga, Dhlamini and Mazwani) and formed the Crocodile Gang to carry out sabotage against the Smith government.
After basic military training in Tanzania, led the gang to Umtali (now Mutare), where Joseph Shasha became their liaison contact.
The gang attacked Nyanyadzi Police Camp, then a bridge at Chikwizi, and killed Rhodesian Front member Pieter Andries Oberholzer in Melsetter District.

With police closing in the gang split; Mazwani, Mlambo and Dhlamini were captured and sentenced to death, while Ndangana escaped to Zambia hidden in a banana lorry via the Chirundu crossing and was received in Lusaka by Herbert Chitepo.
Sent to Ghana for military training, completed the course in 1965 and was then chosen for advanced training in China.

Moved to Tanzania as a member of the ZANLA General Staff, helped set up Itumbi Training Camp (Chunya District, Mbeya Region), trained its first group of guerrillas and helped establish the Mugagau camp.
Posted to Lusaka to work with Chitepo at the Liberation Centre, then elevated to the ZANLA High Command later that year.
Appointed ZANLA Chief of Operations, overseeing military planning and activity inside and outside the country.
Kidnapped and held at Chifombo Camp in eastern Zambia, enduring near-starvation, until released after Tongogara and some Zambian soldiers intervened.

After Chitepo's assassination, was arrested with other senior ZANU leaders by Zambian authorities and held without trial at Mpimba and Mukobeko prisons until legal help arranged by his brother Hyena won his release in December 1976.
Went to Maputo for administrative and coordination duties and frequently visited ZANU camps such as Tembwe, Tete, Nyadzonia and Chimoio.

Elected to the ZANU Central Committee as Deputy Secretary for Production, Construction and Development, and the following year was posted to Mudzingadzi in Mozambique, where he met his future wife Annah-Lois Nyahangare.

Returned to Zimbabwe and won the Chipinge seat in the House of Assembly; two years later he became Deputy Minister of State for Paramilitary Training, coordinating the training of several thousand militia members.
Re-elected to the ZANU-PF Central Committee at the party's Second Congress.
Lost his parliamentary seat, and with it his deputy ministership, in the general election but was appointed Senator for Manicaland later that year.
Died in an accident near Nyazura and was buried at the National Heroes Acre on June 30.

summary: Rwizi Grafton Ziyenge (born 1933) trained in building and became a trade unionist, serving as secretary-general of the Building Artisans' Union from 1964 until ill health forced him out about a decade later. Active in the ANC, NDP and ZAPU youth wings before joining ZANU in 1963, he later helped lead the internal People's Movement as its National Organising Secretary and attended the Lancaster House Conference. After independence he served as an MP, deputy minister of works, Central Committee member, senator and Governor of Mashonaland East. He died in a car accident near Marondera in January 1990 and was buried at the National Heroes Acre.

Went to a training school (Domboshawa, name truncated) in 1948 and earned a Diploma in Building in 1951.
Began working the year after qualifying.
Joined the African Artisans Union.
Was active in the youth wings of the ANC (Southern Rhodesia), the NDP and ZAPU, earning a name as a dedicated nationalist.
After the split in ZAPU joined ZANU at its formation and served as its Highfield District Treasurer.
Became secretary-general of the Building Artisans' Union, a post he gave up about ten years later because of ill health.
As National Organising Secretary of the People's Movement, ZANU's internal wing, attended the Lancaster House Conference that led to independence.
Elected to the House of Assembly representing Mashonaland East.
Appointed Deputy Minister of Works (a ministry later tied to Construction); a 1982 appointment follows but is partly lost at the page edge.
Appointed Governor of Mashonaland East, during which the province saw notable development in roads, schools, clinics and dams.

Appointed to the Senate and re-appointed Governor of Mashonaland East.
Died in a car accident near Marondera and was buried at the National Heroes Acre on January 13.

summary: Edward Ndlovu (born 1926 in Gwanda) was schooled at mission schools and in South Africa, where he joined the ANC, before returning to Bulawayo in 1951 and moving into trade unionism and nationalist politics. He held senior posts in the ANC, NDP and ZAPU, including representing the NDP in Cairo and serving as ZAPU secretary for foreign affairs, was detained in 1959, and left the country in 1963 to further the armed struggle. A co-founder of the ZANU-ZAPU Joint Military Command (1972) and the Patriotic Front (1976), he became PF-ZAPU MP for Matabeleland South at independence and, after helping forge the unity accord, a deputy minister of energy, water resources and development. He died on 3 September (year illegible in the OCR) and was buried at the national shrine.

timeline.text: Born at Mbeba in the Manama area of Gwanda.

Started school at Madume and moved to Manama Mission, his family paying fees by supplying milk to the missionaries at Madume; later passed Standard Six at Tsholotsho and studied at an institute in South Africa.
Obtained a Joint Matriculation Board certificate (and, per garbled text, a Junior certificate).
Joined the African National Congress of South Africa (text just before this is garbled).
Returned to Southern Rhodesia and took an accounts job with Messrs J. Wolfe in Bulawayo.
Became a founder member of the African Voice, led by Benjamin Burombo.
Joined the Commercial Workers Union and worked with Joshua Nkomo, then secretary-general of the Railway Workers Union, to organise trade unionism.
Elected deputy secretary-general of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress when its Bulawayo branch merged with the City Youth League.
Detained at Khami Prison with other nationalists when the ANC was banned.
Became active in the National Democratic Party and rose to be its secretary.
Sent to Cairo to represent the party in Egypt and other Arab states, staying until after ZAPU was banned in 1962.
Elected deputy secretary of the People's Caretaker Council and in August was one of five ZAPU executive members who left the country to advance the armed struggle.
Became ZAPU secretary for Foreign Affairs.
Helped form the ZANU-ZAPU Joint Military Command (1972) and the Patriotic Front (1976).
Elected PF-ZAPU Member of Parliament for Matabeleland South.
Elected PF-ZAPU secretary for political organisation at the party congress.
Re-elected to Parliament for the Gwanda constituency.
Appointed a deputy minister following the ZANU (PF) and PF-ZAPU unity accord, which he had helped forge.
Died while Deputy Minister of Energy, Water Resources and Development, and was buried at the national shrine.

summary: Willie Musarurwa (born 24 November 1927 in the Chinhoyi District) came from a family of 14 children, worked on farms as a youth, studied at mission schools and Goromonzi, and trained as a teacher before turning to journalism. He edited African Weekly, Bantu Mirror and Parade in the nationalist era, helped found the NDP, was detained from 1964 to 1974 and edited detainee publications, then took part in the unity talks behind the Patriotic Front and was its co-spokesman at Lancaster House. After independence he became the first black editor of The Sunday Mail, sat on the ZBC board and ran a public relations firm, while also chairing the Children's Protection Society. He died on 3 April 1990.

timeline.text: Born in the Chinhoyi District, one of 14 children.
As a youth ran away with his brother Morris from cattle herding to work as tobacco graders near Darwendale, then worked for a farmer in Trelawney, where he first saw exploitation at first hand.
Schooled at Nyamangara, Marshall Hartley Mission and Howard Mission, then entered the pioneer group at Goromonzi Secondary School, where he ran a bush barber shop for pocket money.
After his Cambridge School Certificate trained as a teacher at St. Augustine's Mission, Penhalonga.
Taught at Epworth Mission while regularly writing articles for the press.
Supported the Youth League and the African National Congress.
When the ANC was banned went underground with others to form the National Democratic Party, of which he was a founder member.
Attended Princeton University in New Jersey as a Parvin Fellow.
Became active in the liberation struggle on returning in 1963, was arrested in 1964 and detained until 1974, editing publications at Gonakudzingwa such as Gonakudzingwa News and Zimbabwe Review.

Took part in repeated talks on ZAPU-ZANU unity that led to the Patriotic Front (1976) and attended the Victoria Falls, Salisbury, Geneva, Malta and Lancaster House conferences, serving as the Front's co-spokesman at Lancaster House.
Lived in exile in Zambia, where he was ZAPU's Secretary for Publicity and Information.
Stood in the general election in Mashonaland on the party-list system but was not elected.
Appointed editor of The Sunday Mail (its first black editor), later joined the ZBC board as deputy chairman, and was asked to leave the weekly after editorial controversies.
Teamed up with Cephas Msipa to found the public relations consultancy MT & BS (Private) Limited, of which he was managing director until his death.
Welcomed the unity of PF-ZAPU and ZANU-PF, for which he had worked quietly behind the scenes.
Published in Parade a review of the press in Zimbabwe's first decade of independence, one of his last works; died on April 3.

summary: Ernest Kadungure (born 13 February 1942 in Chivhu) was educated at mission schools, worked briefly for an oil company and moved to Zambia in 1964, resigning a ministry job in 1968 to join the liberation war. After training in Tanzania he became a ZANLA chief instructor and a member of the reconnaissance team that prepared the 1972 north-eastern offensive, later holding the party posts of Secretary for Education and Culture and Secretary for Finance. After independence he held several ministerial posts (Transport and Power; Youth, Sport and Recreation; State for Defence; Political Affairs) and sat on the ZANU (PF) Central Committee and Politburo responsible for youth. He died at Parirenyatwa Hospital aged 48 on 31 May 1990 after a long illness.

timeline.text: Born in Chivhu.
Schooled at St. Thomas and Daramombe Mission in Chikomba District, then Loreto Mission and St. Augustine's, Penhalonga.
Worked briefly for an international oil company (garbled passage).
Moved to Zambia, where he trained and later worked in a ministry, apparently Lands and Natural Resources (garbled).
Resigned from the ministry post to join the liberation struggle.
After his first military training in Tanzania became chief instructor at one of ZANLA's training camps.
Helped prepare the opening of the north-eastern front as part of the ZANLA reconnaissance team.
Sat on the ZANU Central Committee at Chimoio as Secretary for Education and Culture, later taking over as Secretary for Finance.
Elected to the House of Assembly and appointed Minister of Transport and Power.
Became Minister of Youth, Sport and Recreation, a post he held until 1984.
Appointed Minister of State (Defence) in the then Prime Minister's Office.
Elected to the ZANU (PF) Central Committee and then given a youth-related party post (Secretary for Youth, read from garbled text).
Re-elected to the House of Assembly and appointed Minister of State (Political Affairs) in the President's Office, responsible for Youth Affairs and National Service.
Died at Parirenyatwa Hospital after a long illness, aged 48, while sitting on the Central Committee and Politburo responsible for youth.

name: Sarah Francesca Mugabe
title: Cde
roles: Teacher
First Lady of Zimbabwe
Deputy Secretary of the ZANU (PF) Women's League (1978)
Patron, Mutemwa Leprosy Centre, Mutoko (1981)
Executive Chairperson, Child Survival and Development Foundation in Zimbabwe
First Secretary of the united ZANU (PF) Women's League and Secretary for Women's Affairs in the Politburo (1989)
education: Achimota Secondary School (Ghana)
Qualified as a teacher
summary: Sarah Francesca 'Sally' Mugabe (born 1931 in Ghana), known as Amai, was a Ghana-born teacher who married Robert Mugabe in 1961 and quickly joined the nationalist struggle, receiving a five-year sedition sentence in December 1961 for leading a women's protest. She left Rhodesia for Tanzania, lost her only son to cerebral malaria in Ghana in 1966, then lived in London and Mozambique, mobilising support for the liberation war and championing women. After independence she devoted herself to children's welfare and the Mutemwa Leprosy Centre and in 1989 became first Secretary of the united ZANU (PF) Women's League. She died of a kidney ailment on 27 January 1992 and was the first heroine buried at the National Heroes Acre.

timeline.text: Born Sarah Francesca Hayfron in Ghana.
Attended Achimota Secondary School and qualified as a teacher, meeting Robert Mugabe when both taught at Takoradi Teacher Training College.
Married Robert Mugabe in Salisbury and was at once drawn into nationalist politics.
Charged with sedition and sentenced to five years after leading women to the Prime Minister's office to protest the 1961 Constitution; she appealed and was restricted to her Harare home.
Left for Tanzania before her appeal was heard, where nationalist leaders were planning a government-in-exile.
Gave birth to her only son, Nhamodzenyika, after a difficult pregnancy marked by high blood pressure and little medical care.
The couple separated for their child's sake: she took the baby to her parents in Ghana while Mugabe returned to Rhodesia and was jailed on arrival.
Her son died of cerebral malaria in Ghana and the Rhodesian authorities refused to let Mugabe attend the funeral.
Studied and worked in London, lobbying British MPs for the release of political detainees in Rhodesia, until the couple reunited in 1974.
In Mozambique became a mother figure and counsellor to young guerrillas and raised financial, diplomatic and material support, especially in Scandinavia.
Elected Deputy Secretary of the Women's League at the first ZANU (PF) Women's Congress, held in Mozambique.
As Prime Minister's wife campaigned for women's rights and helped turn the Women's League into a strong pillar of ZANU (PF).
Became patron of the Mutemwa Leprosy Centre in Mutoko, raising funds and helping reduce the stigma around leprosy.
Became patron of many children's centres, started projects to rehabilitate prostitutes, and was invited to be Executive Chairperson of the Child Survival and Development Foundation in Zimbabwe.
With UNICEF help set up the Child Survival and Development Committee for Zimbabwe and raised international awareness of children's plight in Southern Africa.
Elected first Secretary of the united ZANU (PF) Women's League and Secretary for Women's Affairs in the Politburo.
Died in Harare of a kidney ailment and was laid to rest at the National Heroes Acre on February 1 as its first heroine.

notes: College name read as 'Takoradi' (OCR 'Takarodi')
Bio appears to end with the 1989 Women's League paragraph on photo 092256; no closing line seen, so check nothing follows it
Burial year not printed (assumed 1992)

name: Lameck Chikanga Makanda
title: Cde
roles: Former Senator
Member of the ZANU (PF) Central Committee
Member of the African National Congress of Southern Rhodesia and the National Democratic Party
Founder of the People's Movement pressure group
Internal leader at the 1976 Geneva Peace Talks
summary: Lameck Makanda (born 1912 in Mvuma) was a veteran politician described as one of the 'nationalist elders' at Heroes Acre, who joined the ANC and then the NDP and was charged with mobilising people for the armed struggle once the NDP was outlawed. He took part in the early petrol-bomb phase, was imprisoned for four years and restricted, but kept the party's internal work going after other leaders went abroad. He attended the 1976 Geneva talks, formed the People's Movement as a pressure group, and joined the Senate at independence in 1980, urging land redistribution and respect for traditional rituals. He died in Harare and was buried at the National Heroes Acre on 7 November 1992.

timeline.text: Born in Mvuma.
Joined the African National Congress of Southern Rhodesia, then the National Democratic Party after the ANC was banned, mobilising people against colonial rule.

After the NDP was outlawed and peaceful protest was judged to have failed, was charged with mobilising people for the armed struggle and was at the forefront of its early petrol-bomb attacks on factories, mines and farms.
Was imprisoned for four years and restricted, yet kept the party's internal activities going after most leaders left to fight from outside.
Attended the Geneva Peace Talks as one of the internal leaders.
Returned to Rhodesia and formed the People's Movement, a pressure group meant to fill the gap left by ZANU (PF)'s departure.
Joined the Senate, known as a strong advocate of land distribution and traditional rituals.
Buried at the National Heroes Acre after dying in Harare.

notes: Death date not printed in the legible intro (only the burial date November 7, 1992 and place of death Harare)
'1960s' for joining the ANC is read from both OCR versions but the ANC was banned in 1959, so verify against the page
'Four years' of imprisonment and the word 'restrictions' come from a garbled right-edge passage

Chairman, Zimbabwe Refugees Association (in England)

summary: Joseph Culverwell (born 10 July 1918 in Johannesburg) was a Cape Town-educated teacher and psychologist whose 27-year career took him across Africa, Iran and England, and who served as a sergeant in the Second World War. Angered by unequal postwar compensation, he joined the nationalist movement, worked with figures such as Nyandoro, Chikerema and Nkomo, became a ZAPU then ZANU member, was jailed in 1967 and later supported the struggle from England, chairing the Zimbabwe Refugees Association. After attending the Geneva and Lancaster House talks he returned in 1979, became a senator and leader of the Senate, then deputy minister of education and later minister of state for national scholarships. He died on 16 July 1993 after a stroke and was buried at the Heroes Acre on 22 July.

timeline.text: Born in Johannesburg while his mother was on a short trip to South Africa.
Attended McKeurtan Primary in Bulawayo, Moffat Primary in Harare and Trafalgar High School in Cape Town.
Elected Secretary-General of the National Association of Coloured Peoples, having earlier served as Secretary of the Coloured Community Service League.
Served as a sergeant in the Rhodesian and British armies in Ethiopia, Somalia, Kenya and Egypt.

Turned to nationalist politics after receiving only a quarter of the compensation given to white servicemen, working with Nyandoro, Chikerema and Nkomo and helping organise the inaugural meeting of the African National Congress.
After graduating in education and psychology (Cape Town and Nottingham) built a 27-year teaching career across Zambia, Kenya, Tanzania, Nigeria, Uganda, Iran and England.
Joined ZAPU and then ZANU.
Imprisoned for 18 months for political activity but after 12 months left to teach in Zambia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and eventually England.

Backed the struggle under ZANU (PF) by obtaining clothes, medicine and ambulances for guerrillas, and chaired the Zimbabwe Refugees Association, which sought jobs, housing and scholarships for exiles.
Was a delegate at the abortive Geneva Peace Talks and later at the Lancaster House Conference.
Returned to Zimbabwe.
Appointed a senator after ZANU (PF)'s election victory and led the Senate for eight years.
Served as Deputy Minister of Education and Culture.
Appointed Minister of State in the President's Office responsible for National Scholarships.
Briefly Deputy Minister of Higher Education before retiring from government and Parliament that year through ill health.
Died at Parirenyatwa Hospital after a stroke and was buried at the Heroes Acre on July 22.

notes: Intro lines (death and burial dates) are absent from the column OCR and were read from the whole-page OCR
Burial year not printed (assumed 1993); book paragraphs are not in chronological order, so event order was rearranged

name: Samuel Mayor Urimbo
title: Cde

summary: Samuel Mayor Urimbo, popularly called Mayor Urimbo, was a pioneer ZANLA fighter who rose from ordinary combatant to ZANU (PF) national commissar in 1977. His wit and charisma earned him the label 'soul of the Party', and he is credited with devising the Gukurahundi programme of dismantling settler institutions and creating liberated zones. A former tobacco factory worker from Gutu, he was politicised in Zambia, trained in Tanzania and later sat in Parliament for Ndanga/Zimuto until ill health ended his term in 1990. He died in September 1993, leaving a wife and eight children.

timeline.text: Born in Gutu in Masvingo province.
Attended Whete Primary School, then went on to Gutu Mission for secondary schooling.
Worked as a machine operator for the tobacco firm BAT until the company sent him to Zambia as an instructor, where he joined the independence party UNIP.

timeline.date: At the formation of ZANU in 1963
timeline.text: Became a member of the ZANU youth wing as soon as the party was formed.
Joined ZANLA and received military training in Tanzania.
Back in Zambia he led a clandestine reconnaissance and weapons-ferrying operation towards the Mt Darwin/Mavuradonha area of the north-east.
Took part, with Ernest Kadungure and others, in the delicate operation of moving the spirit medium of Mbuya Nehanda from the Mavuradonha area to Tete Province in Mozambique.
Became ZANU (PF) national commissar and mobilised, recruited and politically oriented thousands of young people joining ZANLA in Mozambique.
Elected Member of Parliament for Ndanga/Zimuto.
Gave up his parliamentary seat because recurring ill health forced him to.
Died on September 7 and was buried at Heroes Acre on September 11, survived by his wife and eight children.

summary: Christopher Ushewokunze was a lawyer and economist from Shurugwi who turned student activism against UDI into a career in public service. After detention, expulsion and study in Britain, he taught law in Zambia and at the UN Institute for Namibia before returning to Zimbabwe as Secretary for Mines in 1980. There he created the Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe, later led the Zimbabwe Development Corporation and served as Minister of Trade and Commerce, admired for credibility and candour. He died in a road accident in January 1994, leaving his wife and five children.

timeline.text: Born in Shurugwi as Christopher Machingura Mugwagwa Ushewokunze.
Enrolled as a law student at the University of Rhodesia and Nyasaland and became active in nationalist politics.
Led a student committee that organised protests against Ian Smith's moves to declare UDI.
Expelled from the university and detained at Gonakudzingwa, where he met Joshua Nkomo and other nationalist leaders.
Released after a year and escorted by police to the airport to leave for Britain on a British Council scholarship; continued law studies at Edinburgh.
Enrolled for a Masters degree at London University.
Qualified as a barrister at Middle Temple.
Joined the University of Zambia as a law lecturer.
Served as senior law lecturer at the United Nations Institute for Namibia.
Spent four months as legal consultant to UNCTAD's Zimbabwe Project.
Appointed Secretary for Mines and created the Minerals Marketing Corporation of Zimbabwe as sole marketer of the country's minerals.
Left the Ministry of Mines to head the newly formed Zimbabwe Development Corporation, set up to indigenise key parts of the economy.
Became Minister of Trade and Commerce, pushing indigenisation and reassuring the public during economic reform.
Killed in a car crash near Chegutu; buried at the national shrine on January 22 as its 21st hero.

summary: George Nyandoro was one of the most dynamic founders of Zimbabwe's liberation movement, active from the 1940s in multi-racial groups before helping launch the City Youth League and the African National Congress as its Secretary-General. Detained after the 1959 Emergency, he later went to England for medical treatment, then served ZAPU as secretary-general while living in Zambia until 1979. After a brief ministerial role he retired from politics for business, leading Art Corporation for nearly two decades. He died in June 1994 at 68, survived by his wife, seven children, 11 grandchildren and a great-grandchild.

timeline.text: Born at St. Mary's Mission in Mhondoro District.
Worked at the Rhodesia Herald in Salisbury, then as an accountant at City Stores, teaching himself book-keeping and some law.
Entered anti-colonial activity through the British African National Voice Association and the Inter-Racial Association, which he soon dismissed as talking shops.
Helped form the City Youth League with James Chikerema, Edson Sithole, Dunduza Chisiza and others, later renamed the African National Youth League.
Co-founded the African National Congress with Joshua Nkomo as President, Chikerema as Vice-President and himself as Secretary-General.
Attended the first All-Africa People's Conference in Accra.
Arrested under the State of Emergency with other ANC leaders and jailed at Khami or restricted to Gokwe.
Released to travel to England for treatment of tuberculosis of the spine.
Led a team of lobbyists at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference in London, then moved to Zambia as ZAPU secretary-general.
Returned to Zimbabwe and served in the Zimbabwe-Rhodesia government's lands and rural development ministry before leaving active politics.
Led Art Corporation, becoming its first black chairman and a respected businessman on numerous boards.
Died aged 68 and was buried at the National Heroes Acre on June 29.

summary: Sidney Malunga was a Bulawayo teacher turned civic activist, ZAPU official and later ZANU (PF) leader. He campaigned against the 1972 Pearce Commission proposals, was detained by the Rhodesian authorities, and after independence rose to the Central Committee and to Parliament for Mpopoma. Known as an outspoken debater who scrutinised government spending, he also worked on hospital equipment supply and the Matabeleland Zambezi water project. He died in a road accident in August 1994.

timeline.text: Born; did primary schooling in Filabusi.
At Emphandeni Mission, where he did secondary school and teacher training, George Silundika introduced him to politics by lending him political books.
Became active in civic affairs while teaching at a community school in Mpopoma, Bulawayo, and helped found the Mpopoma Lease Holders Association.
Played a key part in forming a Bulawayo residents' association (BURA) and held office in a trade-union federation.
Served as secretary of the ZAPU Nketa branch and held other party and People's Caretaker Council posts.
Campaigned fiercely against the Pearce Commission's settlement proposals and was arrested and held at Wha Wha, Kwekwe and Connemara prisons.

timeline.date: in time for the Lancaster House talks
timeline.text: Freed from detention just in time to attend the Lancaster House talks that led to the 1980 independence.
Became one of five Deputy National Organising Secretaries of the party.
Elected a member of the Central Committee.
Elected Member of Parliament for Mpopoma Constituency.
Elected to the new united ZANU (PF) Central Committee following the ZANU (PF)-PF ZAPU Unity Accord.
Won respect as a parliamentarian on the Public Accounts Committee and select committees, challenging overspending and indiscipline in ministries and criticising Acts and by-laws.
Died in a car accident in Bulawayo; buried at the national shrine on September 3.

summary: Justin Chauke was a highly regarded ZANLA commander from Nuanetsi District who joined the struggle after working as a driver in Zambia. He trained in Tanzania in 1968, took part in early infiltration and reconnaissance along the Zambezi, and rose to the General Staff and High Command with responsibility for logistics. After detention in Zambia in 1975 he held field commands including Gaza Province, then served on the Central Committee until 1984. Ill health ended his army career and he ran a rehabilitation centre near Beatrice until his death in October 1994.

timeline.text: Born William Hathlan Hanyani Maseke Chauke at Mupapa, Chanyanga, in Nuanetsi District.
Left school after Standard Four for lack of a place, went to Zambia and worked as a driver for the UN Economic Commission for Africa.
Was drawn into the liberation struggle through Josiah Tongogara and his friend Mayor Urimbo.
Left Zambia for Tanzania with 110 recruits escorted by Tongogara; the group reached Itumbi Training Camp despite desertions on the way.
Was among the first trained guerrillas, led by Mayor Urimbo, to infiltrate Zambia.
Joined a team doing reconnaissance along the Zambezi River up to Kariba.
Went with Mpofu and Shumba to Tete in Mozambique to work with Frelimo.
Became a member of the General Staff and later of the High Command, responsible for logistics.
Arrested and detained for questioning by Zambian police after the death of Herbert Chitepo; freed the following year.
Joined the Central Committee as deputy Secretary for transport and welfare, a post held until the 1984 Congress; commanded in Gaza Province during the war.
Demobilised through ill health and appointed Superintendent of Enslindale Rehabilitation Centre in Beatrice, serving until his death.
Reverted to ordinary Party member status at the 1989 Congress.
Died at home in Ringa Resettlement Area after a long illness, survived by his wife and seven children.

summary: Isaac Mukusa, known in the struggle as Sarudzai Chinamaropa, was a Kariba clerk who joined the nationalist youth league and then ZANLA. He commanded Chimbichimbi Camp in Zambia and helped mobilise the north-eastern front, including the capture of Gerald Hawkesworth and the evacuation of Mbuya Nehanda's successor medium. Detained in Zambia in 1975, he joined the Central Committee and High Command in 1977, and after independence ran Ruwe Rehabilitation Centre until his death in November 1994.

timeline.text: Born in southern Zambia while his father was working there; the family lived mostly in Hurungwe, Mashonaland West.
Schooled in Kariba to Standard 5, then worked as a clerk for the Central African Power Board collecting visitor fees at the powerhouse.
Experienced racial discrimination at work and joined the Youth League of the nationalist movement.
Recruited into ZANLA after a talk by Henry Hamadziripi, trained at Itumbi Camp in Tanzania and took the Chimurenga name Sarudzai Chinamaropa.
Returned to Zambia as commander of Chimbichimbi Camp, where his knowledge of both banks of the Zambezi and local languages was valuable.
With Justin Chauke and others, shifted strategy to reconnaissance and mass mobilisation, and with Badza, Tungamirai and a spirit medium helped open the north-eastern front.
Took part in capturing Rhodesian land development officer Gerald Hawkesworth and taking him to Zambia unharmed, a propaganda success showing the war was against oppression, not whites.
Helped safely evacuate the successor spirit medium of Mbuya Nehanda to Zambia.
Imprisoned at Kabwe in Zambia with other ZANLA cadres after the assassination of Herbert Chitepo.
Released to attend the abortive Geneva Conference.
Elected to the Central Committee at the ZANU Congress and appointed to the High Command.
Became superintendent of Ruwe Rehabilitation Centre, a post held until his death.
Died, survived by his wife and two children.

summary: Albert Nxele, with the Chimurenga name Buffalo Mongol Mugaradzakasungwa, was a Matabeleland-born teacher and ANC activist in South Africa before returning to join the NDP and ZAPU. He underwent training in the Soviet Union and became commander of the Kongwa and Morogoro camps in Tanzania, training many future leaders. He later served in national security in Lusaka and helped secure the Patriotic Front at Lancaster House. After independence he was treasurer of the War Veterans Association and a security officer, dying in December 1994.

timeline.text: Born in Kezi District, Matabeleland South; completed standard six at St. Patrick's School in Bulawayo.
Taught for a time before going to work in Johannesburg.
Joined the African National Congress in South Africa and later organised ANC protest against the Rivonia treason trial.
With Stephen Nkomo, Makhatini Gunduza and others, formed a burial society for Zimbabweans in Johannesburg, the Sons of Southern Rhodesia Self-help Association.
Returned home, joined the National Democratic Party and rose to district chairman.
After the NDP ban, was sent by ZAPU with six other cadres for military training in the Soviet Union.
On return, assigned to open Kongwa Military Academy in Tanzania as camp commander, with Lookout Masuku and Nikita Mangena under him.
Took charge of Morogoro Camp, the first OAU-sponsored training camp, which trained leaders such as Solomon Mujuru.
Appointed Assistant Director of National Security based at party headquarters in Lusaka after the release of political leaders.
Organised security for the Patriotic Front leadership during the Lancaster House talks.
Returned to Zimbabwe; after independence was demobilised and a foodstuffs co-operative he formed with other ex-combatants failed for lack of funds.
Elected national treasurer when the War Veterans Association was launched in Chinhoyi.
Collapsed and died at his Marlborough home; buried at the national shrine on December 30, survived by his wife and two children.

notes: Soviet training date 'April 4, 1961' printed before 1966 return and may be misprinted/misread (NDP was still active in early 1961)
Burial year not printed in intro (assumed 1994)

summary: Guy Clutton-Brock was an English social worker and Anglican lay missionary who moved to Rusape in 1948 and became a friend and adviser to black nationalists. He helped the ANC draft its constitution, defended Chief Tangwena's community, and was detained in 1959 before founding Cold Comfort Farm. Deported later for allegedly supporting terrorists, he kept campaigning from Wales and after independence led the UK Britain-Zimbabwe Society. He died in January 1995 and his ashes were scattered at Heroes Acre that August.

timeline.text: Born in Northwood, England, second son in a middle-class family of two boys and two girls.
Married Molly Allen after studying history at Cambridge and training at a theological college in Oxford.

timeline.date: during and after the Second World War
timeline.text: Worked as a social worker in the slums of London, experiences that shaped his socialist and Christian ideals.
Came to Southern Rhodesia with Molly as lay missionaries of the Anglican Church, based at St. Faith Mission in Rusape, working as an agricultural adviser promoting co-operatives.
Helped nationalists including George Nyandoro, Maurice Nyagumbo and James Chikerema draw up the constitution of the African National Congress of Southern Rhodesia.
At the ANC's inaugural congress he stressed national unity regardless of race, colour or creed.
Publicly backed Chief Tangwena and his people against forced eviction, angering the colonial government.
Detained without trial, which drew international condemnation; on release he set up Cold Comfort Farm, a refuge for fugitive combatants.
Cold Comfort Farm was declared unlawful soon after an incident involving Didymus Mutasa, its assets were seized a year later, and he was deported in February on allegations of aiding terrorists.
From Wales he continued lobbying the British government against the Smith regime and supported detainees' families and political prisoners.
Elected president of the United Kingdom chapter of the Britain-Zimbabwe Society.
Died; his ashes were scattered at Heroes Acre on August 11, 1995.

summary: George Mudukuti, from Gutu, became a nationalist organiser with the NDP and ZAPU youth wing before training in China, Ghana and Egypt and joining ZANU. He was among the first to take up arms and took part in sabotage of railways, then endured long detention alongside Mugabe, Muzenda and other leaders. After helping lead the People's Movement he attended Lancaster House, entered Parliament and the Senate, and later led construction projects in Masvingo. He died in 1995 at his home.

timeline.text: Born in Gutu, Masvingo.
Entered nationalist politics by joining the NDP as organising secretary of the Highfield branch.
Joined ZAPU after the NDP ban and chaired its youth wing.
Received military training at the Nanking Military Academy in China, and also trained in Ghana and Egypt.
Assigned to the ZAPU office in Tanzania, where he crossed over to join ZANU at its formation.
Was among the first Zimbabweans to take up arms and one of five combatants who began a programme of internal sabotage.
With other comrades, attacked a locomotive at Victoria Falls and the Masvingo railway line to hit the settler economy.
Arrested and held in long detention at Wha Wha with Robert Mugabe, Simon Muzenda, Eddison Zvobgo and Leopold Takawira, and also at Gonakudzingwa, Sikombela and Salisbury Maximum prisons.
After release helped form the People's Movement, ZANU's internal wing, becoming its Deputy and Administrative Secretary.
Attended the Lancaster House conference as part of the ZANU delegation.
Stood for election in Mashonaland Central on a ZANU (PF) ticket and was later appointed MP for Masvingo after Nolan Makombe became President of the Senate.
Appointed senator after being elected to the Central Committee at the party's second congress.
Elected MP for Masvingo North, and chaired a construction co-operative that built rural schools and Mahoto Dam.
Collapsed and died at home; buried at the National Heroes Acre on June 2, survived by his wife and eleven children.

Death year not printed in the intro lines read (1995 inferred from burial date)

summary: Ariston Chambati was an administrator, politician and businessman who helped found the NDP and served ZAPU in exile, studying in the United States and at Oxford. He was a ZAPU diplomat at Geneva and Lancaster House, became Zimbabwe's ambassador to Bonn, and helped build the ZANU-ZAPU unity of 1987. He later became chairman and chief executive of T.A. Holdings and entered the Cabinet as Finance Minister in 1995. He died that October after a short illness.

timeline.text: Born; schooled at Bradley Institute, Howard Institute and Tegwani Secondary School in Plumtree, then worked for Harare firms.
Joined the City Youth League in Harare and later became treasurer of the Mbare branch of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress.
Became one of the founding members of the National Democratic Party; later joined ZAPU and wrote pamphlets against white supremacy.
Went abroad to study after ZAPU was banned, earning degrees in the USA and a doctorate at Oxford.
Awarded the African Institute Scholarship; in 1970 received a Lincoln College Middle Eastern Research Grant.
Elected Deputy Secretary General of the ANC (ZAPU).
Attended the Geneva Conference as Secretary to the ZAPU wing of the Patriotic Front delegation.
Became ZAPU's Secretary for Research in Lusaka and joint-Secretary of the Patriotic Front delegation at Lancaster House.
Elected to the first independent Parliament for ZAPU in Mashonaland West and appointed Ambassador to Bonn in October.
Returned home and, from 1984 to 1987, helped promote the ZANU-ZAPU unity that led to the 1987 Unity Accord.
Joined the board of T.A. Holdings as a trainee manager and rose to Chairman and Chief Executive, also sitting on boards such as Barclays Bank of Zimbabwe and African Lakes Corporation.
Appointed to the ZANU (PF) Central Committee.
Won the Makonde seat and was appointed Finance Minister, giving up lucrative business posts; soon presented a budget and promoted funding for black businesses.
Died after a short illness; survived by his wife Dianna and five children.

summary: Herbert Ushewokunze was a doctor and fiery orator who entered politics as a student leader in South Africa and later opposed the Pearce Commission in Zimbabwe. In 1976 he left his medical practice to run ZANLA's health services in Mozambique, training paramedics and opening camp clinics. As independence Minister of Health he introduced free basic care and backed traditional medicine, later holding several other portfolios and senior ZANU (PF) posts. He died in December 1995 as Harare provincial chairman.

timeline.text: Born near Marondera as the last child of a Wesleyan Methodist family; his father died weeks before his birth and an uncle raised him.
Studied medicine at the University of Natal, where he became President of the Black Medical Students Union and joined the Pan African Congress.
Joined South African protests against pass laws that led to the Sharpeville massacre.
Returned to practise medicine in Bulawayo, the first black doctor to run a private nursing home (Marondera Clinic), with surgeries in Gweru and Kwekwe and a free clinic in Gokwe.
Helped form Mashonaland United Football Club (now Zimbabwe Saints) and joined ZANU's youth branch, recruiting youths underground.
As vice-chairman of the ANC, helped organise the black population's rejection of the Pearce Commission.
Left his medical practice to join ZANLA in Mozambique, becoming Secretary for Health, Central Committee and High Command member.
Set up clinics in guerrilla camps and refugee settlements and trained paramedics into a ZANLA medical corps that also served Mozambicans.
Became Zimbabwe's first Minister of Health and introduced free basic medical care for the low-paid and unemployed.
Held Home Affairs, then Transport (1984-88), Political Affairs (1988) and Energy, Water Resources and Development (1990-93) before leaving government.
Elected to the Central Committee and became Secretary for Commissariat and Culture.
Won the Chinamora seat; in 1990 became MP for Highfield, Harare.
Died as ZANU (PF) chairman for Harare Province; laid to rest December 12, survived by 21 children.

summary: Willard Zororo Duri was an exceptionally gifted student from Manicaland who left university in 1975 to join ZANLA in Mozambique. He rose to territorial commander and General Staff intelligence officer in Gaza province, then completed his degree after independence and worked in the President's Office. He became ZANU (PF)'s Manicaland security officer and later provincial chairman, and was a Non-Constituency MP who observed elections abroad. He died with two daughters in a road accident in April 1996, just before taking up an ambassadorial post in Cuba.

timeline.text: Born in Nyazura District, fourth child in a family of eight girls and two boys.
Sat his Junior Certificate at Hartzell High School after primary school at Rukweza.
Achieved seven distinctions at 'O' Level at St. Augustine's Mission, a national record.
While studying civil-engineering-oriented sciences at the University of Zimbabwe, left with other students on foot for Mozambique to join the armed struggle.
After military and political training was deployed in Gaza province, a harsh semi-arid zone under threat from the Smith regime's apartheid ally.
Rose to territorial commander and General Staff member specialising in intelligence, working with ZIPRA forces to identify enemy targets.
Resumed his studies at the University of Zimbabwe.
Completed a science degree (read as physics and computing), joined the President's Office computer division and was elected ZANU (PF) security officer for Manicaland.
Served as ZANU (PF) provincial chairman for Manicaland.
Appointed Non-Constituency Member of Parliament and later monitored elections abroad in Cambodia, South Africa and Mozambique.
Killed with two daughters in a car accident near Rusape while returning to Mutare from independence celebrations, before taking up an ambassadorial post in Cuba.
