summary: A Harare-born former postal worker, Stanford Tofa Shamu (war name Solo Maimbodeyi) secretly recruited youths for the armed struggle in the 1960s and crossed into Mozambique in 1974 to join ZANLA. After training at Mgagao in Tanzania he commanded a detachment in Gaza Province, fighting boldly until a 1977 gunshot wound left him in a wheelchair. After independence he worked at the national broadcaster, served the party in Harare, and helped set up the War Veterans Association and ex-combatant rehabilitation efforts. He died in 1996 from war-related injuries and was buried at the national shrine as the 33rd hero.

timeline.text: Born in Harare.
Attended Chirodzo Primary School in Mbare, then took a job with the Postal Services and studied privately for O Levels.
Swept up in nationalist politics and, after the parties were banned, secretly recruited young people for the armed struggle despite the threat of jail or death.
Crossed into Mozambique with Air Commodore V. R. Zimondi and others to join ZANLA.
Arrived while the liberation war was in turmoil after the Nhari-Badza rebellion, and made a determined effort to tell the leadership that the recruits were there to fight.
After a year of waiting, the group was sent to Mgagao in Tanzania for military training.
Deployed in Gaza Province among the first group opening up that war zone and served as a fearless Detachment Commander.
Was shot in the waist while trying to rescue a colleague and remained wheelchair-bound for the rest of his life.
Joined the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation as a commissionaire and was later promoted to VTR Editor.
Served the ruling party in Harare in committee roles and was known for settling internal disputes.
Helped found the War Veterans Association and spent much of his time on programmes to rehabilitate ex-combatants.
Died in Harare of injuries from the war and was buried at the national shrine as the 33rd hero, survived by his wife and two children.

summary: Garikayi Magadzire, known as Gary, came from a poor Shurugwi farming family and overcame fee problems and expulsions to train in agriculture. As a government agricultural demonstrator he quietly supported the nationalist cause, was detained around UDI, and later aided guerrillas and survived an assassination attempt. He co-founded an adult literacy body, promoted farmers' savings clubs and co-operatives, led small-holder farmers at the Lancaster House talks and went on to head the national farmers' union and serve on agricultural boards. He died in Harare in October 1996, aged 59.

timeline.text: Born at Tivugari Village in Shurugwi, one of eight sons and twelve daughters of the peasant farmer Tamayi Magadzire.
Got a clerical job at Gaths Mine but was demoted to garden boy for being under-age; Rev. Samkange then sponsored his Standards 5 and 6 at Pakame Mission.

Was expelled from Tegwane Mission for being a Seventh Day Adventist rather than a Methodist, then spent about a year at Tsolo College in South Africa before being expelled for entering a whites-only dormitory.
Graduated from Mzingwane College at Essexvale (now Esigodini).
Joined the Ministry of Native Agriculture as a demonstrator based in Fort Victoria (Masvingo).
Met Joshua Nkomo, a teacher at Mzingwane, who opened his eyes to racial injustice and led him to join the National Democratic Party.
Was present at the founding of ZANU in Gweru.
Detained just before UDI and released in mid-November 1965.
Resigned from government service to join Windmill Fertilizer Company while secretly assisting both ZAPU and ZANU.
Helped two teachers found an adult literacy organisation, now called ALOZ.

Survived an assassination attempt when the policeman sent to kill him turned out to be his uncle and only cut his hand; mobilised Harare black businessmen to supply guerrillas at George Tawengwa's farm.
Served as vice-president of a farmers' union and was later elected president of the Zimbabwe National Farmers' Union.
Led small-holder and communal farmers' representatives at the Lancaster House talks in London.
After a merger of farmers' bodies he became first president of the new union, a post he held until death.
Died in Harare at age 59 from diabetes and blood pressure complications.

summary: Stephen Vuma, born in Shurugwi, entered nationalist politics after leaving Dadaya Mission in 1958 and was jailed and restricted in the early 1960s. In exile he ran party accounts from Dar-es-Salaam and studied national economic planning in Kiev, building a career of more than 31 years in party financial administration. After returning in 1980 he handled PF-ZAPU finances, served as MP for Silobela from 1990 to 1995 and later became ZANU-PF Deputy Secretary for Finance in the Politburo. He died in his sleep at his Gweru plot in May 1997.

timeline.text: Born at Ghogo in Shurugwi, third son among ten children of the farmer Sesulelo Willie Vuma.
Left Dadaya Mission and joined active politics, completing part of his secondary schooling by correspondence.
Worked for the Posts and Telecommunication Corporation in Harare and mobilised people for the nationalist struggle as the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress grew popular.
Was arrested and sent to jail.
Was restricted at his father's plot in Silobela, after visiting restricted leaders such as Takawira, Nkomo and Mugabe to discuss sending a delegation to the United Nations.
Was arrested again after returning from consultation journeys and held at a maximum security prison in Salisbury.
Was appointed to go to Dar-es-Salaam to manage party accounts and, passing through Zambia, was recommended for military training.
Studied at the Kiev Institute of National Economy in the Soviet Union, earning an MSc in National Economic Planning plus two diplomas, while raising funds for the liberation movement.
Returned home after years in exile, mostly in the Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, and became PF-ZAPU secretary for finance and financial director of its companies.
Was elected Member of Parliament for Silobela.
Lost the Silobela seat to Margaret Msimbe and turned to farming at his Gweru plot.
Died in his sleep at his Gweru plot while serving as ZANU-PF Deputy Secretary for Finance; survived by two wives and six children.

summary: Born into the Marange chiefly family near Mutare, George Marange trained as a teacher at Makerere University in Uganda and taught in Manicaland for about ten years. He joined the ANC in 1958 and then the NDP and ZAPU, holding regional and national posts, and was detained from 1964, during which he taught and represented fellow detainees. Fluent in Shona and Ndebele, he worked for ZAPU-ZANU unity, helped lead to the Patriotic Front, attended Lancaster House and later promoted the Unity Accord. He served as an MP from 1990 and died in Mutare in August 1997 aged 67.

timeline.text: Born at Old Umtali (now Hartzell) into the prominent Marange chiefly family.
Left Hartzell for Makerere University in Uganda, where he earned a teaching certificate, a public relations certificate and a diploma in public administration and social welfare.
Returned to Southern Rhodesia and taught for about ten years in schools around Manicaland.
Joined the Southern Rhodesian African National Congress led by Joshua Nkomo, working alongside Enos Chikowore.
Joined the National Democratic Party after the ANC ban and became its Manicaland Regional Secretary, a post he kept in ZAPU; later became PCC Deputy Treasurer.
Was detained and moved between Wha Wha, Marandellas, Gwelo, Gonakudzingwa, Salisbury and Khami prisons, living in Camp 4 at Gonakudzingwa alongside Msika, Nkomo and Nkala.
Taught fellow detainees who wanted to study and was elected chairman of the detainees' committee to present their problems to prison officials.
Was elected ZAPU Organising Secretary for Youth.
Encouraged unity talks between ZAPU and ZANU that led to the formation of the Patriotic Front.
Served as a ZAPU delegate at the Lancaster House Conference.
First stood for election to Parliament.

timeline.text: Was appointed PF-ZAPU National Organising Secretary and member of the National Task Force on Unity, and promoted the Unity Accord in Manicaland.
Won election as a Member of Parliament, representing a constituency outside his home area, and was re-elected in 1995.
Died in Mutare aged 67.

summary: Nolan Makombe, born near Masvingo, worked as a teacher, health inspector and radio technician before giving about 30 years to nationalist politics from the late 1950s. He led the NDP and then ZANU in Masvingo, endured repeated detention and torture, and composed 'Nyika Yedu yeZimbabwe', which became ZANU's anthem during the struggle. After independence he served as President of the Senate and Constitutional Deputy State President, then as Speaker of Parliament from 1990 until retiring in 1996. He was also a church leader, and died at Parirenyatwa Hospital in May 1998 aged 66.

timeline.text: Born in the Zimuto area of Masvingo, one of twelve children of the teacher Taruvinga Joramu Makombe.
Taught at Zimuto Mission, then took a Public Health Inspector course (1953-55) while working for the City of Salisbury in Norton.
Worked as a radio technician for Golden Electronics in Bulawayo and earned a technical diploma with a South African college.
Joined the youth movement of the African National Congress and became active in the Second Chimurenga struggle in Masvingo.
Was elected NDP Provincial Secretary for Masvingo, holding the post until 1961 and keeping it in ZAPU.
Became the first ZANU Provincial Chairman for Masvingo, serving until 1979.
Was arrested when ZANU was banned and held at Wha Wha until 1966, then moved to Sikombela with leaders such as Mugabe, Sithole, Zvobgo and Takawira.
Was detained again in 1971-72 and 1977-79 and tortured, including being tied up in a helicopter from Masvingo to Buffalo Range.
Composed the song 'Nyika Yedu yeZimbabwe' while in restriction; it became ZANU's national anthem during the liberation struggle.
Attended the Geneva Constitutional Conference as a ZANU delegate.
Was released from Wha Wha but restricted to the Bulawayo area; after Lancaster House he campaigned in Masvingo, where ZANU PF won all 11 seats.
Was appointed President of the Senate, which made him Constitutional Deputy State President.
Was elected to the ZANU PF Central Committee and re-elected Senate President the following year.
Led Zimbabwe delegations to parliamentary conferences abroad and held office in the Inter-Parliamentary Union and Commonwealth Parliamentary Association groups.
Became Speaker of the Parliament of Zimbabwe when the single-chamber system began.
Retired from active politics.
Died at Parirenyatwa Hospital aged 66; survived by his wife Iris, seven children and eleven grandchildren.

summary: Rodgers Mangena, known by the war name Nikita, was a brilliant Zimbabwean schoolboy who was expelled for leading a fees strike, fled to Zambia and gave up a Rhodes scholarship to join ZAPU's armed struggle in 1965. After training in Algeria and Tanzania he became a top ZIPRA commander, an ideological influence and editor of its magazine, and was Chief Political Commissar of ZIPA in 1974. He joined ZAPU's delegations to the Geneva and Malta conferences. He was killed in a landmine explosion in Zambia in 1978 and his remains were laid at the National Heroes Acre in August 1998.

timeline.text: Born at Fort Rixon in Insiza District, one of four children of Bakayi Mangena and Elizabeth Mangena (nee Ngwenya).
Excelled at Namande and Musume schools and was school captain at both Musume and Chegato Secondary School.
Led a student strike over fees at Chegato, was expelled aged 18, and crossed into Zambia with his aunt's help to join his uncle in Chingola.
Finished form two at Chingola Secondary School first in the whole school and turned down a Rhodes scholarship to join the liberation struggle.
Was among the first volunteers when ZAPU recruited cadres for the armed struggle, despite criticism from his school staff that it wasted his talents.
After initial training he and Andrew Mafu, Philip Maphosa and Tapson Sibanda went to a military academy in Algeria, then to Kongwa and Morogoro in Tanzania.

When ZAPU's army was renamed ZIPRA and the Chikerema-Nyandoro group left, he was appointed to a senior command post under Commander in Chief Jason Ziyaphapha Moyo and joined the Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Council.
Is credited with giving ZIPRA ideological clarity through his commitment to Marxism-Leninism; edited 'The Combat Diary' and wrote the poem 'Forward'.
Was appointed Chief Political Commissar when the joint ZIPRA-ZANLA force ZIPA was formed; ZIPA soon disintegrated.
Took part in the ZAPU delegation to the Geneva Conference and later the Malta Conference.
Died in a landmine explosion in Zambia's Southern Province while inspecting bases that had been attacked by the enemy.
His remains were buried at the National Heroes Acre.

summary: Philemon Makonese, from Zaka in Masvingo, lost jobs as a teacher and a bank worker for bringing nationalist politics into his workplaces. In 1960 he was among the first youths to volunteer for military training abroad, later trained in China and qualified as an oil engineer in 1967, the first Zimbabwean to do so. He represented ZAPU in Egypt from 1968 to 1972, then helped run the party's organisation and was elected Secretary for Welfare, Culture and Sports in 1975. He died in a Lusaka car accident in 1979 and his remains were reburied at the National Heroes Acre in 1998.

timeline.text: Born in the Zaka District of Masvingo province.
Became involved in nationalist politics while teaching and was dismissed for allegedly politicising students; then joined a bank and was fired again for bringing politics into banking.
Joined the African National Congress of Southern Rhodesia and became a member of the NDP youth wing.
Was one of the first youths to volunteer for military training abroad, walking with three compatriots for most of the way to Zambia.
Was welcomed in Zambia by ZAPU leaders including Chikerema, Nyandoro, J. Z. Moyo and Silundika, then went to Tanzania, enduring hardship without losing his resolve.
After meeting Joshua Nkomo, was arranged to go to China with three other cadres for military training.
Graduated with a science degree in oil engineering, the first Zimbabwean to hold such a qualification.
Served in Egypt as ZAPU's deputy representative, building lasting diplomatic ties between Zimbabwe and Egypt.
Returned to ZAPU headquarters to take charge of the party's organisation.
Was elected ZAPU Secretary for Welfare, Culture and Sports at the People's Congress.
Married Fezela Majola, who was working for the South African ANC in Lusaka.
Died from injuries in a car accident in Lusaka, Zambia.
His remains were reburied at the National Heroes Acre.

summary: Herbert Mahlaba, born in Shurugwi and known in the war as Clement Gaza, was radicalised at Solusi College and joined ZANU's youth wing in 1963. He helped run an underground People's Movement, recruited cadres, fled the country for military training, and in 1978 held a post in the Patriotic Front's Combined Defence Council in Maputo. After independence he served in the army until 1987 as a lieutenant-colonel, then entered Parliament and government and became Governor and Resident Minister of Midlands. He was associated with the Zimbabwe-Mozambique Friendship Association and died in a car accident near Lupane in December 1998 at age 52.

timeline.text: Born in Shurugwi.
Joined Solusi College for secondary education, reaching A Levels, after earlier schooling that ended with Standard Six at Hanke Mission.
Became involved in nationalist politics at Solusi and joined ZANU's militant youth wing when the party was born.
After ZANU was banned, helped found an underground People's Movement whose main base was in the Midlands.
Recruited cadres for military training in neighbouring countries for over ten years, until the Rhodesian authorities got wind of his activities.
Escaped to Botswana, then Zambia and later Tanzania, where he received military training.
Trained at Nachingwea in Mozambique.
Was appointed to a senior post in the Patriotic Front's Combined Defence Council based in Maputo.
Was a delegate at the Lancaster House peace talks that led to independence.
Joined the new civil service, then enlisted in the Zimbabwe National Army as Director of Manning Records.
Retired from the army as Director of Army Public Relations with the rank of lieutenant-colonel, having earned a BA honours degree while serving.
Became a Member of Parliament and government minister, and was later appointed Governor and Resident Minister of Midlands, serving until his death.
As Midlands Governor, became linked with ZIMOFA's work of giving food, shelter and medicine to Mozambican refugees displaced by civil war.
Died in a car accident near Lupane aged 52; survived by his wife and four children.

summary: Patius Ruocha Gumbo, known as Charles and by the war name Tigwe, was a boiler-maker from Gutu who crossed into Mozambique in 1975 to fight and trained at Tembwe. After independence he served in the integrated army from the rank of major, earning a reputation as a strategist in the Mozambican civil war and holding many command posts. He later served on the truce Joint Verification Commission in Mozambique and was the SADC Task Force Operations Director during the DRC intervention, finishing as Brigadier General Staff at Army Headquarters. He died in Harare in April 1999 and was the first serving soldier declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Gutu, the tenth child in a family of eight boys and six girls.
Attended Mundondo School for his primary education.
Completed O Levels at Lower Gweru Secondary School and then trained as a boiler-maker.
Slipped into Mozambique to join the liberation war, was trained as a guerrilla at Tembwe and took the Chimurenga name Charles Tigwe.
Was attested as a major in the integrated Zimbabwe National Army, a post charged with building unity among former enemies.
Distinguished himself as a brilliant strategist during the Mozambican civil war and took part in recapturing many towns from enemy control.
Held a wide range of command posts, including company commander, battalion second-in-command, military academy instructor, deputy commander of the parachute group and commander of the commando group.
After peace talks ended the Mozambican conflict, stayed in Mozambique as a member of the truce's Joint Verification Commission.
When the Democratic Republic of Congo, threatened by rebels, asked fellow SADC members for help, served as SADC Task Force Operations Director and helped repel the rebel advance.
At the end of that tour he was appointed Brigadier General Staff at Army Headquarters.
Died in Harare after a short illness and was buried later that month as the first serving soldier declared a national hero; survived by two wives and three sons.

summary: Daniel Madzimbamuto, born in Murehwa, studied at Munali in Zambia, worked in Northern Rhodesia and South Africa, and rose from the Salisbury Youth League and the ANC to ZAPU's Central Committee. He was one of the country's longest-serving detainees, held from 1959 with only short breaks until 1975, and used the time to earn a University of London law degree. He and his wife Stella challenged Ian Smith's regime in a case that reached Britain's Privy Council. In exile he sat on ZAPU's war council, represented ZAPU on the Patriotic Front joint committee, and attended the Geneva, Malta and Lancaster House talks before a post-independence career at the Posts and Telecommunications Corporation. He died of heart failure on May 2, 1999 and was buried at the national shrine as the 44th hero.

timeline.text: Born in Murehwa.
Attended Chitate and Jakopo Primary schools and then Murewa Mission for Standard Six in 1948.
Studied on a bursary at Munali Secondary School in Zambia, a school noted for producing leading nationalists.

After a brief stint as a broadcaster in Northern Rhodesia, moved to South Africa and married Stella (nee Nkolombe), working in a carpentry shop and a circus company; on returning home he worked as a salesman driver for Lever Brothers.
Joined the Salisbury Youth League and, when it merged with the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress under Joshua Nkomo, was elected chairman of the Highfield Branch.
Was detained after the first state of emergency and held at Khami, Gweru, Shurugwi and Marondera prisons until January 1964.
Became a ZAPU Central Committee member and Secretary for External Affairs and Logistics, but was free for only a few months.

Was detained again at Wha Wha and Gonakudzingwa and spent about ten years in Gweru or Harare maximum security prisons until 1975, when he was released to attend the abortive Victoria Falls Constitutional Conference.
Used his long detention to earn a University of London law degree, A Levels in economics and history, and several certificates and diplomas.
With his wife Stella, challenged the legitimacy of Ian Smith's government in a case heard by Britain's Privy Council, which made the regime an international concern.
Went into exile in Zambia to prosecute the armed struggle as a member of ZAPU's war council and central committee.
Was appointed ZAPU's representative on the Patriotic Front joint committee and took part in the Geneva and Malta constitutional conferences.
Served as ZAPU's legal advisor at the Lancaster House peace talks.
Joined the Posts and Telecommunications Corporation as deputy postmaster-general and stayed until retiring in 1998.
Died of heart failure and was buried at the national shrine as the 44th hero; survived by his wife Stella, two sons and two daughters.

summary: Joshua Nkomo, born in Kezi in 1917, trained as a carpenter and teacher before studying social science in South Africa and working as a railway welfare officer and trade unionist. He led successive nationalist parties (ANC, NDP, ZAPU, PCC), spent about ten years restricted or detained from 1964 and later commanded ZIPRA in the armed struggle. After independence he served in government, was dropped in 1982 amid unrest in Matabeleland, and was central to the 1987 Unity Accord, later serving as a Co-Vice President. He died in July 1999 aged 82 and was mourned by huge crowds.

timeline.text: Born in Kezi District to Thomas Nyongolo Nkomo, a community leader and lay preacher of the London Missionary Society.
Travelled to Adam's College in Natal to study carpentry and, on the train, met Enoch Dumbutshena and Herbert Chitepo, a meeting that drew him towards politics.
Graduated in South Africa, returned home, married Johanna Fuyana and became a social welfare officer with Rhodesia Railways in Bulawayo.
Became Secretary of the Railway Workers' Association and by 1955 was president of the Federation of African Workers' Unions.
Elected President of the African National Congress of Southern Rhodesia and, at Huggins's invitation, attended the London conference on federation, returning strongly opposed to it.
Left the railways to start an auctioneering and insurance business in Bulawayo, the first African to run such a venture.

After the 1958 All Africa People's Congress in Ghana pushed nationalists towards armed struggle, the 1959 emergency banned the ANC while Nkomo, then in Egypt, escaped arrest and ran an external office in London for 18 months.
Became president of the newly formed National Democratic Party (NDP).
Led the NDP delegation to the constitutional conference under Sir Edgar Whitehead, boycotted the resulting elections, saw the NDP banned in December and launched ZAPU as its president.
ZAPU was banned and its leaders restricted for three months; Nkomo, in Zambia, floated a government-in-exile idea that Sithole, Dumbutshena and Nyerere resisted.
Returned home, was restricted at Kezi for three months, then addressed a United Nations committee in New York.
The Dar es Salaam executive under Ndabaningi Sithole voted to oust him, so he formed the People's Caretaker Council while ZANU was founded in August.
Arrested and restricted at Gonakudzingwa, then confined for ten years at places including Gwelo Prison and Buffalo Range, with only three-monthly family visits from 1969.
Appeared in public only three times in detention, meeting Harold Wilson, George Thomson and the Peace Commission at Nuanetsi.
Released without warning and flown to Zambia, where the ANC lacked effective leadership.
After futile peace efforts he resolved to escalate the war; ZANU and ZAPU formed the Patriotic Front and he led ZIPRA as Commander-in-Chief.
ZAPU won about 20 seats in the first elections; he turned down the largely ceremonial presidency and accepted the Home Affairs ministry.
Dropped from government with colleagues as civil unrest gripped Matabeleland; he briefly went into exile, returned about a year later and later won a Bulawayo (Magwegwe) parliamentary seat.
ZAPU and ZANU signed the Unity Accord; he then served briefly as Senior Minister and afterwards as Co-Vice President until his death.
Died in Harare and was buried at the national shrine on July 5 before a record crowd, survived by his wife Johanna, three children and grandchildren.

summary: Sikwili Moyo, born in 1923, rose from trade unionism in Bulawayo to become a nationalist organiser and later a guerrilla commander. He helped organise the 1948 strike and revive the ANC, left for Tanzania in 1962 to run arms logistics, led ZIPRA's reconnaissance unit and joined its Revolutionary Council. After independence he served as MP for Gwanda and on the ZANU (PF) central committee until his death in October 1999.

timeline.text: Born (birthplace not legible in the text).
Bulawayo unions formed the Federation of Bulawayo African Workers Union with 32 affiliates, and Moyo, a Commercial Workers Union executive member, left his job to work for it full-time.
With labour leaders including Benjamin Burombo and Jason Moyo he organised the largest recorded strike in colonial Southern Rhodesia's history.
Young militant unionists including Moyo set out to revive the moribund ANC in Bulawayo, teaming up with Nyandoro, Chikerema, Edson Sithole, Hamadziripi and other radicals in Harare.
The Southern Rhodesia African National Congress was formed in Harare under Joshua Nkomo, with Moyo as organising secretary for Matabeleland.
The ANC was banned and its leadership, Moyo included, was arrested.
After release he worked in the successor parties, the NDP and ZAPU, which was formed in 1961.
When the Rhodesia Front banned ZAPU he left for Tanzania.

After military training in Ghana he handled the movement of arms and ammunition into Southern Rhodesia from Tanzania and helped recruits travel for training in Egypt, Algeria, the Soviet Union and China.
Caught at Kapiri Mposhi by Northern Rhodesian police smuggling weapons from Mbeya, he served a one-year jail term alongside Amos Ndlovu.
As Commander of the Reconnaissance Unit he sent small guerrilla groups into the country, then was recalled and seconded to the Soviet Union for further training.
Returned and was elected to the Revolutionary Council of ZIPRA.
Served as a Patriotic Front delegate at the Lancaster House talks that led to independence in 1980.
Elected Member of Parliament for Gwanda.
From the Unity Accord period he sat on the central committee of the united ZANU (PF) and served as a non-constituency MP.
Died of liver complications, survived by a wife and three daughters.

summary: Cephas Cele was a teacher from Gwanda who left Southern Rhodesia for Zambia in 1963 and joined ZAPU's external wing. Trained as a guerrilla at Morogoro in 1967, he commanded ZIPRA's western front, headed personnel and training and eventually served as its Commissar and Second-in-Command. After independence he worked in demobilisation and as a government social welfare officer and took part in the process leading to the 1987 Unity Accord. He died of diabetes in Bulawayo in July 2000 aged 65.

timeline.text: Born in Gwanda, the fourth child and only son among six children of Sithundi and Sihlahlena Cele.
Attended Glassblock Number 2 School and Hope Fountain Mission for primary education.
Completed secondary education at Inyathi Mission.
Began teaching at Ncema Primary School and then at Glassblock Number 2 School, becoming active in the NDP Youth League and joining ZAPU at its birth.
Left teaching for Zambia in search of better work and joined ZAPU's external wing.
Trained as a guerrilla at Morogoro in Tanzania alongside Solomon Mujuru, with Nxele, Mangena and Masuku among the instructors.
Impressed in combat tactics, he was made ZIPRA Commander for the western front, including joint operations with Umkhonto we Sizwe.
Returned to ZIPRA headquarters in Zambia as Chief of personnel and training.
During the ZAPU leadership crisis, when exiled cadres detained Jason Moyo, Silundika and Edward Ndlovu, he took on extra administrative duties until their release in 1971.
Nikita Mangena became ZIPRA Commander with Lookout Masuku, the Commissar, as his deputy.
After Mangena's death Masuku replaced him as commander and Cele moved up to Commissar, working on political induction of recruits and sitting on ZAPU's supreme Revolutionary Council.
Took up work in a directorate handling demobilisation of former fighters and their return to civilian life.
Later worked as a Government social welfare officer until he retired.
Took part in events and meetings leading up to the Unity Accord.
Died of diabetes at his home in Bulawayo aged 65 and was buried at the national shrine a week later, survived by his wife Debra, eight children and 14 grandchildren.

summary: Ndabaningi Sithole, raised in Matabeleland North and Shabani and educated in mission schools, became a teacher and ordained minister before entering nationalist politics. He served the NDP and ZAPU, then broke away in 1963 to lead the new ZANU, was restricted, then jailed from 1966 and convicted in 1969 over an alleged plot against Ian Smith. He lost the leadership of the mainstream ZANU, lived for a time in exile in the United States, returned to sit in Parliament and died in December 2000. A prolific author, he was formally conferred national hero status in August 2022.

timeline.text: His family moved to Shabani; he dropped out of a Methodist mission school against his father's wishes, then worked as a kitchen boy while attending night school.
Ran away again against his father's wishes to join Dadaya Mission School.
Finished Standard Six top of his class, earning a 10-pound Beit Bursary for Waddilove Training Institute and later a two-year primary teaching course.
Gained a Senior Certificate of Education and later graduated through distance learning.
Singled out as a key figure in the Dadaya School strike, his political baptism, a background incident to the rise of African nationalism.
Appointed to the teaching staff at Mount Selinda United Church of Christ Mission in Manicaland.
Studied at Newton Theological Seminary in Massachusetts, USA.
Returned from the USA and was appointed Principal of Chikore Central Primary School and as a minister of the gospel.
Became President of the African Teachers' Association and a year later treasurer of the NDP under Joshua Nkomo, then was forced by missionaries to resign teaching.
After the NDP was banned and ZAPU formed, he was elected its Chairman.
Exchanged the pulpit for full-time politics.
With Mugabe, Nkala, Tekere, Midzi and Hamadziripi he broke away from ZAPU to form ZANU.
At ZANU's first congress in Gwelo his speech became the cornerstone of its policy of war and direct confrontation.
From restriction he issued the Sikombela Declaration giving Chitepo full powers to prosecute the war from Zambia, enabling the exiles to set up the Revolutionary Council (Dare reChimurenga).
Moved to Salisbury Prison under indefinite detention and, three years later, was convicted of plotting to assassinate Ian Smith and other ministers, receiving six years.
Released in the Detente era and took part in the Lusaka unity talks of December 1974 that produced the African National Council under Bishop Muzorewa.
After being removed from the leadership of the mainstream ZANU, he contested the 1980 elections with a reorganised ZANU.
Lived in voluntary exile in the United States, then returned to Zimbabwe, resumed politics and won a parliamentary seat.
Died at Mercy Fitzgerald Hospital in the USA at age 80, survived by his second wife and six children.
The Second Republic under President Mnangagwa bestowed National Hero status on him.

summary: Border 'Madzibaba' Gezi was born in Guruve in 1964 and joined the liberation struggle as a teenager, working with ZANLA as a mujibha and later as a political commissar at an assembly point. After independence he rose through youth structures, local government and ZANU-PF in Mashonaland Central, serving as MP, provincial chairman and Governor while championing land redistribution. He became a Cabinet minister and then the Party's National Secretary for the Commissariat, leading a restructuring drive. He died in a road accident on 28 April 2001 and was buried at Heroes Acre.

timeline.text: Born at Gezi Village in Guruve District, first-born of Moses Chibarara, a peasant farmer.
Made contact with ZANLA forces in the Mvurwi area, received training and teamed up with other young rural 'mujibhas'.
Used his youth and Johane Masowe Church membership to slip through the Rhodesian security net while working as a mujibha.
His organising talent earned promotion to political commissar, serving Alpha Assembly Point at Hoya in Muzarabani during the ceasefire.
Left the assembly point to finish his schooling at Holy Rosary Secondary School in Mvurwi.
Served as Mazowe District Youth Secretary and sat on the white-dominated Umvukwes Rural District Council, resisting councillors who opposed rural infrastructure.
Elected Mashonaland Central Youth Provincial Secretary for Information and Publicity and held the post until 1987.
Won the Muzarabani seat by a large margin and served on parliamentary committees including Standing Rules and Orders, Public Accounts and Security Ministries.
Elected ZANU-PF Provincial Chairman for Mashonaland Central and restored unity in the province, which the Party swept in the 1995 and 2000 elections.
Became Governor and Resident Minister for Mashonaland Central and campaigned tirelessly for land redistribution.
Mashonaland Central under his leadership returned one of the strongest 'yes' votes in the constitutional referendum.
Won the Bindura constituency seat in the parliamentary elections.
Appointed to Cabinet by President Mugabe as Minister of Youth Development, Gender and Employment Creation, launching economic empowerment projects.
Appointed National Secretary for the Commissariat at the Special ZANU PF National People's Congress and began restructuring the Party.
Died in a car accident near Mvuma while travelling to Masvingo to disburse 1.6 million dollars to community self-help projects.
Buried at Heroes Acre.

He recruited young people for the guerrilla war, organised the 1975 escape of Mugabe and Tekere into Mozambique, and was jailed for his part. After independence he was an MP and long-serving minister (Lands, Home Affairs, Defence) and a senior ZANU (PF) official in commissariat and later transport and welfare. He died in a car accident in May 2001 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in the Devedzo area near Rusape, fourth son in a family of three girls and four boys.
Attended St Vincent Primary School, where he was class monitor and a prefect early on.
Joined politics at 16 through youth leagues of successive nationalist parties and mobilised youth in Makoni and Rusape.
Studied at St Annes Mission in Wedza, becoming chairman of the debating society.
Went straight from school to join Didymus Mutasa and Guy Clutton-Brock at Cold Comfort Co-operative Farm near Harare, later becoming vice-chairman and handling cropping.
After the regime banned Cold Comfort (Clutton-Brock deported, Mutasa jailed), he became managing director of the co-operative remaining members moved to, working with Chief Rekayi Tangwena.
Helped recruit young people for guerrilla training with Maurice Nyagumbo, Rev Basil Nyabadza and others, and contacted FRELIMO to host evicted Tangwena people and trainees.
Masterminded the night escape of Robert Mugabe and Edgar Tekere from Highlands via Nyanga, with Chief Tangwena guiding them into Mozambique.
Arrested after the escape, held at Nyanga, Rusape, Mutare and Salisbury Maximum prisons, tortured, and sentenced to 15 years with six suspended.
Released after serving about four years to attend the Lancaster House Conference as a ZANU (PF) delegate.
Appointed ZANU (PF) Administrative Secretary for Manicaland, was arrested over statements at St Augustine in Penhalonga and bailed two weeks before the elections.
Elected MP for Manicaland and appointed Deputy Minister of Lands, Resettlement and Rural Development.
Became minister of the combined Lands, Agriculture and Rural Resettlement ministries (a resettlement of about 42,000 families is mentioned), then moved to Home Affairs and later Defence.
Served as Political Commissar for Manicaland until a People's Congress made him Deputy Politburo member for Production, Construction and Development.
Appointed National Secretary for Commissariat and Culture and director of elections.
As Defence Minister worked for peace in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Zimbabwean troops fought alongside SADC allies.
Appointed Secretary for Transport and Welfare at the Special People's Congress, a post he held until his death.
Died in a car accident in Nyanga, was declared a national hero by the Politburo and buried at Heroes Acre three days later.

summary: Chenjerai Hunzvi grew up in a poor rural family in Chikomba and was jailed as a teenager for nationalist activity. He served ZAPU and ZIPRA in Zambia, trained in Romania and represented ZAPU in Poland before qualifying as a medical doctor and practising in Harare. He rose to lead the national war veterans association, secured pensions and compensation for ex-combatants and led the farm occupations from February 2000, and was also elected MP for Chikomba. He died at Parirenyatwa Hospital on 4 June 2001, aged 51.

timeline.text: Born at Chiminya village in Chikomba District into a poor rural family; his father worked as a foreman at Bata Shoe Company in Gweru and later in forestry and dip-tank supervision.
Attended Highfield Secondary School and obtained his O Levels.
Detained at Wha Wha for political activities, interrupting his schooling; he shared cells with Willie Musarurwa and is described as the youngest political activist arrested.
Arrested for leading demonstrations against British Prime Minister Harold Wilson.

Detained at Gonakudzingwa Restriction Camp for taking a London Observer journalist to interview Joshua Nkomo and another leader about the Pearce Commission, then restricted to his home area in Chikomba.
As a wanted man, fled Rhodesia and joined the ZAPU external wing in Lusaka, Zambia.
Appointed director of Security in the ZAPU/ZIPRA Revolutionary Council in recognition of his hard work.
Joined the ZANU and ZAPU delegations to Maputo for the formation of the Patriotic Front.

Sent to Romania by Jason Moyo for training in re-integration and rehabilitation of freedom fighters, earning a Diploma in Resocialization in Bucharest, then worked at Zimbabwe House in Lusaka as Director of Foreign Affairs.
Left for Warsaw as ZAPU Chief Representative, and later that year served on the ZAPU team at the Lancaster House talks.
After independence returned to his studies and completed a medical degree; while studying in Poland he married a Polish woman.
Returned home, joined the Ministry of Health and did his housemanship at the Parirenyatwa Group of Hospitals.
Moved to Marondera General Hospital and became Secretary for Health and Child Welfare, later Vice-Chairman, of ZANU PF Mashonaland East Province.
Transferred to Harare Central Hospital as a casualty officer, where he was given war victims compensation claims to handle and grew committed to war veterans' welfare.
Rose from vice-chairman (1992) to chairman (1994) of the Harare provincial war veterans body and became national chairman of the ZNLWVA in 1995.
Around his re-election, led thousands of war veterans in demonstrations over the government's neglect of ex-fighters, which ended with the promised pensions being paid.
Under his leadership the ZNLWVA imported tractors, opened businesses, set up the Zexcom investment fund and won statutory recognition for war veterans.
After the rejection of the draft constitution, led war veterans onto white-owned farms, defying international criticism and court rulings.
Elected Member of Parliament for Chikomba.
Died at Parirenyatwa Hospital, Harare, aged 51.

summary: Clement Muchachi, born in Shurugwi in 1925, was educated at mission schools and Goromonzi and studied further by correspondence before working as a clerk and in commerce in Bulawayo. He entered nationalist politics in 1952 as a Bulawayo ANC branch secretary and stayed active through the SRANC, NDP and ZAPU, taking on youth and recruitment duties and helping set up training camps. After roughly a decade or more in detention or restriction, he became independent Zimbabwe's first Minister of Public Works in 1980 and later sat on the National Consultative Assembly following the Unity Accord. He died in Gweru in October 2001 aged 76 and is described as accorded national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in the Matondo area of Shurugwi.
Attended mission primary schools, then Goromonzi, where he was a prefect and debating-society chairman; completed A Level by correspondence and studied through the University of South Africa.
Worked about four years as a clerk in the Native Education Department before moving into commerce in Bulawayo.
Became branch secretary of the Bulawayo African National Congress, helped found it in Bulawayo and was elected to its leadership.
Played an active part in merging the ANC with the Harare-based Youth League into the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress and became a senior member.
After the SRANC was banned, joined the newly formed NDP, holding senior posts, sitting on the Bulawayo African townships committee and serving as Secretary for Youth in charge of recruitment.
Helped nationalists such as Emmerson Mnangagwa avoid harassment by settler agents and helped establish military training camps.
NDP was banned; per the text ZAPU was banned eight days later and most of its leaders were restricted for three months.
Spent about ten years in prison or restriction, held first at Gonakudzingwa and then at Hwahwa Prison in Gweru.
Later detained at Harare Prison.
Appointed first Minister of Public Works of independent Zimbabwe, leading a reconstruction programme of schools, clinics, houses, dams and roads until 1982.
After the Unity Accord, appointed to the National Consultative Assembly, where he served until his death.
Died in Gweru aged 76.

summary: Cain Nkala was born in 1958 in the Gwanda area and worked in Bulawayo before leaving in 1977 to join ZIPRA, where he trained in Zambia and Angola, served as a medic and commander and was integrated into the national army as a lieutenant. After demobilisation in 1983 he taught briefly, became active in residents' and war veterans' affairs and rose to chair the Bulawayo war veterans' association. The book presents his leadership of farm occupations in Matabeleland from 2000 as his main legacy. In 2001 he was abducted, tortured and killed, and his decomposed body was found in a shallow grave near Solusi University on 13 November 2001.

timeline.text: Born at Mtshabezi Mission Hospital, Gwanda District.
Schooled at Sitezi Primary and Mtshabezi Secondary, then took a two-year certificate course in metalwork and agriculture.
Moved to Bulawayo to join his parents, joined the Inyathi Youth Club in Mpopoma and worked as a machine operator at G and D Shoes.
Inspired by a rally speech by Joshua Nkomo at Mahova Shopping Centre in Mpopoma, left with other youths for Zambia via Botswana to join the liberation struggle.
Trained at Nampundu Recruits Camp and Freedom Camp, where he became medic to a group of 300 ZIPRA cadres.
Was in the first group trained by Cuban instructors at Boma Training Camp in Angola and became an infantry platoon commander.
Selected for further training in military strategy and administration, then deployed in the Kariba area.
Rose to commander of an anti-aircraft battery in the First Regular Battalion and held the battalion's position firmly when Rhodesian forces attacked, causing heavy enemy losses.
Crossed into Zimbabwe, reported to the Gwayi River Mine Assembly Point and was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a lieutenant.
Demobilised from the army.
Worked as a temporary teacher and took an active part in the Magwegwe Residents Association.
Having joined the war veterans association at its start, rose to become Bulawayo provincial chairman.
Led Bulawayo war veterans in farm demonstrations and occupations, masterminding farm demonstrations across the Matabeleland region.
Re-elected provincial chairman in recognition of his resolute stand on the land issue.
Also served on the Bulawayo ZANU (PF) executive committee and the Provincial Land Committee, and led the creation of a War Veterans Widows Association for Bulawayo.

Abducted, tortured and killed; his decomposed body was dug up from a shallow grave at Norwood Farm near Solusi University, and the same group is alleged to have killed Limukani Luphahla on 29 October 2001.
President Mugabe condemned the abduction, torture and killing and vowed that the perpetrators would be brought to justice.

summary: Bernard Chidzero, born in 1927 near Hatfield in Harare, rose from Kutama Mission to universities in Lesotho, Canada and Britain, earning a doctorate in 1958 and writing a Shona novel. He built a long United Nations career, becoming Deputy Secretary-General of UNCTAD and campaigning for UN Secretary-General, while supporting the nationalist cause through the NDP and exile scholarship such as an economic survey of Zimbabwe. After independence he left the UN to become Zimbabwe's first Minister for Economic Planning and Development and later Senior Minister of Finance, steering market-oriented reforms until 1995. He died on 8 August 2002 aged 75 and was buried at Heroes Acre on 11 August.

timeline.text: Born at Arlington Estate near Hatfield, Harare, the eldest of seven children.
Completed Standard Six at Kutama Mission in Zvimba as a consistently top student.
Obtained a Bachelor of Arts degree (psychology) at Pius XII University College in Lesotho after matriculating in Natal.
Completed a degree in Political Science at the University of Ottawa in Canada.
Published his first Shona novel, Nzvengamutsvairo, while still a student.
Received his doctorate after thesis work begun at McGill, and married Micheline at Nuffield College, Oxford.
Joined the National Democratic Party while working abroad.
Began his UN career as an Economic Affairs Officer with the UN Economic Commission for Africa in Addis Ababa.
Was part of the delegation that went to London to press for recognition of African interests in the new Southern Rhodesian constitution.
Promoted to director of the UN Special Fund Programme, then became UNDP resident representative in Nairobi.
Moved to Geneva as Director of the Commodities Division of UNCTAD.
Promoted to Deputy Secretary-General of UNCTAD.
Invited by Robert Mugabe at independence, left UNCTAD, joined the Senate and became the first Minister for Economic Planning and Development in May.
Convened the ZIMCORD conference to raise funds and introduced reforms that moved the economy from a rigid command system to a flexible, market-oriented one.
As a member of the World Commission on Environment and Development, shared in producing the report Our Common Future.
Appointed Senior Minister of Finance, Economic Planning and Development.
Campaigned for UN Secretary-General and came close to winning.
Retired from public life, then served as Special Economic Adviser to the Government until the year before his death.
Died aged 75, four days before he was due to receive the Order of the Zimbabwe Star, which he would have been the first to receive.
Buried at Heroes Acre.

summary: Charles Dauramanzi, from Gutu, was a ZAPU youth who was arrested in 1962, skipped bail and went into exile, becoming one of the earliest ZAPU cadres trained in China. He recruited fighters inside Rhodesia, served on the Revolutionary Council and the General Staff, and in 1973 joined the High Command in charge of logistics. After independence he commanded brigades and ended his army career in 1994 as a Major-General, receiving four campaign and service medals. He later ranched cattle on a farm bought in Chivhu in 1984 and died on 23 February 2003.

timeline.text: Born in Chief Mukaro's area, Gutu, the fourth of eight children (six boys and two girls).
Attended Bako Primary School and Selous Missionary College.
Worked for a year as a salesman for Rothmans of Pall-Mall and became active in politics as a ZAPU youth.
Arrested for taking part in anti-government strikes, skipped bail and left for Tanzania through Lusaka.
Became one of the earliest ZAPU cadres to receive military training in China.
Deployed back into Southern Rhodesia to recruit fighters, working with figures including Simon Muzenda and Emmerson Mnangagwa.
Served on the Revolutionary Council, handling reconnaissance, recruitment and logistics.
After the Revolutionary Council was disbanded in 1968 and the Dare reChimurenga created in 1969, was named to the General Staff.
Elevated to the High Command with responsibility for logistics.
After independence commanded 3 Brigade and the Presidential Guards Brigade, then served as Director Liaison at Ministry of Defence headquarters.
Was awarded the Independence, Liberation, Ten-Years Service and Mozambican Campaign medals.
Bought a commercial farm in Chivhu and began cattle ranching, well before the Fast Track Land Reform Programme.
Retired as a Major-General after a 14-year army career.
Died.

summary: Swithun Mombeshora, born in Mhondoro in 1945, was detained as a schoolboy for protesting against colonial rule and again over UDI before qualifying as a doctor in 1972. After working in government hospitals he went into private practice in 1976 and used it to help the liberation struggle by treating and supplying injured fighters. Elected MP for Makonde in 1980, he joined government in 1981 and held a string of posts, from deputy agriculture minister to Governor of Mashonaland West and minister of Mines, Transport and Communications, and Higher Education. He led the Red Cross Society of Zimbabwe from 1998, died on 17 March 2003 and was declared a national hero two days later.

timeline.text: Born in the Mhondoro Communal area of Chegutu District.
Attended Nyamasanga and St Mark's primary schools, then St Augustine's Secondary School in Penhalonga.
Briefly detained with fellow students at St Augustine's for demonstrating against the colonial government.
As an A-Level student at Fletcher High School in Gweru, joined street protests against UDI and was again arrested and detained.
Completed his medical degree at the University College of Rhodesia and was appointed Medical Officer at Mpilo Hospital.
Was promoted from senior officer in pediatrics and obstetrics and gynaecology to Government Medical Officer at Marondera.

Left government service for private practice, treating patients in Mabvuku and Mbare while quietly running liberation errands and supplying injured fighters with medicine and clothing until independence.
Won the Makonde seat in Mashonaland West in the first non-racial elections.
Gave up three private surgeries to join the independence government as Deputy Minister of Agriculture.
Went on to serve as Deputy Minister for Lands, Agriculture and Rural Resettlement and Minister of State for Local Government, Rural and Urban Development.

As Governor and Resident Minister of Mashonaland West he saw landlessness first hand, strengthening his support for land reform; he also headed the Mines, Transport and Communications, and Higher and Tertiary Education ministries.
Joined the Zimbabwe Red Cross as a volunteer and was elected Mashonaland West provincial chairperson.
Unanimously elected national president of the Red Cross Society of Zimbabwe, and re-elected in 2001.
Chaired the Red Cross federation's HIV/AIDS Scaling Up Committee for Southern Africa, sat on its Disaster Relief Commission and travelled widely to bring drought relief to needy families.
Died at his home in Borrowdale, aged 58.
Declared a national hero.
Buried at Heroes Acre.

summary: Stephen Nkomo, younger brother of Joshua Nkomo, began his activism in South Africa with the ANC and SACTU before returning in 1959 to lead NDP and ZAPU structures in Bulawayo. After fleeing to Zambia in 1964 he served ZAPU as a diplomat in North Africa, helped establish guerrilla camps and ZIPRA, and later ran the manpower department in Lusaka. Following independence he was an MP, a deputy foreign minister and a leading figure in the 1987 Unity Accord, then Governor of Matabeleland South where he chaired land redistribution. He died on 20 April 2003 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born at Antelope in Matobo District; he was the younger brother of the future Vice President Joshua Nkomo.
Attended St Joseph's Mission School at Kezi, then Empandeni and Mzingwani, working for various companies to pay his school fees.
Left the country for South Africa.

In Johannesburg joined the African National Congress alongside Robert Resha, Duma Nokwe and Alfred Nzo, became a founder member of SACTU, and with Albert Nxele formed the Sons of Mzilikazi Society for Zimbabweans living in South Africa.
Helped organise the People's Congress at Kliptown that produced the Freedom Charter and campaigned against the Bantu Education Bill.
Returned from South Africa to join the struggle for Zimbabwe's liberation.
With the founding of the National Democratic Party he became chairman of its Impi Branch and was then raised to chairman of the party in Bulawayo District.
When ZAPU was formed he was elected to the Bulawayo District executive chaired by Lazarus Nkala.
Co-opted by Major Findo Mpofu onto an underground committee; was later arrested over a firearm allegation and mocked the regime in court by joking about a lizard.
Escaped into exile in Zambia after men he had recruited were arrested for alleged possession of arms.
After serving as ZAPU's diplomat in Egypt, was appointed ZAPU representative to Algeria, the Maghreb and Francophone states, using fluent French and Arabic to win material and financial support.
Helped open camps for liberation fighters in Egypt, Algeria, Libya and even Palestine and was instrumental in founding ZIPRA, ZAPU's fighting arm.
Elected a member of the Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Council.
Tasked with heading the Department of Manpower at PF ZAPU's external headquarters in Lusaka, stressing self-reliance in food production.
Elected PF ZAPU Member of Parliament for Matobo and held the seat for ten years; received the Independence Gold Medal.
At the PF ZAPU National Congress elected to the Central Committee and appointed Secretary for External Affairs.

Elected to the Central Committee and Politburo at the united PF ZAPU-ZANU PF Congress after helping prepare the 1987 Unity Accord, and became Secretary for External Relations; awarded the Liberation Silver Medal and the Liberation Decoration.

Served as Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs, then in 1992 became Governor and Resident Minister of Matabeleland South, driving projects such as colleges in Gwanda and the Trans-Limpopo Frontier Initiative.
As Governor chaired the Provincial Land Distribution Committee at the start of the Fast Track Land Reform Programme, pushing for landless people and farm workers to benefit.
Died on 20 April; the ZANU PF Politburo declared him a national hero on 22 April; buried at Heroes Acre on 25 April, survived by two daughters, three grandchildren and one great grandchild.

summary: Johanna Nkomo, known as Mama MaFuyana, was born into Nguni royalty in the Matobo District and married Joshua Nkomo in 1949 after meeting him while working at a Bulawayo convent. For years she raised their children largely alone while he was detained or on struggle missions, and she endured pressure and threats from the Rhodesian authorities, including a 1977 plot against her youngest child that pushed her into exile in England and East Germany. Robert Mugabe praised her quiet dignity and loyalty to the cause, and she kept working for national unity after independence. She died in June 2003 aged 76 and was buried at Heroes Acre.

timeline.text: Born in the Matobo District to Paul Silwalume Fuyana and Maria Sithunzesibi Mbambo, the second of three children, within Nguni royalty.
After primary schooling at St Joseph's and Empandeni she worked as a girls' hostel matron at the Dominican Sisters' Convent in Bulawayo for two years.
At the convent she was introduced to Joshua Nkomo, then in his early thirties, who asked her to marry him.
After initial difficulties the couple married and set up home at the Railway Compound in Bulawayo.
Their first child, Themba, died in infancy.
Later children were born: Thandiwe Barbara (1 June 1954), Ernest Thuthani (11 November 1955, now late), Michael Sibangilizwe (29 September 1958) and the last-born Sehlule (24 August 1964).
While her husband was repeatedly detained or away on risky struggle missions she raised and educated the children single-handedly.
Threw a can of baby milk powder at security personnel in defence of little Sehlule and was held at Commonage as a result (details garbled).
The Rhodesian regime hatched a plan to kidnap her young child Sehlule in revenge for the death of a priest at a mission in Gwaai that it blamed on freedom fighters.
Fearing for her family she left the country, staying briefly in England before going to the German Democratic Republic.
After independence the conflict between the two sister liberation movements did not weaken her commitment to unity and peace; the text breaks off while describing her later work.
Died aged 76 after complaining of severe stomach pain.
Buried at Heroes Acre.

summary: Robert Marere, a Buhera-born artisan trained in building and carpentry, entered politics through the African Artisans Association and the Youth League and joined the SRANC and then the NDP. He was repeatedly detained between 1959 and 1965, was part of the 1976 Geneva delegation led by Robert Mugabe and later helped mobilise support through the People's Movement. After independence he was an MP for Mashonaland East and a Deputy Minister for housing and public construction, promoting building brigades. Nyagumbo's book credits his grocery shop with feeding party officials, and he died on 7 September 2003 aged 84.

timeline.text: Born in the Buhera District and attended several mission schools for primary education.
Completed Standard Six at Domboshava Training School, then took a two-year industrial course that qualified him as a building and carpentry artisan.
Joined the African Artisans Association, a trade body campaigning for African artisans, which drew him into politics.
Joined the Youth League and became a member of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress when it was formed on 12 September.
Detained at Khami Prison after the SRANC was banned, then held at Selukwe (Shurugwi) and Marandellas (Marondera); studied bookkeeping while imprisoned.
After release was elected to an office (title illegible) in the Highfield branch of the newly formed National Democratic Party; the NDP was banned in 1961.
Detained at Wha Wha Prison after the banning of ZANU.
Briefly released, then locked up again at Salisbury Prison the same year.
Part of the delegation led by Robert Mugabe in settlement talks with the British and Rhodesian governments in Geneva.
Mobilised and organised people around the pro-Patriotic Front People's Movement and recruited young Zimbabweans using his own vehicle and resources.
At independence became a Member of Parliament for the ruling party in Mashonaland East.
Appointed Deputy Minister of Housing responsible for rural housing.
Became Deputy Minister of Public Construction and National Housing, promoting building brigades inspired by visits to Cuba.
Died aged 84, survived by his wife Magnet and seven children.

summary: Simon Muzenda, affectionately called Mzee, rose from a Gutu rural upbringing to become a teacher, carpenter, trade union and nationalist organiser in Bulawayo and Mvuma. He held office in the NDP, ZAPU and ZANU, endured long detention in the 1960s and early 1970s, and later worked with Robert Mugabe from Zambia and Mozambique and at the Lancaster House talks. After independence he held top office and ended as Vice President, remembered also as a cultural figure and land reform advocate. He died in September 2003 aged 80 and was buried at the National Shrine.

timeline.text: Born in Gutu District; began primary school late at 14 at Nyamande, then went to Gokomere Mission.
Went to Domboshawa where he trained as a teacher.
Turned down a scholarship to train as an agricultural demonstrator, unwilling to enforce the colonial cattle de-stocking programme.
Taught at Empandeni Mission, where he first met the young teacher Robert Mugabe.

Went to South Africa for carpentry training, taught at Mazenod Catholic School in Mayville, Durban until 1950, was inspired by Reverend Michael Scott's fight against the Group Areas Act, then returned home, married Maud Matsikidze and settled in Bulawayo.
In Bulawayo worked as a clerk and in factories before opening his own workshop in Barbourfields, where he was active in the Barbourfields Tenants Association.
Elected Secretary-General of the British African National Voice Association (African Voice), headed by Benjamin Burombo, gaining national prominence.
Moved to Mvuma and started a carpentry business.
Became involved in the SRANC as it opened branches in Southern Province.
Became chairman of the NDP's Mvuma Branch and was elected Organising Secretary of Victoria Province at the Bulawayo congress.
When the Whitehead regime banned the NDP he took his place in ZAPU as Administrative Secretary of Fort Victoria.

Banned from the Tribal Trust Lands and (per fragmentary text) arrested at Zvishavane over an alleged seditious speech, defended by Herbert Chitepo; sentenced to 12 years but served two at Salisbury Prison.

After ZANU was outlawed he was detained at Wha Wha and later Sikombela, reunited with Robert Mugabe, and also moved among Gwelo and Harare camps with Takawira and Malianga; recruited young people for military training in Ghana and China.
Released during Anglo-Rhodesian negotiations and campaigned against the Pearce Commission proposals, calling them a suggestion to commit political suicide.
Posted to Zambia as Deputy Administrative Secretary of the ANC to help unify liberation forces under the Zimbabwe Liberation Council; in 1974 organised recruits in camps in Zambia and Tanzania.
Moved to Zambia and kept contact with Mugabe, later joining him in Mozambique to prosecute the war and helping resolve the crisis after Herbert Chitepo's assassination.
Attended talks (venue illegible) preceded by the ZANU-ZAPU pact that created the Patriotic Front.
Took part in the Lancaster House talks and criticised perceived British bias.
At Independence assumed one of the highest offices, Deputy Prime Minister (partly legible), later serving as Vice President.
Died aged 80 and was buried at the National Shrine on 24 September; Mugabe called him a veteran freedom fighter and the soul of the nation.

summary: Norman Zikhali, a Mberengwa-born teacher turned textile and garment trade unionist in Bulawayo, used union platforms to press wage claims and to oppose the Pearce proposals. He recruited young people for the liberation war, was detained until 1979 and earned a law degree through private study while held. Elected MP for Pumula-Magwegwe in 1990, he served as a deputy minister for youth development and championed land redistribution and local development until he left Parliament in 2000. He died in Bulawayo on 24 November 2003.

timeline.text: Born to a peasant family in Chief Ngungumbane's area, Mberengwa District.
Taught at Ngungumbane Primary School, then joined Security Mills, a textile factory in Bulawayo.
Took part in the huge Makokoba march in Bulawayo protesting the banning of the NDP, held alongside similar demonstrations in Gweru, Harare and other towns.
As Secretary General of the Southern Rhodesia Tailors and Garment Workers Union he confronted clothing employers in a deadlock over a one pound weekly rise for about 10 000 African workers.
Urged European and Coloured workers in the clothing industry to join African workers in the union in the name of unity.
Used union structures to oppose the Pearce constitutional proposals, retorting that no one should accept half a loaf while others had full loaves.
Led the Bulawayo Textile Workers Union as Secretary General under Joseph Msika, recruited young people for the liberation war and was seen as a very dependable underground contact.

timeline.date: after ZAPU's banning in 1962 and of successor parties
timeline.text: Arrested with other nationalist leaders, held at Wha Wha near Gweru and then Connemara Prison, where he stayed until 1979.
Studied privately in detention and obtained a Bachelor of Laws degree through a South African university.
Elected Member of Parliament for Pumula-Magwegwe in Bulawayo and soon appointed Deputy Minister of Political Affairs for youth development.
Told constituents that many people had become squatters because of land hunger, reflecting his push for land redistribution.
Left Parliament after driving projects such as Amhlope Secondary School, brick housing to replace mud huts and women's and youth self-help schemes.
Died at his Bulawayo home and was buried at the national shrine, survived by his wife, six children and eleven grandchildren.

summary: Julia Tukai Zvobgo, born in Shurugwi, trained as a teacher and in domestic science before marrying nationalist Eddison Zvobgo. She endured harassment and accusations of passing messages to her detained husband, then studied in Britain and the United States, earning diplomas and degrees. After joining ZANU in 1963 she served as Administrative Secretary for Women's Affairs in Mozambique, returned in December 1979 with the election team, was briefly jailed during the 1980 campaign and went on to be MP for Zvishavane and a Women's League and Central Committee figure. She retired from active politics to run family business and died of a heart attack in Harare on 16 February 2004.

timeline.text: Born into the Whande family of Shurugwi and raised in a peasant household with two brothers and five sisters.
Completed her lower Teacher's Certificate at Gutu Mission and taught for a while.
Went to Usher Mission for a Diploma in Domestic Science, where she met her future husband Eddison Zvobgo.
Stayed at home expecting her first child after marriage while her husband left for studies in the United States; later witnessed his arrest on his return and his 18-month sentence.
Became a member of ZANU at its formation.
ZANU's banning led to her husband's detention and restriction at Sikombela and other camps; she endured harassment and torture over accusations of smuggling messages to detainees.
Studied in Britain at Hillcroft in Surrey and then on a United Nations scholarship at Leeds Polytechnic, earning a Diploma in Institutional Management in 1971.
Continued her higher education in the United States where her husband was studying and teaching.
Obtained a BA in political science at Lewis University, Illinois.
After her husband left to join the armed struggle in Mozambique she moved to Notre Dame University and obtained a Master of Science in Administration.
Joined her husband in Mozambique, was elected Administrative Secretary for Women's Affairs and became one of the pioneers of the Women's League.

Among the first ZANU PF cadres to return to Zimbabwe after the Lancaster House conference as part of the Election Directorate, helping set up the party office on the road now named Robert Mugabe Road.
Held for about two weeks for allegedly assisting ZANLA forces in the Zvishavane area and released after the polls, then elected Member of Parliament for Zvishavane.
Elected Secretary for Publicity and Information in the Women's League.
Re-elected to Parliament.
Retired from active politics to concentrate on family business.
Died at her house in Harare after a heart attack, survived by her husband and three children.

summary: Mark Dube, known in the war as Joshua Misihairambwi, grew up near Esigodini and became a trade unionist in Harare before joining ZANU in 1963. After several detentions in the 1960s he left for Botswana in December 1972 and reached ZANLA via Zambia and Mgagao camp in Tanzania, serving as commissar and instructor and later in the Lancaster House process. In 1980 he advised the Ceasefire Commission and he later served as Governor of Matabeleland South. Nicknamed Monomutapa for urging fighters to meet at a whites-only hotel after victory, he died on 28 July 2004 aged 69.

timeline.text: Born in Esigodini, the fourth of nine children, raised by his grandmother; completed Standard Six at Nkulumane but lacked resources to study further.
Moved from Bulawayo to Harare seeking work; racial discrimination and low pay pushed him to fight the colonial system.
Became active in the trade union movement with colleagues including Thomas Mswaka and Titus Maluleke.
Jailed under the Law and Order Maintenance Act for allegedly inciting workers to protest poor conditions, held in Salisbury then Marondera for nine months.
With Titus Maluleke formed the Zimbabwe Labour Organisation after a union split; as Administrative Secretary he ran Southern Province towns including Fort Victoria, Mvuma, Shabani and Selukwe.
Joined ZANU after the ZAPU split, became an organising secretary and attended the party's founding at Enos Nkala's Highfield home on 8 August.

Arrested after the blowing up of a Rhodesia Railways locomotive in Fort Victoria; found not guilty of leading the attack but held in 90-day restriction at Wha Wha and re-detained for a further 90 days.

In restriction studied bookkeeping and secretarial subjects, witnessed Leopold Takawira's beating by a prison superintendent at Gweru and met captured guerrilla Watson Chihota, which stirred his resolve to join the armed phase.
Moved from Gweru Prison to Wha Wha and then Sikombela where the ZANU leadership was held.
Released from Sikombela, restricted to a 15-mile radius of Bulawayo, stayed at his parents' home in Essexvale and later worked for a businessman until 1970.
During the Pearce Commission he organised people to reject the proposals while police and special branch kept him under watch.
Left the country through Plumtree into Botswana, was briefly jailed there and interviewed by J. P. Moyo.
Flown to Zambia with five comrades, met ZANU leaders in Lusaka and moved to Mgagao Camp in Tanzania with 52 other recruits.
Completed military training but stayed at Mgagao as a commissar and military instructor on the General Staff.
Fragmentary text suggests Mgagao cadres, Dube among them, rejected Detente, chose new commanders including Rex Nhongo and sought safe passage to continue the war.
Part of the group that went with Rex Nhongo from Tanzania to Mozambique (place name partly legible) after FRELIMO allowed ZANU and ZAPU to operate there.
Fragmentary text places him in the Lancaster House process, including a trip to London and consultations with the High Command in Mozambique.
Made Military Advisor to the Ceasefire Commission and nominated as a ZANU PF parliamentary candidate.

Served as Governor of Matabeleland South; afterwards turned to private ventures and farming, travelled widely and took part in making two films, one in ZANLA camps in Mozambique with Yugoslav sponsorship.
Died at his sister's home in Luveve, Bulawayo, two days after returning from South Africa where he had sought treatment.

summary: Tichafa Samuel Parirenyatwa was born in 1927 near Rusape and trained in South Africa, qualifying in 1957 as the first black medical doctor in Rhodesia. He used his professional standing to win over white colleagues while devoting his growing free time to the nationalist struggle, becoming Deputy President of ZAPU. In 1962 he was murdered by state security agents who tried to pass the killing off as an accident. A major Harare hospital now carries his name.

timeline.text: Born near Rusape in Makoni district to Sophia and David Deme Parirenyatwa; both sides of the family had ties to early black resistance to colonial rule.
The family left Rusape and settled in Murehwa, where he later attended primary school.
Moved on to Howard Institute and then Adams College in Natal, South Africa, aiming for a professional career.
At Fort Hare University he earned a BSc in Biology and became a leading organiser in the African National Congress Youth League branch there.
Won a place at Witwatersrand Medical School as one of the first few black students, and took part in the Defiance Campaign against apartheid laws, nearly being expelled from South Africa.
Qualified as a medical doctor, becoming the first black medical doctor in what was then Rhodesia.
Worked among hostile white colleagues but earned their respect through skill and professionalism, and became a household name among black people.
Was posted to Antelope Mine Hospital in Kezi, where local whites at first resented him but later opposed his transfer back to Harare.
Left government service and opened a private practice so he could give more time to the nationalist cause.
Was elected Deputy President of ZAPU and, after the earlier party was banned, pushed for a more resolute approach against settler rule.
Toured the country building party structures, set up a research unit for the party and stressed discipline and professionalism.
Was killed by security agents about 15 km from Shangani while travelling to Bulawayo on party business; the killers staged it as a car accident at a level crossing.
The government later named one of the main hospitals, Parirenyatwa Hospital, in his honour.

summary: Eddison Zvobgo rose from a rural mission-school background to earn degrees in Lesotho, Britain and the United States, finishing as a lawyer with a doctorate. He was one of the founders of ZANU in 1963 and its main constitution drafter and publicity chief, and spent close to ten years in prison and restriction for the cause. He served as the Patriotic Front's legal voice at the 1970s negotiations and held a string of cabinet posts after independence until 2000. He died in August 2004 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born into a church-minister's family as the eldest child of a very large family near Fort Victoria.
Began schooling at Jichidza Mission and later moved through Chibizhe Mission and Waddilove Institute before secondary school.
Joined the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress, starting his political career.
Became a founder member of the National Democratic Party and won a scholarship to study at Pius XII University College in Lesotho.
While studying in the United States, was made the NDP Chief Representative to the United Nations and the Americans, a role he kept for ZAPU after the NDP was banned.
Returned home and in August helped found ZANU, drafting the party constitution and serving as Executive Secretary for Information and Publicity.
Elevated to Deputy Secretary-General at the first ZANU Congress in Gweru, a post he held until 1977.
After ZANU was banned, was held at Wha Wha, tried and convicted over a statement made at the congress, and jailed in Salisbury.
Was re-arrested at the prison gate on release, served with a restriction order and sent to Sikombela Camp in Gokwe.
Moved with other leading nationalists to Salisbury Prison, where he stayed until November 1971.
Obtained an LLB degree from the University of London while in Salisbury Central Prison.
Released and restricted to Highfield, where he became a fierce critic of the Pearce Commission.
Was grudgingly admitted as an Advocate of the High Court of Rhodesia.
Joined the Patriotic Front legal team at the Geneva Conference, later serving at the Malta and Dar es Salaam talks in 1978.
Elected Deputy Secretary for Publicity at the Chimoio Conference, taking charge of information.
Acted as chief spokesman of the Patriotic Front and legal adviser to ZANU-PF at the Lancaster House Conference.
Served as ZANU Director of Elections, was elected MP for Masvingo Province and became Minister of Local Government and Housing.
Served as Minister of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, later holding State, Public Service, Mines and finally Minister without Portfolio posts until 2000.
Died at St Annes Hospital in Harare after a long illness; he was later declared a national hero.

summary: Solomon Tawengwa studied economics in India before joining the family business, which he then used to feed, clothe and fund freedom fighters and to recruit youths for training in Mozambique. After independence he rose through Harare city politics to become Deputy Mayor, MP for Highfield and the city's first Executive Mayor, known for housing for the poor and programmes for street children. He was also a respected businessman and company director and a senior ZANU PF official. He died in October 2004 aged 64.

timeline.text: Finished Standard Six after attending Mutukwane, St Margaret's and St Anne's schools.
Left Goromonzi High School and went to university in India.
Graduated with a BA in Economics and Political Science in India, where he helped form the African Students Association.
Returned home and joined his father's well-established family business.
During the liberation war used the family business to supply transport, food, clothing and money to freedom fighters in the Wedza, Chiduku, Dorowa and Marondera areas.
Recruited young people for military training in Mozambique and used the Mushandirapamwe Hotel in Highfield as a recruiting point and meeting place for ZANU PF stalwarts.
Served as a Harare city councillor.
Was Deputy Mayor of Harare, and in 1986 was elected ceremonial Mayor.
Became Member of Parliament for Highfield.
Became the party's candidate and the first Executive Mayor when the post was introduced, serving until his resignation in 1999.
Resigned as Executive Mayor, after housing and street-children programmes for which he is remembered.
Died at his Highlands home in Harare aged 64, after diabetes and kidney complications.
