summary: Ruth Chinamano was born in South Africa in 1925, trained as a teacher and married Josiah Chinamano in 1950 before moving with him to Rhodesia. She became a committed nationalist, leading ZAPU's women's wing, enduring detention and restriction, and later taking part in the 1979 Lancaster House talks. In independent Zimbabwe she served in Parliament, speaking on women's progress, social evils, health and pan-African concerns, and remained on the Central Committee until her death on 2 January 2005. The party accorded her national heroine status.

timeline.text: Born in Griqualand, South Africa, one of five children of a teacher father and a teacher mother.
Won a scholarship to St Matthew's College but was expelled with other girls after protesting against a white principal; she then worked nine months as a domestic servant.
Trained as a teacher at Maria Zell Teacher's College in East Griqualand.
Began teaching at Lourdes school on the Cape-Natal border in Umzimkulu.
Met her future husband Josiah Chinamano while on holiday in Port Elizabeth.
Married Josiah Chinamano in King William's Town and then moved with him to Rhodesia.
Appears to have accompanied her husband to the United Kingdom, where she attended political meetings (OCR very poor).
In Rhodesia was introduced to nationalists James Chikerema and George Nyandoro and joined the African National Congress, stepping up her fight against discrimination.
Became active in ZAPU's People's Caretaker Council in Highfield and its women's wing (ZAWU).
Was detained at Gonakudzingwa, apparently as the only woman among the first four political detainees there, and later moved to Wha Wha.
Was elected ZAPU secretary for Women's Affairs and Central Committee member at a Zapu congress held on 27 and 28 September while abroad visiting her children (year unclear).
Was one of the PF ZAPU delegates at the Lancaster House Conference.
Entered Parliament under the proportional representation system as the Lupane member (details garbled).
Served as a non-constituency MP in the third Parliament.
Used parliamentary motions to push for restrictions on beerhalls near schools, harsher penalties for rape and deliberate AIDS spread, and tax rebates for AIDS-awareness work.
Was retained in the Central Committee at the 4th People's National Congress of ZANU (PF) and saw Joyce Mujuru elected Vice President.
Died aged 80; the Politburo accorded her national heroine status.

summary: Witness Mangwende grew up in Buhera and became known from his school days for challenging colonial teaching and authority. Arrests, expulsions from Zimuto and the University College of Rhodesia and restriction pushed him abroad, where he earned a doctorate and then served ZANU in Maputo. After independence he was Zimbabwe's Foreign Minister for most of the 1980s and later held several other ministries, ending as Governor of Harare. He died of diabetes in February 2005 aged 59.

timeline.text: Born in the then Charter district and raised in Magunda village, Marume, Buhera.
Finished primary school at Marume and Makumbe schools.
Entered Chibi Secondary School, run by the Dutch Reformed Church, where he challenged a white teacher's colonial version of history and religion.
Did his O Levels at Zimuto, a hotbed of nationalist teachers, and defied a white principal there.
Mobilised fellow students against UDI and, with others, was arrested, detained and tortured by Special Branch without giving in.
Completed A Levels at Goromonzi and briefly attended the School of Social Work before leaving for politics.
Enrolled at the University College of Rhodesia, first for law and then for an honours history degree, and became a prominent student leader.
Helped organise Africans against the Pearce Commission and led the famous Pots and Pans demonstration over discrimination against African lecturers.
Was expelled from the university and restricted to his home area after campus unrest sparked by Ian Smith's racist song; later escaped via Botswana to the United Kingdom.
Completed his doctoral thesis and married Eben Yananiso Takavarasha.
Obtained his doctorate in the UK, then went to Maputo as ZANU's representative in the host Foreign Office handling fighters' welfare and diplomacy.
Was appointed Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs by Prime Minister Robert Mugabe and became an MP for Mashonaland East.
Served as Foreign Minister, setting up Zimbabwe's foreign missions and campaigning at the UN for Namibia's independence.
Was appointed Minister of Information, Posts and Telecommunications by President Mugabe.

Reassigned to the Ministry of Education and Culture.
Became Minister of Transport and Communications.
Appointed the first Governor and Resident Minister of Harare Metropolitan Province.
Died at the Avenues Clinic in Harare after a battle with diabetes, aged 59.

summary: Enos Chikowore was born in 1936 near Chivhu, trained as a teacher and clerk and entered nationalist politics in 1958 through the youth wings of the early parties. Known as General Chedu, he led youth sabotage actions in the 1960s and later worked in Zambia for the war effort before studying in Britain. After independence he sat in Parliament and held several ministries including Local Government, Public Construction and National Housing, and Transport and Energy. He died in April 2005 aged 69 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Chikowore Village in the Chief Mutekedza area near Chivhu.
Trained as a teacher at Waddilove, taught briefly, then studied bookkeeping by correspondence and joined the accounts department of Central African Airways.
Entered politics by joining the youth wing of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress.
With other nationalists helped form the National Democratic Party after the ANC was banned.
When the NDP was banned in December of that year, he led a youth wing that fed into the birth of ZAPU.
Became the first National Secretary for Youth Affairs when ZANU was formed after the nationalist split.
As 'General Chedu', headed Highfield-based youth sabotage missions, using dynamite from mines such as Shabanie and Mashava.
Left for Zambia, helped form the Dare reChimurenga and recruited cadres, shuttling between Lusaka and Dar es Salaam; he survived a serious car accident that left a spinal problem.
Went to the UK to study, earning a Diploma in Public Administration at York and then studying law at Leeds, while acting for ZANU among students.
Elected to Parliament at Independence and soon after held junior ministerial posts.
Appointed Minister of Local Government, Rural and Urban Development, and also served as Minister of Public Construction and National Housing, where he pioneered a national housing scheme.
Appointed Minister of Transport and Energy, a post he held until his resignation (year cut off in OCR).
At the ZANU PF National Congress he criticised senior officials who ignored the call to give up extra farms.
Died at his Harare home aged 69, shortly after his former Kadoma constituency was narrowly lost to the opposition.

summary: Winston Changara, born in Mount Darwin in 1954, left school as the liberation war reached his area and became a ZANLA fighter, training in Tanzania and helping open the Mutoko front. He later did intelligence and close-security work for Robert Mugabe, then joined the police at Independence and rose to Senior Assistant Commissioner. As Aide de Camp to Mugabe and head of the Police Protection Unit, he professionalised VIP protection. He died in March 2006 and was remembered as a humble, generous man who supported community projects and enjoyed fishing.

timeline.text: Born in Changara Village under Chief Kandeya in Mount Darwin, the fourth child in a family of ten.

His secondary schooling at Mavhuradonha was cut short when the war escalated; Rhodesian soldiers descended on the school and nearby villages, and pupils were rounded up and beaten, which pushed him to join the liberation struggle.

Linked up with a detachment of freedom fighters, was soon made a section commander over other recruits because of his bravery, and carried guns and ammunition to the front, a task demanding fitness and a flooded Zambezi crossing.
His group survived a fierce ambush by combined Portuguese and Rhodesian troops at Banirambuya (Nehanda's Vlei) and escaped unscathed.
Was arrested on the way to Tanzania for military training, taken to Zambia, and after release stayed with national chairman Herbert Chitepo, who died in a car bomb the same year.

Taken to Mgagao camp in Tanzania where he trained in military engineering, led farming self-reliance work in his company, and as a company commander helped draft the Mgagao Declaration rejecting Ndabaningi Sithole's leadership.
Passed a gruelling selection process under General Rex Mujuru, including a 60-kilometre armed march, and was among the first of an elite group of 400 combatants sent to open new fronts.

Was part of a 30-strong section that opened the Takawira sector in Mutoko and fought in the first big battle at the Haramba Mountains, where a local informer exposed the fighters and several Rhodesian aircraft were shot down.
Was wounded in Mutoko, recovered in Mozambique and became base commander at Tete; Josiah Tongogara talked him out of demanding a return to the front.
After the Tembwe attack he was sent to Yugoslavia for a two-month security and intelligence course, then posted to the Party offices in Dar es Salaam.
Performed close-security duties for the then ZANU leader Robert Mugabe in Tanzania, and in 1979 was promoted to the General Staff; during this time he met his Tanzanian wife Buppe.
Was attested into the Police Force as a Patrol Officer, then moved to the President's Office (CIO Branch 5) for VIP-protection courses.
Returned to the Zimbabwe Republic Police, became Aide de Camp to Prime Minister Mugabe and was promoted Inspector, later rising to Senior Assistant Commissioner.
Introduced his future bride to Mugabe and Julius Nyerere during a 1983 state visit to Tanzania, and married her in 1984.
Attended a command and staff course at Bramshill Police College in England and on return was also made Officer Commanding the Police Protection Unit.
Turned the former Ministerial Guard Unit into a professional VIP security unit and extended it to all provinces.
Was recently appointed chairman of a committee to raise funds for the reburial of fallen freedom fighters.
Died at Parirenyatwa Hospital after a short illness; President Mugabe praised his service in protecting the nation's leadership.

summary: Tichaona Jokonya was a teacher turned student activist who fled Rhodesia in 1966, studied abroad and organised ZANU students and the London branch. Returning in 1979 he laid the Party's groundwork in Salisbury, then built a long civil-service and diplomatic career as ambassador to Ethiopia and the OAU and as Zimbabwe's envoy to the UN and WTO. He helped shape the unity-accord ministry, African trade positions and the country's land-reform case abroad. After heading a tourism body he won the Chikomba seat and served as Information Minister until his death in June 2006.

timeline.text: Born in Chivhu.
Attended Lourdes and Kutama mission schools, qualified as a primary teacher and taught for six years while studying by correspondence.
As a student activist, joined protests against the Unilateral Declaration of Independence.
Dropped his University of Rhodesia degree to escape persecution, slipped out via Botswana to refugee camps in Francistown, and took a leadership role in the ZANU student movement in exile.
Was in Lusaka by the end of the year.
Went to Kenya to resume university studies; while there he took part in a tour of Africa promoting the Southern African independence struggle, starting his contacts with future African leaders.
After graduating he took up a Commonwealth Scholarship at Sussex University in the UK.
Served as Secretary of the Party's London Branch under Didymus Mutasa, helping coordinate visiting leaders while also teaching in Birmingham.
As a ceasefire neared, the Party told him to return home and take a university job in order to lay political groundwork; he helped set up a secret underground cell at the university.
Once the ban was lifted he launched the Salisbury North branch as its Secretary and helped organise the homecoming rally addressed by the President at Zimbabwe Grounds in Highfield.
Was recalled from the university to become a Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Culture, where he helped set up most of the Youth Training Centres.
Served as Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the OAU, chairing its Advisory Committee after being re-elected five times and negotiating the PTA protocols that fed into COMESA.
Headed the Ministry of Political Affairs as Senior Permanent Secretary, which was created to consolidate the ZANU-ZAPU Unity Accord of 22 December 1987.

Was Zimbabwe's Permanent Representative to the UN in Geneva and Vienna, argued the case for land reform, and as WTO representative chaired the Africa Group of trade negotiators ahead of the 1999 Seattle meeting.
Came home to chair the 10th Conference of the Parties to CITES amid Western pressure over ivory sales and Zimbabwe's land policy.
At the UN in New York he also dealt with Zimbabwe's involvement in the DRC and helped oversee electoral transitions in Malawi and Mozambique.
Worked in the Office of the President and Cabinet and then became Chief Executive of the tourism authority (year garbled).
Left the tourism authority to return to active politics and won the Chikomba parliamentary seat on a ZANU PF ticket, later becoming Minister of Information and Publicity.
Was found dead in his hotel room on the day he was due to address parastatal heads under his Ministry.

summary: Armstrong Gunda grew up in Mbare, Harare, and joined ZANLA in Mozambique in 1975 after being politicised by colonial injustice. After training at Tembwe and in China he became a detachment commander, and at Independence he moved into the Zimbabwe National Army. Over a long career he commanded battalions, led training institutions, headed the Presidential Guards Brigade and finally 1 Brigade, reaching Brigadier General in 2004. He earned independence, liberation, service and campaign medals (including Mozambique and DRC) and was declared a national hero, leaving a wife and four children.

timeline.text: Born; grew up in the high-density suburb of Mbare in Harare where he did his primary schooling.
Attended St Killian's Mission near Rusape and was politicised early by the injustices of white rule.
Joined the liberation struggle in Mozambique as a ZANLA member, taking the Chimurenga name Armstrong Tangwena.
Trained at Tembwe, went to China for more specialised military training, and on return was deployed to a sector in a Mashonaland province.
By the time of the ceasefire he was a detachment commander operating in Tangwena Sector.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army at Independence and soon commissioned a lieutenant.
Served as Officer Commanding first of 41 Infantry Battalion and then of 42 Infantry Battalion.
Was entrusted with further responsibilities as a battalion second in command and continued to show integrity and dedication.
Headed the Training Wing at the Directorate of Army Training and was Brigade Major for 1 and 2 Brigades in 1982 and 1984-85.
Worked as Staff Officer Grade One (Training) at the Directorate of Army Training.
Was Commandant of the Recruit Training Depot (1995-96) and then of the All Arms Battle School (1996-98).
Commanded the Presidential Guards Brigade.
Promoted to Brigadier General, the rank he held until his death.
Took command of 1 Brigade.
Was unanimously declared a national hero, praised by Didymus Mutasa and Army Commander Lieutenant General Philip Sibanda as a loyal soldier, trainer and administrator.

summary: Gideon Lifa, known in the struggle as Rodello Tichavakunda, left Rhodesia for Mozambique to fight, trained at Nachingweya, instructed other recruits and entered the ZANLA General Staff in 1979. He served under Tongogara in Maputo and led the funeral parade after Tongogara's death. After Independence he rose through the Zimbabwe National Army as a battalion and brigade commander and in senior staff and training posts, attending courses in Zimbabwe, Australia and the UK. He retired in 2005 as a Major General due to ill health, died in June 2007 aged 49, and was declared a national hero; he left a wife and seven children.

timeline.text: Disillusioned by the racism and brutality of the Smith regime, he joined the liberation struggle in Mozambique and served at camps including Nyadzonya and Doroi.
Was present at the Nyadzonya attack and the same year was among the first group of cadres sent for basic military training at Nachingweya.
Because of outstanding performance he became an instructor and trained a later intake of combatants before being nominated for officer cadet training.
Attended the regular officer cadet course at Nachingweya Institute, which prepared him for leadership in the defence forces to be formed at Independence.
Appointed a member of the General Staff and posted to Maputo, where he worked with ZANLA commander Josiah Magama Tongogara.
When Tongogara died he was made Funeral Parade Commander and carried out the task to the admiration of onlookers, including Mozambican authorities.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army and commissioned a lieutenant in August 1981 (attestation date partly garbled).
Served as a battalion commander, including 22 Infantry Battalion, where he led its integration and stabilisation.
Held a senior staff post at Army Headquarters responsible for organisational design and establishments (dates garbled, apparently 1982-1985).
Commanded 95 Brigade, exercising command and control during the Mozambique campaign and border-control operations.
As a Brigadier General at Army Headquarters and later Director Army Training he handled staff duties, research and development and coordinated regional training exercises (dates garbled).
Retired from the army with the rank of Major General because of ill health.
Died at West End Clinic in Harare after a long illness, aged 49, barely a week after another hero's burial.
Was unanimously declared a national hero; Defence Minister Sydney Sekeramayi said the status honoured his service before and after independence.

After Independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army's Signals Corps and rose to Brigadier General, serving as commandant of the Signals School, commander of the Signals Corps and later brigade commander. During the DRC deployment he protected an eastern sector and helped repel an attack on Kabinda in 1999. He died of cancer in July 2007, was declared a national hero by the ZANU PF Politburo, and left a wife and three children.

timeline.text: Born at Ntiko village in Gwanda, Matabeleland South.
Passed his Ordinary Level examinations at Lundi Mission Secondary School in Masvingo.
After clashes with oppressive colonial laws arising from his youth politics, he left for Zambia to join ZIPRA.
Trained as a combatant by ZIPRA under Joshua Nkomo's command and was deployed to Hurungwe for military operations.
Was pulled from the front and sent to the Soviet Union for specialised military signals training, later serving in ZIPRA under Tshinga Dube.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army in the Signals Corps and commissioned lieutenant on 31 August 1981 (day partly garbled).
Served as second in command of 1 Signals Regiment.
Was on the directing staff at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Was Commandant of the Zimbabwe School of Signals, training Signals specialists.
Served as Deputy Commander of the Zimbabwe Signals Corps.
Was Acting Commander of the Signals Corps, then Commander from April 1994 until about February 2001 (end year garbled).
While deployed at Mbuji-Mayi in the DRC he held off an attempt by rebels and the Rwandan army to attack Kabinda until a mechanised brigade arrived and defeated them in July 1999.
Was Chief Instructor of the Intermediate Staff Course for Congolese senior and general officers at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Commanded 4 Infantry Brigade.
Served as Brigadier General Inspectorate at Army Headquarters.
Died at West End Hospital after a long battle with cancer, aged 52 as printed.
The ZANU PF Politburo unanimously conferred national hero status on him.

summary: Masala Sibanda was a ZIPRA liberation fighter born in Nkayi District who joined nationalist politics as a youth in Bulawayo and was detained at Gonakudzingwa in 1966. After guerrilla and Soviet military training he served in ZIPRA's logistics structures, rising to Deputy Head of Logistics in the High Command and building forward bases along the Zambezi. He joined the national army at independence as a Major, retired in 1999 to work on locating and caring for fighters' graves in Zambia, and remained active in ZANU PF in Bulawayo until his death in 2007 at 61.

timeline.text: Born in Nkayi District to Bafo Sibanda and Jessy Ngwenya.
Entered politics young as a member of the Youth Wing of the Mpopoma and Tshitshisa branch in Bulawayo.
Was detained by the colonial authorities at Gonakudzingwa Restriction Camp along with other cadres.
After release he went into Zambia to join the armed struggle and underwent rigorous guerrilla training.
Was chosen for further military training in the Soviet Union.
Was seconded to various sectors of the ZIPRA military structures and helped create ZAPU's military wing that led to ZIPRA.
Attended the Conference of Militants in Lusaka during the ZAPU crisis in Zambia, which set the way forward to the Turning Point strategy, and worked with commanders at rear and front.
Was appointed to the ZIPRA Headquarters Logistics Department and helped organise the Zimbabwe People's Army (ZIPA) in Mozambique.

Was promoted Deputy Head of Logistics in the ZIPRA High Command as ZAPU launched its Turning Point Strategy, and set up forward logistic bases at Sinazongwe, Kabanga, Mapatiziya and other Zambezi areas.
Met Alphonsina Mubuyaeta in Zambia; they later married.
During the ceasefire stayed behind with a few men to look after the ZIPRA stores.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a Major and served in the Army Headquarters Quartermaster Branch.
Retired after nineteen years of army service and was assigned to Museums and National Monuments to identify graves, rehabilitate shrines and compile the list of fighters who died in Zambia.
Led yearly teams to memorial sites in Zambia, and later served ZANU PF in Bulawayo as Welfare and Transport Secretary and sat on the Mafela Trust board.
Died after ten days in Mater Dei Hospital, Bulawayo, aged 61; heroes status was conferred posthumously.

summary: Isaac Lintshwi Nyathi was born in 1936 in Mangwe District and worked as a school clerk and railway fireman in Bulawayo, where his home became a resistance hub. Detained by the Special Branch, he went to Zambia in 1964, studied Economics in the Soviet Union, and fought in the 1967-68 battles before becoming PF-ZAPU's head of research and later its envoy in Sweden and Eastern Europe. After independence he sat on the ZAPU Central Committee, won a parliamentary seat in 1985 and served as a diplomat before dying of diabetes complications in December 2007 at 71.

timeline.text: Born at Sanzukwi area, Mangwe District, Matabeleland South.
Worked as a school clerk at Mbizo Primary School in Luveve, Bulawayo, until 1961.
His house in Mpopoma South became a resistance centre where freedom fighters and even ANC asylum seekers were fed and funded, while he worked as a railways fireman.
Was arrested several times by the Rhodesian Special Branch, ending in six months' detention at Hwa Hwa Prison.
After release he crossed into Zambia to join the armed struggle and was assigned to study Economics in the Soviet Union.
Returned to Zambia after completing his studies.
Took part in the Hwange (1967) and Sipolilo (1968) battles.
Became PF-ZAPU Head of Research in Zambia after gaining a doctorate in Economics, and joined the Revolutionary Council, a post held until 1979.
Was appointed PF-ZAPU representative in Sweden, later covering Eastern Europe from Berlin, and advised ZAPU on economics at the Lancaster House Conference.
Returned home and was elected a ZAPU Central Committee member (served 1980-1987).
Won the Bulilima-Mangwe parliamentary seat on a PF-ZAPU ticket but did not complete the term (details garbled).
After the Unity Accord was signed he was appointed to an ambassadorial post, apparently in Nigeria (garbled).
Served as a diplomat in Kuwait.
Died at Mater Dei Hospital in Bulawayo after a long fight with diabetes, aged 71.

He had the honour of hoisting the new national flag in April 1980 and then built a long army career, culminating in command of SADC allied forces in the DRC and promotion to Lieutenant General on retirement. timeline.text: Became secretary and then chairman of the African National Congress branch in Masvingo, then slipped out of the country to Zambia and got initial military training at Mgagao, Tanzania.
Was picked for the ZANLA General Staff and served as an instructor at the Mgagao camp, teaching future senior figures including Chiwenga, Shiri, Chihuri and Zimondi.
Led a group of cadres to join the Zimbabwe People's Army (ZIPA), where ZANLA and ZIPRA trained together at Mgagao.
Relocated to Mozambique to head external training and specialised artillery training.
Was appointed to the ZANLA High Command, serving as the Training deputy in Block 12 at Chimoio.
Was deployed in Gaza Province to cripple the Rutenga railway line and later joined 550 ZANLA troops under Josiah Tungamirai who attacked Mutare.
Was part of the ZANLA command that held the Mavhonde base in a five-day battle against Rhodesian forces, a turning point in the war.
Was the first citizen to hold and hoist Zimbabwe's new national flag at the independence handover at midnight.
Was commissioned as Brigadier General and served at Army HQ from mid-1981.
Commanded an infantry brigade and took part in Mozambique operations securing Zimbabwe's economic lifelines against Renamo (dates and brigade garbled).
Served as Director of the Army Services Corps at Army Headquarters.
Was re-appointed Brigadier General, Quartermaster Staff at Army Headquarters.
Sat on the Joint Verification Commission in Mozambique.
Served as Brigadier General, General Staff at Army Headquarters.
Was Chief of Staff, Administration at Army Headquarters.
Was Chief of Staff, General Staff at Army Headquarters.
Commanded the SADC Allied Forces in the DRC, taking charge of operations, the fragile ceasefire and the transition after President Laurent Kabila's assassination.
Served as Chief of Staff General at Army Headquarters.
Retired as a Major General and was promoted to Lieutenant General in recognition of his service.
Died after a long illness; the President praised him as a great strategist.

summary: Lloyd Gundu was born in Marondera in 1946; his family's eviction from their land and his early protests against colonial laws pushed him into nationalist politics. He trained in Tanzania and China, bombed the African Daily News offices in 1964, was sentenced to death, saw it commuted and was released only in April 1980 after 16 years. He then built a career in the President's Department intelligence services, with postings in Bonn and London and director-level roles, before serving as ambassador to Yugoslavia and then Sudan. He died in June 2008 aged 61 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born first of nine children (four boys, five girls) in Marondera; the family was later forced to move to Murehwa on 17 July 1951 after white authorities took their land.
Was expelled from school for protesting colonial repressive laws.
While working as a salesman in Salisbury he became Secretary-General of a youth league (name garbled, 'Hassim').
Left for Zambia to join the liberation struggle.
Went to Tanzania for military training.
Went with six other cadres to China for training in urban guerrilla warfare and sabotage, graduating in September.
After operations in Mutare, Kwekwe and Harare and the blowing up of the African Daily News offices in Salisbury, he was arrested.
His death sentence by hanging was confirmed but remained unexecuted.
His sentence was commuted to life imprisonment because he was a juvenile; he was held at Harare Central then Khami Maximum Prison, and joined underground prison committees.
Was released from prison two days before independence after 16 years.
Was appointed an Intelligence Officer in the President's Department, External Branch.
Took on Evaluation and Collection Divisions and the Liberation Movements Desk, channelling assistance to bodies like the ANC.
Served as Liaison Officer/Counsellor at the Zimbabwe Embassy in Bonn, Germany.
Held the same post at the Zimbabwe Embassy in London.
Served as Assistant Director and then Deputy Director of the External Branch.
Became Director in the Counter Intelligence Branch.
Became Director for Special Projects in the Director General's office, then moved to the Foreign Affairs ministry and served as ambassador to Yugoslavia (start and end dates damaged).
Took up his post as Zimbabwe's ambassador to Sudan in Khartoum.
Died aged 61 while serving as ambassador; declared a national hero.

summary: Elliot Tapfumaneyi Manyika was born in Chiweshe in 1955 and became a political activist while at Kutama College, which led to a five-year prison sentence in 1974. After independence he studied further, joined the ZANU PF Youth League and rose through party and civil-service roles to become Governor of Mashonaland Central, MP for Bindura North, a minister and the party's National Political Commissar. He was also known for motivating members through music. He died in a road accident in December 2008 at 53 on his way to monitor party elections, and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born at Rosa Clinic in Chiweshe, Mashonaland Central.
Sat Ordinary Level examinations at Kutama College.
Was arrested for allegedly writing and circulating subversive statements against the Rhodesian regime while awaiting his O-level results, and was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.
Was freed under strict conditions limiting his movement and political activity, including regular reporting to police, which ended his Advanced level studies.
Joined the ZANU PF Youth League with Border Gezi and helped form the 21st February Movement.
Became the youngest ZANU (PF) provincial secretary for administration.
Held administrative posts in the civil service and Foreign Affairs ministry, with a promotion in March 1992 (titles unreadable).
Became a party committee member and Deputy Secretary for Information and Publicity.
Posted as Zimbabwe's High Commissioner to Malawi until 2000, when he was reassigned.
Became Mashonaland Central Governor and Resident Minister, driving the land reform programme and building schools and clinics.
Became Bindura North MP and Minister of Youth, Gender and Employment Creation, and (as listed) ZANU-PF National Political Commissar.
Was appointed Minister Without Portfolio and led a countrywide research team on socio-economic and political issues.
Was re-elected as Member of Parliament in 2005 and again in 2008.
Died in a road accident on the Zvishavane-Mbalabala Road while travelling to Gwanda to monitor party provincial elections, aged 53; the Politburo declared him a national hero.

summary: Gordon Sibanda was a ZIPRA officer who joined nationalist politics in the NDP in 1959, then ZAPU, and trained in Algeria and at a commando school before serving as commissar, instructor and camp commander in Tanzania. He rose to head ZIPRA's intelligence, communications and reconnaissance, ran Zambezi infiltration missions, sat on the Joint Military Command and became ZAPU's representative in Libya. He joined the Zimbabwe National Army in 1981, retired as a Major in 1999 aged 51, took up farming and party work, and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Joined the National Democratic Party as a Youth League member, later moving to ZAPU.
Went to Zambia, worked briefly for Anglo-American on the Copperbelt, and served as a ZAPU publicity secretary (wording garbled).
Joined ZIPRA, ZAPU's armed wing, under the guidance of senior nationalists including George Nyandoro, and left for military training via Tanzania and Egypt.
Started training in Algeria as one of 91 recruits; a group of 19 educated trainees, including him, was then selected for special training at Cherchell.
Underwent commando training at Skinder Commando School, then moved to Kongwa Camp in Tanzania where he became a political commissar.
Was Chief Instructor at a training camp (Morogoro), teaching tactics, topography and close combat.
Served as camp commander at Morogoro, then became a member of the Joint Military Command created by ZIPRA and ZANLA in Mbeya.

Headed intelligence, communications and reconnaissance, running Zambezi crossings; survived a boat sinking and was rescued after three days on an island; also led a raid at Mana Pools capturing nine rifles.
Kept his intelligence, communications and reconnaissance post when ZANLA and ZIPRA formed the Zimbabwe People's Army (ZIPA).
Was appointed ZAPU Chief Representative in Libya, handling military matters including training.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a Green Board Officer (lieutenant colonel equivalent), later confirmed at lieutenant, then captain and finally major.
Held ZNA posts including commanding officer at Bulawayo depot, battalion commander in Mutare, school of infantry officer, and company commander posts in Bulawayo and Masvingo.
Retired at age 51 from the army.
Took up farming in Gwaai while mobilising for the ruling party, serving as a district political officer in Bulawayo province (wording damaged).

summary: Vitalis Musungwa Zvinavashe, known as Fox Corner, was born in Gutu in 1943, worked as a fish trader and mechanic trainee, and joined ZANU in Zambia before training in Tanzania in 1968. He rose to the ZANLA High Command and ZANU Central Committee, was detained by Zambia after Chitepo's death, and led intelligence and reserve forces during the war. After independence he held brigade and staff commands, became ZNA commander in 1992 and first commander of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces, steering UN, SADC and DRC deployments. He retired in 2003, became a farmer, senator and Politburo member, and died of cancer in March 2009.

timeline.text: Born in Zinhata Kraal, Gutu District, and went to Masema and then Jersey Tea Estate primary schools.
Trained in the fish industry and became a small-scale fish trader between Southern and Northern Rhodesia.
Moved to Northern Rhodesia and became a trainee mechanic at the CMED in Lusaka.
Took guerrilla warfare training at Chunya Camp in Tanzania under William Ndangana and was made camp political commissar.
Returned to Zambia with ZANLA comrades, forming a group that later became the High Command and opening operational sectors along the borders.
Was elected to the ZANLA Military Council and commanded the Botswana-Zambia border sector responsible for recruitment, training, intelligence and infiltration.
Was elected to the High Command and appointed provincial secretary of the Malawi(?)-Mozambique-Zimbabwe (MMZ) Front until the 1974 detente.
After Herbert Chitepo's assassination he and other High Command members were detained in Zambia until 1976, then cleared of charges and released.
At the ZANU Chimoio Congress was elected to the Central Committee and made Deputy Chief of National Security and Intelligence.
After the ceasefire he remained in Mozambique commanding the ZANLA Reserve Force and handling ZANU's external affairs.
Joined the Zimbabwe National Army as Brigadier General, commanded 3 Infantry Brigade in Manicaland and led the first ZNA troops guarding the Beira Corridor.
Was promoted Major General and made Chief of Staff for General Staff matters, and briefly led ZDF troops in Mozambique.
Took command of the ZNA as Lieutenant General after the retirement of Solomon Mujuru (Rex Nhongo) and oversaw the Somalia UNOSOM deployment, followed by Rwanda and Angola missions.
Became the first Commander of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces under the amended Defence Act.
Chaired a Harare meeting on the idea of an African Standby Force.
Helped deploy forces in Lesotho and SADC allied forces in the DRC, chairing the defence chiefs of Angola, DRC, Namibia and Zimbabwe.
Founded Tynwald Pre-school, Primary and Secondary Schools.
Received an honorary doctorate from the University of Zimbabwe and retired from the army, handing over to General Constantine Chiwenga.
Joined the ZANU PF Central Committee and Politburo (2004), became Secretary for Indigenization and Empowerment and Senator for Gutu (2005), and joined the War Veterans Board (2006).
Died of cancer at Manyame Air Base Hospital aged 66 (as printed); the Politburo declared him a national hero the next day.

summary: Wilford Lizart Sibanda, known in the struggle as Johnson Fletcher, was a Matabeleland-born carpenter who used his employment with the Johnson and Fletcher company to support the liberation war. After moving to its Livingstone branch in Zambia he helped ZIPRA and its ANC allies cross into Rhodesia and kept supply bases and reconnaissance units going. After independence he looked after former ZIPRA facilities, then served ZAPU as an adviser and contributed to the Unity Accord. He later ranched cattle until his death in 2009.

timeline.text: Born at Ncema in Umguza District, Matabeleland North.
Trained as a carpenter at Inyathi Boys Institution after finishing Standard six.
Began working for a Bulawayo company called Susman.
Worked for Johnson and Fletcher in Bulawayo while becoming active in anti-colonial politics.
Asked to be transferred to the Johnson and Fletcher branch in Livingstone, Zambia, where he took the Chimurenga name Johnson Fletcher and recruited and helped cadres for the war.
Joined the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress, later moving through the NDP into ZAPU.
Moved to the Zambian branch for his own safety as an intelligence net tightened around him.
Appointed chairman of ZAPU's Southern Region and kept operational camps and reconnaissance units supplied around Livingstone, working with colleagues such as Buche, Zitshe Moyo and Stollamu Ndlovu.
Maintained logistics bases and crossing points (Mlibizi and other camps near Livingstone) and helped ZIPRA fighters cross into Rhodesia by passing them off as company employees.
Helped the combined ZIPRA and ANC (Umkhonto we Sizwe) forces cross the crocodile-infested Zambezi River.
Was entrusted with looking after the facilities from which ZIPRA forces had operated during the war.
Retired and became an adviser to ZAPU, and later served as an adviser in the process leading to the Unity Accord.
Died after a long illness; he was cattle ranching at Fig Tree in Matabeleland South at the time and was buried at Lady Stanley Cemetery.

summary: Akim Mathew Ndlovu, nicknamed Hatari Ngozi for his intolerance of indiscipline, rose from NDP youth activism in Bulawayo to become commander of ZIPRA, ZAPU's armed wing. He trained in the Soviet Union, organised cross-border deployments from Zambia and cooperated with the ANC's Umkhonto we Sizwe. He later served as ZAPU's representative in Tanzania and military adviser to Joshua Nkomo in Lusaka. After independence he was a Member of Parliament, spent years in exile after 1982, and returned after the 1987 Unity Accord before retiring because of ill-health.

timeline.text: Born in Mberengwa District, Midlands Province.
Worked as a clerk at Lobels Bakeries, and also at the Ministry of Public Construction and Rhodesia Railways.
Became a political activist by joining the National Democratic Party as youth chairman of the Iminyela Branch, and took part in sabotage against the Rhodesian regime.
Was detained by the Special Branch for his activism, and continued despite harassment by the white minority regime.
Left the country to join the liberation struggle in Zambia.
Led a group of cadres who went for military training in the former Soviet Union.
Returned to Zambia, joined ZAPU cadres trained in China and North Korea to form ZIPRA, and was appointed its commander.
Ordered two simultaneous deployments of ZIPRA cadres into Rhodesia for combat.
Sent sabotage sections into the country.
Was approached by the ANC's Umkhonto we Sizwe to plan the war together, leading to joint ZIPRA-MK platoon deployments into Rhodesia.
Was posted to Dar-es-Salaam as ZAPU representative dealing with training and OAU liberation committee supplies.
After Joshua Nkomo's release from detention, was recalled to Lusaka as military adviser to the ZAPU president, serving until independence in 1980.
Was elected Member of Parliament for Matabeleland South.
Left for Zambia amid political disturbances and then sought refuge in Norway until the 1987 Unity Accord.
Returned and was elected to the ZANU PF Central Committee, but retired from active politics after a short time because of ill-health.
Died in Bulawayo after a long illness, aged 74.

summary: Standrek Chitekedza was a factory worker from Mount Darwin who crossed into Zambia in 1973 to join the liberation war and rose through ZANLA as a section commander, instructor and provincial field commander in Tete. After independence he moved through the Air Force of Zimbabwe into the national army, holding battalion, brigade and training commands and leading troops in the DRC. He earned several service and campaign medals and was known for loyalty, professionalism and care for his troops. He died in 2001 and was first buried at the Mashonaland Central provincial shrine before being reburied at the National Heroes Acre in 2004.

timeline.text: Born in Mount Darwin, second child in a family of peasant farmers with five boys and one girl.
Began primary school and later moved to St Albert's Mission, where he studied to Standard six.
Worked as a moulder at FIBRO Plastics in Harare, where he became aware of colonial injustice.
Crossed the Zambezi River to join the liberation struggle in Zambia and trained at Chakwenga Camp the same year.
After service as a ZANLA Section Commander in Tete, went for advanced training at Mgagao in Iringa, Tanzania.
Specialised in anti-aircraft weaponry, became an instructor at Mgagao, and later that year joined the ZANLA general staff as Camp Security Officer.
Reassigned as Chief Instructor at Tembwe ZANLA Training Camp in Mozambique.
Commanded attacks on Rhodesian Security Forces at Mudzi and Mutoko and led the re-opening of an operational sector in Tete Province.
Led six combatants in an attack on the Salisbury fuel depot, described as a turning point of the war.
Appointed Provincial Field Operational Commander of Tete Province, taking over from Air Marshal Shiri, after opening a provincial base in the Takawira Sector in 1978.
Reassigned to command ZANLA forces at Dendera Assembly Point.

timeline.date: After the attainment of Independence in 1980
timeline.text: Joined the Air Force of Zimbabwe as a Squadron Leader and attended an Anti-Air Defence Commander's Course in Scotland.
Transferred to the Zimbabwe National Army and promoted to Lieutenant Colonel.
Commanding Officer of 53 Infantry Battalion, then Presidential Guards posts between 1982 and 1984 and acting brigade commander until 1988.
Commandant of the All Arms Battle School in Nyanga, then Central Ammunition Depot Commander at Darwendale (1992 to 1994) and Harare District Commander (1994 to 1998).
Appointed Deputy Commander of 2 Brigade and shortly afterwards its Commander, a post held until his death.
Deployed on the Eastern Front in the DRC under Operation Sovereign Legitimacy, where he planned and executed operations praised by Zimbabwean and SADC allied commanders.
Died after a short illness aged 50; buried at the Mashonaland Central Provincial Heroes Acre.
His remains were exhumed and reburied at the National Heroes Acre.

summary: Joseph Wilfred Msika began as a teacher and then a Bulawayo furniture and textile worker, rising to lead trade unions before becoming a founding figure of the main nationalist parties. He was repeatedly arrested and detained, studying for higher qualifications in custody, and remained loyal to Joshua Nkomo through the ZANU split. After independence he held cabinet posts, helped negotiate the Unity Accord of 1987 and later served as Vice President of Zimbabwe and ZANU-PF second Secretary. He was also a football patron, land-reform and humanitarian supporter, and was declared a national hero on his death in 2009.

timeline.text: Born at Nyariri Village under Chief Negomo, Chiweshe, the first son of his father's second wife in a polygamous household.
Attended the Salvation Army's Howard Institute until Standard 6, then trained as a carpenter-teacher at Mount Selinda and passed the Junior Certificate by correspondence.
Taught woodwork at Usher Institute in Matabeleland while becoming active in nationalist politics.
Joined Bauden and Striver, a Bulawayo furniture company, rising from cabinet maker to supervisor and leading hand.
Left Orkin Lingerie for a better-paying job with a Johannesburg-based clothing firm, and later became a clerk, then Chief Clerk and administrative officer at Consolidated Textile Mills in Bulawayo.
Took up trade unionism through the Textile and Allied Workers' Union, helped form the Federation of Bulawayo African Workers Union and later led the Federation of Southern Rhodesia unions.
Took part in founding the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress, with Joshua Nkomo as president and Msika elected treasurer.
Was detained with other ANC leaders at Khami Maximum Security Prison, where he met nationalists from Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
Was elected a councillor in the newly formed NDP, and in December 1961 became founding Secretary for Youth Affairs when ZAPU replaced the banned NDP.
ZAPU was banned and he and the leadership, except Nkomo who was abroad, were arrested; a regime report blamed them for a wave of sabotage in 1962.
Was in Dar es Salaam when ZANU split from ZAPU and walked out in protest of the move to depose Nkomo, staying loyal to him.
After the PCC was banned he was re-arrested and held in prisons and detention camps including Gonakudzingwa, using the time to complete Ordinary and Advanced Level and study with UNISA.
Flew to Zambia with other ANC leaders to meet Frontline State leaders and take part in the Victoria Falls Bridge Conference, which ended in deadlock.

After the Smith-Nkomo talks failed, went to London to release the contents of the talks; he later joined Patriotic Front delegations to the 1976 Geneva talks and later conferences up to Lancaster House.
Was elected Senator and appointed Minister of Natural Resources and Water Development, a post held until differences arose in the new united government.

timeline.date: after the death of Josiah Chinamano (year garbled)
timeline.text: Was elected Vice President at a congress following the death of Josiah Chinamano.
As a member of the four-man Unity Committee, helped bring about the Unity Accord that created the unified ZANU-PF.
Appointed Senior Minister of Public Construction and National Housing, then Minister of Local Government and Urban Development until 1995, also serving as ZANU-PF National Chairman.
Became Patron of the Zimbabwe Football Association, taking over from the late Vice President Simon Muzenda.
Died at West End Hospital in Harare aged 85 and was declared a national hero by the ZANU-PF Politburo.

education: Mwembe (lower primary) and Mnene (primary)
Dadaya Mission for secondary, then a scholarship to Tegwani Secondary School in Plumtree
African Junior Certificate and Matriculation

summary: Richard Chemist Hove was a Midlands-born clerk who studied commerce in India and then joined ZANU's exile structures in Zambia, later serving as its representative in Western Europe and in its information and external affairs departments. He was detained in Zambia after Chitepo's assassination in 1975 and went on to Mozambique and Patriotic Front conferences. After independence he was Zimbabwe's first Minister of Public Service and held several other ministries before becoming Planning Commissioner. He was also a farmer, chairman of Finhold, and at his death ZANU PF Secretary for Economic Affairs and Senator for Mberengwa.

timeline.text: Born in the Midlands Province.
Educated at Mwembe, Mnene and Dadaya Mission, then won a scholarship to Tegwani Secondary School in Plumtree, where he excelled in matriculation.
Worked as a school clerk after finishing secondary school.
Worked as a clerk for Shell Oil in Bulawayo for four years and joined the Bulawayo Residents Association, which strengthened his nationalism.
Left to study at Sydenham College, University of Bombay in India, where he rallied diplomatic and material support for ZANU and became president of the African Students Association.
Graduated with a Bachelor of Commerce, then went straight to Lusaka to join the liberation struggle, working in the Party's headquarters.
Became a member of ZANU's Revolutionary Council alongside figures such as Herbert Chitepo, Noel Mukono and Percy Ntini.
Was appointed Chief Representative of ZANU in Western Europe, based in London, travelling widely to win support.
Was recalled to Lusaka and given a secretary post in the Dare reChimurenga, representing the Party at many conferences.
Reassigned to head and reorganise the Department of Information and Publicity in Zambia, in charge of broadcasting.
Was detained with other ZANU leaders in Zambia after the assassination of Herbert Chitepo, released before the Geneva Conference, and then went to Mozambique.
Became Deputy Secretary for External Affairs, replacing Webster Gwauya and serving under Mukudzei Mudzi.
Was part of the Patriotic Front delegation to the Commonwealth Conference in Lusaka and later left Maputo for a Patriotic Front conference in Dar-es-Salaam.
Became Zimbabwe's first Minister of Public Service and Member of Parliament for Mberengwa.
Held ministries of Home Affairs (1981 to Feb 1982), Trade and Commerce (1982 to 1985), Mines (1985 to 1990) and Defence (1990 to 1992).
Served as Planning Commissioner in the Office of the President.
Elected to the Central Committee and made Chairman of the Midlands Province.
Appointed to the Finhold Board, becoming its chairman in 2004.
Died at St Annes Hospital in Harare aged 77 after a long battle with diabetes.

summary: Misheck Chando, known in the war as Cde Makasha, was a Murewa farm boy who quit school over forced labour and entered nationalist politics through ZAPU and later ZANU. After arrests and an escape from a planned execution he crossed into Mozambique, trained in Tanzania and rose to command the Gaza front, including a daring train derailment near Rutenga. He was wounded in 1970s fighting and stayed on a standby force after the ceasefire. After independence he worked in the army, a school and veterans' bodies before becoming Senator for Bindura-Shamva, and died in a road accident in 2009.

timeline.text: Born at Jakopo Village in Murewa District, the eldest son of his father's first wife in a family of 21 children.
Attended Jakopo Primary School, later Murewa Primary School and Chiveri Farm School in Bindura, where forced farm labour made him drop out before finishing Standard Six.
Joined ZAPU and was an activist until 1969, leading youth road-blocking and other sabotage in Salisbury townships.
Evaded a police manhunt by going underground in Murewa and led an action codenamed Zhanda, destroying water tanks and tobacco barns of white farmers in the Shamva area.
Was arrested with six colleagues, held and tortured at several police stations, then released.
Joined ZANU and worked in the Hoya area of Muzarabani, passing intelligence about police patrols to freedom fighters.
Was arrested again after a betrayal, learned of a plan to execute him by firing squad, and escaped with the help of a sympathetic policeman.
Crossed into Mozambique, was received by FRELIMO and taken to Chifombo camp, then led ammunition-carrying groups and recruits including Teurai Ropa, whom he helped through malaria.
Was sent to Mgagao in Tanzania for training and afterwards became Deputy Commander of a special unit that recaptured bases lost in the 1974 rebellion.
Commanded a section in which Teurai Ropa served in a political role.
Was appointed Provincial Field Operational Commander and opened Gaza Province for the war, defending against Rhodesian and South African forces.
Commanded the group that blew up the railway and derailed a Rhodesian goods train near Rutenga.

Was shot in both legs at Vorga Railway Siding near Malvernia, spent eight months in Maputo Military Hospital, and later became Deputy Camp Commander at Chimoio and commander of Maroro, Fingwe and Doroi camps.

timeline.date: In 1979 at the beginning of the ceasefire
timeline.text: Remained in Mozambique with 250 guerrillas as a standby force until returning to Zimbabwe in April 1981.
Served in the Zimbabwe National Army and was elected Deputy Secretary of ZANU PF in Mashonaland Central.
Worked as boarding master at Chindunduma Secondary School and later for the Zimbabwe-Mozambique Friendship Association.
Elected Senator for Bindura-Shamva, after earlier roles on the National Consultative Assembly (1999) and with the ZNLWVA (2005), and a land reform farm in 2001.
Died in a vehicle accident on the Harare-Shamva-Bindura road, aged 68.

summary: Sunny Ntombiyelanga Takawira, called Amai Takawira, was a Filabusi-born nurse who married ZANU founding Vice President Leopold Takawira in 1955. She hosted early nationalist meetings, raised the family alone after his arrest in 1964 and smuggled messages to the detainees, and she suffered beatings and attacks herself. After independence she served as Senator for Midlands, helped found a training centre for former fighters at Melfort and continued to shelter veterans. She died in January 2010 and was declared a national heroine, the fifth heroine buried at the national shrine.

timeline.text: Born (nee Dube) in Dube village, Filabusi, the second child and oldest girl of seven.
Her family was moved by the Rhodesian government to Nkayi, where she grew up in a drought-prone area with poor soil.
Trained as a nurse at Mnene Mission Hospital and first worked at Gokwe Hospital.
Married Leopold Takawira at Gokwe, becoming stepmother to his three children, and joined Harare Central Hospital as a pioneer nurse in casualty and outpatients.
Had three children of her own (Samuel, Leo Tafirenyika and Gertrude); a stepson, Patrick, died in 1959.
Hosted early nationalists' secret meetings at her home on Jabavu Drive in Highfield.
After ZANU was banned and her husband imprisoned, raised the family alone and smuggled letters and information into and out of Hwahwa, Gonakudzingwa, Sikombela and Salisbury Central Prison.
Her husband died in custody after torture and neglect; she learned of it from his colleagues.
Treated nationalists and wounded fighters as a nurse in Highfield, joined wives' demonstrations and was detained, beaten and tortured after being betrayed.
Her home was attacked, injuring her children Gertrude and Leopold Jnr; her sons Sam and Tafi joined the liberation struggle.
Welcomed fighters returning from Mozambique at the Salvation Army Church in Mbare, retired from nursing after being appointed Senator for Midlands, and set up a training centre at Melfort Farm.
Walked from Melfort to the Harare Post Office to raise funds for wounded war veterans.
Was diagnosed with an ovarian cyst found to be benign, but the operation led to complications.
Died at her Mt Pleasant home after leaving the Avenues Clinic, aged 82; the ZANU PF Politburo declared her a national heroine.

summary: Sabina Gabriel Mugabe, known as Tete, was a sister of Robert Mugabe who worked as a teacher, nutrition and community-development educator, and long-serving ZANU PF legislator. She grew up at Kutama, trained as a teacher, and moved from NDP and ZAPU activism into the founding circle of ZANU, later studying abroad in nutrition, economics and fashion. She served about two decades at Silveira House, carried much of the Mugabe family's upkeep while her brother was in prison or exile, and from 1985 sat in Parliament championing orphans, rural people and women. She died at 80 after years of ill health following strokes.

timeline.text: Born at Kutama Village in the Zvimba area into a large family; her brother Robert Mugabe later became national leader.
Finished her primary schooling at Kutama Mission as a day pupil.
Began teacher training at Empandeni Teachers' Training College in Bulawayo.
Taught at Benhura and Ngezi schools in Mhondoro before moving to Mhandu school in her home area.
Helped found Highfield Community School and took part in other community projects.
Entered politics through the NDP as its local secretary, mobilising young people, some of whom sabotaged colonial equipment while others left to train as freedom fighters.
Became instrumental in forming ZANU and was among its earliest women members.
Started a dress-making project in Chegutu to give women practical skills.
Left the country for the United Kingdom under an assumed name as political tension rose, and studied abroad.
Continued overseas studies, including fashion and design at a Paris academy, collecting several certificates before returning home.
Taught and lectured at Silveira House in Chishawasha for about 20 years, 12 of them as head of its Applied Nutrition and Development Department.
Campaigned actively for ZANU PF in Mashonaland West after the Lancaster House settlement.
Was widowed when her husband, Johannes Zhuwawo, died.

Elected provincial Secretary for Women's Affairs, and when the ZANU PF Women's League was launched became its Secretary for National Production; she also drove the Matunu Training Centre co-operative in Manicaland.
Elected MP for Makonde East in 1985, then for Zvimba from 1990, and returned again in 1995 and 2000, pressing for orphan centres, rural development and women's emancipation.
Attended the Beijing World Women's Conference in China and was noted as a woman from Southern Africa who sat in Parliament at the same time as her sons (wording garbled).
Suffered successive strokes, in 1985 and 2005, that damaged her brain and left her ailing.
Ill health stopped her from offering herself for re-election.
Died at the Avenues Clinic in Harare aged 80, leaving four children.

summary: Ephraim Sango Masawi grew up in rural Mashonaland Central and became a youth leader in the nationalist movement. As a young activist he led underground sabotage, rallied youths against the Pearce settlement proposals, and helped channel recruits into the armed struggle. After independence he held youth, council and parliamentary posts in Mbare, helped launch the 21st February Movement, and later served as Governor and Resident Minister for Mashonaland Central and as the party's Deputy National Political Commissar. He died of leukemia at 61.

timeline.text: Born in the Musana area of Mashonaland Central, the last of ten children (five boys and five girls).
Attended Mutanhaurwa and Mupandira primary schools near home, then St Peter's Kubatana in Highfield and later community schools nicknamed 'Manzou' for his secondary education.
Joined classmates in resisting the ill-treatment of black people under the settler regime and was elected chairman of the ZAPU youth wing, then called ZHANDA.
Took part in underground work, mobilising youths to carry out economic sabotage such as burning white-owned property in Salisbury and tobacco crops on white farms around the city.
Used his political awareness to rally support, especially among youths, for a NO vote to the Pearce proposals.
Was part of a network of activists recruiting youths for the armed struggle in Mozambique, and was told by the party to stay in Harare, with Ken Madora, to coordinate recruitment.
As a leader of the youth wing of the People's Movement, the internal wing of ZANU (PF), survived two bomb attacks while working against rival groups and Rhodesian agents.
Elected unopposed youth chairman of ZANU (PF) Mbare District after independence.
With other senior figures helped found the 21st February Movement; in the same year he was also elected a ward councillor for Mbare (details garbled).
Entered Parliament after the death of veteran nationalist Cde Nyagumbo and was returned again in the 1995 general elections.
Served the party as Deputy Secretary for Information and Publicity and as a Politburo member.
Served as Resident Minister and Governor of Mashonaland Central.
Died of leukemia aged 61 while serving as Deputy National Political Commissar.

summary: Welshman Mabhena was a teacher from Nkayi who became one of the early nationalists, joining the NDP and then ZAPU, where he managed the movement of arms and supplies to ZIPRA forces. His activism cost him 17 years in prison between 1962 and 1979, during which he completed advanced schooling and later a commerce degree. After independence he served as a PF-ZAPU MP and Deputy Speaker, helped negotiate the 1987 Unity Accord as ZAPU Secretary General, and then became ZANU PF provincial chairman, Minister of State and Governor of Matabeleland North. The book adds that he turned to the opposition late in life, and that he died aged 86.

timeline.text: Born at Zinyangeni in Nkayi.
Attended Zinyangeni Primary and Inyathi Mission, went to Tiger Kloof in South Africa for secondary school, then returned to teach at Inyathi Mission School before entering politics.
Joined the NDP, one of the pioneers of political activism against white rule in the early 1960s.
Arrested with Cdes William Mbambo and Mswelamboya Sibanda for possessing weapons meant for a ZIPRA operative; he and his colleagues refused to name the recipient despite harsh torture.
Tried and sentenced to five years in prison, which he served in Salisbury.

timeline.date: on ZAPU's formation (as read from OCR)
timeline.text: After the NDP was banned, joined ZAPU and took charge of coordinating logistics for moving arms and materials to ZIPRA forces on the front line, working under the watch of Rhodesian intelligence.
Spent a total of 17 years in prison because of his political activities.
Used prison time to study, reaching Advanced Level, the Fellowship of the Association of Certified Bookkeepers of South Africa, and later a UNISA commerce degree.
Elected Member of Parliament for Nkayi on a PF-ZAPU ticket.
Elected Deputy Speaker of Parliament and, as ZAPU Secretary General, contributed greatly to the talks leading to the ZANU-ZAPU Unity Accord.
Appointed ZANU PF Matabeleland North Provincial Chairman.
Appointed Minister of State for Political Affairs and later Governor of Matabeleland North, serving until his retirement in July 2000.
The book notes that late in life he turned against ZANU PF to embrace opposition politics (text cut off).
Died at the age of 86.

summary: Nevison Nyashanu, known by the war name Ndazo Nganga and the nickname Sharp Shooter, was a ZAPU nationalist from a village under Chief Nyashanu who studied by correspondence and later earned university qualifications. After military training in the Soviet Union in 1964 he organised ZIPRA activity and recruitment inside Rhodesia, which brought restriction, detention and severe torture. Flown to Britain for treatment in 1974, he later became Deputy Secretary General of PF-ZAPU, helped bring about the Unity Accord, and served as Buhera North MP and in international parliamentary forums. He died at his estate in December 2010, survived by his wife Shamiso and many children and grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born at Mukanganga village under Chief Nyashanu, the first of seven children (three girls and four boys).
Completed primary school in the Paramombe circuit and then went to Dadaya Mission for later standards.
Became an active member of the African National Congress and in 1960 sat on the NDP committee for Buhera and Charter districts.
Studied for the General Certificate of Education through correspondence, later adding diplomas and degrees.
Posted as ZAPU students' representative in Zambia, based in Lusaka and for a time Chingola.
Received military training at a camp in Kiev, Ukraine, in the Soviet Union.

Assigned by the ZAPU leadership to logistics and reconnaissance work and ZIPRA operations across Zimbabwe, recruiting cadres for training in Mozambique and Zambia; the Smith regime confined him to within about 12 miles of Harare.
Arrested and restricted at Gonakudzingwa after the colonial state of emergency in Highfield.
A further state of emergency led to his detention in several Rhodesian prisons.

Mobilised women to demonstrate at what is now Africa Unity Square and was jailed for four months; held and tortured at Goromonzi Police Lockup, called the Torture Centre, including in a specially built cell and with electric shocks.
Transferred to Gweru Prison, joining other detained ZAPU cadres; later moved again (1973) and released because of failing health after being told he needed treatment within four months.
Flown to the United Kingdom for medical treatment, where he acted as a vibrant ZAPU representative while its leader was in detention.
As Deputy Secretary General of PF-ZAPU under Welshman Mabhena after Cde Msipa's resignation, helped formulate and implement the Unity Accord with ZANU PF.
Elected to the Central Committee and appointed Deputy Secretary for Political Education (reading garbled).
Became MP for Buhera North and drove projects such as schools, bridges, dams and Murambinda Growth Point.
Led or took part in delegations to Inter-Parliamentary Union conferences, presenting papers on Zimbabwe and joining the Parity Working Group on women's participation in politics.
Died from complications of hypertension.

summary: Corneous Nhloko, who also went by a name beginning Victor, was a youth cadre who took up the liberation struggle in the 1960s and returned home in December 1979. After independence he joined the President's Department as an intelligence officer and rose steadily, heading counter-intelligence work in Harare, serving in the external branch and as liaison officer in Lagos, training new officers, and finally helping run operations in the Midlands. The book portrays him as a strategist and dedicated patriot. He died at 63, was buried in Silobela and was declared a National Hero, leaving his wife Irene and three children.

summary: David Karimanzira was a highly educated ZANU (PF) politician and administrator born in Murehwa District. A student activist who clashed with colonial authorities at Dadaya and at the University of Rhodesia, he received a suspended sentence in 1973 and then left for the UK, where he studied at Oxford and Birmingham and worked for the party in exile. After independence he served in the Transport ministry and in business management, then as MP for Murehwa and minister of youth, lands, higher education and information. From 1996 until his death in March 2011 he was Resident Minister and Governor, first for Mashonaland East and then for Harare, and held the post of party Secretary for Finance.

timeline.text: Born at Chitowa in Murehwa District, the sixth of eight children.
Suspended for three months at Dadaya after a demonstration with other black students against discrimination at the school.
Took part in political activities in Highfield, a stronghold of black nationalist politics.
Enrolled for a bachelor's degree at the University of Rhodesia, completing it in 1973.

Arrested with national hero Witness Mangwende for organising a student demonstration, held in Harare Prison, refused to plead guilty, and received a six-month sentence with hard labour that was suspended on condition he stay within 20 kilometres of Salisbury.
Persecution led him to leave and join the liberation struggle's diplomatic front abroad; before going he had worked as a teacher at Highfield Community School.
Studied for a teaching certificate and a master's in educational administration at Oxford University.
Held various ZANU (PF) posts in the United Kingdom, beginning with the Birmingham branch; he met and married Rungano Ushewokunze in London.
Gained a master's in educational psychology at Birmingham and the following year enrolled for a doctorate there; also earned a transport administration diploma from Dalhousie University.
After independence joined the Ministry of Transport as Under Secretary, becoming Deputy Secretary in 1982.
After party work in Harare Central District and as Matabeleland coordinator, became ZANU PF Secretary for Finance for Mashonaland East province, which then included Harare (reading partly garbled).
Joined a Harare organisation as Deputy General Manager and became General Manager a year later (name garbled).
Elected MP for Murehwa and appointed Minister of Youth, Sport and Culture, serving to 1987.
Served as Minister of Lands, Agriculture and Rural Settlement.
Served as Minister of Higher Education and Technology.
Moved to the Information, Posts and Telecommunications portfolio.
Appointed Resident Minister and Governor of Mashonaland East.
Reassigned as Resident Minister and Governor of Harare Metropolitan Province, a post held until his death.
Died at West End Clinic aged 64, survived by his wife Rungano, two sons and a daughter.

summary: Livingstone Muzariri, known in the war as Menard Negidi, left school in Wedza to join the liberation struggle, entering Zambia in 1973 and training at Mgagao in Tanzania. He became an instructor, served the party as political commissar in Botswana and in administration in Maputo, and rose into the ZANLA General Staff. After independence he joined the President's Department and climbed from trainee officer to Director Counter Intelligence, Internal Branch Director and, in 2003, Deputy Director General of the Central Intelligence Organization. A successful farmer whose land was shown to visitors as a Land Reform success, he died of liver cancer, was accorded national hero status, and left his wife Esther and five children.

timeline.text: Born at Chironda village in Wedza, the youngest son in a family of nine.
Attended Chironga and Nyamhara primary schools and Mavuradonha for secondary school, but gave up his education to join the liberation struggle.
Entered Zambia through the Ruya area and was based at Teresera Base Camp in the Chifombo area under Chief Chatikobo.
Went on to Tanzania, receiving six months of initial military training at Mgagao, and then did an Instructor's Course at the same base.
Served as an instructor at the camp.
Posted to Botswana as a Political Commissar in the party office under Cde G. Hlatshwayo (Mao Tongai), staying about a year.
Recalled to Maputo, Mozambique, to work in the party's Administration Department, his last posting before independence, and rose to the ZANLA General Staff.
Back from Mozambique, served as Liaison Officer at the Bindura Assembly Point in Mashonaland Central.

After being sent by the party on a basic intelligence course, was brought into the President's Department as a Trainee Intelligence Officer, later rising to Intelligence Officer and head of the 'B' desk.
Promoted to Senior Intelligence Officer and deployed to Bulawayo to oversee organisation operations in Matabeleland.
Promoted to Divisional Intelligence Officer and moved to Mashonaland Central as Deputy Regional Head for Harare and Mashonaland provinces.
Elevated to Provincial Intelligence Officer and deployed to Masvingo.
Promoted to Director Counter Intelligence.
Transferred to the Internal Branch as Branch Director.
Appointed Deputy Director General of the Central Intelligence Organization, a rank he held until death.
Died of liver cancer at St Anne's Hospital in Harare aged 56.

summary: Edgar 'Two Boy' Zivanai Tekere, a founding member of ZANU, was born in 1937 and nicknamed for his football skills. After leaving teacher training he worked in Harare, studied commerce and marketing by distance, and entered nationalist politics through the Youth League, NDP and ZAPU. Detained and restricted after ZANU's ban in 1964, he later crossed into Mozambique, became ZANU Secretary General in 1977, and served briefly as a minister after independence until he was dropped in 1981 following an acquitted murder trial and criticism of government policy. Expelled in 1989, he led the Zimbabwe Unity Movement in a presidential race and died of prostate cancer in June 2011 aged 74, being buried at Heroes Acre; his wife Pamela and daughter Maidei survive him.

timeline.text: Born in Nyang'ombe village.
Gained the nickname '2-Boy' for his football skills, said to be like playing two people in one.
Began teacher training at St Augustine Mission and became increasingly involved in politics, travelling from Penhalonga to Salisbury as a Youth League member.
Lost interest in teacher training and moved to Harare, where he worked at the SPCK bookshop and rose to costing clerk.
The ANC was banned by the colonial government, pushing nationalists to regroup.
Helped found the NDP; after its ban in 1961 he was part of the formation of ZAPU and held a Salisbury district post.
Heavily involved in preparing the First ZANU Congress, where he was elected to a party post (title garbled); after ZANU was banned he was among the leaders arrested.
Held at Sikombela and then Gokwe with other restricted ZANU leaders, from where the Sikombela Declaration authorised exiled members to wage the armed struggle.
Detained at prisons including Connemara and Kwekwe, remaining focused on the armed struggle.
Released with other ZANU leaders after the Lusaka Unity Accord.
Crossed into Mozambique with Robert Mugabe to spearhead the struggle there.
Took part in the ZANU delegation to the Geneva Conference.
Elected Secretary General when the party was reorganised at Chimoio after the Geneva talks collapsed, and ran the party's daily affairs from Maputo.
Part of the ZANU (PF) delegation to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Lusaka and addressed the UN General Assembly in New York.
Attended the Lancaster House Conference as part of the ZANU (PF) delegation.
Credited with inviting Bob Marley to perform at Rufaro Stadium at independence; appointed Minister of Manpower Planning and Development.
Put on trial for allegedly killing a white farm manager, Gerald Adams, and acquitted on the ground he acted in the interest of state security.
Removed as minister after speaking against government policy; he stayed on as party Secretary General for a time and later was Manicaland provincial chairman until 1987.
Expelled from the party and formed the Zimbabwe Unity Movement to contest the presidential election (year reads 1999 in OCR) which he lost.
Died of prostate cancer at Murambi Gardens Private Hospital in Mutare aged 74 and was buried at the national Heroes Acre.

summary: Andrew Muntanga was a Tonga man from Binga who began on the path to the priesthood in Zambia before politics and the ZAPU cause drew him into the liberation struggle. He organised people in Binga, survived imprisonment, escaped abroad, and served ZIPRA as deputy commandant of the Guerilla Works Camp in Lusaka and as a delegate to the settlement talks. After Independence he represented Binga in Parliament twice, pushed local development, and helped bring ZAPU people into ZANU PF after the Unity Accord. He retired because of poor health and died in July 2011.

timeline.text: Born in Binga.
Began his schooling (Sub A and Sub B) at a Catholic school.
Entered a seminary at St Mary's to continue his primary schooling while preparing for the priesthood.
Moved to Northern Rhodesia, finished primary school and did secondary education at Chikuni while training for the priesthood.

timeline.date: during his priesthood training in Zambia
timeline.text: Was first drawn into politics through UNIP under Kenneth Kaunda, and heard of ZAPU's work back home.
Returned to Rhodesia, met ZAPU leaders in Bulawayo and went to consult the detained Joshua Nkomo at Gonakudzingwa, then began mobilising people across Binga on foot and opening party branches.
After release from Hwahwa, resolved to go to Zambia through Botswana to join the armed struggle.
Was arrested for recruiting cadres, jailed at Khami with other ZAPU activists, escaped and flew to London where he worked with veteran nationalists for ZIPRA camps in Zambia.
Redeployed to the Guerilla Works Camp in Lusaka as Deputy Commandant under Stephen Nkomo, handling ZIPRA manpower development and logistics.
Rose to the ZIPRA Revolutionary Council and was chosen as a delegate to the failed Geneva conference and later the Lancaster House Conference.

After Lancaster House, joined the ZIPRA logistics advance party into Zimbabwe, helped identify assembly points in Matabeleland North and was elected to the PF ZAPU Central Committee as Deputy National Organising Secretary.
Served as the first post-Independence MP for Binga and drove construction of schools, clinics and the Binga District Hospital.
Played a part in the negotiations leading to the Unity Accord, then mobilised people into ZANU PF structures in Matabeleland North.
Recalled by the Binga community to stand again, won, and served as MP until 2000; also served as provincial commissariat secretary until 2000 before retiring through ill health.
Died; the party later unanimously agreed to confer hero status on him.
