summary: Solomon Mujuru, known in the war as Rex Nhongo, grew up in Chikomba and left school and work to join the liberation struggle in the 1960s. Trained in several countries, he moved from ZIPRA to ZANLA, opened the north-east front and led the 1972 Altena Farm attack. He became a top ZANLA and ZIPA commander and a key figure in the Mgagau period and in shifting the war to semi-conventional operations. After Independence he was the first commander of the Zimbabwe National Army, retired as full General in 1992, then served as an MP and farmer until he died in a fire in August 2011.

timeline.text: Born at Mabukwa Village in Chikomba, the seventh of nine children.
Attended Kwenda Mission and Rufaro primary schools before proceeding to Zimuto Secondary School near Masvingo.
Organised a student demonstration at Zimuto Secondary School, which appears to have ended his time there.
Left his salesman job at Dunlop to join the liberation struggle.
Imprisoned and detained at Khami Prison for inciting and taking part in political activity in Bulawayo.

Left the country, was sent with others to Moscow for a six-month communications and intelligence course, fell ill, returned to Dar es Salaam, then trained at Morogoro, in Bulgaria (artillery) and Egypt.

Quit the ZAPU military wing with several colleagues after internal disputes and, despite Tanzanian rules against defection, persisted until ZANLA accepted him; he was then trained under the Chinese and waited at Kongwa transit camp.
Appointed to lead a group of 45 fighters from Tete in Mozambique into Rhodesia to open the north-east front, becoming the first sector commander and taking the war name Rex Nhongo.
Commanded about 21 guerrillas in the attack on Altena Farm, regarded as the start of resumed guerrilla warfare that spread across the country.

After the death of Herbert Chitepo and the arrest of ZANU leaders in Zambia, escaped to Mgagau in Tanzania and effectively led the external wing, convincing Nyerere to let the war continue and securing a farm for food production.
Voted commander of ZIPA, the joint ZANLA-ZIPRA force, and served as ZANLA Chief of Operations under Josiah Tongogara; admitted to the ZANU Central Committee.

Kept directing the war as Chief of Operations after the 1977 restructuring; the Grand Reef attack (December 1977) and the Rutenga railway attack (1978) showed ZANLA's semi-conventional reach, and combined ZANLA and ZIPRA operations were sanctioned.
Under his leadership came the Salisbury Oil Depot attack and letter and parcel bombs in towns; the battles of Mapai (5 to 10 September) and Mavhonde pushed the Rhodesians to Lancaster House.

Led the advance platoon into Zimbabwe to prepare for the arrival of the PF ZAPU and ZANU PF leaders and run assembly points; at Independence he was attested into the ZNA and commissioned Lieutenant General.
Appointed Commander of the Zimbabwe National Army and oversaw the integration of ZANLA, ZIPRA and Rhodesian forces.
Appointed a member of the ZANU PF Politburo.
Promoted to full General on retirement.
Sworn in as Member of Parliament for Chikomba, helped spearhead the Land Reform Programme and later gave up the seat in 2009.
Died in a fire at his farm.

summary: Chilisi Bhuka Ngwenya was born in the Plumtree area, worked as an assistant manager at Meikles and then joined ZIPRA. After training in Tanzania and the Soviet Union he served as an intelligence officer and later as ZAPU's representative in Botswana, where he coordinated logistics and care for wounded guerrillas. He was ambushed and captured in 1979, tortured and held for a year, and the damage to his health later contributed to his death. After Independence he served in the Zimbabwe National Army, mostly in public relations and intelligence, retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel; he died in December 2011 and was declared a national hero later.

timeline.text: Born at Hikwa Village in the Plumtree area.
Worked as an Assistant Manager at Meikles Number Two.
Joined ZIPRA, the military wing of ZAPU, at Luthuli Camp.
Sent with others to Morogoro, Tanzania for basic military training, completed in 1972.
Returned to Zambia and was deployed along the Zambia-Rhodesia border as an intelligence officer.
Went to the Soviet Union for intelligence training with other future senior figures, then returned to Zambia and was deployed to Botswana.

Monitored recruit movements, gathered information on Rhodesian forces, liaised with Botswana authorities and arranged medical care for wounded ZIPRA and Umkhonto we Sizwe fighters; later took over as ZAPU representative there.
Was ambushed and captured by Rhodesian forces about 30 km before Kazungula while delivering a new truck to ZAPU headquarters in Lusaka; held in Bulawayo, tortured and interrogated for a year.
Survived and was released from jail when Zimbabwe became independent.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a private and then commissioned as an officer; posted to Army Headquarters Public Relations Directorate as officer commanding shows until January 1983.
Promoted Temporary Major and appointed Public Relations Officer.
Promoted Deputy Director of the Public Relations Directorate.
Promoted Substantive Major.
Posted as Second-in-Command of the Zimbabwe Intelligence Corps in Harare, a post held until 1 July 1991.
Moved to the Military Intelligence Directorate as an analyst and retired on 30 June, being promoted Lieutenant Colonel on retirement.
Died in a Bulawayo hospital; buried at Plumtree.
Posthumously declared a national hero.

summary: Edson Ncube was a Tsholotsho-born teacher and carpenter-trained businessman who entered nationalist politics in 1959 and moved through the NDP, ZAPU, PCC and ANC-Z. He was jailed, restricted and detained repeatedly by the Rhodesians, including for opposing UDI and the republican referendum and for helping recruit fighters. After Independence he held provincial ZAPU posts, then helped fold ZAPU into ZANU PF after the Unity Accord, serving in the Central Committee and Politburo and as MP for Mpopoma. He also led residents' and church projects in Bulawayo, farmed commercially, and died in 2012 survived by five children and three grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born as the only child of his family in Tsholotsho District.
Studied carpentry at Inyathi and Hope Fountain missions and earned a Certificate of Carpentry.
Joined the African National Congress; the same year, while teaching at Daramombe, white Rhodesian policemen questioned him about the banned ANC, which launched his political career.
Taught in Bulawayo at Mpumelelo Primary School; after the NDP was banned in 1960 he was active in political activism at Stanley Hall.
Chaired the Gwaai Development Association, a ZAPU wing, working closely with John Landa Nkomo.
First arrested while a teacher at Maphisa for resisting UDI and sentenced to 18 months.
Held at Khami Prison for rejecting the republican referendum.
Mobilised people to vote against the Pearce Commission proposals and was elected publicity secretary of a nationalist body (name cut off).
Joined Boka Group's Bulawayo operations as a sales representative and rose to branch manager and group marketing head for Matabeleland, the Midlands and Masvingo.
Restricted to a 15-mile radius of the Bulawayo Post Office and detained for recruiting freedom fighters; later held at Marandellas (Marondera) Prison until the ceasefire period.
Elected ZAPU Provincial Secretary and later Provincial Chairman.
After the Unity Accord, appointed Co-Chairman of a provincial body in Matabeleland North, a post held until 1989.
Served as Member of Parliament for Mpopoma and took part in parliamentary committees.
Died after anaemia; recognised as a national hero for his pre-Independence record.

summary: Kantibhai Patel was born into a peasant family in Gujarat and left university to work in Zambia, where he organised shop workers and became involved with the ANC and UNIP. After moving to Rhodesia in 1961 he joined NDP and ZAPU, turned Indian community bodies toward supporting African nationalism and suffered police raids on his home and shop. After Independence he rose through ZANU-PF as Senator, MP, Central Committee and Politburo member, and ran philanthropic and friendship projects. He died in 2011 and was cremated in Harare.

timeline.text: Born into a peasant family in Dharmaj, Gujarat, India.
Cut short his university studies and went to Zambia, where he worked as an assistant for a year.
Formed a Shop Assistants' Union against colonial injustices, lost his job and was unemployed for two years before teaching at Greenacre School in Kalomo.
Built links with the ANC and later UNIP and became a member of the Kalomo Provincial Race Relations Committee.

Moved to Rhodesia, joined the NDP and ZAPU with other progressive Indian Zimbabweans and was elected to the Asian Association executive, where he radicalised members towards supporting African nationalism.
Was appointed ZAPU District Treasurer for Norton.
Helped organise Gandhi Centenary celebrations in Rhodesia.
His house and shop were twice ransacked by colonial police after NDP and ZAPU were banned.
With other Indian community members, started the Sarasvati Education Trust to fund scholarships for black students expelled from the University of Rhodesia.
Lost his wife.
Served on the ZANU-PF Harare Central Branch executive as treasurer and later as Provincial Finance Secretary.
Appointed Senator by Prime Minister Mugabe.
Appointed a non-constituency Member of Parliament.
Elevated into the ZANU-PF Central Committee at the party congress.
Elected Member of Parliament and served on parliamentary committees including public accounts.
Re-elected to the Central Committee and then elevated to the Politburo; also served on the Child Survival and Development Foundation board and led the Zimbabwe-India Friendship Association.
Died in Johannesburg after a fall and was cremated in Harare.

summary: Stanislaus Mudenge was a gifted pupil from Zimuto who studied history, was expelled from university for protesting UDI, detained at Gonakudzingwa, and then earned degrees in England. He worked as an academic in Sierra Leone and Lesotho and as ZANU's external secretary before returning in 1980 to build the Foreign Ministry as Permanent Secretary. He later served as UN representative, Masvingo North MP and a Cabinet minister in higher education and foreign affairs, defending the Land Reform Programme and expanding universities. He also wrote award-winning historical works on the Mutapa state and died in October 2012.

timeline.text: Born in Zimuto, Masvingo, in a family of six.
Attended Gaths Mine Primary School in Mashava, then Gokomere Mission upper primary from 1954.
After excelling at Goromonzi, enrolled for an Honours degree in History at the University of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
Led student protest against UDI, was expelled and detained at Gonakudzingwa.
After release, moved to England and graduated in history from the University of York.
Elected Secretary for Information of the ZANU Students' Union in the United Kingdom, then pursued a doctorate at the University of London.
Began his academic career at Fourah Bay College in Sierra Leone, later becoming Senior Lecturer, Dean and Director of Strategic Planning at the National University of Lesotho.
Became ZANU Secretary for External Affairs in Lesotho.
Returned and joined Government as Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, building it up from scratch.
Served as Zimbabwe's Permanent Representative to the United Nations.

Served as ZANU PF education secretary in Masvingo North and was elected MP for the area; rose in party and civil service, later Deputy Secretary for Commissariat and Culture in Masvingo Province and then Central Committee member.
Appointed Minister of Higher Education and helped set up NUST, the Chetsanga Commission, the Zimbabwe Open University concept and work towards BUSE; then moved to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Defended the Land Reform Programme internationally as it reached its peak.
In his second tenure as higher education minister, backed the Harare Institute of Technology Act (2006), the establishment of Lupane State University and ZIMCHE (2007).
Re-elected MP for Masvingo North and appointed Minister of Higher and Tertiary Education; also Secretary for External Affairs in the Politburo.
Collapsed and died in his Masvingo hotel room aged 70.

summary: Landa John Nkomo grew up in the Tsholotsho area of Matabeleland and became a teacher before entering nationalist politics in the late 1950s. He was repeatedly detained, joined ZAPU's external leadership in Lusaka, and survived a parcel bomb in 1977. After independence he held many ministerial posts, helped negotiate the 1987 Unity Accord, chaired ZANU-PF, served as Speaker, and rose to Vice President. He also funded a rural secondary school in Tsholotsho and died in January 2013.

timeline.text: Born in the Gwaii Reserve area, now Tsholotsho, Matabeleland North, as the third child and eldest son of his family.
After Standard 6 at Solusi Mission he moved elsewhere to study privately for the Junior Certificate, which he obtained in 1956.
Qualified as a teacher and began his political career as a founding member of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress.
After the Congress was banned he stayed active in the youth wings of its successor parties, the NDP, ZAPU and the People's Caretaker Council.
Became a founder member and first secretary of the radical Mpopoma Residents Association in Bulawayo.

Clashed with the Native Commissioner for Tsholotsho and was briefly jailed, then arrested again for political activity, moved between prisons and was restricted at Gonakudzingwa for two and a half years; he studied for O and A levels while detained.
Joined the newly formed African National Council, serving as Secretary for Education and later Deputy Secretary-General (1973).
Served as ZAPU Secretary for Administration at its Lusaka headquarters, a post he kept until 1985.
Took part in forming the Patriotic Front, joined ZAPU's Central Committee and the Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Council, and attended the Geneva Conference with the ZAPU delegation.
Attended the Malta Conference and survived a parcel bomb that killed ZAPU Second Vice President Jason Ziyaphapha Moyo, suffering lasting injuries.
Elected to Zimbabwe's first Parliament and served as Deputy Minister of Industry and Energy, then Minister of State in the Prime Minister's Office from 1982 to 1984.
Played a key role in the PF ZAPU delegation, led by Joseph Msika, in the unity talks that produced the Unity Accord and the merged ZANU-PF.

Was Minister of Labour, Manpower Planning and Social Welfare and introduced the National Social Security Scheme; he also sat in the ZANU-PF Central Committee and Politburo from 1988 to 1999 and spoke at the founding of the Zimbabwe War Veterans Association and ZIPEDRA.
Elected President of the 80th International Labour Conference in 1993 and Chairman of the ILO Governing Body in 1994, steering several ILO committees.
Served as Minister of Local Government, Rural and Urban Development (later restructured to include National Housing), pushing local government reform and the Traditional Leaders Act.
Elected ZANU-PF National Chairman for five years and re-elected in December 2004 for another five.
Was Minister of Home Affairs, then Minister of Special Affairs in the President's Office responsible for Lands, Land Reform and Resettlement (2003 to April 2005).

Elected Speaker of Parliament until 2008, became a non-constituency Senator in August 2008, and in February 2009 was made Minister of State responsible for the national healing organ; he later became Vice President of Zimbabwe.
Awarded an honorary doctorate in Business Administration and Development by Solusi University.
Died at a Harare hospital after a long battle with cancer.

summary: John George Mayowe, known in the struggle as Robert Mandebvu, was drawn into politics as a student at the University of Rhodesia and left in 1975 after Herbert Chitepo's assassination. In Mozambique he trained at Tembwe, taught political education and directed Chitepo College, earning Tongogara's confidence. He then served ZANU abroad in Libya and Scandinavia, and after independence worked in media administration and diplomacy, ending as ambassador to the DRC. He died in Johannesburg in 2013.

timeline.text: Born to George Mayowe and his wife; he did primary schooling at St Anthony Primary School.
As a history student at the University of Rhodesia he joined furious protests after the car-bomb assassination of ZANU chairman Herbert Chitepo in Lusaka.
Abandoned university and crossed into Mozambique with the first big group of university students to join the armed struggle.
Reached the Junta military camp near Vila Pery (now Chimoio), where recruits met Robert Mugabe, and helped organise the swelling ranks of recruits.
Moved with others to a new camp on the Nyadzonia river and gave political education to fighters there.
Received military training at Tembwe camp in Tete Province, Mozambique.
Redeployed to a camp in the Chimoio area, met his future wife Tendai Mheta there, led the political research department and then became Director of Chitepo College of Party Ideological Instruction.

Won the notice of ZANLA commander Josiah Tongogara, who recommended him for the ZANLA General Staff; with John Chimbande he helped produce liberation-war ideological material including the Mwenje II booklet.
Left the Directorship to serve as ZANU Chief Representative in Libya, following up on military training.
Appointed ZANU Chief Representative to Sweden, Denmark, Norway and Finland.
After Independence he worked in media administration, apparently as Secretary-General of the Zimbabwe Mass Media Trust and later at Zimbabwe Newspapers (page badly garbled).
Appointed Ambassador to Romania and Bulgaria, where he negotiated for experts to fill vacant skilled posts back home.

Later recalled and redeployed to Foreign Affairs head office in a policy and research directorship, also chairing a committee linked to Southern Sudan and its independence process (readings uncertain).
Appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Democratic Republic of Congo, a post he held until his death.
Died in Johannesburg, South Africa, after succumbing to an illness, and was mourned by President Mugabe as a loyal cadre.

summary: Jevan Maseko, known in the struggle as Enock Tshangane, was a Bulawayo nationalist who served prison and restriction terms in the 1960s before leaving for Zambia. He trained in Tanzania and the Soviet Union, rose through ZIPRA to Chief of Operations and then Chief of Staff, and survived a 1978 landmine attack. After independence he became a Major General, helped integrate the three armies, and later served as deputy minister, governor and ambassador. His medals included the Liberation Medal (Gold) and the Grand Officer of the Zimbabwe Order of Merit.

timeline.text: Born (year taken from the heading's life dates).
Took party office in Mpopoma Central, Bulawayo, as secretary and later deputy.
Joined other young nationalists in a fierce reaction to the Rhodesian Prime Minister's address at a stadium as resistance and arrests of leaders intensified.
Arrested and sentenced to three years with hard labour at Khami Prison along with fifteen other detainees.
After release from Khami he was restricted at Gonakudzingwa alongside leaders such as Joshua Nkomo and Joseph Msika.
Released, worked briefly as a carpenter in Bulawayo, then left Rhodesia through Botswana for Zambia to join the struggle.
Trained in infantry at Morogoro Camp in Tanzania for nine months and was appointed platoon commander.
Worked as a military instructor and chief of staff of the camp, then trained further as a battalion commander in the Soviet Union.
Served as a commandant and was deployed to Mozambique as a deputy chief when the Zimbabwe People's Army (ZIPA) was formed.
Sent to Zambia, where he was incorporated into the ZIPRA High Command.
Became ZIPRA Chief of Operations.
Survived a landmine attack on his vehicle on the Zambezi front that killed ZIPRA commander Alfred Nikita (surname illegible).
Appointed ZIPRA Chief of Staff, a post he held until Independence.
After being attested into the Zimbabwe National Army in 1980 he was made a substantive Major General.
Appointed Chief of Staff, Administration and Quartermaster; he helped integrate ZANLA, ZIPRA and the Rhodesian Army through the Joint High Command.
Retired from the Zimbabwe National Army.
Served as Deputy Minister of Political Affairs (1988-1990), sat on the ZANU PF Central Committee for Harare (1989-1994) and was Governor of Matabeleland North (1990-1992).
Was Ambassador to Algeria (1993-1994) and then to the Russian Federation (1995-1999).
Served as Ambassador to Cuba; his later appointment as Ambassador to Angola could not be taken up because of ill health.
Died aged 70.

summary: Kanengoni left for the liberation war in August 1975, surviving the Nyadzonia attack and training at Nachingwea in Tanzania. After independence he protected the ZANU leadership and built a long career in the Central Intelligence Organisation, rising to Deputy Director Internal. He also became a prosperous farmer and businessman, a party official in Mashonaland Central, and a patron of schools, clinics, seed schemes and youth projects, earning the nickname Cde Yahwe. The ZANU PF Politburo declared him a national hero.

timeline.text: Angered by colonial oppression, he left the country on foot via Machipanda to join ZANLA in Mozambique.
Was in the Nyadzonia camp and survived the brutal Rhodesian attack there, then was moved to another camp.
Formed part of the first group of 750 trainees at Nachingwea in Tanzania, nicknamed Songa Mbele and trained by Tanzanian forces.
Returned to Harare as part of the team giving protection to the ZANU leadership under Robert Mugabe, staying at Mount Pleasant Holding Centre as a liaison officer.
Served as an auxiliary patrol officer in the Zimbabwe Republic Police (date and later details illegible).
Joined the Central Intelligence Organisation and worked in its government-protection directorate, receiving training in securing government premises and key national installations.
Received intelligence training in Cuba and held a headship in the government-protection unit around January 1986.
Promoted to Assistant Director Internal, handling administration of the Internal Branch.
Promoted to Deputy Director and then Deputy Director Internal for counter-subversion and serious crimes.
During a restructuring he was placed in the Director General's office to handle special projects.
Named chairman of a CIO committee that supported the Land Reform Programme, and became a successful farmer himself.
Was redeployed as Deputy Director Internal, the post he held when he died.
Chosen by Mashonaland Central Province to chair the successful Mazowe District fundraising committee.
Voted ZANU PF Secretary for Administration for Mashonaland Central Province, working to improve livelihoods in Mazowe communal lands.
After his death the ZANU PF Politburo declared him a national hero.

After independence he moved from local government into the Air Force of Zimbabwe, rising from Flight Lieutenant to Air Commodore and holding senior equipment and defence-policy posts. He later led the National Railways of Zimbabwe and helped revive it. He died in August 2013 after a road accident near Insiza.

timeline.text: Born in the Mwacheta area of Chipinge, first of eight children of Cephas and Agnes Karakadzai.
At 18 left Mount Jersey Secondary School with a group of students and crossed into Mozambique at Espungabeira to join the armed struggle.
Moved from Machazi and Chibawawa camps to Chimoio Camp for military training.
Selected for political education at Chitepo (Wampua) Ideological College; his nom de guerre was Hip Level.
After the ceasefire he and his detachment went to an assembly point, and during that period survived a landmine blast near the Mavuradonha Mountains.
At Independence joined the Ministry of Local Government as a Promotion Officer.
Married Sylvia Mukudu; they later had five sons.
Left Local Government in 1983 and joined the Air Force of Zimbabwe as a Flight Lieutenant in 1984.
Appointed Base Equipment Officer, later Staff Officer Grade 1 Equipment.
Became Acting Director Equipment in 1989 and was confirmed in the post in 1991.
Later appointed to an operations-related Director-General post and then Deputy Secretary for Defence Policy and Procurement (dates and wording unclear).
Promoted to Group Captain and then Air Commodore, the rank he held until death (years illegible).
Appointed General Manager of the National Railways of Zimbabwe, where he turned the company around, introduced commuter trains and secured funds for rail steel from China.
Died at Mater Dei Hospital in Bulawayo after a road accident the previous evening.

summary: Enos Mzombi Nkala was born in Filabusi and worked a string of jobs in Bulawayo and Harare before the Native Land Husbandry Act and settler injustices pushed him into nationalism. He led the 1960 Seven Thousand March, served as treasurer of ZAPU and then of ZANU, which was founded in his Highfield home in 1963. He spent about twelve years in detention, then became a cabinet minister after independence before resigning from government around 1989. He died in Harare in August 2013, remembered by Mugabe as a staunch, unyielding fighter.

timeline.text: Born in the Filabusi area of Matabeleland South; he later went by the name Mzombi during the struggle.
Worked as a laboratory assistant at Rhodesia Cement at Colleen Bawn, then in a Bulawayo clothing factory.
Moved to Harare and worked as a newspaper vendor, clerk, insurance broker and then at the Bantu Times, where he met Nathan Shamuyarira and wrote for magazines such as Parade and Drum.
Joined the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress.
Led the Seven Thousand March in Salisbury (Harare) demanding better conditions and the end of the State of Emergency.
Elected Deputy Secretary General of the new NDP under George Silundika, and was arrested for a fiery speech; his trial collapsed after he insulted the white judge.
Became assistant to Joshua Nkomo, and after the NDP ban became Treasurer of the newly formed ZAPU; he was also convicted of making a subversive statement that year.
Was a founding member of ZANU, formed in his house in Highfield, and served as its Treasurer under Ndabaningi Sithole.
At the ZANU first Congress in Gwelo he pushed for a more confrontational line, and soon afterwards was arrested and held at Sikombela Detention Camp.
Held in Salisbury, Connemara, Hwahwa, Sikombela and Gonakudzingwa for about twelve years alongside Sithole, Takawira, Tekere, Nyagumbo and Mugabe, and helped conceive ZANU's armed wing.
While detained he studied by correspondence, taking on law and commerce degrees at once before dropping law, and could not finish his courses because of the harsh conditions.
After release from prison he campaigned vigorously for ZANU around the Lancaster House period, drawing the attention of Britain's last governor, Lord Soames.
Became a cabinet minister (apparently Finance first), later holding other portfolios until 1985 and then Defence.
Resigned from government and stayed politically inactive until his death.
Died at a private hospital in Harare after a long illness affecting his heart and kidneys.

summary: Kumbirai Kangai was a teacher from Masvingo area schools who entered nationalist politics through the NDP, ZAPU and then ZANU. After studying in the United States and rallying support for ZANU there, he joined the exiled leadership, sat on the second Dare reChimurenga, and was jailed in Zambia in 1975 before taking a Central Committee post in 1977. After independence he represented Buhera South and held several ministries, and as Lands and Agriculture minister in 1997 he faced Britain's refusal to fund land purchase. He died on 24 August 2013, remembered by party leaders as a fearless and principled cadre.

timeline.text: Born to a teacher father, Jemiel Mukomana Kangai, and Josina (nee Mupambirei); his father's frequent transfers meant he attended several primary schools.
Attended Zimuto Secondary School for Forms 1 to 4 after completing Standard 4 to 6 at Makumbe Mission.
Began teaching at Zimuto Primary School, where one of his pupils was the future General Solomon Mujuru, then moved to Nyashanu Mission for two years.
Became politically active in support of the National Democratic Party while working as a teacher, attending meetings by night and teaching by day.
Was transferred to Murehwa District and taught at Muchinjike and Rupange schools, where his political activity grew.
Joined ZAPU at its formation after the NDP was banned.
Joined ZANU soon after it was formed, was arrested after evading police for a long time, and was later released.
Went to the United States on a scholarship to study Public Health and Clinical Laboratory Pathology at the University of California.
Studied Medical Technology at the same institution and was elected Secretary for Publicity in a US-based Zimbabwean organisation.

timeline.date: during his studies in the USA
timeline.text: Rallied American public opinion and support for ZANU and was elected ZANU chief representative for North America.

timeline.date: after his studies, late 1972 per OCR
timeline.text: Answered a call for Zimbabweans abroad to join the struggle, left America and moved on to Africa, eventually reaching Zambia.
Was elected to the second Dare reChimurenga of ZANU as Secretary for Transport and Social Welfare.
Was jailed with other Dare members by the Zambian government over the killing of Herbert Chitepo, a crime actually carried out by Rhodesian Selous Scouts.
Was released along with some colleagues after pressure so that they could attend the Geneva Conference.
When Robert Mugabe assumed full leadership at Chimoio, he was elected to the Central Committee in charge of Transport and Social Welfare and worked to improve conditions for refugees in Mozambique.
Was part of the ZANU delegation at the Lancaster House Talks in London.
Won the Buhera South seat in the House of Assembly after ZANU's landslide and became Minister of Labour and Social Welfare.
Became Minister of Industry and Technology and kept his Central Committee seat at the second ZANU Congress held at Borrowdale Race Course.
Was re-elected for Buhera South and soon afterwards appointed to another ministerial post whose title is cut off in the text.

As Minister of Lands and Agriculture he received a letter from British minister Clare Short rejecting any special British duty to pay for land purchase, which began a lasting dispute over land reform.
Died after collapsing at home and being taken to a local clinic; he was survived by wife Miriam, twelve children and several grandchildren.

summary: Misheck Tanyanyiwa left school early to join the liberation struggle in 1975, trained with ZANLA in Tanzania and then trained other cadres in Tanzania and Mozambique, rising to Detachment Commander. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army, helped build 1 Commando Battalion and became its first black commanding officer, introducing parachuting and reconnaissance training. He later held brigade and headquarters appointments, represented Zimbabwe in the DRC peace commission, and served as Defence Attache in China, where he died in 2013. He received several service and campaign medals including the Grand Officer of the Zimbabwe Order of Merit.

timeline.text: Born as the fifth of twelve children and the eldest son in a family of seven girls and five boys; he left school early because he wanted to join the liberation war.
Joined the liberation struggle and received training in Tanzania under ZANLA.
Went to Nachingwea as one of the instructors training new recruits.
Was moved back to Mozambique with other trainers by Tanzanian forces after internal disturbances in the liberation movement.
Moved to Inhaminga in Mozambique, where he carried on training cadres; the highest wartime post he held was Detachment Commander.
Was stationed at Beira for a period at the end of the war (his assignment there is not legible).
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a private soldier, given the equivalent of Major rank, and went through integration at the Zimbabwe Military Academy.
Took part in dissolving the Rhodesian Light Infantry and forming 1 Commando Battalion, then passed the selection and training for the unit and completed a Special Forces Commando Course at Wafa Wafa.
Became the first black and first former guerrilla Commanding Officer of 1 Commando Battalion, tasked with turning it from a white-dominated elite outfit into a loyal national unit.
Introduced parachute jumping and reconnaissance training in the Commando unit and led it in early Mozambique deployments against RENAMO in the Beira Corridor.
Handed over command of the Commando unit to a successor (name garbled) after a spell as an instructor.
Was promoted to substantive Lieutenant Colonel.
Was promoted to Colonel and posted to a brigade headquarters, serving as acting brigade commander from May 1989 to February 1990 and then commander of 4 Infantry Brigade until 1992.
Was promoted to Brigadier General.
Served as Brigadier General Administration at Army Headquarters, then returned to command an infantry brigade from 1997 to 2000.
Helped negotiate the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement and headed Zimbabwe's delegation to the Joint Military Commission during the DRC campaign.
Was posted to ZDF Headquarters as Director General Public Relations.
Was sent to China as Defence Attache during the Look East period and worked to deepen military training and exchanges between the two countries.
Died in Beijing; he was survived by wife Mariah (nee Nyabocho), three children and two grandchildren.

summary: Eric Gwanzura was a builder, teacher and trade unionist from Zvimba who built schools, houses and a famous stadium for black communities in Salisbury. He used trade unionism to organise workers, helped drive the 1960 strike and moved into nationalist politics with the NDP and later ZANU-PF. He is also said to have joined delegations to the Geneva and Lancaster House negotiations, settled in Chegutu where he ran Cafe Capri, and served as a Senator. He died on 9 December 2013 after collapsing at home.

timeline.text: Born at Mashonganyika Village in Zvimba to Reverend Enock Gwanzura, a founding member of the Apostolic Faith Mission, and Maria (nee Gara).
Attended Govathema Primary School and Kutama College, where Robert Mugabe was also a student, then trained as a builder at Waddilove.
Taught at Sandringham High School and then at Kawara Primary School, a Salvation Army school in Mhondoro, about two years at each.
Moved to Salisbury and started a construction company aimed at building schools for black children shut out of better white-only schools.
Built Gwanzura Stadium in Highfield with his brother, which became the first FIFA-approved soccer stadium in the country.
Built housing for urban Africans and was invited by Major Lewis of the Salvation Army to work at Usher Institute in Matabeleland improving infrastructure for black communities.
Turned to trade unionism and, with Reuben Jamela, pushed for the formalisation of unions across Southern Africa.
Helped organise the well-known Rhodesian strike and was described as the mastermind of African township resistance in urban areas.
Was one of the revolutionaries, with Joshua Nkomo, Michael Mawema, George Silundika and Morton Malianga among others, linked to the National Democratic Party.
Built a communication network linking the exiled leadership with freedom fighters and politicians inside Rhodesia, travelling abroad to carry news and take back instructions.

Served as a Senator in the new Parliament and held committee positions.
Took part in the negotiations leading to the Unity Accord between ZANU-PF and PF-ZAPU (partly legible).
Died after collapsing at his home in Chegutu; he was survived by two wives, nineteen children and 65 grandchildren.

summary: Harold Chirenda, who fought as Elliot Masengo, was among the first ZAPU cadres trained in Algeria and became a ZIPRA training chief, instructing many future commanders and launching early sabotage missions. After 1978 he represented ZAPU in Bucharest and joined the Patriotic Front delegation at Lancaster House. In the Zimbabwe National Army he held training, operations and sports posts, wrote the order that launched the Mozambique campaign, led an infantry battalion, and served as military attache in Botswana before retiring in 1995. He died in 2014 and was declared a National Hero by the ZANU PF Politburo.

timeline.text: Born in Mbare, Salisbury, with the nom-de-guerre Elliot Masengo.
Was among the first group of 19 cadres sent to Ksar El Boukhari in Algeria for basic military training.
Was picked for the Officer Cadet Course at Cherchell Military Academy, graduating in 1966, and later trained as a commando.
At Cherchell he met Samora Machel, Ali Halimeh and Yoweri Museveni, who were doing similar training.
Was appointed an instructor at the ZIPRA Morogoro camp in Tanzania, teaching field engineering, guerrilla warfare and topography to future senior commanders.
Led a first infiltration into Rhodesia with Kheli Malaba and Joshua Moyo to blow up the water engine at Chirundu Sugar Estates.
After ZAPU's military wing became ZIPRA, served as Deputy Chief of Personnel and Training, becoming Chief of Training in 1976.
Took part in a second infiltration crossing at Kazungula with Cephas Cele and was later made substantive Director of Training in the ZIPRA High Command.
Survived the landmine blast that killed ZIPRA commander Nikita Mangena, and was sent to Bucharest as ZAPU Chief Representative until independence.
Was part of the Patriotic Front delegation at the Lancaster House Conference and married Florence Ngwenya in Bucharest.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a Lieutenant Colonel.
Became Chief Instructor at the Zimbabwe Military Academy, worked with the British training team on integration, and wrote Operation Sledgehammer, which began Zimbabwe's involvement in Mozambique.
Became GSO 1 Sports, was the first Zimbabwe Defence Forces delegate to the international military sports council CISM, and lobbied for the ZDF's admission at Lagos.
Helped found Black Rhinos Football Club, which rose to the Super League and later won the league and reached the African Club Championship semi-finals; he earned the nickname Go Bhora.
Took command of 43 Infantry Battalion and took part in Operation Chipoko against RENAMO south of the Beira Corridor.
Was posted back to the Directorate of Army Training as GSO 1 Sports.
Served as military attache at Zimbabwe's High Commission in Botswana, also covering Angola and Namibia.
Retired from the Zimbabwe National Army.
Died at United Bulawayo Hospitals after a long illness, having been declared a National Hero by the ZANU PF Politburo.

summary: Brigadier General Zingoni, born in 1954 in the Masvingo area, left school for lack of money and worked as a health clerk in Masvingo before slipping across to Mozambique in 1976 to join ZANLA. He served as a medical officer through the war after training in Tanzania. After independence he trained in Korea, Nigeria and Zimbabwe, held command and staff roles in the Zimbabwe National Army, and served in the Mozambique and DRC campaigns, ending as Director Operations of the SADC Task Force in Kinshasa. He earned a long list of medals including the Liberation and Independence medals and the Order of Merit, and died in May 2014.

timeline.text: Born in a village in the Masvingo area under Chief Mapanzure; he left school after the Junior Certificate because of money problems.
Moved to Bulawayo to find work and save for further study, which he could not do until after independence.
Was introduced to nationalist politics in Bulawayo and joined anti-Pearce Commission demonstrations.
Got a job with the Ministry of Health and became a health orderly clerk at the provincial medical office in Masvingo, where he saw colonial brutality and racial segregation first hand.
While sent to Chiredzi on a cholera control team, he slipped away with two friends and crossed into Mozambique at Chikwalakwala (now Sango Border Post).
Was received by FRELIMO, taken to Machipanda and joined ZANLA, where his medical background led to hospital work, and later did military training at Chimoio under Augustine Chihuri.
Returned from a six-month course at the Multinational Medical Institute in Tanzania and was deployed at Tembwe, then to Chaminuka Sector as a Section Medical Officer.
Rose from Platoon to Detachment Medical Officer and then to ZANLA staff and sector medical level until the ceasefire in December 1979.

Went to the DPRK for infantry commander training, was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a private and later promoted to Captain after standardisation training at the Zimbabwe Military Academy.
Was among the first officer contingent sent to Nigeria to help turn the guerrilla force into a professional army, then served as an officer in the ZDF.
Held command, training and staff posts from low-level to top headquarters, and in Mozambique led a battalion guarding the road, rail and pipeline link.
Served as Commander Western Front and then Director Operations at the SADC Task Force Headquarters in Kinshasa under Lt Gen Valerio Sibanda, and organised the Task Force's withdrawal from the DRC.
Completed his O and A levels by correspondence after independence and was pursuing doctoral study alongside the ZDF Commander and other officers when he died.
Died; he was survived by wife Wadzanai Virginia (nee Mabeza) and three children.

summary: Nathan Shamuyarira began as a teacher, then became a leading African journalist, rising to editor of the Daily News and head of African Newspapers Ltd before resigning over racial policies. Recruited to ZAPU in the early 1960s, he joined the ZANU breakaway, studied at Princeton and lectured in Dar-es-Salaam. After independence he served as a long-time minister, notably reshaping Zimbabwe's media institutions and later serving as Foreign Minister. President Mugabe praised him as an architect of the country's modern information sector, and he died on 4 June 2014.

timeline.text: Born to Tafirenyika Shamuyarira, a Methodist evangelist, and Maria; he had a brother, Musa, and a sister, Evelyn.
Attended Waddilove Mission for primary school and teacher training, then completed his secondary education by correspondence.
Taught at Tegwani School in Plumtree and then taught animal husbandry at Domboshawa Training Centre.
Left teaching for journalism, starting as a cub reporter with African Newspapers Ltd.
Became editor of the Daily News.
Went on a six-week tour of Britain and a three-month tour of the United States with Commonwealth journalists, which he saw as an attempt to win over Third World reporters.
Held the post of Editor-in-Chief of African Newspapers Ltd until he resigned over its racial policies.
Persuaded by Dr Samuel Parirenyatwa to join ZAPU, he became an active member helping shape its policies.
Was part of a ZAPU delegation led by Joshua Nkomo to the United Nations in New York to press for recognition of Africans' right to self-determination (OCR garbled).
Was among the leaders who broke away from ZAPU to form ZANU, and the following year left Southern Rhodesia to study Political Science at Princeton.
After graduating, lectured at the University of Dar-es-Salaam while remaining involved in his country's politics.

As a government minister he spearheaded decolonisation of the media, creating the Zimbabwe Mass Media Trust, the national news agency ZIANA, the Zimbabwe School of Mass Communication and Zimbabwe Newspapers, and reshaping the public broadcaster.
Started community projects for women and communal farmers in the Makonde area, including a farmers' warehouse and a school scholarship scheme.
As Foreign Minister he raised Zimbabwe's profile as a non-aligned, Pan-African state, and Zimbabwe hosted several major world summits during his term.
Died at West End Clinic in Harare from a chest infection; he was survived by wife Dorothy and a daughter.

summary: Stanley Sakupwanya was a Bulawayo-born doctor who started in nationalist youth politics in the 1950s and joined ZAPU in 1961. He smuggled dynamite into Rhodesia for sabotage, was arrested, then fled and trained as a doctor in the Soviet Union, returning to treat guerrillas and help the movement from Zambia. After independence he served as a Lieutenant Colonel and army medical officer, then worked at Mhangura Mine, and later took party and Senate roles after the Unity Accord. He died on 1 July 2014 as ZANU-PF Party Secretary for Welfare for the Disabled.

timeline.text: Born in Bulawayo to pharmacist Steven Urayayi Sakupwanya and Estella (nee Mashingaidze), the second child in a family of seven.
Attended primary school in Bulawayo and then Moeng College in Botswana, determined to become a doctor despite racist ridicule from a white pharmacist.
Began his political life in the African National Congress Makokoba Youth Wing.
Joined the National Democratic Party Youth League when it was formed, and later joined ZAPU at its formation in 1961 after the NDP was banned.
Moved to Barbourfields, was elected youth chairman, and helped recruit youths for military training, raise funds and smuggle weapons.
While working as a Rhodesia Tobacco Company sales representative he smuggled dynamite chargers from Zambia for sabotage of railway lines, until a friend's loose talk led to his arrest.
After release he left Rhodesia for Zambia and then went to the Soviet Union to study medicine, where he became President of the Zimbabwe Students Union.
Completed his medical studies and went back to Zambia.
Was detained at Lilongwe Airport in Malawi, while on the way to his mother's funeral, because of the many countries he had been visiting.
Was involved in arrangements for the burial of Jason Moyo, killed by a parcel bomb by Rhodesian forces.
Was unable to attend the Lancaster House Conference because fighting between Tanzania and Uganda disrupted communications, then returned with the advance team after the ceasefire.
Was integrated into the ZNA as a Major and appointed Senior Medical Officer, later becoming a substantive Lieutenant Colonel.
Retired from the army in 1983 and worked as a Senior Medical Officer at Mhangura Mine until 1986.
Was elected to the ZAPU executive and helped bring ZAPU and ZANU-PF together; he later joined the ZANU-PF Central Committee and the Politburo.
Served as Senator for Nyanga South (constituency and start year partly legible).
Died at Parirenyatwa Hospital while Party Secretary for Welfare for the Disabled; he left children and 15 grandchildren (other details garbled).

summary: Major General Eliah Bandama was a Chipinge-born soldier whose life changed after a 1975 school strike at Chikore Mission led to his arrest and exclusion from schooling. He fled to Mozambique, was jailed briefly as a suspected spy, then trained as a ZANLA fighter and engineer, was wounded in 1977 and received further training in China. After the 1979 ceasefire he joined the first group integrated into the Zimbabwe National Army and rose through the ranks, serving in Commando Regiment, a UN peacekeeping contingent and a regional deployment, eventually commanding 3 Infantry Brigade. He died of Burkitt's leukemia in July 2014.

timeline.text: Born in the Musikavanhu area of Chipinge to Zacharia Bandama and a mother named Chikozomba; grew up in Chipinge District.

During a student strike at Chikore Mission after expulsions, an administration block was burnt; he was among six suspected ringleaders held, tried, caned with eight cuts and released, then barred from formal education in Rhodesia by the Minister of Education.
With two close friends he slipped out to Mozambique (Espungabera, then Maputo) to join the struggle, but was arrested as a suspected Rhodesian police agent and held at Posto Machazi.
Freed from Posto Machazi on Mozambique's Independence Day and moved to Chibawawa (Toronga Camp), where he was taught politics and bayonet fighting.
Went to Tembwe Training Camp and trained in engineering, then passed through Chimoio and was deployed to Gaza Province.
Suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his left knee and thigh when helicopters attacked his section at Chomupani; sent back to Mozambique for treatment.
Chosen by General Rex Nhongo to go for further training in China with two other comrades.
Had a bullet removed from his left knee in Guangzhou, then trained in engineering, mobile warfare and politics before returning via Ethiopia and Tanzania.
After meeting Josiah Tongogara at Pasichigare Base, he was redeployed to Chitepo Sector as a Detachment Political Commissar and fought there until the ceasefire.
Part of the advance team into Zimbabwe; attested into the ZNA as a Private and then given officer status, among the first guerrillas integrated into the army.
Promoted to Lieutenant and married Winnie Florence Chatindo the same year.
Posted to Commando Regiment, where he served in various positions.
Later commanded an infantry battalion that formed part of Zimbabwe's contingent to the UN operation in Somalia (UNOSOM II); exact dates not legible.
Deployed under Operation Sovereign Legitimacy (OSL), apparently as officer in charge of logistics at Eastern Front headquarters (reading uncertain).
Died at West End Hospital after succumbing to Burkitt's leukemia while serving as commander of 3 Infantry Brigade.

summary: Lloyd Kotsho Dube was a Matabeleland-born nationalist, academic and diplomat. After early work as a law clerk and bank employee in Rhodesia and involvement in the 1960 protests, he served ZAPU abroad as a representative at the United Nations and in the UK and Western Europe. He worked in American university publishing and teaching, earned a doctorate, then ran PF-Zapu's publications from Lusaka and joined the Lancaster House delegation. In independent Zimbabwe he held party posts, served as ambassador in France and elsewhere, and chaired the NRZ board before dying at his Bulawayo home of diabetes.

timeline.text: Born as the fifth and last child of Malandi Dube and Tshiziwa Ncube in Matobo District, Matabeleland South.
Took part in the large 1960 demonstration against Sir Edgar Whitehead's government demanding release of detained nationalists.
Worked as a law clerk at the Harare attorneys Coghlan Welsh and Guest.
Worked at the then Bank of Rhodesia and Nyasaland.
Became ZAPU's representative to the United Nations and the Americas, based in New York, and later also covered the UK and Western Europe from London, lobbying and petitioning at the UN.
Served as Research Associate and Associate Editor at the University of Massachusetts Press, and headed development dialogues and the African students association at the university.
Earned a PhD in Policy Studies and became Assistant Professor at Morehouse College in Atlanta, later at the University of Georgia (1976 to 1978).
Moved to Lusaka as Director of Information and Editor-in-Chief of PF-Zapu publications such as Zimbabwe People's Voice, Combat Diary and Zimbabwe Review.
Member of the PF-Zapu delegation at the Lancaster House talks that led to independence in 1980.
Wrote a scholarly work apparently on Zimbabwe's education policies (title garbled).
Served on a national structure helping implement unity between ZANU-PF and PF-Zapu; also held national party posts in publicity/elections (titles garbled).
Took a diplomatic course before his first ambassadorial posting to France.
Organised President Mugabe's state visit to Portugal.
Ambassador to France, Spain, Portugal, the Vatican and UNESCO; became Dean of Commonwealth Ambassadors accredited to France and facilitated two presidential visits to Pope John Paul II.
His advocacy for solar energy at UNESCO led to the Solar Summit held in Harare, where President Mugabe was elected chairman of the World Solar Commission.
Served on the boards of the Zimbabwe Investment Centre and the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation.
Appointed Ambassador to Nigeria, then to Zambia from 2004 to 2006.
Chairman of the NRZ board of directors.

summary: Justice Andrew Mutema was a Bikita-educated academic high-flyer who joined the liberation war as a teenager after meeting freedom fighters at school. He endured a hard journey to Mozambique, nearly being executed by mistake, and was later sent to Romania for anti-aircraft radar and air defence training. After demobilising in 1982 he entered the legal service, rising from assistant magistrate to regional magistrate and then senior president of the Administrative and Labour Courts. He became a High Court judge and a COMESA Court principal judge, was declared a national hero, and died in August 2015.

timeline.text: Born into a family with seven girls and two boys, to Peter Chigweshe and Elizabeth (nee Mhurai) Mutema, under Chief Chiwara.
Attended Silveira Secondary School in Bikita and came top of about sixty candidates in the Junior Certificate, earning a bursary for himself and one other student.
First met freedom fighters who came from Mozambique to Silveira to give political education; he then attended pungwes and listened to the Voice of Zimbabwe.
He and Englebert Rugeje tried to leave for Mozambique but met sectoral commander Henry Muchena, who advised them; they shelved the plan and returned to school.
A group of young recruits including Mutema, Rugeje, John Chipembere, Michael Rinowanda, Leonard Mafume, Francis Chanyau and Josiah Sithole set off on foot from Bikita towards Mozambique.
In Chipinge Rugeje's brother-in-law, who worked at the District Administrator's office, grew suspicious and reported them, but the group escaped Rhodesian detection and continued.
In Mozambique the group was stripped and put in a pit awaiting execution, but Cde Henry Muchena learned of the arrest and saved them; they then reached Chibabawa camp and were deployed in battalions.
Selected with about 200 cadres for training in Romania, studying Romanian and sciences at Timisoara and then specialising in anti-aircraft radar and air defence artillery systems.
Romanian training courses ran from June 1980; he returned to Zimbabwe around Heroes Day (August) 1982.
Chose demobilisation into civilian life.
Attended a combined magistrates, prosecutors and presiding officers course at Domboshava Training Centre run by the Ministry of Justice.
Returned to Domboshava for six-month extended magistrates training and joined the Ministry of Justice as an assistant magistrate.
Appointed Magistrate after a short attachment to the prosecutions department; later earned an honours degree at the University of Zimbabwe.
Rose through Senior Magistrate (1990), Provincial Magistrate (1994) and Regional Magistrate (1997).
Appointed Senior President of the Labour Court after earlier serving as Senior President of the Administrative Court.
Appointed Judge of the High Court of Zimbabwe and worked in Harare until 1 February 2013.
Became Senior Judge of the High Court in Bulawayo.
Became Principal Judge in the First Division of the COMESA Court of Justice.
Collapsed at home, was rushed to Mater Dei Hospital in Bulawayo and died the next day.

summary: Dr Sikhanyiso 'Duke' Ndlovu was a Mberengwa-born educator and nationalist who studied in South Africa and the USA while working as a radiographer and social worker. He joined ZAPU in Bulawayo, helped create an education programme for detainees at Gonakudzingwa, and later represented ZAPU in the USA and directed its schools in Zambia. After independence he founded ZDECO, joined the ZANU-PF Central Committee and Politburo, and served as a deputy minister of higher education and as Minister of Information and Publicity. He died in September 2015 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born at Mnene Mission Hospital in Mberengwa, second of thirteen children of Akem and Emelia (nee Mutengwa).
Completed Standard Six at Mnene Mission School, where friends nicknamed him 'Duke of Edinburgh' for his big-word debating; he paid fees by growing groundnuts.
Went to Natal, South Africa, and took his Junior Certificate and matriculation at Marrian Hill High School.
Worked at YMCA stores on Rissik Street, Johannesburg, to raise money for university.
Enrolled for a BA in Social Studies (Social Work) at the University of Natal, studying part-time as the apartheid university act barred blacks from white universities.
Moved from boiler-making work in a hospital laundry to radiographer training at McCord's Zulu Hospital and was appointed to take charge of a unit there (text cuts off).
Was manhandled by a white station master after entering a waiting room (apparently whites-only), but insisted on his ticket and threatened to sue for assault, and was allowed to continue his journey.
ZAPU was banned following the bombing of White City Stadium, as the political struggle in Bulawayo intensified.
While at Gonakudzingwa he helped set up an education programme for detainees, sourcing correspondence course materials from institutions in England.

Released from Gonakudzingwa but placed under house arrest in Mpopoma with a 24-hour guard; was tasked by Dr Nkomo and the executive with carrying a message to ZAPU's external leadership and went to Lusaka the same year.

Studied in the USA (diploma, BA in Sociology, public administration masters, doctorate in education), worked as a clinical social worker, chaired the ZAPU branch there, and presented Zimbabwe's case to the UN Human Rights body.
Returned to Zambia and became Director of ZAPU Schools at Victory Camp and J Z Camp.
After the bombing of J Z Camp, became Special Assistant to ZAPU President Joshua Nkomo and managed a Lusaka building that served as a hide-out for Nkomo.
Founded the Zimbabwe Distance Education College (ZDECO) and served on the PF-ZAPU Central Committee until 1987.

Joined the ZANU-PF Central Committee, was elected to the House of Assembly, and served as Deputy Minister of Higher Education (year read as 1994 but uncertain), helping prepare ground for Midlands State University and the Zimbabwe Open University.
As ZANU-PF Deputy Secretary for the Commissariat in the Politburo, ran the party's mass mobilisation machinery.
Served as Minister of Information and Publicity (2007-08) and was ZANU-PF candidate for Pelandaba-Mpopoma in the March 2008 parliamentary election.
Rowdy opposition elements in Bulawayo burnt a college belonging to him.
Died at Mater Dei Hospital after an asthma attack and subsequent stroke; the Politburo declared him a national hero.

summary: Aguy Clement Georgias was a Mashonaland-born boilermaker and draughtsman who worked on major industrial and pipeline projects before building Trinity Engineering into an award-winning firm employing more than 500 people. After independence he used his business to support the army and the wider economy, championed the in duplum rule, and entered politics as a Senator and deputy minister. When the West put him on its sanctions list he personally funded a legal challenge in the European General Court, fighting the measures at his own expense. He died of heart and kidney failure and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born on 22 June in Mashonaland; year and district are illegible.
Trained as a boilermaker and draughtsman before taking work at industrial sites.
Joined the team working on the Number 4 blast furnace at the Rhodesia Iron and Steel Company (RISCO), later Zimbabwe's largest steel producer.
Worked on the Feruka oil pipeline from Beira in Mozambique to Mutare, and later at Hippo Valley on steam boilers.
Started his own engineering business from modest beginnings with one welding machine and a single oxygen/gas set, then built a larger enterprise after spotting demand for durable tri-axle trailers.
Moved his business from elsewhere to Harare (then Salisbury) and built products that became a favourite among farmers in communal and resettlement areas.

At independence he was among the few well-off Africans committed to transferring the economy to rightful owners, expanding his equipment and winning contracts from the Zimbabwe National Army and food/bottling firms.
Fought for the enforcement of the 'in duplum' rule, which stops lenders charging interest beyond the capital sum.
Joined national politics, serving as a Senator and later in a deputy-ministerial post.
Was placed on the European Union's sanctions list; Trinity Engineering also suffered heavy losses.
Was detained overnight at Heathrow while in transit to the USA and sent back to Zimbabwe, challenging the deportation.
Used his own money to file an application in the European General Court against the sanctions; he lost but the sanctions list was later revised downwards.
Died of heart and kidney failure at AMI Hospital; the Politburo declared him a national hero.

summary: Victoria Fikile Mahamba Chitepo was born in Dundee, South Africa, and educated at Adams College, the University of Natal and Birmingham, becoming a trained social worker. She married Herbert Chitepo in 1955 and moved to Southern Rhodesia, where she became involved in nationalist politics and women's organisations such as the YWCA and Zenzele Club. After his death she kept up his unfinished work and later served as a government minister. She was declared a national hero after her death on 8 April 2016.

timeline.text: Born Victoria Fikile Mahamba Sithole at Dundee in KwaZulu/Natal region, third child of Alice and Enock Sithole in a family of children including four girls.
Appointed Deputy Head girl at Adams College in Natal at age 19, known for her eloquence.
Taught at Inanda Seminary near Durban.
Studied social science at the University of Natal, then took a post-graduate course in social work at Birmingham University, where she met with racism on campus.
Did three months of specialised study in social psychology at London University and met Herbert Chitepo, whom she had known from Adams College.
Married Herbert Chitepo and relocated to Southern Rhodesia.
Became first secretary general of the Young Women's Christian Association (YWCA) in Rhodesia and promoted self-help groups such as the Zenzele Club.
Was present when ZAPU was formed and continued women's work, visiting ZAPU detainees, giving them books and hosting nationalists at home.
After her husband's death she took on his unfinished mission and cared for the children (husband's death year not printed in the legible text).
Appointed Minister of Natural Resources and Tourism (start year garbled), serving until 1990, then Minister of Information, Post and Telecommunications.
Involved in setting up vocational training initiatives such as the Jairos Jiri-linked centres and the Herbert Chitepo Training Centre, and in the Zimbabwe Children's Trust.
Died; the nation mourned, and the Politburo declared her a national hero.

summary: Vivian Mwashita Muchicho was a woman combatant who crossed into Mozambique in June 1975 to join ZANLA. She trained at Chimoio, served as an instructor, survived the Nyadzonya and Chimoio attacks and took part in ammunition-carrying and frontline work in Tete. After independence she worked at ZANU-PF headquarters and in the Central Intelligence Organisation, then entered politics as MP for Harare South and Senator for Mvurachena. She helped found the Female Ex-Combatants Organisation and the War Veterans Association, and died in 2016.

timeline.text: Crossed into Mozambique with a group of women recruits to join ZANLA in the liberation war.
Survived the Rhodesian attack on Nyadzonya camp after being moved there from Villa de Manica.
Trained in guerrilla warfare at Chimoio under instructors who included Augustine Chihuri (Cde Steven Chocha) and Lot Sibanda.
Spent four months in Ethiopia, where she began work as a military instructor at Tatek Military Base.
Back in Mozambique, survived the Rhodesian air bombardment of Chimoio.
Was among those ordered by ZANLA Chief of Defence Josiah Tongogara to return and help bury the hundreds of comrades killed; the scenes stayed with her and moved her to tears for the rest of her life.
Answered the call to the battlefront and was deployed in Tete Operational Province under Cde Shiri.

Joined a large contingent of women combatants who carried ammunition, explosives and weapons loads of up to 50kg from Zumbo on the Mozambican border via Chidodo to fighters inside the country, walking for up to seven days.
Worked at ZANU-PF headquarters on Manica Road in Harare, guided by senior party figures including Tony Gara.
Later joined the Central Intelligence Organisation, where she served until retiring in 1995.
With colleagues including Irene Zindi and Margaret Dongo, formed the Female Ex-Combatants Organisation (FECO) to advance the interests of women ex-combatants.
Helped build a wider War Veterans Association, registered and launched in 1989 with financial help from First Lady Sally Mugabe.
Received the Liberation War Hero Bronze Award and won the Harare South parliamentary seat.
Became Zanu-PF Senator for Mvurachena, a constituency that took in Harare South, Sunningdale and Waterfalls.
Worked to improve housing in her constituency, helped found several housing cooperatives and taught skills such as soap-making and bread baking.
Died, survived by her husband Peter Muchicho, three children and six grandchildren.

summary: Dr Rati Muchemwa was a Zimbabwean doctor who turned political through student activism at Fletcher High School and later ZANU support work in Britain, helped by encouragement from Herbert Chitepo. He gave up medical practice in the UK to serve ZANLA in Mozambique, running health care at Chimoio and other camps, surviving the 1977 Chimoio attack and representing ZANU at World Health Organisation meetings. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army, becoming Director Medical Services and eventually a Brigadier General. He was survived by his wife, three children and one grandchild.

timeline.text: Attended Fletcher High School in Gweru, where he began organising fellow students to discuss the abuses of colonial rule.
The Rhodesian government, recognising his ability despite his activism, granted him a state scholarship.
After a second scholarship, moved to Britain to continue his medical studies at the University of Birmingham.
Qualified with a bachelor's degree in medicine and surgery (MBChB) at Birmingham.
While in Britain, worked with exiled activists such as Simba Makoni, recruited other students and raised money for the war effort that was sent to ZANU headquarters through a secret route.
Met ZANU chairman Herbert Chitepo in Birmingham; Chitepo urged him to join the liberation struggle and he replied that he would do so once his current commitment ended.
Left Britain to join the struggle; after a rigorous vetting he was accepted as a genuine cadre and sent to ZANLA headquarters at Chimoio.

At Chimoio joined Dr Sydney Sekeramayi and Dr Herbert Ushewokunze at Parirenyatwa Referral Hospital; the three doctors cared for sick and wounded fighters and refugees and introduced public health measures such as compulsory use of toilets.
Deployed to Doroi Refugee Camp, where he brought daily deaths from disease and malnutrition under control within two months.
Appointed member of the General Staff and ZANLA Forces and Camp Medical Officer at Chimoio; he also trained medical staff for the front and bases.

Survived the Rhodesian attack on Chimoio, in which a colleague was killed when an ambulance they were using was hit; he later operated at Chimoio City Hospital and then treated casualties at a rear base hospital.
Underwent military training at Takawira Base Two.
Represented ZANU at the World Health Organisation conference in Geneva with ZAPU's Dr Bango, winning resolutions for WHO medicine and supplies to liberation-held areas and refugee camps.
Served as Chief Medical Officer at Mavonde Operational Base, then as medical officer at Tembwe responsible for medicines, vaccines, equipment and training medics.

Attended another WHO conference with a ZAPU colleague and helped win adoption of Patriotic Front resolutions by a large majority despite British, Australian and Canadian resistance linked to the Internal Settlement.
Helped prepare ZANLA's move into Zimbabwe, was appointed to the Cease-fire Commission and became one of three pioneer doctors of its Medical and Logistical Services Command.

After joining the Zimbabwe National Army as a Major and Senior Medical Officer, was promoted to Colonel and later became Director Medical Services; also rescued victims of a bomb blast at 88 Manica Road that year.
Completed the Joint Command and Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
As a Colonel during the Mozambican Campaign, took part in operations around Gorongoza (details garbled).
A promotion or appointment is recorded, most likely to Brigadier General (text garbled).

summary: Dr Charles Utete was born in Chivhu and became a political scientist who taught in the United States and at the University of Rhodesia/Zimbabwe. He then became one of independent Zimbabwe's most influential civil servants, rising to Chief Secretary to the President and Cabinet and helping steer the post-1980 public service and the 1987 Unity Accord. He chaired the Lands Review Committee that guided the Fast Track Land Reform Programme and retired around 2003 before taking many board positions. He died at home in Harare on 15 July 2016 and was described by the President as a national hero.

timeline.text: Took up a teaching post at Montclair State College in New Jersey after his studies in the United States.
Returned home and joined the University of Rhodesia (now University of Zimbabwe) as a Senior Lecturer in Political Science, later serving as a faculty dean.
At the university worked alongside Dr Misheck Sibanda, later his successor as Chief Secretary, and took part in a ZANU district structure with the late national hero Tichaona Jokonya.
Held a senior organisational role connected to the Non-Aligned Movement summit.
Contributed to shaping the post-1980 public service and uniformed forces and to the Unity Accord that joined ZANU-PF and ZAPU.
Moved into the top civil service post in the Office of the President and Cabinet, where he headed the secretariat that carried out Cabinet and presidential directives.
During the Renamo blockade of the Beira corridor, argued for alternative trade routes for the country.
Served as Chief Executive for a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting held in Harare.
Chaired the Lands Review Committee, whose first report set out guidelines for implementing the Fast Track Land Reform Programme.
Retired after 23 years as a senior civil servant; at his farewell the President praised him as a central figure in the government system.
After retiring, sat on public and private boards, chairing the Industrial Development Corporation, Seedco Zimbabwe and Astra Industries.
Became a director of Zimpapers and later its chairman.
Served on the National Economic Consultative Forum's anti-corruption taskforce, arguing that public attitudes to bribery had to change.
Died at his home in Harare, aged 77; the President called him an intellectual of renown who helped transform the civil service.

summary: Cephas Msipa was born in 1931 in the Midlands and trained as a teacher, rising through teachers' associations and early nationalist parties. His activism led to a teaching ban, detention and a 1966 escape, followed by years working for ZAPU and editing The Zimbabwe Times. After independence he was a deputy minister, Minister of Water Resources and Development, Midlands Governor and Minister of State for State Enterprises and Indigenisation, and he held many board roles and a Midlands State University honorary doctorate. He was also a philanthropist and author of a memoir, and was remembered at his death as a veteran nationalist.

timeline.text: Born in the Siboza area of Shabani District, the first of ten children.
Took up his first teaching post at a primary school (name not legible), studying for his school certificate and A-levels on the side.
Moved to Kwekwe to teach at Amaveni Primary School, where he challenged the headmaster Mr Greenfield over racially discriminatory conduct.
Began organising meetings for the African National Congress and was active in RATA, being elected secretary but later removed for questioning discriminatory practices.
Transferred to Shingirayi School in Salisbury (now Harare).
Promoted to head Mhofu Primary School in Highfield, using the post to mobilise teachers and was voted chairman of the Highfield RATA branch.

With Enos Nkala and others, helped persuade Robert Mugabe to take up the post of Secretary for Information and Publicity in the National Democratic Party, then resigned from teaching to take up political work.
Married Charlotte Sithabile at St Martin's Church, Amaveni, Kwekwe.

Appointed to a senior post at Crowborough No. 1 School in Mufakose but was suspended for his politics; went on to become RATA vice president and then president, confronting the settler government over injustices to African teachers.
Banned from teaching, arrested and held at Gonakudzingwa and Harare prisons, then escaped in 1966 in protest at the Unilateral Declaration of Independence and was listed as a wanted terrorist.
Worked in disguise as a farm labourer at Cold Comfort Farm alongside Didymus Mutasa and Guy Clutton-Brock; when Clutton-Brock was deported he went into hiding for weeks before being captured.
Took part in the nationalist movement of the mid-1970s and was elected National Secretary for Education of ZAPU, helping educate many liberation leaders.
Co-founded The Zimbabwe Times and edited it; the paper was banned in 1978 and he was detained until 1979.
Chosen as one of the nationalists who took part in the Lancaster House talks leading to independence in April 1980.
Served as Deputy Minister of Youth, Sport and Recreation and Deputy Minister of Manpower Planning, then became Minister of Water Resources and Development in 1982.
Played a key part in the process that united ZANU and ZAPU, working with Joshua Nkomo and Robert Mugabe.
Served as Governor of the Midlands Province.
Served as Minister of State for State Enterprises and Indigenisation, then was reappointed Midlands Governor in 2000 until retirement (around 2008).
Set up the C. G. Msipa Scholarship Trust for needy but gifted students (2009) and published his memoir In Pursuit of Freedom and Justice (2015).

summary: Chanetsa grew up in colonial Rhodesia and went into exile in the late 1960s, joining the liberation struggle in Tanzania and Mozambique. He worked in ZANU protocol and security roles, including as Chief of Protocol at Chimoio and in advance teams for Robert Mugabe's delegations. After independence he continued in protocol and party work, was invited to Namibia-linked SWAPO activities in the early 1990s, then became MP for Hurungwe East, Governor and Resident Minister of Mashonaland West, and later MP for Hurungwe North. The Politburo unanimously declared him a national hero and he was survived by his wife Beatrice and children.

timeline.text: Left Rhodesia for exile, reaching Mwanza in Tanzania where he furthered his education and joined other nationalists in the liberation effort.
Deployed at the ZANU office in Tanzania to carry out protocol and security duties; that year he met his future wife Beatrice, who worked in the Tanzanian judiciary.
While at Chimoio, was appointed Chief of Protocol.
Went to Khartoum in Sudan as part of an advance team preparing for Robert Mugabe's delegation at an Organisation of African Unity summit.
Travelled to Britain around the Lancaster House Agreement and helped ask Zimbabwean students abroad to return home and assist in the coming elections.
After independence continued in protocol work, helping train young officers and develop diplomatic staff (text fragmentary).
Became the first ZANU-PF district chairman in Tengwe, Hurungwe.
Invited by SWAPO and stayed there until 1995 (role not legible).
On returning to Zimbabwe, won the Hurungwe East seat in a by-election, and soon afterwards was appointed Governor and Resident Minister of Mashonaland West.
As governor, oversaw the Land Reform Programme in his province and was instrumental in the Magunje Irrigation Scheme, the Chiroti bridges and Hurungwe prison (dates garbled).
Ended his tenure as Governor and Resident Minister; that year became MP for Hurungwe North.
Was unanimously declared a National Hero by the ZANU-PF Politburo in recognition of his contribution to the country.
