summary: James Murozvi was born in Bikita and trained as a teacher before fleeing Rhodesian conscription to join ZANLA in 1975. He taught refugee children, trained as a soldier and in Tanzania, then led small units at the front and served in Gaza Province until independence. In the Zimbabwe National Army he held staff, brigade and intelligence posts, worked for General Zvinavashe, served as Defence Attache in London and rose to Brigadier General and Director General Defence Strategic Planning. He later headed war veterans' welfare at a ministry, died in April 2017 aged 60, and was survived by his wife Joyce, four children and two grandchildren.

timeline.text: While at teachers' college, was targeted by Rhodesian authorities for forced National Service, which pushed him towards the liberation fighters.
With other young men and women, slipped into Mozambique through Mount Selinda to join ZANLA.
Stayed briefly at Espungabera and Machasi, then at Chibawawa camps where he taught refugee children arriving daily across the border.
Selected for military training at Takawira 2 Camp in Chimoio, where he showed strong military ability.
Chosen for further training in the Songa Mbele group; sailed to Tanzania on the ship Mapinduzi, where he first met Charles Wekwete.
Took a Senior Tactics Course as one of 110 outstanding trainees, then returned to Mozambique with Wekwete and others to command small units at the front.

Reassigned to Gaza Province as a detachment security officer; at the ceasefire he was ordered to join a ZANLA force that stayed clandestinely in operational areas rather than going to assembly points.

Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army, posted to Army Headquarters as a General Staff Officer Grade 3, and the same year posted to the Grey's Scouts (now Mounted Regiment), among the first former guerrillas to join that white-dominated unit.
Selected for a 36-member group of former ZANLA officers sent for a pre-integration course at Inkomo Barracks and then Staff College Camberley in the UK.
Promoted to Captain and appointed Personal Staff Officer to the Chief of Staff, General Staff, then Major General Vitalis Zvinavashe.
Posted as Brigade Major at 2 Infantry Brigade, taking part in Operation Butterfly (Beira Corridor) and Operation Cobweb (Nyamapanda-Zobwe Corridor) to protect Zimbabwe's route to the sea.
Posted to the Directorate of Army Training as a General Staff Officer Grade 2, and promoted to Major on 1 March 1986.
Posted to the Military Intelligence Directorate as Staff Officer Grade 1 Evaluation; in intelligence work he helped ANC Umkhonto we Sizwe fighters move through Zimbabwe into South Africa.
Served as Personal Staff Officer to General Zvinavashe, first at Army Headquarters and, from 1994, at Zimbabwe Defence Forces Headquarters.
Received promotions in the mid-1990s, the later one to Colonel (dates garbled).
Appointed Defence Attache in the United Kingdom during tense relations over the Land Reform Programme.

Held posts as Director Operational Requirements, Deputy Commander of an infantry brigade, a staff officer at the National Defence College and from 2 February 2011 Director General Defence Strategic Planning.
Seconded to the Ministry of Welfare Services for War Veterans as Principal Director responsible for war veterans' welfare.
Collapsed outside his home and died on arrival at Westend Hospital, aged 60; his daughter had given birth that same night.

He later worked on the security of ZAPU leader Joshua Nkomo and survived an enemy attack in 1979. After independence he served in the police and the President's Department, then climbed the intelligence ranks to Assistant Director for the Western Region by 2013. He is portrayed as a humble, approachable leader despite his senior rank, and died in 2017 survived by his wife, eight children and six grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born in Gwanda District, Matabeleland South, the sixth child in his family.
Completed primary schooling at a school whose name is not legible.
Attended Mzinyathini Secondary School, then moved to Gwanda Secondary School for 1974 to 1975 and never finished Form Three.

Dropped out of school and crossed into Botswana to join ZIPRA, one of eight recruits (pupils and teachers) who left Gwanda on foot; he was based at Selebi Phikwe near Francistown, then moved to Nampundu base in Zambia under Ahmed Gutu.
Sent to Tanzania for eight months of basic military training at Mgagao and Morogoro under Sam Fakazi, alongside ZANLA recruits.
Deployed to Chakwenga Guerrilla Training Camp under Philip Valerio Sibanda, where he helped screen and vet recruits and provided security for the trainees.

Picked for specialist security and intelligence training (including VIP protection) in Varna, Bulgaria, serving as deputy commander and political commissar of a group led by John Pinda that became the core of ZAPU's National Security Organisation.
Returned from Bulgaria, served on the southern and eastern front, and was later recalled to Lusaka for security work around ZAPU leader Joshua Nkomo.
Survived an enemy attack on Nkomo's residence that aimed to harm the ZAPU leader and cripple the party (details partly legible).
Came home at Independence as part of a VIP protection team under Albert (surname not legible) and received a medal (name not legible) for his liberation-war contribution.

Transferred to Bulawayo.
Promoted to Security Aide I and later transferred to Masvingo Province (year of transfer cut off).
Promoted to Senior Security Aide in 1989 and Chief Security Aide in 1991, then sent to Chinhoyi as deputy head of the regional CSU unit.
Transferred from the CSU to a government protection division (GPS).
Took part in a war-veterans verification exercise, using his struggle experience and intelligence background to expose impostors, some of whom were imprisoned (timing not legible).
Promoted to District Intelligence Officer and moved from the GPS to an internal intelligence branch.
Rose to provincial intelligence posts in Matabeleland South, with a direct promotion on 4 June 2005, handling oversight duties there.
Promoted to Assistant Director for the Western Region, covering Matabeleland North and South, Bulawayo, Masvingo and the Midlands.
Died aged 57 according to the whole-page text; survived by his wife, eight children and six grandchildren.

summary: Godfrey Chidyausiku was born in 1947 near Domboshava and was among the first pupils at St Ignatius College before reading law at the University of Rhodesia. He became an advocate in 1973, helped found the African Bar Association, won the Highfield seat in 1974, defended jailed nationalists, and represented ZANU at the 1979 Lancaster House Talks. After independence he was an MP and deputy minister, then Attorney-General and finally Chief Justice, remembered as a fearless nationalist who defended the Constitution. He died in South Africa in May 2017 aged 70, survived by two wives and ten children.

timeline.text: Born at Domboshava, the seventh of eight children of Nyamayaro Chidyausiku and Shingaidzo Helen (nee Chiweshe).
Started at Mutake Primary School in Domboshava, then did Standards 2 to 6 at Makumbe Mission.
Attended St Ignatius College in Chishawasha as one of its pioneer students, a school set up for black pupils, and was made a prefect for his leadership qualities.
Studied Law at the University of Rhodesia, joined fellow students in protesting against Smith's 1965 UDI, and went into private legal practice after graduating.
Married Mary Machekera (six children) and became an advocate.
With Katsere, Edison Sithole, Wilson Sandura, Edison Zvobgo, Sylvester Maruza and others, formed the African Bar Association to tackle the legal problems faced by black lawyers and ordinary Africans.
Stood in the Rhodesian general election and won the Harare African Roll Constituency (Highfield).
Defended black political activists jailed by the colonial regime, among them Ushewokunze, Marere, Sithole, Tsvarai and Dr Munyaradzi.
Attended the Lancaster House Talks for ZANU, chosen for his legal qualifications and loyalty to the struggle.
Elected MP for Mashonaland East, which led to his appointment as Deputy Minister of Local Government and later further ministerial posts (partly legible).
Appointed Attorney-General.
Appointed Chief Justice of Zimbabwe by the President.
As head of the judiciary during the Land Reform Programme, was a firm defender of the Constitution and judicial independence, resisting pressure from outside critics (partly legible).
Died of liver and kidney complications at Morningside Clinic in South Africa, where he had been flown for treatment, aged 70.

Retirement age/date and other items on p.178 (a commission around 1992, a November 2009 item) are garbled and not recorded.

summary: N. K. Ndlovu, born in 1930 in Insiza District, trained in leatherwork and taught at several mission and community schools before giving up paid work in 1965 to commit fully to the liberation of Zimbabwe. He was active in successive nationalist parties from 1957, co-founded the Bulawayo United Residents Association, was detained several times including at Gonakudzingwa until 1968, and later served ZAPU's War Council, caring for cadres and refugees in Zambia and Angola. After independence he led ZAPU's Matabeleland South election campaign, held party posts, became a Luveve councillor and the first black Mayor of Bulawayo, and later sat in ZANU PF bodies. He died of prostate cancer on 29 May 2017 aged 86.

timeline.text: Born at Gwatemba in Filabusi, Insiza District, one of eight children of Khutshwekhaya Shamisi Ndlovu and Ndayeni Dube.
Started school at Majini Mission in Beitbridge, then attended Zezani, Gwatemba Primary (1940) and Wanezi Mission (1945 to 1947).
Studied leatherwork, tannery, English, geometry and building at Mzingwane Government Industrial School, a hub for the political awakening of African students, and earned a leatherwork certificate.
Began teaching at Zezani School, with later posts at another primary school (1953), Matopo Mission and Empandeni Mission.
Taught at Jairos Jiri Institution for the Disabled in Bulawayo, then gave up his paid job to commit fully to the liberation struggle.

Took part in the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress from its start, moving from trade unionism into mainstream politics, and married Betty Sibanda, a teacher from Matobo District (five children).
Joined the National Democratic Party as a card-carrying member after the earlier party was banned.
Co-founded the Bulawayo United Residents Association with Jason Moyo, Grey Bango and Senator Chief Mutasa and became its first chairman.
Offered himself and was elected to represent the Bulawayo African Townships when the white authorities created African Townships Advisory Boards (date not legible).
Detained and held at Gonakudzingwa Restriction Camp with other nationalist leaders, released in 1968.
Briefly detained for campaigning against the Pearce Commission proposals, then elected Vice President of the African National Congress after Canaan Banana had escaped the country (year not legible).
Detained for recruiting and feeding ZIPRA guerrillas, then re-arrested and held at Whawha after joining Pearce Commission protests.
Served on the ZAPU War Council, coordinating a programme to support revolutionary fighters and looking after refugees and trainees at camps such as Nampundwe Transit Camp.
After ZAPU camps in Zambia were closed following brutal attacks, visited surviving cadres, helped bury those killed, and visited camps in Angola to see to their welfare.
Returned to Zimbabwe after the Lancaster House Talks and chaired the Matabeleland South Elections Committee for ZAPU's campaign.
Selected to the ZAPU Central Committee, serving as Secretary for Transport and later Secretary for Welfare.
Elected Councillor for Luveve; his organising ability and discipline later saw him elected the first black Mayor of Bulawayo (year cut off).
Later served in ZANU PF structures, including the Politburo and the Central Committee (dates unclear).
Died of prostate cancer at his daughter's house in Bulawayo, aged 86.

notes: Heading not legible; name taken from p.178 text, and hero status is not printed in the available OCR (null).

summary: Shuvai Ben Mahofa, born in Masvingo Province, left a nursing course, met her husband Ben Mahofa in 1958, and joined nationalist politics in 1959 through the NDP, ZAPU and ZANU while running income-generating projects for African women. She worked as a community officer in Gutu and, during the war, as a collaborator who fed, treated and informed guerrillas and helped organise pungwes. After independence she was a Gutu councillor, the longest-serving MP for Gutu South, deputy minister in several ministries, a Senator, Minister of State for Masvingo, a Politburo member and Women's League leader. She was declared a national heroine, the ninth heroine to be interred at the National Heroes Acre, and was survived by four children and 27 grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born in Masvingo Province, the fifth of nine children (five girls and four boys).
Began primary school in 1948, then attended Muzobwi school (1950 to 1952) and a mission school for Standards 4 to 6.
Went to Morgenster Mission to train as a nurse but did not complete the course.
Met Ben Mahofa, then an agricultural extension officer in Zaka; the couple had six children.
Joined the National Democratic Party, later joined ZAPU after the ban, and in 1963 joined ZANU.
Worked with African women on income-generating projects, which led to her appointment as Provincial Coordinator for NGOs in Masvingo (then Fort Victoria), coordinating home-based women's activities.
Earned a Diploma in Community Development at Domboshava Training Centre.
Took a post in Gutu District reporting to the District Administrator (title partly legible), coordinating projects that empowered women for about two years.
Served as a war collaborator, supplying food and medical supplies, treating sick or injured fighters, passing on information about Rhodesian activity, helping move weapons and organising pungwes.
Elected Councillor for Tirizi Ward; she remained in local government work until 1984 (partly legible).
Elected MP for Gutu South, a seat she held for 23 years, earning the moniker Chikoforo (a cultivator).
Appointed Deputy Minister for Women's Affairs by President Mugabe, serving seven years.
Drafted into the Women's League National Executive as Secretary for Transport and Social Welfare and became a ZANU PF Central Committee member.
Became Deputy Minister for Political Affairs, a portfolio she held for five years.
Elected National Secretary for the Commissariat in the Women's League.
Assigned as Deputy Minister in the Gender and Youth Development Ministry.
Elected Senator for Gutu.
Appointed Minister of State for Masvingo Provincial Affairs, later drafted into the Politburo, and was Women's League Secretary for Security at her death.
Died; she was then declared a national heroine, the ninth heroine to be interred at the National Heroes Acre.

summary: George Rutanhire was born in Hwedza in 1949, attended St Albert's Mission in Mt Darwin and trained as a Catholic catechist before helping wounded Frelimo fighters and joining the armed struggle. A leg wound kept him from the front, so he did administrative and mobilisation work, represented ZANU in Sweden in 1974, and held political education roles for ZANLA cadres at Mgagao. After independence he was MP for Mashonaland Central, deputy minister for youth, party chief whip, a figure in the Unity Accord talks and in forming the war veterans association, and later a Politburo member. He died on 19 August 2017 of renal failure at Karanda Mission Hospital, survived by his wives and eight children.

timeline.text: Born Peter Clever Musanhu at Ruzane village in Hwedza and baptised in the Roman Catholic Church.
As a student at St Albert's Mission School in Mt Darwin, joined a hunger strike over ZANLA cadres in Chinhoyi (wording garbled; 1965 appears nearby).
Was taken by the Catholic Church to Hwange to train as a catechist, then returned to Mt Darwin and worked at Chimbuwe Centre.
Won the trust of Frelimo forces by helping wounded fighters recover in local homesteads, working with some local chiefs.
Joined the armed struggle; at Chifombo camp his main duties were political orientation and mobilising the masses, and he composed Chimurenga songs with comrades (partly legible).
Shot in the leg in a fierce battle; the bullet lodged in the bone and could not be removed, which kept him from returning to the front.
Part of a ZANU group in Sweden, working with sympathetic socialists to source material support for the struggle; met Dr Sekeramayi among students there.
Recalled to Mgagao by General Magama Tongogara, where he had political and ideology duties and composed a song (title partly legible).
With Cde Makudo and a few others, went to Tanzania to deliver the Mgagao Declaration to President Nyerere, with copies for other leaders.

Led trained cadres from Beira to Dar es Salaam (eight days on the ferry Chamachamapinduza), then led a group to joint training at Nachingwea, where he was arrested and imprisoned (wording garbled, linked to Ndabaningi Sithole's schemes).
Drafted and supervised a ZANLA campaign programme for the first elections, and was involved in a heroes trust effort to exhume and rebury comrades without decent burials (partly legible).
Elected MP for Mashonaland Central, a seat he held until 1985, and compiled Selected Speeches of Robert Gabriel Mugabe, published by Books for Africa in 1983.
Appointed Deputy Minister for Youth, Sport and Recreation and elected to the ZANU PF Central Committee.
Elected Party Chief Whip in Parliament and later played a part in the 1987 Unity Accord talks between ZANU and ZAPU.
Appointed ZANU PF Chairman for Mashonaland Central.
Held another ZANU PF post, legible only as Secretary for Gender and ... (title unclear).
Appointed again to a party post and later became a Politburo member, a position he held until his death (partly legible).
Died of renal failure at Karanda Mission Hospital in Mt Darwin; President Mugabe called him a giant of the struggle.

summary: Maria Msika was born in Botswana in 1928, schooled there, and moved to Zimbabwe to train at the Usher Institute, where she met and in 1946 married the future Vice President Joseph Msika. She backed his nationalist activism through years of harassment, his detention, and the loss of a young child, raising the family largely on her own. An industrious entrepreneur, she ran a fish and chips business in Bulawayo and taught women handicraft skills; her home was attacked with grenades in January 1977, leaving her with a permanent limp. She was survived by three children, eight grandchildren and ten great-grandchildren, and the Party and its Women's League agreed to confer heroine status on her.

timeline.text: Born in Botswana into a family of six children and grew up there.
Attended primary school at Tsesebe and a Catholic secondary school in Gaborone before relocating to Zimbabwe.
Enrolled at the Usher Institute in Matabeleland for professional training and met her future husband, who was teaching woodwork there.
Married Joseph Wilfred Msika in Tsamaya, Botswana.
Stood by her husband as he took up nationalist politics, and was harassed by the colonial administration from time to time while he was imprisoned.
Lost a two-year-old child while her husband was in detention (camp name reads like Gonakudzingwa) and bore the grief without him.
Raised the family largely alone through her own enterprise while her husband remained in detention.
Rhodesian forces targeted her family home in Pelandaba; she survived two grenade attacks, one of which injured her leg and left her with a permanent limp.
At independence she was an accomplished businesswoman running a well established fish and chips business she had founded in Bulawayo, alongside knitting and crocheting ventures.
Worked with Mama Mafuyana and others in a women's club in Mpopoma that taught handwork and helped women sell their goods at the City Hall and as far as Botswana.
After her death the then ZANU PF spokesperson, Cde Si... Moyo, described her as a courageous, humble and kind-hearted mother figure who left a legacy of dedication and patriotism.
ZANU PF and its Women's League unanimously agreed to confer heroine status on her in recognition of her role during and after the liberation struggle.

summary: Timothy John Stamps, born in Surrey in 1936, qualified as a doctor in Wales and moved to Rhodesia in 1968, rising to become Salisbury's Chief Medical Officer. He refused to follow racially discriminatory health policies and was dismissed in 1974, after which he worked on community health projects, joined the city council and helped fund rural clinics and hospitals in independent Zimbabwe. He later served as Minister of Health and Child Welfare and as a health adviser in the Office of the President and Cabinet, and was known for his stance on HIV/AIDS. He died on 26 November 2017, survived by his wife Cindy and his children and grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born in Surrey, the younger of two children of Edward Stamps and Winnifred Dunkley.
Admitted to study medicine at the Welsh National School of Medicine.
Finished his medical degree and began a two-year period of practical hospital training, completed in 1959.
Registered as a medical practitioner, among the youngest doctors in the United Kingdom at that time.
Married Elizabeth Craig Raby; the couple had children, including one they adopted.
Left the UK for colonial Rhodesia to join its Public Health Service, partly because he opposed performing abortions that British law required of him.
Appointed Deputy City Health Medical Officer for Salisbury and rose through the ranks.
Became Salisbury's Chief Medical Officer.
Clashed with the racist authorities when he tried to extend health facilities to marginalised black people, and was victimised as a result.
Dismissed as Chief Medical Officer after resisting a directive to discriminate against black patients; in the same year he earned a law degree at the University of Rhodesia.
Worked in community health projects and chaired the UN-sponsored Freedom from Hunger campaign.
Elected to the Salisbury City Council; around this time he and his wife Elizabeth separated.
Raised funds abroad to build clinics and community hospitals in rural Zimbabwe, working closely with the Ministry of Health.
Married Cindy Elaine Willis, daughter of Ronald Willis, a district officer he had met while on the city council.
Became patron of a Zimbabwean trust (name and purpose garbled in the OCR).
Served as Minister of Health and Child Welfare (appointment years not legible) and campaigned against the spread of HIV/AIDS.
Died of a lung infection at Borrowdale Trauma Centre.

summary: John Chimbandi was born in Wedza in 1951 and studied in Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland before leaving a school job to join the liberation struggle, training militarily and reaching the front in 1973. He became a political commissar and then ZANU PF's chief representative for East Africa in Dar-es-Salaam. After independence he spent decades in the foreign service, including postings in Bonn, Beijing, Tehran and finally as Consul General in Beira, continuing his career despite a health setback that paralysed his left side. He died on 2 June 2018, survived by his wife Leocardia and three children, and the Politburo declared him a National Hero.

timeline.text: Born at Zviyambe in Wedza to Anna and Martin Chimbandi.
Completed his secondary schooling (years read from damaged text).
Studied at the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland and earned a degree that included Political Science.
Began his working life at a school in Botswana (post partly illegible), then left to join the intensifying liberation struggle and received military training.
Deployed to the war front after his training and rose through the ranks.
Served as Field Operations and Camps Political Commissar.
Appointed ZANU PF Chief Representative for East Africa (Tanzania, Kenya, Madagascar, Uganda, Burundi, Rwanda) at the OAU Liberation Committee in Dar-es-Salaam, mobilising funds and political backing.
Part of the delegation to the Pan-African Conference in Arusha, Tanzania, on the plight of African refugees.
Joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as Assistant Secretary for Africa and the Middle East and coordinated policy on liberation movements such as the ANC, SWAPO and PLO.
Married Leocardia, whom he met in 1980; they had three children.
Acting Under Secretary for Administration and Finance.
Studied at Oxford and obtained a postgraduate diploma in International Relations.
Under Secretary for the Non-Aligned Movement Secretariat.
Minister Counsellor at the Zimbabwe Embassy in Bonn, Germany.
Minister Counsellor at the Zimbabwe Embassy in Beijing, China, after posts as Under Secretary for international organisations and for policy and research.
Minister Counsellor at the Zimbabwe Embassy in Tehran, Iran.
Deputy Director of the Americas Department in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Consul General at the Zimbabwe Consulate in Beira, Mozambique, until retiring at the end of September 2017.
Died after battling chronic lung disease and an enlarged heart; the ZANU PF Politburo declared him a National Hero.

summary: Thokozile Mathuthu came into politics through the ZAPU Youth Wing in the 1970s, supporting guerrillas as a collaborator while working in clerical and teaching jobs, and married Jonathan Mathuthu in 1977. After independence she rose through the ZAPU and then ZANU PF women's structures, helped with the Unity Accord process, and served as Governor and Resident Minister of Matabeleland North from 2005 to 2013, reportedly its longest-serving governor. She later served as Deputy Minister for Information, Media and Broadcasting Services and ZANU PF Deputy Secretary for Women's Affairs, and was studying at the Zimbabwe Open University when she died of cancer in 2018. She was declared a National Heroine and was survived by her husband and four children.

timeline.text: Attended primary school and then went on to secondary education (years read from damaged text).
While working as a temporary teacher, met the harsh Rhodesian policies of low wages for blacks, racist recruitment and placement, and general disenfranchisement.
Joined the ZAPU Youth Wing committee and became a war collaborator, risking her life to help freedom fighters.
Married Jonathan Mathuthu; the couple had four children, two boys and two girls.
Working as a wages clerk at a mine, she passed on information and fed fighters, and helped house and supply ZIPRA comrades until the 1979 ceasefire.
After independence served on the committee of the Kamativi ZAPU Women's League.
Deputy Chairperson of the ZAPU Women's Wing for Nengasha District in Hwange.
Played a part in the task force that drove the integration of PF ZAPU and ZANU, leading to the Unity Accord.
Secretary for Administration in the Provincial Women's League of Matabeleland North and part of the committee dealing with the separation of Matabeleland and Bulawayo provinces.
District Coordinator for ZANU PF Hwange District, then National Executive Women's League Secretary for Transport and Social Welfare (1997-1999).
Deputy Secretary (2000) and then Secretary (2005) for Transport and Social Welfare in the Politburo.
Provincial Governor and Resident Minister for Matabeleland North, overseeing projects such as Lupane State University and the Bubi-Lupane Dam.
Served on the Constitutional Parliamentary Committee (COPAC).
Took part in a delegation to Shanghai in 2011 and in March 2012 led a delegation to China for a leadership training course; became ZANU PF Provincial Chairperson for Matabeleland North in 2012.
Secretary for Transport and Social Welfare in the Women's League and Secretary for Gender and Culture in the Politburo; Deputy Chairperson of the Pan African Parliament in 2015.
Appointed Deputy Minister for Information, Media and Broadcasting Services and helped drive the broadcasting digitalisation programme.

summary: Phinias Makhurane, born in Gwanda in 1939, studied Physics and Mathematics in Salisbury and became the first black Zimbabwean to obtain a science PhD, at Sheffield. He taught and led departments at the University of Zambia and the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland, then held senior posts at the University of Zimbabwe and became NUST's Vice-Chancellor in 1991. He chaired many national and regional education and research bodies, including ZIMSEC, SIRDC and ZIMCHE, and wrote an autobiography. He died on 1 December 2018, survived by his wife Lydia, four children and six grandchildren, and was declared a National Hero by the Politburo.

timeline.text: Born in the Gungwe area of Gwanda, the last of nine children of Likeleli Galabwe (nee Moyo) and Mvomoli Tsukuta Makhurane.
Began secondary school at Mnene and moved the same year to Chegato High School.
Transferred to Zimuto High School and then Fletcher High School, where he finished secondary school and was among the first Lower Sixth pupils.
Enrolled at the Rhodesia and Nyasaland University (now University of Zimbabwe) to study Physics and Mathematics and met Lydia Madaila Tlou.
Married Lydia Madaila Tlou.
Went to Sheffield University in the UK, earning a Master's in Physics and Chemistry and a doctorate in Solid State Physics within 39 months, the first black Zimbabwean science PhD.
Took up a post at the University of Zambia and was involved with a committee of the International University Exchange Fund, which raised Scandinavian money for Southern African students.
Left the University of Zambia for the Botswana campus of the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland as senior lecturer and reader in Physics.
After chairing the physics department and serving as Dean of Applied Science, was Deputy Rector of the university.
After Zimbabwe's independence, joined the University of Zimbabwe as Deputy Vice-Chancellor (year not legible).
Became Vice-Chancellor of NUST and led its growth into a centre of excellence, helping shape its master plan and physics facilities.
Appointed by President Mugabe as technical advisor to the Minister of Higher and Tertiary Education (wording garbled).
Chaired the Scientific and Industrial Research and Development Centre (SIRDC); in 2005 also took over the Edward Ndlovu Memorial Library Board of Trustees.
Received honours including honorary doctorates, a Presidential Certificate of Distinction for science and technology education, and fellowship of the Zimbabwe Academy of Sciences.
Died of diabetes and hypertension at Mater Dei Hospital in Bulawayo; the Politburo declared him a National Hero.

summary: Oliver 'Tuku' Mtukudzi, born in 1952 into a musical family, began recording in 1975 and became one of Africa's best-known musicians through the Black Spirits and his distinctive blend of traditional and modern styles, reaching more than sixty albums according to the book. He also composed for film, founded an arts centre in Norton, worked as a philanthropist and activist, and served as a UNICEF regional goodwill ambassador. He collected many local and international awards and honorary degrees. He died on 23 January 2019, survived by his wife Daisy and four children, and became the first musician declared a National Hero.

timeline.text: Born to Samson Mtukudzi and Jessica Mudarikwa of Madziva, the eldest of six children.
Grew up in a musical household where both parents sang, and his father's early death gave him a strong sense of responsibility as the first-born.
At age 23 released his debut single 'Stop after Orange'.
Joined the Wagon Wheels band alongside other noted musicians after becoming acquainted with Thomas Mapfumo in a Harare studio.
Released a hit single (title garbled, begins 'Dzan...') inspired by black people's hardships under white rule during the Second Chimurenga, and used his music to spread revolutionary messages.
Formed the Black Spirits and released the hit album 'Ndipeiwo Zano'.
Added a keyboard to his sound under the influence of South African producer West Nkosi and blended traditional and modern styles into his own distinctive music.
Split from the Black Spirits for two years and sang with other groups such as the Zig Zag Band in Kwekwe.
Won an M-Net award for best soundtrack for the film Neria.
Released an album (title not legible) that went to the top of Zimbabwe's music charts in its first week.
Won a KORA Award for best African male artist and a lifetime achievement award, plus a University of Zimbabwe honorary Arts degree.
Founded an arts centre in Norton (name begins 'Pak...') to nurture young artistes.
Appointed UNICEF Regional Goodwill Ambassador for Eastern and Southern Africa, campaigning for children's rights and against AIDS stigma.
Honoured by the Government of Italy with the Cavaliere of the Order of Merit.
Received honorary doctorates from the International Institute of Philanthropy and from Great Zimbabwe University.
Died at Avenues Clinic in Harare after a long illness with diabetes.
President Mnangagwa announced the unanimous decision to confer National Hero status, making him Zimbabwe's first musician to receive it.

summary: Callistus Ndlovu (1936-2019) was a nationalist, academic and politician from the Plumtree area who studied at Empandeni and in Lesotho. He joined the NDP and ZAPU, earned a Master's in History in New York and represented ZAPU at the United Nations while teaching at American universities. After independence he served as MP, Minister, Senator and ZANU-PF provincial chairman and later headed Zipam. He died in South Africa in 2019 and was declared a National Hero.

timeline.text: Born in the Plumtree area, the eldest of four children.

After primary school ending in 1953, studied at Empandeni Secondary School, where he met future national hero Tarcissius Silundika, who encouraged his academic and political aspirations; he then trained as a teacher at Empandeni.
Joined the National Democratic Party when it was formed.
Joined ZAPU after the NDP was banned.
Won a scholarship to study at Pius XII University College in Lesotho, rallied fellow students to nationalist politics and was elected chairman of the ZAPU students and residents branch there.
Elected President of the Student Representative Council for a year, organising protests against racial discrimination and repressive laws.
Became Secretary for Publicity of the National Union of the Basutoland Students.
Graduated with a BA in History, returned to Bulawayo to teach at Empandeni, Mafakela and Mpopoma High Schools, and was held for 90 days at Khami Prison.
Left Rhodesia to study in New York, earning a Master's in History, and was elected ZAPU chairman (location garbled) in late 1967.
Joined the board of directors of the Encyclopaedia Africana and became an Associate Professor of History at City University of New York, after a professorship at a Long Island university.

Became a member of ZAPU's Revolutionary Council and its representative to the United Nations and North America, setting up an office near UN headquarters that coordinated external relations and supplies for combatants.
Granted Freedom of the City of Minneapolis (1972); the following year received a distinguished-teaching award and the Agrey Fellowship of the Edward Hazen Foundation.
Attended the Geneva Conference as chief political advisor to ZAPU, and later the 1979 Lancaster House conference that led to independence.
Returned home and was elected Member of Parliament for Mzingwane, a seat held until 1985; he later joined the ZAPU Central Committee.
Served as a Minister: a first portfolio from 1982 (name illegible), Mines from 1983, then Industry and Technology from 1984 to 1989; also elected ZANU-PF chairman for Matabeleland North.
Appointed a Senator.
After the Unity Accord, elected a member of the ZANU-PF Central Committee.
Executive consultant with the Treger Group and member of a private-sector committee promoting Zimbabwe-Botswana trade; in 1995 became chief executive of Calding Consultants.
Director-General of the Zimbabwe Institute of Public Administration and Management (Zipam); also chaired the foundation taskforce for Gwanda State University.
Died in South Africa; the ZANU-PF Politburo unanimously declared him a National Hero.

Worked as a teacher after leaving school.

Crossed into Mozambique with other cadres via the Gonarezhou-Mapai-Barragem-Xai-Xai route and reached the Xai-Xai ZANLA Transit Camp.
Given the task of setting up a special school for refugee children, mostly Shangani, which ran until it was moved to Tete Province.
Served on the base administration at Matenje Base, which later became (name garbled) an institution linked to the Chitepo School of Ideology.
Integrated into the Zimbabwe National Army and commissioned as an officer, later rising through Lieutenant Colonel and Colonel to Brigadier General (dates garbled).
Held staff and directorate posts, including Directing Staff and Chief Instructor roles at the Zimbabwe Staff College and a directorship in public / civil-military relations (details garbled).
Attended a command and staff course in Nigeria and other courses at the Zimbabwe Military Academy and Staff College (1980s, dates garbled).

Received the Independence, Liberation, Service and Long and Exemplary Service medals plus campaign medals for Mozambique and the DRC (Operation Sovereign Legitimacy); an Order of Merit award is also mentioned.
Died at West End Hospital after a short illness; the Politburo unanimously accorded him National Hero status.

summary: Misheck Velaphi (1937-2019) was a teacher-trainee who was politicised at Howard Training Institute and left teaching for full-time activism, joining the NDP in 1960. He trained in Egypt, helped bring the first weapons into Rhodesia from Congo in 1966, and was later jailed for seven years, meeting Emmerson Mnangagwa in prison. After release he worked as a ZIPRA intelligence officer, took part in the talks that led to the 1987 Unity Accord and held ZANU-PF posts in Bulawayo. He was accorded National Hero status after dying in 2019.

timeline.text: Born at Mambale, Seula Village, the eldest in a family of five.
Began primary school in 1946, completed Standard Four at Samanyoni School and did Standard Six at Cyrene Mission School.
Enrolled for teacher training at Howard Training Institute, Mazowe, where teachers and nationalists such as James Chikerema and George Nyandoro stirred his political interest.
Joined other politically conscious youths meeting at Stanley Square, Bulawayo, to discuss how to win freedom, believing no one would free them but themselves.
Quit the Institute and teaching for full-time politics after a racial insult (being herded into a table-manners lesson), walking out and never going back.
Joined the National Democratic Party and took part in the 'Zhii' uprising in Bulawayo, which left 12 people dead and convinced him the regime could only be removed militarily.
Went to Zambia for a year, where he and eleven other cadres taught each other to handle guns and guerrilla tactics.
Underwent six months of military training in Egypt; after the NDP ban he sought weapons in Tanzania without success, then went to Kenya to consult Joshua Nkomo.
With colleagues raided Congolese rebels in Congo, drugging them and taking their guns, bombs and ammunition: the first weapons brought into Rhodesia and the start of the armed struggle.
Repeatedly crossed the Zambezi to source weapons and helped run a logistics office in Bulawayo to receive and distribute them.

Arrested with weapons and explosives and sentenced to seven years, held at Khami Prison where he met Emmerson Mnangagwa; kept in a shack in isolation for 36 months, then moved to Gwelo (until 1972), Gonakudzingwa and Salisbury prisons.
Released after outwitting security officers; from 1974 to 1977 worked as an intelligence officer for ZIPRA.
Sent by PF ZAPU on ceasefire-related duties (wording garbled) and worked in its electoral directorate sourcing campaign material.
Worked as an accountant at a veterans' investment holdings firm, later becoming a housing officer with Bulawayo City Council.
Played a pivotal role in the peace talks that led to the Unity Accord, then worked to build ZANU-PF party structures.
Died at United Bulawayo Hospitals; the Politburo unanimously agreed to accord him National Hero status.

summary: Dumiso Dabengwa (1939-2019), nicknamed The Black Russian, was born in Tsholotsho, worked as a teacher and bank employee, then joined the NDP and ZAPU and trained in Moscow in 1964. He headed ZIPRA's intelligence division during the liberation war, was jailed after independence but acquitted, and joined ZANU-PF after the 1987 Unity Accord, serving as Home Affairs Minister from 1992 to 2000. He left ZANU-PF in 2008 to revive ZAPU and founded a development foundation. He died in 2019 on his way home from India and was accorded National Hero status.

timeline.text: Born at Mavela, Tsholotsho, the second child in a family of eight.
Attended Mavela Primary School and Emzingwane Secondary School, then taught at Phakame School before taking a job with Barclays Bank in Bulawayo.
Joined the NDP and, after its ban, ZAPU; his youth-league activism led to repeated harassment and arrests.
Moved to Zambia to mobilise for the liberation struggle and met his future wife Zodwa Khumalo; they married in Bulawayo in August 1980.
Part of one of two groups of ZAPU cadres sent to Moscow for training, where he gained military and security-intelligence skills and the nickname 'The Black Russian'.
Took part in early armed-struggle battles of 1967/68 (campaign names garbled).
Headed ZIPRA's intelligence division during the war and cooperated with ZANLA and Umkhonto weSizwe; at one point helped Robert and Sally Mugabe escape Rhodesia via Botswana on their way to Ghana.
Arrested and jailed with Lookout Masuku and others on treason charges, but acquitted.
Persuaded by Joshua Nkomo to join ZANU-PF in the spirit of the Unity Accord.
Appointed to chair a Matabeleland water project (name partly garbled).
Served as Minister of Home Affairs for eight years.
Lost a House of Assembly contest as a ZANU-PF candidate in 2000 and was defeated again in the March 2005 parliamentary election.
Announced support for Simba Makoni's presidential candidacy at a Bulawayo press conference and the same year left ZANU-PF to revive ZAPU.
Founded the Dumiso Dabengwa Foundation, a non-profit promoting an alternative model of development cooperation (year not legible).
Died while travelling from India to Zimbabwe after a liver-related illness; the Politburo unanimously accorded him National Hero status.

summary: Njini Ntuta (1924-1984) was a Tsholotsho-born nationalist who worked in a tannery, where he met Joshua Nkomo and was drawn into politics. His activism led to detention, after which he set up a shoe-making business in Bulawayo. He later helped lead local opposition to the Pearce Commission settlement proposals, and after independence became MP for Tsholotsho and a Deputy Minister before dying in 1984.

timeline.text: Born in the Tsholotsho Communal Land.
Completed Standard Six after attending St Ninians Primary School and Tsholotsho Government School.
Took up tannery training or work at Mavela, Tsholotsho, the kind of skilled work open to Africans at the time.
At the tannery met Joshua Nkomo, who helped shape his nationalist outlook; he became actively involved in nationalist politics.
Arrested and detained by Rhodesian security because of his political activities; finished his education privately while detained.
On release from detention moved to Luveve, Bulawayo, and ran an informal shoe-making business for about five years (date doubtful).
Played a leading role in the campaign against the Pearce Commission's testing of the settlement proposals (surrounding text garbled; possibly detained again).
Elected Member of Parliament for Tsholotsho and served on parliamentary committees.
Appointed Deputy Minister of Mines (and another portfolio, garbled), apparently serving about two years (reading uncertain).
Died four years after independence, survived by his wife Emily and children.

Qualified as a builder while at Mzingwane Government School, then worked in and around Bulawayo, where he found his political calling.
Elected Chairman of the Bulawayo Branch of the Artisans' Union; the next year he became its President and stayed on for another eight years.

Detained at Gonakudzingwa alongside Joshua Nkomo and Joseph Msika on political charges, then moved to Camp 5 and restricted in isolation because the regime feared he would urge young restrictees to take up arms; used the time to pass A-levels and earn a BA by correspondence.
After release, resumed politics and joined the ANC Central Committee.
Elected Organising Secretary of the ANC at the Victoria Falls talks.

summary: Trust Mugoba, who fought as Cde Joseph Zulu, grew up in Mberengwa and Chivhu and joined ZANLA in Mozambique in 1977 at about 18. He trained as a medic, became an instructor and commander who trained over 7000 recruits, and after independence rose through infantry, parachute and staff posts to Major General. He commanded the Eastern Front in the DRC and from 2017 served as Chief of Staff of the Africa Standby Force at the African Union in Addis Ababa until his death. The Politburo accorded him National Hero status.

timeline.text: Primary schooling at Chipinda (Mberengwa), Rambakurimwa (Chivhu) and Chabwira (Mberengwa) primary schools, then Chegato Secondary School; his father had bought a farm at Wiltshire, Chivhu in 1964.
At about 18, crossed into Mozambique through Malvernia (Gaza Province) and reached Xai-Xai as a recruit.
Moved to the ZANLA camp at Chimoio, trained as a medic and completed basic military training at Takawira Training Camp.
Served as a medic at Chimoio Headquarters and survived the Rhodesian Army raid on the camp, then was briefly deployed on operations in Zimbabwe.
Detachment Medic at Mudzingadzi Base, then went to Tanzania for further training and was appointed an instructor for his performance.
Appointed Detachment Commander at Mavonde Operational Base; ten days later was in an accident at Chicamba Dam while leading 76 men to Zimbabwe and was hospitalised at Chimoio until February 1980.
Instructor at Mavhonde Training Camp (moved to Inhaminga in April and Samakweza in August 1980), training over 7000 cadres; then Battalion Commander until June 1981.
Posted to 404 Infantry Battalion as Battalion Second-in-Command; from 1982 a quartermaster staff officer (transport) at Army Headquarters.
Promoted Captain, qualified through Parachute Regiment training, and became Commanding Officer of 2 Parachute Battalion (December), moving to 1 Parachute Battalion in November 1985.
Promoted Substantive Major and Temporary Lieutenant Colonel (March 1986), becoming Substantive Lieutenant Colonel in July 1987.
Deputy Commander Parachute Group (1988), Deputy Director then Director Army Training (1990-91), Commander Parachute Group (February 1992) and promoted Colonel (June 1992).
Director Policy and Public Relations at ZDF Headquarters (January), Commander 1 Infantry Brigade (September) and promoted Brigadier General (October).
Commanded the Eastern Front in the DRC during Operation Sovereign Legitimacy.
Posted to ZDF Headquarters as Director General Operations and Plans.
Appointed Director General Policy, Public Relations and Protocol; promoted Major General in October (year not legible).
Appointed Chief of General Staff at defence headquarters; in this period commanded the SADC special forces exercise at Mahombekombe, Kariba, and later that year Exercise AFRICA II in South Africa.
Seconded to African Union Headquarters as Chief of Staff of the Africa Standby Force in Addis Ababa, a post held until his death.
Awarded the Liberation, Independence, Service, Long and Exemplary Service, Mozambique Campaign and DRC Campaign medals and a Grand Officer Order of Merit award.
Died at a Harare clinic after a short illness; the Politburo unanimously accorded him National Hero status.

summary: Robert Mugabe began as a mission-educated teacher who worked in Zambia and Ghana before entering nationalist politics through the NDP, ZAPU and ZANU. He spent about a decade in Rhodesian detention, then left for Mozambique in 1975 to lead ZANU's armed struggle. After winning the 1980 election he served as Prime Minister and from the 1987 Unity Accord as Executive President until he resigned in November 2017. The book highlights his education drive, pan-African and non-aligned diplomacy and the 2000 land reform, and records his death in Singapore in September 2019.

timeline.text: Born at Kutama Mission in Zvimba to a carpenter father and a mother known affectionately as Mbuya Bona; raised in a strongly Catholic mission community.
Qualified as a teacher and taught at a number of local schools before going to South Africa to study.
Graduated with a Bachelor of Arts from Fort Hare, where he met politically conscious students from across the region and learned of decolonisation politics.
Taught at Chalimbana Teacher Training College in Zambia, then at Takoradi and Apowa in Ghana, where he met Sally Hayfron and was influenced by Nkrumah's Ghana.
After the arrest of NDP leaders including Leopold Takawira, joined a large Highfield march to Salisbury and the next day addressed a crowd of about 40 000.
Resigned from his Ghana teaching contract after two years to enter active politics and was elected to the NDP leadership as publicity secretary, becoming a noted orator.
After the NDP was banned he joined ZAPU in a senior role and was then involved in founding ZANU in 1963.
ZANU and ZAPU were banned and their leaders arrested; Mugabe was held from August 1964 to December 1974 at Salisbury, Wha Wha and Sikombela, studying for several degrees by correspondence.
His young son Nhamodzenyika died of cerebral malaria in Ghana and the Rhodesian authorities refused him permission to attend the funeral.
Released from prison, he escaped into Mozambique with Edgar Tekere, helped by Father Emmanuel Ribeiro, to revive the armed struggle and lead ZANLA.
ZANU won 57 of the 80 seats in the independence election under the Lancaster House agreement; Mugabe became first Prime Minister and formed a national unity government pursuing reconciliation.
Declared education a basic human right, leading to a major expansion of primary and secondary schooling.
A Non-Aligned Movement summit was held in Harare and he became chair of the movement; he was also active in the Front Line States and the Africa Fund.
Signed the Unity Accord with PF-ZAPU leader Joshua Nkomo, creating ZANU-PF; a week later he became Executive President with Nkomo and Simon Muzenda as vice presidents.
Received the World Freedom Against Hunger award and the Africa Prize for Leadership for the sustainable end of hunger, using the prize money to start an agricultural scholarship fund.
His first wife, Sally, died of a kidney ailment.
Rolled out the Land Reform Programme to correct the colonial land tenure imbalance; the book says Western sanctions followed and hampered development.
Served as chairperson of the African Union, urging Africa to be more assertive and to fund its own institutions.
Resigned as President of Zimbabwe after a long political career.
Died in Singapore after a long illness; leaders from Kenya, Russia and Tanzania were among those who paid tribute, and he was accorded national hero status.

summary: Crispan Masuku, known in the struggle as Kid Manzini, was raised in Matabeleland North and joined the liberation war, training in Zambia and Libya, where he specialised in armour. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army and rose from staff officer posts to Brigadier General, serving in logistics, as a diplomat abroad and as General Quartermaster at Army Headquarters. He ended his career as General Manager of Zimbabwe Defence Industries. He died in Bulawayo in May 2020 and was declared a national hero, with a long list of campaign and service medals.

timeline.text: Born in 1958 (year taken from the heading); grew up in Matabeleland North and began primary school in Lupane District.

Was part of a group of about 300 sent to Libya for further military training, specialising in armour.
Completed the Commanders Course, went back to Freedom Camp in Zambia and that same month was moved to the Gwaai River Mine assembly point for the ceasefire programme.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army after independence.
Attended the Company Commanders Course at the Zimbabwe Military Academy.
Completed the Intermediate Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Completed the Command and Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Appointed ordnance staff officer at the rank of Lieutenant Colonel.
Later promoted to Colonel, posted to Defence Forces headquarters in a logistics directorate, then sent on a diplomatic assignment in Africa during which he was promoted to Brigadier General.
Returned from his diplomatic posting and was appointed General Quartermaster at Army Headquarters.
Seconded to Zimbabwe Defence Industries as General Manager, a post he held until his death.
Died at United Bulawayo Hospitals and was buried at Lady Stanley Cemetery in Bulawayo.

summary: Absalom Sikhosana was born in Matobo District and became politically aware as a student in Bulawayo. He worked in the clothing industry and trade unions while active in the ZAPU Youth Wing, went to Zambia for military training in 1977, and after independence worked in municipal unions and later in the ZANU PF Youth League. He helped bring the ZANU PF and PF ZAPU structures together after the 1987 Unity Accord and held party posts up to Politburo level and acting Bulawayo provincial chairman. He died in Bulawayo in May 2020 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Matobo District under Chief Gareth Nzula Masuku, the fifth of six children.
Attended several primary schools, then began secondary school in Bulawayo in 1965 where he came to see the injustices of colonial education.
Left school and worked as a tally clerk at the Bulawayo clothing factory; joined the ZAPU Youth Wing and helped mobilise people to reject the Pearce Proposals.
Elected administration secretary of the ZAPU Mpopoma branch and worked as a regional organiser in the clothing workers union.
After a senior nationalist was detained he became ZAPU secretary general for his region and helped recruit people for the liberation war; he was repeatedly arrested and harassed by the Smith regime.
Exposed by informers, he left the country with others for military training in Zambia and was then assigned to ZAPU's Trade Union Department.
Remained in Zambia until independence, surviving Rhodesian attacks on ZAPU camps.
After demobilisation joined the Bulawayo Municipal Workers Union as Organising Secretary.
Served on the task force overseeing the ZANU PF and PF ZAPU merger and helped unite the two parties' structures.
Elected Secretary for Youth, Publicity and Information of the ZANU PF Youth League at its inaugural national youth conference.
Seconded to Public Services International headquarters in Switzerland as education coordinator for English-speaking Africa.
Returned home after the Switzerland posting.
Served as Deputy Secretary of the Youth League under the late Air Marshal Josiah Tungamirai.
Appointed ZANU PF National Secretary for Youth Affairs in the Politburo, earning the nickname Cde Headmaster.
Nominated to stand as a senator.
Moved from the Youth League to become Deputy Secretary for Implementation of Indigenisation Policy in the Politburo.
Appointed acting Chairman of Bulawayo Metropolitan Province, serving until his death.
Died at United Bulawayo Hospitals and was declared a national hero.

summary: Perrance Shiri left school in Wedza at 18 to join the liberation war, trained in Zambia and Tanzania and rose to become overall ZANLA commander in Tete Province, known for the Mahuwe ambush and the 1978 bombing of fuel tanks in Salisbury. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army, founded 5 Brigade and moved to the Air Force of Zimbabwe in 1984, eventually reaching Air Chief Marshal. After retiring he farmed, promoted Command Agriculture and served as Minister of Lands, Agriculture and Rural Resettlement, helping to negotiate the farmers' compensation deal just before his death on 29 July 2020. The book also records Western sanctions and a 2008 assassination attempt.

timeline.text: Born in Chikomba, Mashonaland East, to Titus and Annotolia, in a large family.
Went to primary school in the Wedza area and then secondary school where he met future Vice President Constantino Chiwenga and became his friend.
At 18, left school with Chiwenga across the border to join the liberation war; trained in Zambia and then at Mgagao camp in Tanzania.
Finished military training, was appointed to a general staff post and assigned as an instructor at Mgagao.
Became overall commander of ZANLA forces in Tete Province, taking over from Cde Mhuru, and led newly trained cadres into Rhodesia.
Planned the Mahuwe ambush, a four-day battle that was a heavy blow to Rhodesian forces and led to the capture of a white District Commissioner.
Led missions including the bombing of oil tanks in Salisbury, which hurt the Rhodesian economy and war effort.
Sent to Romania for a nine-month Artillery Battle Commander's Course.
Commanded the Alpha, Bravo and Charlie assembly points during the ceasefire.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as Joint High Command Liaison Officer at 4 Brigade headquarters in Masvingo.
Posted as Deputy Commander of 2 Brigade in Harare and later that year as founder-commander of 5 Brigade.
Promoted to Brigadier.
Transferred to the Air Force of Zimbabwe at the equivalent rank of Air Commodore as Director General Supporting Services, to help address command problems there.
Played a significant role in the Zimbabwean military deployment in the DRC conflict while serving in senior air force posts (details garbled).
After EU travel sanctions over his support for land acquisition, US President George W. Bush ordered his US property blocked.
Survived an attempt on his life after the June 2008 election.
After retiring from the air force farmed successfully and championed Command Agriculture, then became Minister of Lands, Agriculture and Rural Resettlement, also earning two masters degrees.
Played a pivotal role in the negotiated US$3.5 billion compensation deal with white farmers signed under the President two days before he died.
Died after a short illness; President Mnangagwa paid tribute to him as a stalwart ZANLA commander and he was declared a national hero.

summary: Ruphus Chigudu, known in the war as Mise Chombo, was born in Rusape District in 1955 and schooled locally and at Bernard Mizeki College. An arrest during a 1972 protest and racism at a Bulawayo company pushed him to leave for Mozambique in 1976, where he survived exposure to chemical and biological agents at Doroi, taught cadres, trained at Tembwe and became a platoon commander in Tete. After independence he served as an army officer with several staff and college postings and reached the rank of Brigadier General. He died on 24 September 2020 aged 64 and the Politburo agreed to confer national hero status on him.

timeline.text: Born in Rusape District as the second child of Matthew and Mary Chigudu (nee Mapanga) and raised at Chigudu Village in the Chiendambuya communal area under Chief Makoni.
Attended Chigudu Primary School from Sub A to Standard 6.
Did his secondary schooling at Bernard Mizeki College, where he first became exposed to liberation-struggle politics.
Was arrested in Marondera for demonstrating against the Rhodesian government after a senior nationalist died in detention, then released and went back to school.
After Ordinary Level he went to Bulawayo and worked as a Plant Operator at Rhodox Private Limited, where he saw racist policies favouring white employees.
Left Bulawayo with friends and crossed into Mozambique through Nyakomba in Nyanga, briefly staying at Guru under FRELIMO before being sent on to Chimoio.
Was moved to Doroi Camp, where he and comrades were exposed to Rhodesian chemical and biological agents (including anthrax) and close to twenty comrades died, but he soldiered on.
Was later transferred to the Chindunduma school camp at Chimoio, where he taught young cadres the ideals of the liberation struggle.
Transferred to Tembwe Base in Tete for rigorous basic military training.
Deployed to Chaminuka Sector in Tete Province under Detachment Commander Muchineripi Mabhunu and rose to Platoon Commander through courage and commitment.
Listed as attending a Company Group Commander's Course (post-independence army career, details of early commissioning garbled).
Attended the Intermediate Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Promoted to the rank of Major and posted to the Zimbabwe Staff College, where he served as Directing Staff on the Junior Division.
Took the Joint Command and Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Died aged 64; the Politburo then agreed to confer national hero status in recognition of his contribution.

summary: Collin Moyo, nom de guerre Nyika, was born in Mberengwa in 1954 and left the country in his teens after experiencing colonial forced labour. He trained with ZIPRA at Morogoro in Tanzania, stayed on as an instructor for over 5000 recruits, and later served as a regional commander and Northern Front commander directing large forces from Zambia. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army, held staff and command posts up to Colonel and Brigadier General, and later worked in the President's Office. He died in January 2021 aged 66 and was declared a national hero, holding nine medals for his service.

timeline.text: Born in Mberengwa, Midlands Province, the second child in a large family.
Did primary schooling in Mberengwa and Ordinary Level at Chegato Secondary School.
Pushed by forced labour and other colonial injustices he had experienced, he left the country to seek military training and was airlifted from Botswana to Zambia where ZIPRA leaders received him.
ZIPRA leaders arranged his move to Morogoro Camp in Tanzania, where he began training under Cde Sam Mfakazi among other comrades.
After a six-month mini-commando course, Ghanaian instructors kept him on as an instructor and he trained over 5000 recruits at Morogoro until 1976.

Went back to Zambia and was deployed as Regional Commander in the Luangwa area, planning operations and destroying enemy infrastructure in places such as Guruve, Kachuta, Mhangura, Mutorashanga and Karuru in coordination with ZANLA forces.

As ZIPRA reorganised Rhodesia into Northern and Southern Fronts, he was selected for the military high command, became a member of the Revolutionary Council and commanded the Northern Front from Kafue, Zambia.
Commanded the Kavalamanja battle, which the Zambians gave their own name and which raged for four days near the Zambezi River.
Masterminded an attack that overran an enemy position at Mana Pools.
Commanded an assembly point at the ceasefire.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army and attached to a unit (rest of sentence illegible).

Died aged 66 and was declared a national hero in recognition of his fighting gallantry.

summary: Dizzy Paul Malianga was born in 1935 near Mutare, studied in Zimbabwe and South Africa, and worked as an accountant before joining nationalist politics. He helped found the NDP, served as a ZAPU officer in charge of organising the armed struggle, and from prison helped organise the creation of ZANU in 1963. He was detained and restricted for roughly a decade from 1964 and earned a commerce degree while imprisoned. After independence he served as a Member of Parliament for Mutare West and as a Deputy Minister, and he was a ZANU PF Central Committee member when he died in 2021.

timeline.text: Born at a mission in Mutare, the fifth of ten children.
Gained his matriculation certificate at Ohlange Institute in South Africa after earlier schooling in Zimbabwe and South Africa.

While a branch manager at a departmental store in South Africa, earned a professional accountancy certificate through distance learning; he also became involved with the African National Congress of South Africa.
Returned to Zimbabwe, joined the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress under Joshua Nkomo and took a teaching post in Highfield, Harare.
After the SRANC ban he gave up his studies abroad to work full time for liberation and helped form the National Democratic Party, becoming its Vice President.
Led an NDP delegation to London opposing planned changes to Rhodesia's 1923 constitution and demanding majority rule, then organised a march from Highfield to Harare Central Police Station.
Arrested and charged with subversive statements; his trial was moved to Inkomo Military Camp because of crowds and he got a short prison term.

After release he joined another NDP delegation that rejected the constitutional proposals of Britain's Commonwealth Secretary Duncan Sandys; after the NDP was banned in December 1961 he joined ZAPU and was elected Secretary for Public Affairs with responsibility for organising the armed struggle.
Was served with an order barring him from entering communal lands for fear he would rouse the peasants.
Was barred from addressing or attending gatherings of more than 12 people, then arrested and sentenced to two years under the Law and Order Maintenance Act for subversive statements at rallies.
While in prison he and other comrades organised the formation of ZANU, launched in 1963.
On release from prison he was appointed ZANU External Representative and deployed to its newly established office (location cut off).
ZANU and ZAPU were banned; on his return to Harare in 1964 he was arrested and restricted, first at Sikombela.
Was detained at Salisbury Maximum Security Prison, where he spent the next ten years and obtained a Bachelor of Commerce degree and passed most of a Law degree.
After independence he became MP for Mutare West and Deputy Minister (industry and commerce); other party and ministerial posts are mentioned but are too garbled to extract.
Was re-elected MP for Mutare West and again appointed Deputy Minister of Industry and Commerce.
Died at Parirenyatwa; President Mnangagwa's condolence message called him one of the few surviving nationalists who pioneered the independence struggle.

summary: Sibusiso Moyo, known in the war as Delumuzi, was born at Mnene Mission in Mberengwa in 1961 and joined the liberation struggle as a very young man. He served as a ZIPRA instructor and after the ceasefire became an officer in the new national army, rising through staff and college posts to Major General and Chief of Staff. He gained fame as the spokesperson of Operation Restore Legacy in November 2017 and then became Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade, working to re-engage Western states and strengthen Zimbabwe's role in SADC and the African Union. He died of COVID-19 complications on 20 January 2021 and was honoured as a national hero.

As Foreign Minister he pushed re-engagement with Western countries and promoted the slogan that Zimbabwe is open for business, while also serving in SADC organs and overseeing Zimbabwe's ratification of the AfCFTA and Tripartite free trade arrangements.

summary: Paradzayi Zimondi, born in Mashonaland East in 1947, gave up school to join ZANLA in Mozambique, trained in Tanzania in 1974 and rose from instructor to Manica Province commander and High Command member. After independence he held brigade, presidential guard and military intelligence commands and retired from the army as a Major General in 1996. He then led the prison service from 1998, becoming Commissioner General in 2013, and pushed rehabilitation, open prisons, gender balance and regional cooperation. He died in January 2021 and was survived by three children.

timeline.text: Born in Uzumba District, Mashonaland East, first of seven children of Charles and Abigail Zimondi.
Moved to Salisbury, then left school with other Highfield youths and crossed into Mozambique to join ZANLA.
Underwent military training at Mgagao camp in Tanzania.
Posted to Chimoio, Mozambique, as an instructor, later deployed to Gaza Province and then reassigned to Manica Province.
Became Field Operations Commander in Manica Province, taking over from Cde Happison Muchechetere.
Led ZANLA fighters in several Manica battles, including the Grand Reef battle mounted in reprisal for the Rhodesian attack on Chimoio camp, and was named to the ZANLA High Command.
Was absorbed into the Zimbabwe National Army with the rank of Colonel.
Appointed Deputy Commander of 2 Infantry Brigade.
Promoted to command the Presidential Guard, serving there until 1984.
Transferred to Army Headquarters in a general staff appointment.
Promoted Brigadier General and given command of 1 Infantry Brigade until 1990; protected the Beira Corridor and helped seize RENAMO's headquarters on Gorongoza mountain.
Appointed Director Military Intelligence for the army, a post he held until August 1994.
Named Chief of Defence Intelligence when the army and air force came under a single command structure.
Retired from the army with the rank of Major General.
Appointed Deputy Commissioner of the Zimbabwe Prison Service and went on a study tour of British and Swedish prison systems.
Became Commissioner of the Zimbabwe Prison Service, serving in that title until 2013.
Following the new constitution and the renaming to Zimbabwe Prisons and Correctional Services, became Commissioner General until retiring on 31 October (year garbled, read as 2019).
Founded the Zimbabwe Female Open Prison Trust to drive open-prison development, starting with the Marondera Female Open Prison.
Died of complications in Harare at age 73.

summary: Joel Biggie Matiza was born in Murewa in 1960, left school in 1975 to join the liberation war in Zambia and survived the 1978 Rhodesian raid on Freedom Camp. Sent to Nigeria, he qualified as an architect, returned in 1986 and built a private practice. He entered ZANU PF politics, became MP for Murewa South in 1999 and later a deputy minister, provincial minister and Minister of Transport and Infrastructural Development, driving road, border and airport projects. summary: Moses Griffiths Mpofu was born in 1954 in Nyamandlovu District and joined ZAPU after secondary school, becoming its youth secretary and then crossing into Zambia in 1975 for military training. He worked in ZAPU's security and counter-intelligence department and attended a police command course in the USSR. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe Republic Police, rising through Bulawayo and Harare commands to Deputy Commissioner in 1999 before retiring in 2004. He died in Bulawayo in February 2021 and was declared a national hero.

Finished primary school in Tsholotsho, then attended secondary school in Plumtree from 1969 to 1973.

Appointed ZAPU Secretary for Youth covering areas around Hwange and Victoria Falls (partly garbled).
Crossed the Zambezi into Zambia with other recruits and received initial training at Mwembeshi camp.
Sent to Mgagao and Morogoro camps in Tanzania for further military training.
Posted back to Zambia and placed in ZAPU's National Security and Order counter-intelligence department.
Selected for a police command course at Novocherkassk academy in the USSR, covering criminal investigation and riot management.
Returned to Zimbabwe as part of the ZAPU forces.
Joined the Zimbabwe Republic Police, trained at a police depot and was posted as a Constable (details garbled).

Elevated to Senior Assistant Commissioner and became Officer Commanding Harare Province.
Appointed Deputy Commissioner, serving until retiring on 31 December 2004.
Died at United Bulawayo Hospitals after a long illness, aged 66; the Politburo declared him a national hero.

summary: Emmanuel Francis Ribeiro, born in Chivhu in 1935, trained as a teacher and then as a Catholic priest, ordained in 1964. As a prison chaplain and Highfield priest he supported imprisoned nationalists, sheltered Robert Mugabe and Enos Nkala and helped Mugabe and Edgar Tekere flee to Mozambique in 1975. He was also a prolific church composer, Shona novelist, contributor to the national anthem and flag design, and held a US doctorate in music. He died of pneumonia in June 2021 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Chivhu, fourth of five children of Francis Pires Ribeiro and his wife.
Studied at St Francis Xavier College, Kutama, and Gokomere Mission.
Entered Gweru Teachers College for a Junior Certificate in Education.
Began theology and philosophy studies at Chishawasha Seminary.
Ordained a Diocesan priest.
Published the Shona novel Muchadura, followed by Tonderai in 1969; both won Rhodesia Literature Bureau prizes.
Worked in Mhondoro and Highfield, Harare, and served as prison chaplain at Harare Central Prison, later Assistant Chaplain-General.
As chaplain, met leading nationalists and ministered to jailed Cde Emmerson Mnangagwa and Cde Matthew Malowa, held for a railway bombing in Fort Victoria.
Sheltered Cdes Mugabe and Enos Nkala after their release from prison and helped Mugabe and Edgar Tekere escape to Mozambique.
Introduced vernacular songs and African instruments into Catholic worship after Vatican II and composed many church songs.
Helped with the national anthem and was on the team that designed the national flag.
Researched and recommended national hero status for the Chinhoyi 7 of the 1966 battle.
Enrolled for a master's in music in Bloomington, USA, later earning a doctorate there.
Celebrated 50 years as a priest at St Peter's Kubatana, Highfield, Harare.
Joined religious leaders in the National Elders Forum calling for removal of sanctions on Zimbabwe.
Died of pneumonia at St Anne's Hospital; the Politburo declared him a national hero.

In Mozambique he worked mainly in administration and armaments. After the 1980 integration he rose through infantry brigade commands to Brigadier General in 1994 and was made Major General on retirement in 2004. timeline.text: Born in Chivi District as the third of eight children in a family of modest means.
Went through primary school, which the text names as Venya Primary.
Attended secondary school at a mine school but was pushed out of education by fee demands that excluded many black pupils.
Worked as a general hand in Gweru while studying by correspondence, and saw the harsh treatment of workers living in squalid conditions.
Left Gweru with two companions, crossed into Botswana and joined the liberation struggle, then travelled on to Tanzania.
Received basic military training in Tanzania.
Selected as one of a few cadres sent to Ukraine for light artillery weapons training.
Returned to Morogoro camp, then moved to Beira in Mozambique as the Frontline States pushed to unite the two guerrilla armies.
Served in the administration at Tembwe, handling armaments and clothing for commanders, and was employed under the Tete front.
Moved onto the General Staff, heading a section until the war ended in 1979.
Took part in integrating ZANLA and ZIPRA fighters into the new Zimbabwe National Army.
Commissioned into the army (rank reads Colonel), then commanded a services corps unit from mid-1981.
Married Beatrice Tamburayi (nee Pawandiwa) and was appointed to a Bulawayo command the same year.
Became Acting Commander of 3 Infantry Brigade, and in December 1988 took command of another unit before returning to 3 Infantry Brigade in March 1990.
Appointed Commander of 5 Infantry Brigade and promoted to Brigadier General in 1994.
Took over 2 Infantry Brigade and commanded it until about the start of the new decade.
Was then posted to the DRC deployment, serving as Deputy Managing Director and later Managing Director of an organisation whose name is not legible.
Promoted to Major General on retiring from the Zimbabwe Defence Forces.
After retiring he farmed beans and maize and ran retail and warehouse businesses in Karoi, and helped reorganise the army's Tongogara Football Club.

summary: Nkiwane was a ZAPU stalwart who, after being noticed by Kenneth Kaunda in Zambia, helped organise the party's underground network and smuggle weapons into Rhodesia from Tanzania and Zambia. Some of the arms he moved were used in the 1967 Wankie campaign. After independence he worked in the Ministry of Construction, became a construction partner who developed Bulawayo suburbs, and later retired to farming. He died in July 2021 at 93 and was survived by three children, sixteen grandchildren and thirty great-grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born as the fourth child in his family in a Native Reserve in Matabeleland (location garbled).
Schooled at the Methodist Tegwane Mission, where the Methodist Church was running schools.
Became active in Northern Rhodesian politics, joining a Zambian independence party (appears to be UNIP) and mixing with prominent Zambians.
During Joshua Nkomo's visits to Zambia, Kenneth Kaunda singled out Nkiwane and advised him to work with ZAPU.
After joining ZAPU he worked with comrades such as Jason Moyo to lay the groundwork for armed resistance to white rule in Southern Rhodesia.
Helped recruit Zimbabweans living in Zambia and built an underground network.
Relocated to Mbeya in Tanzania, where he worked with Sixtoi Moyo on moving arms between Tanzania and Zambia.
Took charge of moving weapons such as sub-machine guns and rifles into Rhodesia with comrades including Misheck Velaphi and Kennias Mlalazi.
Used tricks such as showing a smoking pipe as a signal and kept receivers and carriers from contacting each other to avoid arrest.
Weapons he had transported were used in the 1967 Wankie and related ZAPU-ANC campaigns.
Joined the Ministry of Construction, then entered private construction as a partner in Glendenning Construction.
Developed the Cowdray Park and Zonke Izizwe suburbs in Bulawayo before retiring into full-time farming.
Died of prostate cancer at United Bulawayo Hospitals aged 93; the Politburo agreed to give him national hero status.
