summary: Chakabva grew up poor in Murombedzi and worked for a construction company in Harare, at Kariba and then in Zambia, where he became a driver. He was recruited by ZAPU's Nikita Mangena, trained as a ZIPRA fighter in Tanzania, and later fought in the Mavuradonha area and led a large group of fighters before serious injuries ended his front-line service. He settled in Chipinge, married Esther, and took up farming through land reform in 2009. He died in July 2021 aged 78.

timeline.text: Born in Murombedzi District as the sixth of ten children.
Economic hardship under white minority rule meant he could not stay in school because fees were unaffordable.
Found work as a tea boy at Lewis Construction Company in Harare.
Was moved with the same employer to the Kariba Dam project, then relocated to Lusaka, Zambia.
The company moved to Kitwe and he was promoted to driver.
In Kitwe he was recruited by Nikita Mangena to join ZAPU and trained under its armed wing ZIPRA at Morogoro in Tanzania.
Crossed a river border (name garbled, probably the Zambezi) and fought in the Mavuradonha mountains and surrounding areas.
Was part of a team linked to the spirit mediums Mbuya Nehanda, Sekuru Chidyamauyu and another (details garbled).
Was entrusted with a group of about 465 fighters, including 400 who had been under an injured commander named Makasha, in the Shai Shai area on the Limpopo.
Suffered serious injuries in battle, was withdrawn for medical care and afterwards settled in Chipinge because he could not return to the front.
In Chipinge he met Esther (year reads 1975) and they married later (reads early 1989); his injuries kept him out of the army.
Benefited from the land reform programme and began maize, bean and tobacco farming.
Died after a long illness aged 78; the Politburo recognised his contribution to the liberation struggle and to land reform.

timeline.text: Born in a village in Bocha, Manicaland Province.
Finished secondary school, where he was respected as a pupil leader, then moved to Salisbury and stayed with his sister in Mbare.
Took a job at a white-owned photographic company (possibly Kodak) where black workers faced poor conditions, and was politicised by discussions in Mbare.
Left Mutare with his friend Nicholas Nyamupfukudza and crossed into Manica Province, Mozambique, where Frelimo received them.
Met other recruits including Paradzai Zimondi, was taken via Chimoio to Chifombo, and was addressed by Josiah Tongogara.
Joined a group of about 400 cadres moved to Tanzania with Robson Manyika's help for training at Mgagao.
Stayed on at Mgagao after training with a liaison role, then sailed to Beira at the end of the year and moved on to Chimoio.
Operated in Gaza Province, where in a Limpopo River battle he carried an injured Frelimo fighter despite his own rifle wound.
Was hospitalised about two weeks, then left in bandages before full recovery to rejoin his forces.
Was recalled to Chimoio and worked in the security department closely with Tongogara.
Promoted into the ZANLA High Command and appointed Deputy Chief Representative and Military Attache to Zambia.
Was called back to Mozambique to prepare the integration of the armies with Tongogara.
Served as liaison officer in the integration process from offices near the University of Zimbabwe in Harare.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army.
Appointed to command an infantry brigade, taking over from Constantino Chiwenga.
Returned to Army Headquarters as Brigadier General for Administration and Quartermaster, later moving to Operations.
Promoted to Major General and made Chief of Staff for Logistics, moving to Chief of Staff Operations in March 1999 during the DRC deployment.
Recalled from diplomatic service to command the Zimbabwe National Army, a post he held until his death.
Died at the Avenues Clinic in Harare aged 68; the Politburo agreed to honour him as a national hero.

summary: Mpepereki trained as a teacher before leaving Rhodesia for Sierra Leone, where he led ZANU PF cadres as Commissar and raised support for the struggle while studying for a degree. Returning to Zimbabwe he became a soil microbiologist at the University of Zimbabwe, launching a widely praised soya-bean programme for smallholders and winning regional and national research honours. He also chaired the Environmental Management Agency and CMED and sat on several boards. He died of COVID-19 complications in July 2021, aged 70, and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Mberengwa and raised as one of seven children.
Began primary school in Mberengwa, walking about 6 km, and passed with flying colours.
Trained as a teacher at Gweru Teachers College after Chegato Mission secondary school, qualifying in November 1972.
Taught at Moleli High School for two years and used savings to buy clothing for guerrillas.
Left teaching, obtained a driver's licence and passport, crossed into Botswana with Allan Moyo and spent three weeks planning a flight to Sierra Leone.
In Sierra Leone he acted as lead Commissar for ZANU PF cadres, set up a party base and raised funds for lodging, food, clothing and scholarships for comrades.
Graduated with a First Class BSc from the University of Sierra Leone.
Joined the University of Zimbabwe Faculty of Agriculture as a development fellow.
Was awarded an MSc in Soil Science and Microbiology by North Carolina State University.
Met his later wife, and they formally wed in December 1999.
Completed his PhD in Soil Microbiology at the University of Zimbabwe.
Launched the smallholder soya-bean promotion programme, reaching Karoi, Kazangarare, Shamva and Dotito and co-authoring a farmers' production guide.
While leading the Environmental Management Agency, the Chikorokoza Chapera campaign against illegal mining and related damage began.
Received a Long Service Certificate and the IMPRESSA first prize from the African Union for his soya-bean research.
Won the Zimbabwe Presidential Award for distinguished agricultural research.
Died in Harare of COVID-19 related complications aged 70.
Was declared a national hero by the ZANU PF Politburo.

summary: Choeni was drawn into youth politics early and joined the armed struggle in 1974, training in Tanzania as a medical officer and rising to a regional deputy post by 1978. Injuries sustained near the ceasefire ended his army service, after which he built a career in the party at home. He became Provincial Chairman of Matabeleland South and a Central Committee member. He died in 2021 aged 71, survived by his wife Lydia and son Sibusiso.

timeline.text: Born at a rural home as the eldest in a family of several children.
Became heavily involved in youth politics after finishing early schooling.
Joined the People's Revolutionary Army (ZIPRA) and crossed into Zambia, then went to Tanzania for military training.
Completed training and was qualified as a medical officer, then deployed to a front around Gokwe.
Was promoted to Zone Medical man and later to a Zone-level post.
Elevated to deputy regional officer, a rank he held until independence.
Was integrated into the national army but left because of injuries sustained towards the ceasefire.
Returned to Party structures and later to his hometown, rising through Party ranks to the District Coordinating Committee.
Was elected Provincial Secretary for Information and later Vice Chairman of the Province.
Became Chairman of Matabeleland South Province and a Central Committee member, leading from the front.
Died aged 71; the President praised him as a loyal veteran who promoted peace, unity and development.

summary: Ndlovu was a teacher, researcher and journalist who went to Zambia in the 1960s and ran ZAPU's information department, editing the Zimbabwe Review and co-producing a photo book on the struggle. In 1978 he became ZAPU's representative in Algiers. After independence he worked in newspapers, magazine publishing and public relations, and then devoted himself to community and language work, including the TG Silundika Cultural Community Centre and ZILPA. He died in July 2021 and was buried at Lady Stanley Cemetery in Bulawayo.

timeline.text: Born at Dombodema Mission as the fifth of six children.
Completed secondary school and then taught at a mission in Zvimba until 1959.
Did research in social anthropology among the Kalanga of Mangwe district, which produced a book on Kalanga history and culture.
Worked as a journalist for the African Daily News.
After the ZAPU ban, he left Rhodesia for Zambia to help direct the armed struggle.
In Zambia he led ZAPU's Information and Publicity Department and edited its monthly magazine Zimbabwe Review as editor-in-chief.
Published with photographer Zenzo Nkobi the book 'Zimbabwe in the Struggle', combining photographs and stories of the armed struggle and ZAPU refugee camps.
Was posted to Algiers as ZAPU's representative, covering countries including Tunisia, Morocco, Spain, France and West Germany.
Returned to Zimbabwe and joined The Chronicle in Bulawayo, later becoming features and supplements editor for it and the Sunday News.
Moved to Munn Publishing Company as contributing editor and regional manager for Matabeleland, Midlands, Masvingo, Botswana and Zambia.
Joined Lonrho Zimbabwe as a Public Relations Executive.
Was sent by Lonrho to Swaziland as a consultant on a publication project.
After Lonrho retrenchments he lectured in public relations, marketing and journalism, wrote a weekly column and later ran a commercial gardening project.
Spearheaded the TG Silundika Cultural Community Centre and helped form ZILPA to win recognition for marginalised indigenous languages.
Died at United Bulawayo Hospitals after a heart ailment, and was declared a national hero by the Politburo on 20 September 2021.

summary: Jane Lungile Ngwenya, known as NaBigboy, was born in Buhera in 1935 and raised by her grandparents after her father died. A clash with school authorities over racial double standards got her expelled in Standard Six, though she was later allowed to write her exams and then worked as a teacher in Kwekwe. She entered nationalist politics, was jailed in 1959 after a Bulawayo rally and was released with her baby following a protest by white women. Family pressure then forced her to withdraw from activism; she died on 5 August 2021, and the later part of her biography is not legible.

timeline.text: Born in Buhera, Manicaland Province, the child of Gerald Ngwenya and Medina Ngwenya (nee Mushauma).
Her father died and she was raised by her maternal grandparents.
Started primary school at Gwebu in Buhera and moved to Madende Primary the following year; she later recalled how pupils were pushed to speak English and to admire everything white.
Moved to Que Que (Kwekwe) because her grandfather was a policeman, then to Shurugwi in 1947 where she did Standards 4 and 5.
Moved to Charles Wraith, an African school, to do Standard Six.
Was expelled for asking a priest at assembly why Africans could mow a white man's lawn yet were forbidden to walk on it afterwards, and was barred from sitting her exams.
Was allowed to write her exams only after the late Father Kachidza and a Mr McMillan intervened.
After Standard Six she taught in Kwekwe (her pupils included Webster Shamu) and grew determined to see the country freed from white minority rule.
Married George Tinarwo, a driver; he wanted her to be a housewife but her political drive persisted.
Took part in the formation of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress (SRANC) and attended political meetings with her baby on her back.

Arrested after attending a rally of nationalist leaders at Stanley Hall in Bulawayo; held about three weeks at Grey Street Prison (now Bulawayo Prison) with her baby daughter Elizabeth until white women led by a Mrs Watson protested for their release.

After release her husband and family pressed her to give up politics and become a full-time housewife, forcing her to step back from the struggle; her husband had grown wary after repeated police harassment.
Died; the remainder of her story is on a page that could not be read.

summary: Elliot Ngwabe, known as Cde Okello, grew up in Makokoba, Bulawayo, where he protested against settler rule as a youth before joining the SRANC at 18. He rose to a transport role in the party in 1963, trained in Zambia and Algeria, and took part in the September 1964 Zidube Ranch raid, after which he was arrested, escaped in 1965, was recaptured near the Botswana border and held at Khami until the ceasefire. He later held party responsibilities in Matabeleland South and was declared a national hero on 20 September 2021, leaving a wife Wildar, five children and 11 grandchildren. The first page of his biography is unreadable, so birth and early-life details are missing.

timeline.text: As a youth in Makokoba, Bulawayo, he and friends hit back at colonial oppression by stoning the cars of white settlers.
Joined the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress (SRANC) in Makokoba.
Took part in party activities aimed at undermining white minority rule.
Promoted to the transport department of the SRANC.

With other comrades he welcomed Joshua Nkomo at the airport; when police tried to manhandle Nkomo over weapons he had brought in, Ngwabe moved to intervene and was held at Bulawayo's main police station before release.
Crossed to Lusaka for military training and later went to Algeria for further training.
With six other comrades under Moffat Hadebe he attacked Zidube Ranch, a mission meant to seize a Mr Roberts who was linked to emergency declarations and detentions.

The attack went badly with an exchange of fire; the group retreated towards Katopo Hills where villagers, told the men were cattle thieves, attacked them with spears, axes and logs; police in civilian clothes were among them and the comrades were arrested and held at Gwanda then Grey Street Prison.

Escaped from prison with comrades including Moffat Hadebe, Cain Nkala and Clark Mpofu, helped by sympathetic black guards; outside contacts gave them clothes and money and a vehicle to take them to Zambia via Botswana.

In Plumtree they hid from helicopters and ground troops using grass hats, crossed the Ramakgwebane border into Botswana and were later pursued on the road to Francistown; Mpofu was shot in the leg and Ngwabe, trying to help, was struck down and captured.
Taken to Khami Prison, where he met ZANLA detainees including Mnangagwa; an escape attempt failed and he was recaptured and kept at Khami until the ceasefire.
Was released from Khami following the ceasefire.
The ZANU-PF Politburo declared him a national hero.

summary: Mariyawanda Nzuwah was born in Nharira in 1941 and, after outstanding results at Kutama, was sponsored to study in the United States, earning degrees including a doctorate path at Howard University. In America he joined civil rights and labour activism, taught Afro-American Studies at the University of Maryland, founded a journal on southern African affairs and lobbied Congress against minority rule in Rhodesia. After independence he returned to Zimbabwe and rose from university lecturer to Secretary in several ministries and then Chairperson of the Public Service Commission, driving reforms in the civil service. He died on 21 September 2021 and was accorded national hero status; he was survived by his wife Janice, four children and several grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born in Nharira, Mashonaland East, the first of seven children of Mr Nzuwah and Priscilla (nee Chinhakwe).
Started primary school at Nhidza Primary and later moved to another school (name partly legible) to finish primary education.
Went on to Kutama in Zvimba District for secondary education.
Finished secondary school with outstanding results; Catholics running Kutama then identified him for sponsorship to study in the United States.
Enrolled at the University of Minnesota for a degree in Administration and Political Science, where he met his future wife Janice Stevenson.
Spent much time on civil rights work, organising freedom rider protests, and joined trade union activity with the United Auto Workers alongside activist Dr Gary Bush.
Completed his undergraduate studies.
Moved to Washington DC for postgraduate study, graduating in 1967 with a Masters in Philosophy and Administration.
Married Janice Stevenson; they had four children.
Enrolled at Howard University for a doctorate in Public Administration.

Joined the University of Maryland, helped set up its first Department of Afro-American Studies with Dr Mary Berry, and founded the Journal of Southern African Affairs on liberation movements and pan-Africanism.
Lobbied the US Congress with Edson Zvobgo, Dr Busch and Dr Berry to end minority rule in Rhodesia and organised material support for freedom fighters.
Answered the new government's call to return home and joined the University of Zimbabwe as a lecturer.
Joined Government as Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Roads.
Appointed substantive Secretary for Transport.
Appointed Secretary for Local Government.

Appointed Chairperson of the Public Service Commission, where he pushed reforms such as weeding out ghost workers, non-monetary retention incentives like housing schemes and staff buses, HIV and AIDS focal persons and performance units in provinces and districts.
Died at home in Harare after a short illness, aged 80.

summary: Wereki Sandiyani, whose Chimurenga name was Phillimon Gabela, was born in Mashonaland Central and trained as a ZANLA fighter, operating with Frelimo in Mozambique and in northeastern Zimbabwe. He was badly wounded, redeployed in 1975, wounded again and captured, then tortured and had both legs amputated before being sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment. Freed under Zimbabwe's first post-independence amnesty, he worked as a political instructor, served in ZANU-PF, took part in land reform and championed war veterans' welfare. He died on 25 September 2021 aged 66, survived by two wives, seven children and 19 grandchildren, and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: After training he went to Mozambique, stayed with Frelimo comrades, and later crossed the Zambezi River to operate alongside them.
With recruits drawn from Madziwa he joined fighters in the Guwani area, engaged the enemy, was injured but escaped and was carried to Lusaka for medical treatment.
Redeployed after recovering from his first injury as a commander active in several sectors.
In another fierce battle he was wounded in the right leg again and captured by Rhodesian forces.
Taken to a military base (near Mutoko, name partly legible) where he was interrogated and tortured to reveal information on other guerrillas; both his legs were amputated.
Treated in hospital as a prisoner of war, then held in prison awaiting trial.
Sentenced to death for fighting the Rhodesian regime; his first appeal failed but a second appeal commuted the sentence to life imprisonment because of his youth and amputee status.
Freed under the first amnesty granted by President Mugabe and went to Goromonzi Assembly Point to meet fellow comrades.
Later worked as a political instructor at a National Youth Service base in Mt Darwin and received treatment for war injuries.
Went home to Mt Darwin, held several ZANU-PF positions, took part in the Third Chimurenga land reform and was resettled on Plot 26 of a farm in Mt Darwin District.
Died at Mt Darwin District Hospital after a long illness, aged 66; the Politburo unanimously accorded him national hero status.

summary: Simon Khaya Moyo was born in Plumtree in 1945 and, after working at Mpilo Hospital, left Rhodesia in 1968 to join the liberation struggle through Zambia. ZAPU sent him to study at the University of Zambia and Makerere University, after which he served in Lusaka as a close aide to Joshua Nkomo, attended Lancaster House and trained in military intelligence in East Germany. After independence he held government, diplomatic and party posts, rising to ZANU-PF National Chairman and Secretary for Information and Publicity. He died of cancer on 14 November 2021 and was declared a national hero, survived by his wife Margret, two sons and three grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born in Plumtree, Matabeleland South, the second child in a family of nine, to Robert Khaya Moyo and Tiagwa Moyo.

Worked as a research assistant at Mpilo Hospital in Bulawayo, where he became aware of settler injustices.
Left Rhodesia for Zambia via Botswana to join the liberation struggle and was welcomed by the ZAPU leadership in Lusaka.
On ZAPU's direction, completed a diploma in Social Science with merit at the University of Zambia.
ZAPU sent him to Makerere University in Uganda, where he enrolled for a B.A. Honours degree.
Took up a lecturing post in social work in Uganda and helped mobilise support and recruits for the struggle (partly legible).
Went to Lusaka and was appointed secretary and special assistant to the ZAPU leader Joshua Nkomo.
Sent to East Germany for a course in military intelligence, then appointed to ZAPU's Revolutionary Council and Central Committee in Zambia (partly legible).
As Special Assistant to Nkomo, attended the Lancaster House Conference.
After independence served as an Assistant Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs for a period (partly legible).

Later held diplomatic and ministerial posts and senior ZANU-PF positions, including Secretary for Information and Publicity and National Chairman, spearheading the party's ideological school (years illegible).
Wrote two books, including a compilation of his speeches (partly legible).
Died of cancer at Mater Dei Hospital aged 76; the Politburo unanimously accorded him national hero status.

summary: Siwanda Kennedy Mbuso Sibanda was born in Bulilima-Mangwe in 1932 and studied through Solusi Mission and South African institutions, graduating in law from the University of Natal in 1970. Returning to Rhodesia, he joined ZAPU and in 1971 became the first black advocate in Matabeleland, defending political detainees and guerrillas and advising ZAPU on legal and constitutional matters. After independence he worked on constitutional drafting, helped bring about the Unity Accord, sat in Parliament, and served as a High Court judge from 1996 to 2002 before returning to private practice. He also backed football and sport in Bulawayo, died in South Africa on 22 December 2021 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Bulilima-Mangwe District, the first of several children of Jack Sibanda and Volo Sibanda.
Attended Tshabanda Primary School, then Solusi Mission from 1948, finishing Standard 6 in 1953.
Earned a South African junior certificate through correspondence.
Went to South Africa for secondary school but found no place, spending the year as a switchboard operator at the Monte Carlo in Durban.
Enrolled at an institute in Pretoria and obtained the Joint Matriculation Board certificate in 1958.
Enrolled at the University of Natal for a BA and joined the South African Pan Africanist Congress Youth Wing, working with Steve Biko and Griffiths Mxenge in the student movement.
Completed his BA and became a sales representative for Bakers Company Limited in Durban.
Married Leonora Nomampondo Makalima of Ntabankulu, Transkei; they had four children.
Studied law at the University of Natal, graduating in 1970.
Registered as an articled clerk with the right of audience with R. Bugwadeen and Company in Durban.
Returned to Rhodesia, took part in forming the African National Council, joined ZAPU and passed the pupilage exams with the Bulawayo Advocates' Chambers.
Obtained a city permit under the Land Apportionment Act to open an office in whites-only Bulawayo and was admitted as an advocate, the first black advocate in Matabeleland.
Set up chambers in Bulawayo and defended political offenders, detainees and guerrillas.
Practised as a Designated Advocate doing the combined work of advocate and attorney, and took charge of distributing and monitoring political trial cases.
Attended the Lancaster House constitutional conference as a legal adviser to ZAPU (partly legible).
Helped draft, review and finalise the initial Constitution of independent Zimbabwe.

After helping lay the groundwork for the Unity Accord, was appointed to the ZANU-PF Central Committee and became a non-constituency Member of Parliament chairing parliamentary legal and other committees.
Called to the bench and served as a High Court judge in Bulawayo until 2002.
Retired from the bench and returned to private practice in Bulawayo until ill health stopped him.
Died of cancer at Morningside Hospital in Sandton, South Africa, aged 89, and was buried at West Park Cemetery, Johannesburg.

summary: A ZIPRA freedom fighter who walked out of Manama Mission school at 17 in January 1977 and made his way through Botswana to Zambia. He trained militarily and politically, including in the Soviet Union, worked in the ZIPRA Commissariat and survived the Rhodesian bombing of Freedom Camp near Lusaka in 1978. After independence he built a long career in the Zimbabwe Defence Forces, with posts in logistics, staff training and defence policy, and rose to Major General before retiring. He died on 5 June 2022 aged 61 after a long illness.

timeline.text: Born in Matabeleland South, the fifth child in a family of six boys and one girl.
Started primary school before later moving on to secondary education at Manama Mission.
Angered by racial injustice, left Manama Mission aged 17 together with a large group of fellow students to join the liberation struggle.
The group travelled via Botswana into Zambia, where they were received at a ZIPRA reception camp and began military training.
Sent to the Soviet Union for military training, then enrolled at a Higher Political Training School for ZIPRA cadres.
Returned to Zambia and was posted to the ZIPRA Commissariat Department.
Survived the Rhodesian air and napalm attack on Freedom Camp outside Lusaka while comrades around him were killed.
Deployed to Mulungushi Camp and named Commissar of the Kavalamanja Unit, which was being readied for a major attack into Rhodesia.
The unit's deployment plans were thrown into disarray after another air raid (rest of the account falls on an unreadable page).
Served as second in command of 39 Infantry Battalion in the Zimbabwe Defence Forces.
Held the post of Quartermaster Staff Officer Grade 2.
Worked as directing staff at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Served as Quartermaster Staff Officer Grade 1.
Acted as Colonel Logistics.
Directing staff on the senior division at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Held a long posting as Director Defence Policy at the Ministry of Defence (dates and title partly garbled).
Senior directing staff at the Zimbabwe National Defence University.
Moved to the Adjutant General's Pool.
Died after a long illness at the age of 61.

summary: A ZIPRA fighter who left school in Mberengwa district in 1977 to join the struggle through Zambia and was trained in Angola, becoming an instructor and political commissar at Boma camp. He was wounded in a 1979 Rhodesian and South African air attack on the camp. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army in 1980 and rose from company commander to Brigadier General in 2007, serving as Defence Advisor in Addis Ababa and later in senior headquarters posts, and retired as a Major General. The ZANU PF Politburo declared him a national hero after his death; he left a wife, three children and a grandchild.

timeline.text: Attended Danamombe Primary School in Mberengwa for Grade 6 after earlier primary schooling in Harare and at Mnene.
Completed Grade 7 at Asiningira Primary in Mberengwa.
Inspired by students who had slipped away to join the struggle, abandoned his studies and went to Zambia via Botswana to join ZIPRA.
Stayed at Nampundwe Transit Camp in Zambia before being moved on for training.
Was among the second ZIPRA group trained in Angola, doing about three months of basic training and three months of specialisation.
Picked for instructor training, then became a Political Commissar.
Trained successive groups of recruits as an instructor at Boma Training Camp.
Took further conventional and unconventional warfare training at a company commanders course run by Soviet instructors.
Wounded when Boma camp was struck in a joint Rhodesian and South African air operation codenamed Operation Vanity that caused heavy casualties; two fellow instructors died.
Evacuated for treatment, including time in a Luanda hospital, then returned to Boma as Commissar/Instructor once recovered.
Handed over a large group of trained fighters, received a new intake and moved to a new camp at Malanje in central Angola, where guerrilla and conventional training continued alongside ANC cadres.
Returned to Zimbabwe at independence and was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army.
Appointed Company Commander at 16 Infantry Battalion, moving to 36 Infantry Battalion in the same role that September.
Promoted to Lieutenant while at 36 Infantry Battalion.
Moved up to Staff Officer Grade 1 and was later promoted Major (details partly garbled).
Married Sarah Levi.
Promoted to Colonel and took up an administration staff post at Army Headquarters.
Posted to Addis Ababa as Zimbabwe's Defence Advisor, where he defended the Land Reform Programme.
Promoted to Brigadier General while still in Addis Ababa.
Returned home and became Director General Programmes at Defence Forces Headquarters, later heading Defence Economic Development from 2018.

summary: An electrical engineer, businessman and long-serving ZANU PF politician born near Chivhu in 1954 who left school early, worked at the Posts and Telecommunications Corporation and studied at night to qualify. He became politically active as a young man, founded the Kambuzuma party branch in 1978 and later served as councillor, Deputy Mayor of Harare, MP, Senator and, from 2019, Minister of State for Harare Metropolitan Province. He also ran construction and other business interests and led the Zimbabwe Building Contractors Association. He died on 19 July 2022 aged 67 and was declared a national hero; he was survived by his wife Spiwe and two children.

timeline.text: Born in Masinire Village near Chivhu, the first child of the family.
Unable to keep up school fees, took a job with the Posts and Telecommunications Corporation and funded evening classes from his small wage.
Became politically active, acting as a go-between who gathered supplies and carried messages for liberation fighters.
Studied for a Higher National qualification in Electrical Engineering through City and Guilds of London, finishing in 1976, and trained as a telecoms engineer at PTC.
Helped found the Kambuzuma ZANU PF branch and met resistance from the Pfumo reVanhu auxiliary force.
Was attacked by Pfumo reVanhu and shot in the leg, but kept going with help from party cadres.
Moved from PTC to the railways as a Signals Engineer in charge of electrical and electronic signalling design and implementation.
Elected Councillor for Kambuzuma Ward 14 and married Spiwe the same year.
Left the railways to join another employer as a project electrical engineer handling projects and procurement.
Appointed Deputy Mayor of the City of Harare, serving until about October 1984.
Elected Member of Parliament for Kambuzuma Constituency and built up a construction business that became his flagship.
Graduated with a Bachelor of Commerce degree.
Re-elected MP for Kambuzuma and served until 2000.
Elected Vice Chairman of the ZANU PF Harare Metropolitan Provincial Executive, a post held to 2002.
Elected Senator for Harare Metropolitan Province and served as interim provincial party chairman.
Appointed Minister of State for Provincial Affairs and Devolution for Harare Metropolitan Province.
Appointed to the ZANU PF Politburo.
Died of a cardiac arrest at his home aged 67 and was declared a national hero.

summary: Known in the war as Cde Freddie Matanga, he was born near Zvishavane in 1954 and worked at the Government Central Stores before leaving for Mozambique and then Tanzania to train as a ZANLA fighter in 1974. He worked on Mgagao camp food projects, became a commissar and provincial commander in Mozambique and was later sent to Syria as ZANU's representative. He joined the Zimbabwe National Army as a Brigadier General in 1981, retired in 1988, and later held party, board and business roles. He died on 1 August 2022 aged 67, was declared a national hero and was buried at the National Heroes Acre, survived by his wife, six children and ten grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born at Runde Clinic in the Zvishavane area, the third of eight children.
Attended Copper Queen Primary School, then went on to secondary school and finished in 1973.
Took a job at the Government Central Stores.
Driven by racial oppression, crossed into Mozambique with other young people and went on to Tanzania for training at Mgagao Camp, where training ran to 1976.
After initial training, worked on Mgagao poultry and gardening projects that fed the cadres, under the supervision of Gibson Mashingaidze.
Moved to the Mozambique front and became commissar for Tangwena in Manica Province.
Operated in Gaza Province in a commander role.
Sent to Syria as ZANU's representative because of his diligence and commitment.
Oversaw the training of two groups of recruits, several of whom still serve in the army in senior posts.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army with the rank of Brigadier General.
Studied at the Rapid Results and Commercial Careers Colleges.
Married Rosegema Chihoro, then attended the Senior Officers Orientation Course and was made Commander of Harare District Headquarters.
Appointed Brigadier General Quartermaster Staff at Army Headquarters.
Retired from the army and then pursued business and marketing studies.
Chaired a ZANU PF committee looking into war veterans association affairs, investment funds and empowerment projects.
Served as ZANU PF campaign manager for Kwekwe Central.
Sat on the ZBC board and was Deputy General Manager at Anjin Diamond Mining Company.
Served on the board of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces Commission.
Died aged 67 after a long illness at Arundel Hospital in Harare; accorded national hero status and buried at the National Heroes Acre.

summary: Charles Kaneta, known in the war as Cde Santana, was born in Salisbury in 1958 and left school in 1975 to join the liberation struggle in Mozambique. He trained at Chimoio, became an instructor on the 75mm Recoilless Rifle, was further trained in China and took part in the Grand Reef operation. After independence he joined the Zimbabwe National Army and rose from private to Brigadier General through Presidential Guards, artillery and staff postings, ending as Director General Logistics. He earned several degrees and military medals, died in 2022 aged 64 and was accorded national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Salisbury (now Harare), the first child of Nason and Hilda Kaneta.
Finished Standard 6 at Mhakwe Primary School in 1971 and went on to Biriiri Secondary School in Chimanimani in 1972.
The assassination of Herbert Chitepo angered him and his fellow students and pushed him to leave school for the liberation struggle.
Crossed into Mozambique, was guided by villagers to Frelimo soldiers and taken inland to a holding camp with about 200 other recruits.
Passed through several base camps, settled at Toronga (Mangundi) on the Buzi River, helped begin the permanent Chibavava camp, taught Grade 3 at the camp school and heard an address by R. G. Mugabe.
Moved to Chimoio and received military training at Mapinduzi.
Chosen to specialise in the 75mm Recoilless Rifle and became an instructor on it, helping train other comrades.
Selected for further training in China and awarded a diploma by the Chinese PLA Military and Political Cadre Academy in Nanjing, where he and others were visited by Mugabe and Josiah Tongogara.
Flew back to Maputo and was redeployed to Takawira Base Two, joining the instructors who trained a special group of senior party officials.

Redeployed to Pungwe Base Camp and chosen for the night-time Grand Reef operation in Manica Province, led by Tonderai Nyika (later Paradzai Zimondi), after helping with the aftermath of the attack on Chimoio.

Served as an instructor in Manica, was injured, moved between bases such as Tete Base Two and Chimoio because of enemy attacks, trained recruits until the ceasefire and was later repatriated to Zimbabwe.
After a spell at a temporary holding and assembly point he went to Llewellin Barracks for integration and was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a private soldier.
Promoted to Lieutenant after serving as Officer Commanding a headquarters company in an infantry battalion.
Transferred to the Presidential Guards Unit as an administration staff officer for recruitment.
Promoted to the rank of Captain.
Appointed Battery Commander in an Artillery Brigade.
Appointed Commanding Officer of the Presidential Guards Battalion and promoted on 7 November 1996 (rank partly legible, apparently Lieutenant Colonel).
Attended the Battalion Commanders Course in Germany, then in 2000 was posted to Army Headquarters as Personal Staff Officer to the Army Commander, now Vice President Chiwenga.

Completed the China National Defence University college course (2007), then earned a BSc Honours in Political Science (2012) and an MSc in International Relations (2014) at the University of Zimbabwe.
After serving as Defence Attache and then Director General Logistics at Defence Forces Headquarters, he died in 2022 and was accorded national hero status.

summary: Highten Nkomo, who fought as Cde Billy Mzamo, was born in 1952 to parents who had moved to Zambia after losing their land in Tsholotsho. Drawn to nationalist politics as a youth, he overcame his father's attempts to keep him in school and joined the armed struggle. He trained in Tanzania and then in the Soviet Union. He later stayed loyal to the revolutionary party and died of an asthma attack at his rural home on 14 September 2022, leaving a wife, children and grandchildren.

timeline.text: Born to Zimbabwean parents who had moved to Zambia after losing their land in Tsholotsho.
Attended Kapono Primary School and another school whose name is only partly legible.
Became interested in nationalist politics through ZAPU literature and became active in the youth wing of the nationalist movement.
Tried to join the armed struggle but his father objected and involved the Zambian police; a meeting with Zambia's Home Affairs minister decided he should go back to a commercial college in Lusaka.
Slipped away again and this time his father did not follow up; he linked up with other recruits at a camp in Zambia that hosted nationalist fighters.
Was moved to a camp roughly 100 km from Lusaka and then to training in Tanzania alongside recruits who later became senior commanders.
After basic training he was sent to the Soviet Union for specialised military training.
His health deteriorated and he later remained a loyal member of the revolutionary party, ZANU PF.
Died at his rural home in the Dengu area after an asthma attack, aged 70.

summary: Kenneth Manyonda was born in 1934 in Buhera and educated up to Advanced Level at Dadaya Mission. He joined nationalist politics in the late 1950s and rose through the NDP, ZAPU and ZANU in Gweru while also leading the textile workers' union. He was detained for two years in the 1960s, then studied industrial relations and economics in Britain. After independence he held public-service, deputy-minister, Governor and parliamentary posts, famously defeating Morgan Tsvangirai in Buhera North in 2000. He died in November 2022 aged 88 and was accorded national hero status.

timeline.text: Born at Manyonda Village under Chief Nerutanga in Buhera, one of nine children.
Completed Ordinary Level at Dadaya Mission in 1954 and studied Advanced Level there in 1956 and 1957.
After school he worked in industry and commerce and, angered by racial discrimination, joined the African National Congress of Southern Rhodesia, formed that year.
After the ANC was banned he joined the National Democratic Party and became its local branch secretary in Gweru.
Returned to Gweru from a short stay in Livingstone, Zambia, was made Chairman of the ZAPU Gweru Branch and took a job as an accounts clerk at a hosiery firm, where he moved into trade unionism.
Was elected chairman of the factory's textile workers' union branch and then president of the national United Textile Workers Union of Rhodesia.
Became Vice-Chairman of the ZANU Gweru Branch after ZANU's formation and married Ruby Kachuwa.
Arrested and detained for about two years at Whawha, Sikombela and Salisbury prisons for advocating black empowerment.
On release he resigned the union presidency, organised a union newspaper and was elected Publicity Secretary of the African Trade Union Congress.
Left for the UK on a British Government grant to study industrial relations and helped receive and support ZANU PF students there; later earned a BSc in Economics in London and an MPhil at Bradford.
Returned home and worked in the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare as Deputy Registrar in charge of Industrial Relations.
Joined the Post and Telecommunications Corporation as Director of Personnel and helped remove racial imbalances.
Served as Deputy Minister (Posts and Telecommunications), working on rural communication improvements (details partly legible).
Appointed chairman of a rural development council and then provincial Governor for Manicaland.

Re-appointed Governor in April, won the Buhera North primaries and in July resigned to stand in the June 2000 parliamentary election, defeating MDC leader Morgan Tsvangirai and later nicknamed 'Shumba ya Tsvangirai'.
Appointed Deputy Minister of Industry and International Trade, taking part in bilateral and economic talks with foreign countries.

Championed provincial projects including a dam, the Pungwe water project that ended Mutare's water shortages and the Nyanga irrigation scheme; served on the Chairman's panel and as Acting Speaker of Parliament.
Was appointed acting Chief Nerutanga and held the role until his death.
Died at New Marlborough Hospital after a long illness, aged 88.
Accorded national hero status for his contribution before and after independence; the President praised him as a quietly spoken veteran nationalist.

summary: Betty Flora Mtero was born in Shurugwi in 1932 and trained as a Science teacher at Dadaya Mission. With her husband James she joined the nationalist movement, working in the underground committee that supported freedom fighters. She became a pioneer of women's empowerment, a trainer of rural women, a first-of-her-kind African holder of education qualifications and a long-serving ZANU (PF) Central Committee member. She received several awards and an honorary degree, died at home in Harare at 90 and was accorded national heroine status.

timeline.text: Born in Shurugwi, the third of six children of Aaron and Sekai Chikowore.
Attended Marshall Hartley Primary School and then Moleli Secondary School before training as a Science teacher at Dadaya Mission.
Married James Mtero, and the couple later moved with his work to Shabanie, Bulawayo and Fort Victoria.
The couple joined the NDP formed in 1959, then ZAPU after the NDP was banned in December 1961, and later ZANU, with Betty working in the underground committee supporting freedom fighters.
Hosted the funeral of the country's first Black doctor at her Bulawayo home; the Rhodesian regime was then trying to suppress African nationalist activity.
Became the first Zimbabwean appointed assistant training officer for women (Ministry of Internal Affairs, as read), teaching women with Winifred Wilson how to improve their lives and families.
Became the first African to be awarded a certificate in education by the then university and later won an Associateship of the Institute of Education.
Received further training at the University of London.
Moved to Harare after her husband became the first permanent secretary of Education and Culture in the new government (partly legible).
Established the Roger Howman Training Centre in Masvingo and took on several community, women's affairs and children's welfare roles.
Represented Zimbabwe as a delegate at the United Nations women's world forum in Beijing, China.
Won the Ndichiri Mupenyu Award (2008), an honorary master's degree in community development (2009) and the Outstanding Women Award from the national chamber of commerce (2014).
Died peacefully at her home in Glen Lorne, Harare, aged 90.
Conferred national heroine status; ZANU PF war veterans secretary Douglas Mahiya called her a dedicated revolutionary who risked her life for the country's liberation.

summary: Epmarcus Walter Kanhanga was born in 1950 in what is now Chipuriro and was expelled from school in 1968 for political activism before crossing into Mozambique in 1969. He trained as a nurse and fighter, served as a section commander, commissar and provincial commander of Gaza, and played a leading liaison role between ZANLA and Frelimo. After independence he became a Colonel and then Brigadier General, retiring in 1997 before leading the National Parks department and later entering politics as a Guruve North Member of Parliament. He died in his sleep in February 2023 and was conferred national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in what is now Chipuriro, Mashonaland Central, the third of seven children.
Expelled from school after being caned for taking part in student political activism, which also brought him under Special Branch watch.
Crossed into Mozambique through the Chidodo border and was received by Frelimo fighters at Seguranza Base, where he first met ZANLA members.
Taken to Chifombo Base, where he met Solomon Mujuru and Josiah Tungamirai and was put in charge of moving weapons to forward operational bases.
Selected for training at Mgagao Camp in Tanzania, specialised in nursing and served as an intern at two hospitals until the end of 1972.
Deployed to Rhodesia, operating in Mt Darwin and Shamva, and fought his first battle at Gwetera followed by several others.
Became Section Commander and held the Nyamahobogo battleground against attack.
After Chitepo's assassination in Lusaka and the arrest of ZANLA leaders, he was redeployed to Mozambique, took charge of ZANLA forces in the north-east and ran the Tembwe camp.
Served as liaison officer between ZANLA and Frelimo, opened Chimoio Camp and helped run ZIPA.
Appointed Provincial Political Commissar for Gaza Province and took part in the Gaza Attack of 1976.
Returned to the front as Commander of Gaza Province, covering areas around Gonarezhou, Chiredzi and Mwenezi, until replaced by Happison Muchechetere.
Withdrawn and posted to Botswana as ZANLA representative responsible for resources and moving recruits; later helped plan assembly points and served as liaison officer for Chipinda Pools and Dzapasi.

Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army, served as deputy commander of an infantry brigade in 1980, and in 1981 became a substantive Colonel commanding Midlands Province and commander of the Zimbabwe People's Militia.
Married Agines Ramwai Rugoyi at a military wedding in Masvingo attended by Vice President Chiwenga.
Promoted to Brigadier General, the rank he held until retiring from the Defence Forces in 1997.
Joined National Parks and Wild Life in 1998, became Acting Director in 1999 and retired on 30 November 2005 when the department became a parastatal.
Entered politics as ZANU PF district secretary for security and later held directorships and trusteeships.
Elected ZANU PF Member of Parliament for Guruve North and later became a Central Committee member.
Died in his sleep, leaving a wife and four children.
The ZANU PF Politburo agreed to confer national hero status on him, and his province praised him as a man who helped people from all walks of life.

summary: Christopher Mushohwe was born in 1954 in Marange, Manicaland, worked as a clerk in Harare and in 1978 sided with freedom fighters against his white employer, narrowly escaping arrest and joining the fighters in the Gandai mountains. After the war he held party, accounting and State-house administrative posts, then served as a ZANU-PF provincial secretary, Member of Parliament, Senator and Cabinet minister in transport, provincial affairs, youth/indigenisation and information. He also earned multiple doctorates and master's degrees. He died in Harare in February 2023 aged 69.

timeline.text: Born in Chindoti Village under Chief Marange, the 13th of fifteen children.
Employed as a Filling Clerk at Rhodesian Chemicals in Southerton, Harare, and became politically active in the 1970s, meeting freedom fighters on visits to his rural home.
Refused his white employer's order to work the weekend and instead delivered a clothing consignment to freedom fighters.

After an argument with the employer, soldiers handcuffed him and he was beaten and held; he later escaped through a friend and Father Dove at Silveira House and crossed to join freedom fighters at the Gandai mountains.
Assigned to scout targets in Mutare, took a teaching post at Sakubva to cover his work, and identified the Tip-Top shop, which was later bombed.
After the ceasefire he helped set up political structures in Mutare and was elected first secretary for security of the Tonhorai Branch in Devonshire.
Joined the Dairy Marketing Board and on 1 April was appointed the first black Assistant Accountant for the Gweru Branch.
Recalled to Harare to set up an administrative structure at the Prime Minister's State Residence and became Principal Executive Officer (Comptroller).
Tasked by Robert Mugabe to coordinate his study programme until 1990.
Married Penelope Batsirai Mutsago.
Served as ZANU-PF Manicaland Provincial Secretary for Production and Labour, then for Finance.
Elected to the Central Committee in 2000 and to Parliament in June 2000, serving until July 2008.
Became Minister of Transport and Communications.
Appointed Senator and Minister of State for Provincial Affairs and Resident Minister for Manicaland.
Elected Member of Parliament and again served as Minister of State for Manicaland.
Appointed Minister of Youth Development, Indigenisation and Economic Empowerment and Secretary for Economic Affairs in the Politburo.
Served as Minister of Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services (year not legible).
Became Executive Director of the Presidential Scholarship Department in the Office of the President and Cabinet.
Died at his Harare home after a prolonged illness, aged 69.
President Mnangagwa praised him as a key stalwart and loyal cadre whose contributions will be greatly missed; he left a wife and eight children.

summary: Born in 1927 near Chishawasha in Goromonzi, he worked as a teacher, builder and site manager before entering the taxi and bus trade in Mbare from 1956. Despite racial restrictions on African operators he grew a fleet of 27 vehicles and used his buses and offices to help nationalists, which brought a brief detention and later close surveillance through a Reserve Bank directorship. He was also known for charitable and civic board work and for supporting ZANU officials. He died on his farm in Beatrice in June 2023 aged 96.

timeline.text: Started primary school at Chishawasha and later continued at the secondary level there until 1946.
Worked as a teacher at Acturus Mine School.

Joined his father in the construction trade and qualified as a builder, then took a managerial post with the Rhodesian Selection Trust overseeing roads, school grounds and tree planting in Vainona Estates.
Married his first wife, Maria Mtandwa.
Left the Trust at the age of 28.
Started a taxi business at Mbare Musika despite colonial rules that kept Africans out of white-dominated taxi trade, and later got a house in Highfield.
Brought his brother into the business and became part of the first African family to open a taxi rank at Machipisa Shopping Centre.
Married a second wife, Abigail Chigodora, and bought a farm at Muda, Chihota, in what was then the African Purchase Area.
Grew his Easy-way Taxis fleet to eight cars, then sold them and bought two 44-seater Albion buses for the Domboshawa and Bindura routes.
Was arrested and held for two days at Southerton Police Station for lending his vehicle to ZAPU leaders, and was branded a terrorist.
Bought a new 76-seater DAF bus which transformed his business and pushed his fleet to 27 vehicles.
Became close to nationalists such as Edgar Tekere, James Chikerema, George Nyandoro and Robert Mugabe, hosting secret meetings and storing liberation documents at his offices.
Appointed Director at the Reserve Bank of Rhodesia, a post given partly to keep him under watch, yet he kept supporting the liberation struggle.
Acquired industrial property in the Southerton area, previously a white preserve, with a garage and parking used for vehicles of ZANU officials.
Married Coletta Madamombe, with whom he had three children, and was named to the Commission of Inquiry into Racial Discrimination.
Held chairmanship roles in district and Mashonaland East development bodies.
Died at his farm in Beatrice after a long illness, aged 96.

summary: Born in Chipinge in 1923 into a family of three children, Guti had limited schooling under colonial restrictions and began a spiritual journey from 1938, preaching from the late 1940s. He built ZAOGA Forward in Faith Ministries from small beginnings into a church present in over 100 countries, and founded schools, colleges, clinics and a television station. He wrote many books, a study Bible and received numerous honours and awards. He died in South Africa in July 2023 aged 100.

timeline.text: Started primary school at Ngaone but could not continue because colonial schooling barriers discouraged black advancement.
Had a spiritual encounter in a bush in Ngaone village, hearing music in the air and a voice, and later saw a vision of the man who would baptise him.
Had further spiritual experiences that led him to leave formal employment and devote himself to ministry.
Met Gwanzura, the man from his vision, and was baptised the same year.
Began an evangelism journey, according to the fragmentary text.
Travelled and preached widely in these years (details partly legible).
Bought a stand (No. 5448) for a church building in the Highfield area, where the first ZAOGA pastors were formed, and the construction was later completed.
Travelled abroad, and after returning married his sweetheart Eunor.
Bought a farm and set up a Bible training institution; his following kept growing.
After South African congregants asked for a branch, ZAOGA FIF South Africa was established.
ZAOGA spread to Mbeya in Tanzania.
Took part in the 10th independence celebrations, giving a prayer or invocation (wording partly legible).
The church expanded to Europe, other African countries and the United States.
Spearheaded an international leadership summit involving universities and Caribbean participation (name partly legible).
ZAOGA FIF had spread to 106 nations.
Died in South Africa of natural causes at the age of 100.

After graduating he worked in ZAPU's welfare department, sourcing clothes, food and other supplies from friendly countries and caring for refugee families and fighters. He stayed in Zambia after independence to wrap up welfare arrangements and died there in January 1981. The ZANU PF Politburo declared him a national hero in June 1994.

timeline.text: Born as the third of six children at Makhokhoba Clinic, Mzilikazi, Bulawayo.
Started primary school at Mzilikazi Primary, later going to Mzingwane for secondary school and matriculating at Loveday High School in South Africa.
Returned to Bulawayo and worked as a bank clerk at Barclays, Jason Moyo branch.
Joined the ZAPU Youth League and helped recruit other Mzilikazi youths into it.
Crossed into Zambia with fellow cadres, where senior ZAPU officials noticed his academic ability and directed him to study.
Enrolled at the Oppenheimer School of Social Work at the University of Zambia, where he and other students gathered clothes and materials for comrades.
Married Nokuthula Mlambo, also a social work student.
Finished a diploma in social work and chose full-time politics, being attached to ZAPU's social welfare department.
Travelled to supportive countries to study welfare systems and arranged donated clothes, food and ammunition for freedom fighters from Russia, China and Romania.
Led welfare efforts for refugee women and children left in camps while others went for training.
ZAPU leaders asked him to stay in Zambia to finalise welfare arrangements for comrades who remained behind.
Died while preparing to return to independent Zimbabwe.
ZANU PF Politburo posthumously declared him a national hero for his willpower, loyalty, patriotism and contribution to liberation.

timeline.text: Born at Chingwaru village in Guruve as the second of ten children.
Attended Mukwenya Primary School while staying with an uncle, but was sent home when colonial education barriers ended his schooling.
Went to Banket for work and took a job with a white farmer.
Refused to accept a caning from the farm owner and fled to Sinoia, now Chinhoyi, where he joined nationalist politics.
Crossed the border to be trained in Tanzania while still very young.
Returned to Rhodesia under the name David Guzuzu as the youngest of seven fighters.
Fought with six comrades in the day-long Chinhoyi Battle against Rhodesian forces and was killed aged 17, an event seen as the start of the Second Chimurenga.
Then President Mugabe recommended that the seven fighters of the battle be declared national heroes.

Enrolled with a correspondence college, but a wave of nationalism pushed him to leave his studies and join the National Democratic Party Youth Wing.
Moved into trade unionism, then after the NDP was banned joined ZAPU and became a youth leader.
Alongside Dumiso Dabengwa and other activists, helped receive and distribute arms in the early stage of the armed struggle.
Was part of a group of ZAPU cadres sent to Moscow for military intelligence training.
After training was posted to Zambia and then worked as a security officer for ZAPU (details unclear).
Joined a delegation to London seeking funds for the struggle, and after ZAPU's split and reorganisation took charge of party intelligence as Intelligence Director.
Deployed to Botswana, where he was abducted by Rhodesian scouts and never found; he was 36.
Was accorded national hero status for his willpower, loyalty, patriotism and contribution to liberation.

After independence he served as Deputy Commander of the Zimbabwe National Army and became Lieutenant General in 1981, but was arrested in 1982 on treason charges and held until March 1986, despite an acquittal. He died of cryptococcal meningitis at age 46 and was declared a national hero in 1994, with a barracks and a Bulawayo avenue later named after him.

timeline.text: Born in the Gwanda area, one of five children (details partly legible).
Left the country for Tanzania and completed military training there.
His strong performance led to roles as a military instructor and senior ZIPRA political and deputy commander.
Following the death of Nikita Mangena he took over leadership of ZIPRA.
Represented ZIPRA at the Ceasefire Commission and Operations Command, helped agree and put in place the Lancaster House deal, and led the first ZIPRA group home after the ceasefire.
Was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as Deputy Commander under General Solomon Mujuru (Rex Nhongo).
Was promoted to Lieutenant General.
Spoke at a passout parade stressing unity and that the old separate armies had given way to a single national force.
Was arrested and jailed on treason charges alongside Dumiso Dabengwa and others, though they were later acquitted.
Was released from detention.
Died of cryptococcal meningitis at Parirenyatwa hospitals aged 46.
Was declared a national hero along with Nikita Mangena, Artwell Bokwe, Amon Jirira, Jini Ntuta, Edison Sithole, Benjamin Burombo and Dr Samuel Tichafa Parirenyatwa.
Llewellin Barracks on the outskirts of Bulawayo was renamed Lookout Masuku Barracks in his honour.
Government renamed Colenbrander Avenue in Bulawayo in his honour.

Grew up under Mzilikazi's watch and was shaped into a loyal and skilled soldier.
Was appointed by Mzilikazi to lead the multi-ethnic Imbizo Regiment, which guarded the welfare of the kingship.
Married a woman of the Dlodlo clan, sister of Mgandane, one of Lobengula's lieutenants who was decapitated in the 1893 war.
Masterminded the Gadade fight, known as the Battle of Imbembesi, between Ndebele warriors and colonial settlers, in which Major Allan Wilson and members of his column died.
Died in 1893 (circumstances not legible).
Memorials later honoured him: a billboard at the Gadade battlefield and other monuments were put up by the National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe.

summary: James Chikerema was shaped politically in South Africa around 1950, where he met leading ANC figures and co-founded a social club with Maurice Nyagumbo. Back in Rhodesia he became first Vice-President of the African National Youth League in 1957, was named ZAPU vice president while detained, and later acted as ZAPU president during Nkomo's long detention, seeking arms and money abroad. He then helped found FROLIZI, signed the 1974 unity accord, formed the ZDP in 1975, served briefly in the Zimbabwe-Rhodesia government and later joined the Forum Party and the 1999 Constitutional Commission. He died of heart failure in 2006 and was buried at the family cemetery in Zvimba.

timeline.text: While in South Africa he met Nelson Mandela, Walter Sisulu and Oliver Tambo, who inspired him to enter politics, and he joined the South African congress movement.

He was elected chairman of the youth section and, with Maurice Nyagumbo, set up the Central African Social Club in Cape Town to raise political awareness among Rhodesian Africans and other nationalities there.

The African National Youth League was launched at Mai Musodzi Hall in Harare by a group including Mutandwa, Kutama, Parirewa and Nyandoro, and Chikerema, noted for his fiery and emotive style, was elected its first Vice-President.

He helped organise a bus boycott against the Public Order Act in Salisbury (about 200 Africans arrested), joined the Inter-Racial Association and rallied Africans against implementation of a land law (name cut off).
He was detained under a state of emergency declared by Sir Edgar Whitehead, which shook the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland and drew international attention.
While he was in detention ZAPU was formed and he was named its vice president in absentia.
After his release Nkomo sent him to Tanzania and later Zambia to prepare for the training of freedom fighters.
As acting ZAPU president he toured Eastern Europe, Russia and China, addressing a reported two million people in Tiananmen Square, and sought military and financial help.
During Nkomo's detention he and colleagues such as Nathan Shamuyarira and George Nyandoro broke away from ZAPU and ZANU to form the Front for the Liberation of Zimbabwe (FROLIZI).
He signed a unity accord with Abel Muzorewa, Ndabaningi Sithole and Joshua Nkomo, brokered by Kenneth Kaunda and Julius Nyerere.
He formed the Zimbabwe Democratic Party (ZDP).
He was appointed co-minister of transport in the short-lived Zimbabwe-Rhodesia government.
He joined the Forum Party led by Enoch Dumbutshena, Zimbabwe's first black judge.
He served on the Constitutional Commission.
He died of heart failure and was buried at the family cemetery in Zvimba.
President Mnangagwa named him among the heroes being recognised as part of a fuller account of the liberation war.

summary: Benjamin Burombo was an early nationalist and founder of the African Workers Voice Association who resisted racial segregation under white minority rule. He moved from selling religious books and working as a hotel chef in Johannesburg, where Clement Kadalie influenced him, to cattle dealing, insurance sales and a grocery lease in the 1940s that gave him independence and contacts. His speaking skill let him mobilise crowds over wages and land grievances, and he fought the Native Land Husbandry Act. He died in 1959 and the ZANU PF Politburo declared him a national hero on 10 June 1994.

timeline.text: Born into a peasant farming family, one of eight children (five brothers and three sisters), in the Shurugwi area.

Went to Johannesburg, worked as an assistant chef at the Carlton Hotel and met trade unionist Clement Kadalie, who pushed him toward trade unionism.
Returned to Rhodesia and became a cattle dealer in the Selukwe (Shurugwi) District.
Settled in Bulawayo as a salesperson for several insurance societies.
Obtained a lease on a grocery store (location garbled, apparently in Bulawayo), which gave him economic independence and political connections.
Used his oratory, stature and shrewdness to rally the masses over low wages and other economic grievances, pressuring the government's Native Labour Board to respond.

Bitterly opposed the Native Land Husbandry Act, which pushed Africans off productive land, and successfully challenged cases where native commissioners applied it wrongly, inspiring wider resistance to evictions.
Died.
The ZANU PF Politburo unanimously declared him a national hero in recognition of his contribution to liberation.

summary: Godwin Manyerenyere (1946-1966) from Shurugwi left school after Standard Six because of colonial education barriers and worked in his father's shoe business before heading to Mutare. In 1964 he slipped into Mozambique, joined the guerrilla movement and trained there and in Tanzania. He was one of seven fighters who fought the Rhodesian Front at Chinhoyi on 28 April 1966, a battle seen as the start of the Second Chimurenga, and died at 20, unmarried. He is buried at Chemagamba Cemetery in Chinhoyi, and in 2017 Mugabe urged that the seven be declared national heroes.

timeline.text: Born in Makusha Township, Shurugwi, to Watson and Lydia Manyerenyere (nee Dirwai), the second of eight children.
Attended Charles Wraith Primary School up to Standard Six and could not continue because colonial education was designed to keep Africans as casual labour.
Worked as a cobbler in his father's shoe business in Shurugwi.
Left home seeking better prospects and visited an aunt in Mutare.
Crossed into Mozambique with other young men and women and joined the guerrilla movement.
Trained in Mozambique and was recommended for further military training in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania.
Returned to Rhodesia as one of seven young fighters who took on the Rhodesian Front.
Fought the Rhodesian Front soldiers at Chinhoyi in an all-day battle and was killed when the seven ran out of ammunition; the clash marked the start of the Second Chimurenga.
Then President Mugabe recommended that the seven fighters of the Chinhoyi Battle be declared national heroes.

Led students from Mount Selinda and Chikore missions in barricading a road used by colonial settlers; he was arrested and made to report weekly to Nyazura Police Station.
Abandoned his studies to join military training in Zambia.
Selected for further training and sent to the People's Republic of China, then returned to Zambia.
Regrouped with fellow fighters in Mozambique awaiting deployment and joined a sabotage plan against colonial infrastructure.
Deployed with six others to Chinhoyi to cut the Kariba power lines, was betrayed by locals, and was killed after a day-long battle in which the group ran out of ammunition.

After crossing to Zambia in 1963 he was sent to Prague, where he took an Economics degree in 1968, then received military and intelligence training and worked in ZAPU's intelligence structures. He came home in late 1980 and rose to Administrator at Bulawayo City Council. He died on 6 October 2003, was buried at Pelandaba and was declared a national hero; his wife Gloria and son Nkathazo survived him.

ZAPU leaders, noticing his sharp intellect, sent him with other cadres to the Prague School of Economics in Czechoslovakia.
Graduated with a degree in Economics.
Returned to Lusaka with his group for military training and was received by George Nyandoro.
Was brought into ZAPU's intelligence department under Dumiso Dabengwa and sent to the USSR for about three months of military intelligence training.
Back in Lusaka he was deployed to an intelligence camp and later became deputy director of a ZAPU intelligence structure after the capture of Cde Mohadi (details garbled).
Returned to Zimbabwe.
Joined Bulawayo City Council as an administration clerk and later rose to Administrator, the post he held until his death.
Married his long-time sweetheart Gloria Nkomo.
Died of diabetes in Bulawayo aged 64; the ZANU PF Politburo then declared him a national hero for his brainpower, loyalty and contribution to liberation.

summary: Joshua Malinga, born in 1944 in Filabusi, was afflicted by polio at age two and later used a wheelchair, but with help from national hero Naison Ndlovu he trained and studied in Bulawayo and qualified in accounting. Angered by racial and disability discrimination in Rhodesia, he became a disability-rights activist and worked underground with freedom fighters, smuggling letters to jailed nationalists. After independence he rose through ZANU PF and local government, becoming Deputy Mayor and then Mayor of Bulawayo, later a Senator, Politburo secretary for the disabled and Special Advisor to the President on Disability. He lectured and advocated internationally and died of cancer on 8 September 2023 aged 79.

timeline.text: Born in Filabusi, the third of nine children.

timeline.date: at the tender age of two
timeline.text: Was struck by polio, which shaped his childhood and left him restricted to farm chores while peers went to school.
National Hero Naison Ndlovu took him to Bulawayo, where he trained as a cobbler at the Jairos Jiri Centre.
After finishing primary school early, entered Mpopoma High School and passed his exams with distinction in 1965.
Enrolled at Bulawayo Polytechnic to study accounting.
Finished his studies, returned to the Jairos Jiri Centre, rose to top management and won a scholarship to study in the UK.
Came back to Rhodesia and took a job as an accounts clerk in the Government income tax department, where he met discrimination.
Elected chairperson of the National Council of the Disabled Persons of Rhodesia and founded the Disability Rights Movement in Rhodesia.
Built several service stations in Bulawayo suburbs and had other business interests while working underground with freedom fighters and smuggling letters to jailed nationalists.
Served as Deputy Mayor of the City of Bulawayo.
Elevated to Mayor of Bulawayo.
Held the post of deputy provincial chairperson of ZANU PF in Bulawayo Province.
Elected interim (Acting) Chairperson of Mayors and won a Businessman of the Year award.
Served as Deputy Secretary for the disabled and disadvantaged in the ZANU PF Politburo.
Chaired the National Disability Board.
Served as a Member of the Senate of Zimbabwe.
Held the Politburo post of Secretary for the disabled and disadvantaged.
Sat in the Senate as the member representing disabled people.
Appointed by President Mnangagwa as Special Advisor on national disability issues and produced Zimbabwe's first National Disability Policy (appointment year not printed).
Died of cancer at his Northvale home in Bulawayo, aged 79.

summary: Ngwabi Bhebe was born in 1942 in Filabusi, earned a BA at the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland and a PhD in imperial history in London. He taught in Rhodesia, the USA, Sierra Leone and Botswana/Lesotho/Swaziland before joining the University of Zimbabwe, where he rose to Professor of History and Pro-Vice-Chancellor. He conceived and established Midlands State University around 1999, serving as its founding Vice Chancellor and growing it into a multi-campus institution, while also holding many national, regional and international academic posts and publishing widely on Zimbabwean history. He died of diabetes on 16 November 2023 aged 81 and was conferred national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Filabusi; his family soon moved to the Belingwe (Mberengwa) area.
Went on to secondary school and earned his Junior Certificate (year and school name uncertain).
Completed secondary education at Fletcher High School in Gweru.
Began a BA in History and Geography at the University of Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland, graduating in 1967 with excellent grades.
Enrolled with the University of London for a doctorate in Imperial History, going straight to a PhD on his lecturers' recommendation.
Started academic work as a Teaching and Research Assistant at the University of Rhodesia despite his superior qualifications.
Left for the Woodrow Wilson School at Princeton, USA, as a Parvin Fellow and visiting scholar with the Phelps-Stokes Fund.
Became a History lecturer at Fourah Bay College, University of Sierra Leone.
Taught History at the Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland university, holding posts such as Dean of Humanities and History chairperson, and wrote school history textbooks.
Returned home to join the University of Zimbabwe as a History lecturer.
Promoted to Associate Professor of History at the University of Zimbabwe.
Appointed external examiner by the universities of Botswana and Zambia; Malawi invited him in 1991.
Appointed Full Professor of History and promoted to Pro-Vice-Chancellor at the University of Zimbabwe.
Left the University of Zimbabwe to supervise, research, write and try entrepreneurship, developing ideas on decentralising university education.
His concepts led to the founding of the third state university, Midlands State University, despite resistance; he became its founding Vice Chancellor.
Introduced a multi-campus model that opened Zvishavane, Harare and Kwekwe campuses and made the university research-led and solution-driven (dates not printed).
Reading suggests he led the university until about 2016, by which time it was among the country's largest tertiary institutions (garbled).
Died of diabetes at Midlands Private Hospital, aged 81.

summary: Kenny Mabuya, known in the war as Kenny Ridzai, was born in 1952 near Filabusi, grew up in Zambia and left school in 1969 to join ZANLA. After training in Tanzania he fought inside Rhodesia from 1972, surviving ambushes and a spell of mistreatment by FRELIMO soldiers, and later worked in ZANLA security and intelligence, leading the advance group to Lancaster House in 1979. After independence he was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army in 1981, led the Intelligence Corps, became a Lieutenant Colonel and retired in 1994. He died in Harare on 23 January 2024 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Gangabezi Village near Filabusi, the third of six children.
His family moved to Zambia, where they had bought a farm.
Started primary school at Thalimbana Primary School in Lusaka.
Entered Libala Secondary School in Lusaka.
Left school during Form Two and, to avoid being sent back by his ZIPRA brother Shame, enlisted with ZANLA at the ZANU offices in Lusaka.
Was sent to Mbeya in Tanzania en route to Intumbi Camp, where Chinese instructors trained him.
Moved to the Kongwa transit camp in Tanzania.

Returned to Lusaka, went on to Mozambique and Chifombo Camp, fought Portuguese troops on the way, entered Rhodesia and began planting landmines and attacking army routes, helping open the Chaminuka Sector.
Took part in an ambush at Chunya Bridge in Mutoko; afterwards soldiers surrounded his group and he escaped, finally reaching Chief Makuni's area after a three-week walk.
Sheltered in Chief Makuni's homestead with a school pass, mobilised villagers, was betrayed to soldiers but escaped identification as a student.

Crossed into Mozambique, was held and badly treated by suspicious FRELIMO soldiers for three months, then freed by a FRELIMO commander; comrades later vouched for him and he insisted on returning to the front (year not printed).

Was deployed to the Mt Darwin and Centenary area, leading an operational section, later commanding three sections and targeting commercial farm assets that supported the Smith regime (text partly garbled).
Injured in Guruve in a clash with fake soldiers hired by the regime and later became security aide to Cde Chigohwe; in October 1974 went to Chifombo Base to vet recruits against infiltrators.
Became deputy to a Cde Gava in the Military Security Department and was sent for six months of further security studies.
Led the advance group to the Lancaster House Conference, then served at an assembly point in Buhera, Manicaland.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as an officer; commissioned Lieutenant on 18 November 1982.
Promoted Captain in 1984, made Commanding Officer of the Zimbabwe Intelligence Corps in 1985, Major in 1987 and later Lieutenant Colonel in 1990 (rank reading partly garbled).
Retired from the Zimbabwe Defence Forces after continuous service.
Died after a short illness at Westend Clinic in Harare; the Politburo accorded him national hero status.
