summary: Dzimiri was born in Shurugwi in 1958 and left school during the 1970s war to join ZANLA in Mozambique, where he survived both the Nyadzonia and Chimoio massacres. He trained in military intelligence in China and Yugoslavia, served as an instructor and as chief aide to General Tongogara, and helped fold ZANLA fighters into the national army. After a short army and civilian spell he joined the CIO in 1983 and rose to Director level, including a liaison posting in Cuba and the Investments Unit directorship. He died in April 2024 and was declared a national hero by the President and Politburo.

timeline.text: Born in Nyahwa Village, Shurugwi, the eldest of seven children.
Began primary school at Kwarire in Shurugwi, later moving to Matamba Primary and then Hanke Mission, where he finished primary school.
Attended Lower Gweru College for his secondary education.
Angered by racial segregation, left Rhodesia on foot for Mozambique to join ZANLA and received political orientation at Nyadzonia Camp.
Survived the Nyadzonia massacre, then was picked for a security and intelligence course at the Nanking Military Academy in China, earning a diploma.
After more training at Chimoio, operated in Gaza Province until he was pulled out with serious injuries.
Took a second intelligence training course in China.
Became military instructor at the Chaminuka Security and Intelligence Camp in Chimoio, taking over from Kenny Constantine Mabuya, who was away training.
Survived the Chimoio massacre.
Served as chief aide to General Tongogara, sat on the National Security Analysis Group and made secret intelligence incursions into Rhodesia.
Worked as a security and intelligence instructor and trained about 300 cadres who later served in the Prime Minister's Office at Independence.
Went to Yugoslavia for advanced military science training.
Returned and became second in charge at Buffalo Range Assembly Point, helping integrate ZANLA combatants into the Zimbabwe National Army.
Left the national army after a brief spell in the Air Force of Zimbabwe and took civilian jobs, including a municipal police post.
Joined the Central Intelligence Organisation as a security officer and was posted to the Kwekwe station.
Climbed from Senior Security Officer to Intelligence Officer, Assistant Senior Intelligence Officer, Senior Intelligence Officer (moved to Marondera) and Divisional Intelligence Officer.
Moved to Counter Intelligence in December 1999 and was confirmed as Provincial Intelligence Officer the next year.
Transferred to the Internal Branch as Provincial Intelligence Officer for Mashonaland East, leading operations against subversion and supporting the Land Reform Programme alongside Chief Svosve.

Was later promoted to Assistant Director, posted to Havana as liaison officer (a link that led to Zimbabwean doctors and teachers being trained in Cuba), then recalled to a senior Internal Branch operations role and made Director Counter Intelligence.
Redeployed as Director of the Investments Unit, a post he held until he died on 16 April 2024.

summary: Vezha grew up in Chivi, Masvingo, and as a Form Four pupil took part in sabotage of roads used by Rhodesian forces before joining ZANLA in late 1977. He trained in North Korea and joined the Zimbabwe National Army in 1982, then rose through staff, instructor and command posts, including a UN observer mission in Angola. From 2014 he served as personal staff officer to the army commander and then the Defence Forces commander, and he became Brigadier General in 2018. He died in a road accident in Kwekwe in April 2024 and was named a national hero by the President and Politburo.

timeline.text: Born in Zangure Village, Chivi South, the sixth of eight children.
Started primary school at Chihaya; after a school closure in January 1970 he moved through Murezi, Runesu and Chitanga schools and finished Grade Seven in 1975.
Entered Lundi High School in Mwenezi for secondary education.
Led fellow students in digging trenches across the Masvingo-Beitbridge highway and feeder roads used by Rhodesian forces, which put them under surveillance.
After his O-Level studies he joined ZANLA and was trained at the front.
Was stationed at Dzapasi Assembly Point Base 2 and later deployed in Mt Darwin.
Selected for military training in North Korea, where he studied until 1982 alongside future senior officers.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army.
Promoted to Lieutenant and appointed Platoon Commander.
Promoted to Captain and married Veronica the same year.
Held staff posts in charge of staff duties, then company second in command, then operations staff officer.
Chosen to lead a team of international officers on a United Nations Observer Mission in Angola.
Promoted to Major on his return.
Served as Directing Staff at the Zimbabwe Staff College, became Brigade Major of 1 Infantry Brigade in 2000, and returned to the Staff College senior division at the end of 2003.
Promoted to Lieutenant Colonel.
Chief Instructor at the Zimbabwe School of Infantry, then Commanding Officer of an infantry battalion.
Became operations staff officer Grade 1, was promoted to Colonel in 2014 and served as personal staff officer to the Commander of the Zimbabwe National Army.
Became personal staff officer to the Commander Defence Forces.
Promoted to Brigadier General, the rank he held until his death.
Died in a road accident in Kwekwe aged 62 and was subsequently accorded national hero status.

summary: Chaunoita was born in Gutu in 1958 and was pushed out of school by colonial education barriers, which led him to join ZANLA in Mozambique in 1975. He survived the Nyadzonia massacre, trained in military engineering, took a VIP protection course in Yugoslavia and then served as security detail to the ZANLA High Command and as aide-de-camp to Vice President Muzenda. After independence he joined the President's Department (CIO) in 1981 and rose to Director Security and later a Director in the Director General's Office, retiring in 2020. He died in May 2024 after a long illness and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Munoda Village, Gutu, the third of five children.
Started primary school at Gudo, moving to Mataruse Primary in 1970 and then to Gutu Secondary School.
Could not continue his education because of colonial barriers, worked in menial jobs at home and, after meeting freedom fighters from Mozambique and attending pungwes, resolved to join the struggle.
Left for Mozambique with Charles Hwekwete, Colonel Masocha and Amen Sithole, evading arrest, travelling by bus to Mutare and crossing the border on foot.
Stayed at Villa De Manica before moving to Nyadzonia Camp for political orientation.
Survived the Nyadzonia massacre.
Transferred to Tembwe Camp after life-threatening injuries and trained in military engineering.
Selected for a VIP protection course in Yugoslavia, then served as security detail to the ZANLA High Command in Gaza Province.
Deployed to Maputo Province as aide-de-camp to Vice President Simon Muzenda and made a member of the ZANLA General Staff.
Escorted General Tongogara from Maputo to Chimoio and survived the car accident on the return trip that killed Tongogara.
Attested into the President's Department (CIO) as a security officer in the Internal Branch.
Sent to Romania for seven months of training in clandestine investigation.
Promoted to Intelligence Officer.
Moved from the Internal Branch to the Security Branch as Deputy Director Security.
Promoted to Director Security.
Redeployed to the Director General's Office as a Director, the post he held until retiring on 30 June 2020.
Acquired Strathlore Farm in Goromonzi through land reform and farmed maize and wheat.
Died at home after a long illness aged 65 and was accorded national hero status.

summary: Mutsvunguma was born in Makoni in 1957 and left St Augustine Secondary School in 1975 to lead 17 fellow students into Mozambique and join the liberation war. He served in security screening at Nyadzonya, trained in Tanzania, and later worked at the ZANLA High Command as a political commissar instructor alongside figures such as Emmerson Mnangagwa. From 1980 he served in the Zimbabwe National Army, rising from company commander through Major to Brigadier General and attending courses in several countries. He died in June 2024 and was conferred national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Kwaramba Village, Makoni, the eighth of eleven children.
Attended Katsenga and Teikida primary schools and then St Augustine Secondary School in Penhalonga.
Abandoned school, led 17 St Augustine students across the border into Mozambique, and served as security officer screening recruits at Nyadzonya Camp.
Went to Tanzania, where he received initial military training.

Deployed to the ZANLA High Command as a political commissar instructor, advising on political reorientation, analysing world news and drafting political lessons, working with Emmerson Mnangagwa and George Rutanhire.
Helped produce the Zimbabwe News magazine with Henry Muchemwa, Tendayi Chitsotso, Herbert Matanga and George Kashiri.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army and appointed a company commander.
Promoted to Lieutenant.
Promoted to Captain.
Promoted to Major and appointed to a post at Headquarters 2 Infantry Brigade later that year.
Served in an administrative staff officer role (details illegible).
Later career (partly illegible) included senior staff posts, promotion to Colonel and then Brigadier General, and non-military postings such as a marketing role at a defence company.
Died of diabetes at Tariro Medical Centre in Rusape aged 67 and was accorded national hero status.

summary: Chaminuka was born in 1962 in Mashonaland East and left school in late 1977 after student unrest to join the liberation war in Mozambique. He trained as a medical orderly under Dr Sydney Sekeramayi and worked at the ZANLA National Pharmacy, then joined the Zimbabwe National Army in January 1981. He rose to Brigadier General through military intelligence, staff college, personal staff and business development roles and attended many career courses. He died in July 2024 after a short illness and was declared a national hero by the President and Politburo.

timeline.text: Born in Mashonaland East Province under Chief Nemato (as read).
Began primary school at Kapfunde.
Entered St Columbus Secondary School in Honde Valley; in 1976 the school was shut by the Smith regime after many students joined the war, and he moved to St John's (Chikwaka) Secondary School.
Took part in student protests, was spared arrest because of his age, and decided to leave school for Mozambique.
Crossed into Mozambique with five others after a harsh trek, was rescued by a villager and taken to a base, then to Doroi Refugee Camp because of his young age.
Moved to Tembwe Base 2 where he resumed training, then went to Chimoio for a medical training course under Dr Sydney Sekeramayi.
Was deployed to the National Pharmacy, which received, tested, stored and dispatched medicines, and stayed there during the ceasefire in case war resumed.
Returned home to Echo Assembly Point in Nyanga, then to Tongogara Assembly Point in Chipinge, where he was selected for the national army.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army and served under Headquarters 1 Infantry Brigade.
Married Lilian Ndora.

Held a series of posts including Desk Officer in Military Intelligence, Directing Staff at the Staff College, Personal Staff Officer to the Defence Forces commander, Director Military Intelligence and Director Business Development at the National Defence University (dates not legible).
Died at Trauma Centre in Harare after a short illness and was accorded national hero status.

summary: Gibbs Kachana, born Fainos Zungura in Chivi District, left school and mine work to join the liberation struggle in Mozambique, where he trained, held guard command posts and later served in General Tongogara's security detail. He joined the Zimbabwe National Army in 1981, rose through Presidential Guard and staff appointments and became Brigadier General in 1996 while commanding 3 Brigade. He served on regional and international missions and received several service and campaign medals including the Grand Commander of the Order of Merit. He died in April 2000 and was declared a National Hero posthumously in May 2023.

timeline.text: Born Fainos Zungura in Chivi District, third of five children of Tachiona and Ethel Zungura.
Began primary school at Shindi School in Chivi, finished Standard 5 in 1968 and moved to Dare Primary for Grade Seven.
Went on to Lundi High School but was later forced to quit because the colonial system priced African pupils out of fees.
Took a job at Gaths Mine in Mashava, where he saw the harsh colonial treatment of workers first hand.
Turned to political activism and left Chivi with a group of youths on a hard walk to Mozambique to join the liberation war.
Recruited at a refugee camp in Mozambique, trained militarily, took a war name and was made Guard Commander at a camp in Mozambique.
Sent to Romania for further military training.
After returning from Romania he was appointed to the security detail of General Josiah Magama Tongogara.
Attended the Lancaster House talks in London, then stayed in Mozambique with Tongogara while the ceasefire was supervised.
Returned to Zimbabwe at Independence and was deployed at ceasefire assembly points.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as an officer.
Completed the Officers Foundation Course at the Zimbabwe Military Academy and was appointed Lieutenant.
Commanded a Presidential Guard Battalion, then served as a staff officer in the Army HQ Careers Department until November 1984.
Officer Commanding a Presidential Guard Battalion, later Deputy Commander of the HQ Presidential Guards Brigade.
Acting Director of the Food Production Department at Army HQ.
Acting Commander of 3 Brigade.
Promoted to Brigadier General and confirmed as Commander of 3 Brigade, a post listed to April 2000.
Served on missions including the Mozambique and DRC campaigns and a UN peacekeeping mission in Somalia (years unclear).
Died, aged 42 according to the text.
The ZANU PF Politburo under President Mnangagwa posthumously declared him a National Hero.

summary: Edson Sithole rose from a poor rural background and years of casual work to become a lawyer and nationalist organiser, helping found the African National Youth League and holding posts in ZNP, PASU, ZANU and the ANC. He spent long periods in detention and restriction, using that time to earn London and South African law degrees, culminating in a Doctor of Laws in 1974. He took part in the ANC's dealings with the Rhodesian government, including the 1975 Victoria Falls talks. In October 1975 he was abducted with his secretary and never accounted for.

timeline.text: Born in Bikita, the eldest of nine children of Chisingaitwi and Chioniso Sithole.
Started primary school at Bikita, later moving to Devuli School when the settler regime pushed his family to Birchenough Bridge.
After a forced year out of school following Standard Two (1947) while working as a tea picker, resumed at Chikore Mission and passed Standard IV.
Went to Umtali for night school but was tricked by a white farmer into three months of badly paid farm labour.
Escaped to Salisbury, studied at St Peter's night school while working menial jobs, and joined the campaign against the proposed Central African Federation.
Became a news vendor and then a clerk at an African newspaper company, studying privately and passing his Junior Certificate (1954) and A level (1957).
Helped found the African National Youth League with Chisiza, Hamadziripi, Nyandoro, Chikerema and Gonese, serving as interim Secretary-General; it was formally launched on this date.
Offered a US State Department scholarship but could not take it up because of his detention after the state of emergency.
Detained and moved between several prisons; while held at Marondera he drafted the National Democratic Party constitution, smuggled out to Michael Mawema for a new party to launch on 1 January 1960.
Moved with 14 other detainees, including Edgar Tekere, to a restriction area in Gokwe District.
Became Secretary-General of the Pan African Socialist Union formed from ZNP and a trades union congress; completed the LL.B. final in June and was released in July.
Passed the Rhodesian Bar exam and was admitted to the Bar, the second African after Herbert Chitepo; in August he joined the newly formed ZANU.
Elected Publicity Secretary of ZANU; arrested in late September and restricted to Wha Wha and another prison for a year.
Sat the LL.M. examination, was released into a five-mile limit around Salisbury, then sent back to Sikombela where the Sikombela Declaration was signed.
Moved to Salisbury Prison and enrolled for an LL.D. with the University of South Africa.
Released from detention but confined to a two-mile radius of Harare Police Station with daily reporting and a 7 pm curfew.
After the Pearce Commission report, became a leading figure in discussions between the ANC and the Rhodesian Government.
Awarded the Doctor of Laws degree, the only holder in Rhodesia and only African in Southern Africa with it; in June the ANC Central Committee rejected the reported Smith-Muzorewa deal.
Attended the Victoria Falls talks as a leading member of the ANC negotiating team.
Disappeared in Salisbury with his secretary Miriam Mhlanga and was never accounted for.

summary: Jack Mpofu, born Makhethi, left school early, worked in Rhodesia and South Africa, then crossed to Zambia in 1964 and joined ZAPU. He trained at Luthuli Camp, recruited fighters for training in Tanzania, took part in early sabotage and later trained in Russia. He became an instructor, camp commander and in 1976 Chief of Staff and Training, until wounds from a landmine incident ended his formal career. He stayed loyal to Nkomo and to unity after Independence and was accorded National Hero status after his death in July 2024.

timeline.text: Born Makhethi in Mangwe District, the only child of Pewulo Gwakuba Ndebele and his wife.
Started primary school at Tshitshi, later moving to Embakwe Mission but dropping out in Standard Six when fees became unaffordable.
Worked as an agricultural extension worker, then moved to South Africa for farm and mine work before returning to Rhodesia and taking road construction work in Bulawayo.
Crossed into Zambia with Ngozi and Thamu Kadamu, took the name Jack Mpofu, worked in road construction in Lusaka and joined ZAPU.
Trained at Luthuli Camp under Tshinga Dube, then was tasked with recruiting and sent about 200 recruits to Morogoro Camp in Tanzania.
Worked at Mwembeshi Camp with senior ZAPU leaders and led ten comrades to scout Zambezi crossing points near Daka.
With Mazinyane and Matshimini planted explosives under a bridge so that a Victoria Falls goods train was blown over, provoking heavy Rhodesian retaliation and closure of the border.
Stayed loyal to Joshua Nkomo when Chikerema and others broke away to form FROLIZ.
Sent to Russia for further military training.
Returned to Zambia, then served as an instructor at Morogoro in Tanzania under Sam Mfakazi; after disturbances there he moved back to Zambia as an instructor and later Camp Commander.
Promoted to Chief of Staff and Training at ZAPU Headquarters, working closely with Nikita Mangena.
Was injured in the landmine incident that killed Mangena and was sent to Czechoslovakia for treatment.
His injuries prevented him from taking formal employment after Independence.
Married Thokozile.
Died at his Cowdray Park home in Bulawayo after an asthma attack, aged 82.

summary: Elasto Madzingira, known in the war as Ronald Zvenyika, was a scholarship student who left university to join ZANLA in 1978 and served as a trainer of medics. After Independence he studied accountancy, joined the Air Force of Zimbabwe, rose to Group Captain and Director Finance, and later moved to the Army, retiring as Brigadier General in 1995. He held finance, board and commission posts in aviation, broadcasting, electricity and anti-corruption bodies and was active in development work in Chivi. He died in August 2024 and was unanimously accorded National Hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Chivi District, sixth of ten children of Willy and Mherita Madzingira.
Began primary school at Mudadisi, moved to Jaka Primary and finished in 1971.
Attended Fletcher High School after being selected for secondary education.
Won a World University Scholarship allowing study at any Commonwealth university and chose the University of Rhodesia.

Meeting ZANLA fighters such as Simon Mazorodze politicised him; he left studies with five other students to join the struggle in Bikita and was picked to train at the front, taking the name Ronald Zvenyika.
Did further military training at Nyamhinga Camp in Mozambique and served as a medical training officer training troop medics.
Deployed to ZANU PF headquarters in Maputo, where he joined the Secretariat.
Returned to Zimbabwe, then went to Yugoslavia to study mechanical engineering at the University of Zagreb.
Returned home because war injuries stopped him completing his studies, and later that year resumed at the University of Zimbabwe, starting a Bachelor of Accountancy in 1983.
Commissioned into the Air Force of Zimbabwe as a Flight Lieutenant.
Promoted to Squadron Leader.
Promoted to Wing Commander.
Promoted to Group Captain and Director Finance, then transferred to the Zimbabwe National Army.
Retired from active service and was promoted to Brigadier General; afterwards ran philanthropic road, dam and youth skills projects in Chivi.
Appointed a ZANU PF Central Committee member.
Died at his home in Harare, aged 65.

summary: Shadreck Dingaan Ndabambi, nicknamed Dingani Kimati in the war, left Ranch House College in 1975 to join the liberation struggle in Mozambique. He served as a section security officer, survived the 1977 Chimoio attack and later worked in Tongogara's headquarters office on operational and mapping materials. After joining the Zimbabwe National Army in 1981 he built a career in military intelligence and military police and attended several staff and investigation courses. He received service and campaign medals and was accorded National Hero status after his death in August 2024.

timeline.text: Born at Mutoko Hospital, seventh of ten children of Elijah and Monica Ndabambi.
Started primary school at Mutoko, later moving to Kotwa Primary in Mudzi where his father worked for the Ministry of Roads.
Began secondary school at Avilla Mission in Katerere and completed Form One.
Moved to All Souls Mission in Mutoko for the Zimbabwe Junior Certificate.
Enrolled at Ranch House College in Harare for Ordinary Level, where political awareness grew among students.
Left school with a group of four boys to join the liberation struggle, walking at night and crossing into Mozambique via the Gairezi River at Nyamaropa.
Villagers took the group to a Frelimo base where Ndabambi and friends met leaders including Robert Mugabe; he was then moved on for military and intelligence training.
Deployed in Manica Province as a Section Security Officer with the Mutambara Detachment in the Monomutapa Sector.
Severely injured and sent to Chimoio Base Camp for treatment.
Survived the Rhodesian Army attack on Chimoio Refugee Camp and was taken to a camp holding casualties.
After recovering, worked in Tongogara's office at ZANLA Headquarters in Gondola, preparing operational and cartography materials.
Helped safeguard ZANLA materials and documents in Mozambique.
Returned to Zimbabwe and was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army in September as a Second Lieutenant.
Built a career in military intelligence and military police, ending as Brigadier General (dates not printed).
Died, aged 67.

summary: Tshinga Dube, known in the war as Cde Embassy, grew up in Matobo and Bulawayo and was politicised by his family's forced removal and by confrontations at Solusi Mission. He trained abroad, specialised in military communications and engineering, and after Independence helped integrate the armed forces and headed the Army's signals directorate as a Colonel. In civilian life he served in Parliament for Makokoba, held ministerial and party posts including Secretary for Defence, and chaired or directed several public bodies. He died in October 2024 and was accorded National Hero status.

timeline.text: Born at Fort Usher in Matobo District, third of four children of Judge and Jane Lillian Dube.
Started primary school at Fort Usher, then moved to Mzilikazi Primary in Bulawayo and later Solusi Mission for secondary schooling.
His family was forcibly moved from their ancestral land to a remote, desolate area, an event that shaped his anger at colonial rule.
As a Standard Six pupil at Solusi Mission he and schoolmates began openly challenging the authorities.
Trained in Russia, earning an engineering degree in electro-techniques, and specialised in military communications (years not legible).
Served the liberation movement in communications roles, partly from Zambia (details garbled).
At the end of the war was tasked with helping merge the opposing forces, then was commissioned a full Colonel and headed the Directorate of Signals in the new Zimbabwe National Army.
Retired from the army (year not legible).
Held the Secretary for Defence post in ZANU PF, alongside Politburo and Central Committee membership.
Sat as Member of Parliament for Makokoba and served as a Deputy Minister and then Minister in the war veterans portfolio.
Died at Mater Dei Hospital, Bulawayo, aged 83.
The ZANU PF Politburo under President Mnangagwa unanimously accorded him National Hero status.

summary: Jaison Chirinda, who fought under the name William Chezhira Chakaipa, was born in Shamva and crossed into Zambia as a young man, where he joined the liberation struggle in 1965 and trained in several countries. He led one of the two groups sent to Sinoia (Chinhoyi), the clash remembered as the opening of the Second Chimurenga. Captured and sentenced to death, his sentence was reduced to life and he was held in Harare and Khami prisons until 1980. After independence he worked in government, the railways and Parliament and stayed active as a war veteran, dying in October 2024 and being declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Goora, Shamva District, into a family of seven children.
Started primary school at Goora Primary School.
After primary school, travelled to Zambia at the invitation of his elder sister and attended secondary school at Chifombo.
Joined the liberation struggle in Zambia and was picked for military training in Tanzania at Three Leaves Brigade.
His military aptitude led to further training in several countries, including China, Tanzania, Russia and Egypt.
Went back to Zambia to await deployment and then led one of two groups sent into Rhodesia at Sinoia (Chinhoyi); the other group was led by Christopher Chatambudza.
His group, remembered as the legendary seven, fought one of the fiercest battles of the war, which set the stage for the Second Chimurenga.
Was arrested after the Chinhoyi encounters and sentenced to death, a sentence later commuted to life imprisonment.
Served his sentence at Harare Prison alongside fellow revolutionaries including the future President Mnangagwa, and was later moved to Khami Prison in Bulawayo.
Released from Khami Prison at independence.
After independence, worked as a patrol officer and then joined the Ministry of Information, Posts and Telecommunications.
Joined National Railways of Zimbabwe.
Took up work at the Parliament of Zimbabwe, where he stayed until retirement.
Died of diabetes at the CDM Diabetic Centre in Harare.
The ZANU PF Politburo under President Mnangagwa unanimously accorded him national hero status.

summary: Phelekezela Mphoko, known in the war as Cde Report, grew up in Bubi District and trained as an agriculturalist before the racism he saw at work pushed him into ZAPU politics in the early 1960s. He was jailed, trained in the Soviet Union, and rose to become Chief of Logistics in the ZIPRA High Command, running arms and supply for the armed struggle and the ANC/ZAPU alliance. After independence he served in government and then as a diplomat in Mozambique, Austria, Botswana, Russia and South Africa, before becoming Vice President from 2014 to 2017. He died in India in December 2024 and was accorded national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Gwizane village, Bubi District.
Began primary school at David Livingstone Memorial School.
Enrolled for a Diploma in Agriculture at Tsholotsho Agricultural Breeding and Experimental School.
Graduated with a diploma in cropping and animal husbandry.
Left farm work because of racist treatment of workers and joined Dunlop Rhodesia Limited as a moulder, where he found the same injustice and became active in resisting it.
Elected ZAPU Youth Chairman for Mzilikazi Branch and was among the first to register as a ZAPU member, using the alias Report.
ZAPU was banned and he was restricted to his rural home area for three months.

Returned to Bulawayo and led the ZHI-I campaign of arson and sabotage; he was later arrested for retaliating against a police officer who set a dog on youths and sentenced to three years at Khami, then freed on bail pending appeal.
While on bail he defied its conditions to attend the People's Caretaker Council congress at Cold Comfort Farm, which set up an external ZAPU wing to direct the armed struggle.
Chosen by Joshua Nkomo for military training in the Soviet Union, where he studied Military Science and Photo Journalism.
Helped set up the Military Planning Committee and was elected to the ZIPRA High Command as Chief of Logistics under Nikita Mangena.
Joined the Joint Military Command (logistics and supply) of the ANC/ZAPU alliance and ran rehearsals for the Wankie operations at Dan Nang base, Luthuli Camp.
Withdrawn from the front and made ZIPRA Chief of Logistics and Supplies at headquarters, with Masala Sibanda as deputy.
Sat on the OAU ad hoc committee based in Mbeya, Tanzania, that worked to keep ZAPU and ZANU united.
Took part as a delegate in the founding of the Patriotic Front in Maputo and later attended an OAU Liberation Committee meeting in Luanda with Msika and Silundika.
Married Laurinda Mphoko, with Jacob Zuma as best man.
Joined the Ministry of Labour and Social Services.
Moved into the diplomatic service, with a posting in Mozambique as liaison officer.
Appointed liaison officer to Austria, covering UN drug control and the nuclear-test-ban treaty organisation, until 1999.

Appointed Zimbabwe's Ambassador to Botswana; later served as Ambassador to the Russian Federation (where he negotiated Russian use of its veto against sanctions in 2007) and to South Africa (from 2010).
Appointed Vice President of Zimbabwe, a post he held until 2017, after retiring from diplomacy in May 2014.
Died in India after a long illness at the age of 84.

summary: John Mbedzi, known in the struggle as Maworesa, was born near Gwanda and was expelled from school after confronting a racist principal, which marked the start of his resistance. He joined the NDP and ZAPU, spent seven years in detention from 1964, and later sabotaged a white-owned farm before crossing into Mozambique in 1974. In exile he worked as a broadcaster and ZAPU publicity cadre in Mozambique, Zambia and Egypt, and he attended the Lancaster House talks. After independence he became a ZANU PF leader in Matabeleland South and was declared a national hero after his death.

timeline.text: Born at Tshamatengu area near Todds in Gwanda District, the eldest son in a family of six children.
White farmers took over Tshamatengu and his parents were moved to Swereki in Beitbridge District.
Started primary school at Swereki Primary School in Beitbridge and finished Standard Two there.
Moved to Vhutulula Primary School in Zezani for Standard Three, then to Zezani Secondary School in 1956.

Was expelled in Standard Six after he and others attacked a school principal over racial discrimination, then tried and failed to trade cattle hides in Bulawayo because whites would not buy from black traders.
Joined the National Democratic Party when it was formed.
After the NDP was banned he joined ZAPU and was elected its Secretary for Beitbridge District, working with Joshua Nkomo, Enos Nkala and Josiah Chinamano.
After ZAPU was banned he joined the People's Caretaker Council.
Arrested with comrades and held for seven years at Gonakudzingwa, Whawha, Connemara and Sikombela detention camps, studying for O-level exams in detention.
Released but placed under house arrest to stop political activity.

With Musa, Kohomela and Lazarus Mbedzi, cut a fence at Shobi Farm in Gwanda and drove a white farmer's cattle off to communal lands and Botswana; he was detained at Fort Tuli Camp and bailed out by businessman Sam Majoni.
Crossed into Mozambique through Chikwalakwala and went on to Lourenco Marques (Maputo), where he broadcast for six months on Mozambique radio and met his future wife Renni Kibi.
Went to Tanzania to raise resources for ZAPU, where Saul Gwakuba Ndlovu persuaded him to serve the struggle through broadcasting rather than study in Europe.
Moved to Lusaka, Zambia, was welcomed by ZAPU leaders and joined its publicity and information work.
Was seconded to Cairo, Egypt, and attended meetings in Kenya and Tanzania on ZAPU business.
Recalled from Cairo to join the ZAPU delegation to the Lancaster House conference.
After independence he later became a ZANU PF figure and served as Provincial Chairman for Matabeleland South.
The Politburo under President Mnangagwa recognised his service and declared him a national hero.

summary: Chenhamo Chimutengwende became politically active in Highfield as a teenager and rose to lead publicity in the ZANU Youth League before going abroad. He built a career as a writer, editor and journalism academic in London and Nairobi while campaigning for liberation and studying for higher degrees. Back in Zimbabwe he served for decades as a ZANU PF MP, provincial chairman, cabinet minister and finally Deputy President of the Senate. He died in January 2025 and was accorded national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Mashonaland Central Province, one of several children of John and Ronia Nyangoni.
Started primary school in Chiweshe, then moved to Highfield Secondary School in 1956.
Began his political activity at age 14 in Highfield, a centre of nationalist politics.
Elected Secretary for Information and Publicity of the ZANU Youth League.
Received ideological training from Chinese People's Liberation Army experts in Ghana, then went to London and gained advanced diplomas in journalism and television.
Appointed Executive Director of the Europe-Third World Research Centre.
Became Director of the Kwame Nkrumah Institute of Writers and Journalists and joined the editorial board of Black Dwarf, later Red Mole.
Launched The Liberation Struggle, a monthly paper covering liberation movements in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
After an MA in Peace Studies, began a PhD at the same university.
Became Senior Lecturer in Journalism and International Affairs and Deputy Director of the Journalism Programme at City University, and led a delegation of intellectuals to China.
Joined the University of Nairobi as Senior Lecturer and headed its School of Journalism until 1982.
Returned to Zimbabwe as Senior Lecturer at the Zimbabwe Institute of Mass Communications.
Elected ZANU PF Member of Parliament for Mazowe and led school and road building there.
Appointed ZANU PF Provincial Chairperson for Mashonaland Central, a post he held for 17 years.

Elected Deputy President of the Senate and Senator for Mashonaland Central, and later joined the Pan-African Parliament.
Died after a chronic illness; the Politburo then accorded him national hero status.

summary: Solomon Siziba, who fought as Lebanon Ngazimbi, left Manama High School in 1976 and escaped to Botswana and then Zambia to join ZIPRA. He trained as a guerrilla, survived the Rhodesian raids on the Mkushi camps and went to Moscow for further military training in 1979. After independence he served in the Zimbabwe National Army from 1981, holding many command and staff posts, working as Defence Attache in Botswana and retiring as a Major General. He also studied widely and later worked at the National Prosecuting Authority; after his death in January 2025 he was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Matobo District, the first of several children.
Began primary school in Gwanda and later enrolled at Manama High School in 1976.
Left school with classmates including Elson Moyo, Marshal Masera, Albert Ngulube and the future National Hero SB Moyo, and crossed into Botswana to join ZIPRA forces.
Resisted Rhodesian attempts, including a Lutheran pastor's appeal, to make the students return home, and moved on to Zambia where the group was received at CGT Base.
Underwent basic guerrilla training under General Phillip Valerio Sibanda and survived the Rhodesian attacks on the Mkushi camps.
Selected for military training in Moscow; on return was deployed at Solwezi as Reconnaissance Detachment Commander until the ceasefire.
Attested into the Zimbabwe National Army and commissioned with the equivalent rank of Captain.
Later served as Adjutant of 18 Infantry Battalion in Kezi and held a series of command and staff posts, including Commanding Officer of 43 Infantry Battalion and of the All Arms Battle School.
Appointed Defence Attache in Botswana, where he founded the Botswana Military Attache Association and wrote its constitution.
Rose to Deputy Commander of 1 Infantry Brigade and Brigadier General in the Army Inspectorate, retiring as Major General.
After the military he served as Board Secretary and then Director Administration of the National Prosecuting Authority.
Died after an illness; the Politburo then conferred national hero status on him.

summary: John Shumba Mvundura, who fought as Shumba Nyamukwati, grew up in Makoni District and left Harare Secondary School in 1963 under the weight of racial discrimination. He became a ZANU youth leader in Highfield while working in business, and after FRELIMO's 1974 victory he crossed into Mozambique to join the armed struggle. He took part in the Grand Reef attack and was wounded by a grenade, then trained at the Chitepo College of Ideology. After independence he became a diplomat with postings in several countries, held party posts in Manicaland and earned higher degrees; he died in January 2025 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Tarisai Village, Makoni District, the third of nine children.
Started primary school at Dumba Primary, later moving to Handina and in 1960 to Chirodzo for his last primary year.
Entered Harare Secondary School but had to stop in 1963 because racial discrimination blocked African education.
Became a full-time youth activist in Highfield and was made ZANU Youth Chairman for the branch.
Took a job at the Dairy Marketing Board, and in 1967 moved to Zengeni Stores as a manager, later becoming general manager.
Helped lead youths in Highfield who pelted stones at white Rhodesians watching released detainees such as Robert Mugabe, Maurice Nyagumbo, Edgar Tekere and Enos Nkala, forcing them to retreat.
Inspired by FRELIMO's victory in Mozambique, he decided to join the liberation war and crossed into Mozambique.
Endured the harsh Mozambican terrain with fellow cadres, helped by local villagers, and underwent military training.
Returned to Chimoio, Mozambique, and was present around the time of the bomb attack there (details garbled).
Joined a group assembled by Perrance Shiri and the General Staff that crossed back in mid-December and attacked the Rhodesians at Grand Reef near Umtali, then evaded a helicopter pursuit.
Wounded by a grenade after returning from Grand Reef and carried the fragments in his body until his death.
The following year studied Political Science at the Chitepo College of Ideology in Chimoio and then received a ZANU appointment.
Stayed in Mozambique through the ceasefire period, then returned to Zimbabwe and joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and diplomatic service.
Posted in Swaziland, followed by Malawi (1988-93), Libya (2000-04), Nigeria (2004-09) and Cuba (2010-13).
Died at St. Anne's Hospital in Harare after a long struggle with liver cancer, aged 81; the Politburo then conferred national hero status.

summary: Justin Hugh Mupamhanga, known in the struggle as Cde Top 10, left the University of Rhodesia in 1975 after Herbert Chitepo's assassination and joined ZANLA in Mozambique. There he worked in logistics and became a political instructor at the Herbert Chitepo School of Ideology before being sent to study economics in Maputo. After independence he built a long career in the President's Department, as an economics head, intelligence official and diplomat in London, and later as an energy-sector secretary and Deputy Chief Secretary to the President and Cabinet. He died in January 2025 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: After Ordinary level at St Augustine's in Penhalonga he moved to Harare Secondary School for Advanced Level studies.
He enrolled for a general BA degree at the University of Rhodesia, where his political activism began among the students.

Angered by the assassination of Herbert Chitepo in Zambia, he joined a large student protest, then dropped his studies with George Chiweshe and Neville Dembetembe and crossed into Mozambique to join the liberation struggle.
He joined other recruits at Zhunda Military Cantonment outside Vila Pery near Chimoio in Manica Province, where the newcomers met the first trained cadres.
At Nyadzonia he negotiated with the governor of Chimoio for the release of food supplies held back from the recruits.
He became important in the logistics department, receiving and settling new recruits every day.

He was among the first students at the Herbert Chitepo School of Ideology, later becoming one of its trainers of political commissars and helping produce political education material including the Mwenje booklet.
The leadership chose him to continue his studies at Eduardo Mondlane University in Maputo, part of Samora Machel's plan to prepare civic leaders for an independent Zimbabwe.
He remained at Eduardo Mondlane University when Zimbabwe became independent.
He graduated with a BSc in Economics from Eduardo Mondlane University.
He joined the President's Department, working in its economics section.
He was made head of the Economics Division and afterwards Deputy Director External Intelligence.
He was posted to London as Minister Counsellor.
He obtained an MBA from Middlesex University.
Recalled to Zimbabwe to revive the Economics Division, he also served on a task force that arranged maize imports to avert famine.

He was appointed Secretary of what appears to be the energy and power development portfolio, where he pushed for liberalising the fuel industry and for making the national oil company and ZESA more autonomous.
He helped establish the Zimbabwe Energy Regulatory Authority.
He was appointed Deputy Chief Secretary to the President and Cabinet, overseeing implementation and monitoring of government programmes.
He died; the Politburo then conferred national hero status on him.

summary: Elisha Nzirasha Chigudu, known as Cde Tinaye Mutete, grew up in Makoni District and was drawn into nationalist politics as a schoolboy, joining the ZAPU Youth League and being expelled in 1963. He crossed into Zambia in 1964, trained in North Korea, worked as an intelligence operative in Salisbury and was detained for twelve years from 1965. After independence he became a senior civil servant, serving as Permanent Secretary for Home Affairs for a decade and then as Governor of Manicaland until 2008. He died in February 2025 and the ruling party's Politburo honoured his service.

timeline.text: He started primary school at Chigudu Primary School in the Chiendambuya area of Makoni District.
He moved to Cyrene Mission in Matabeleland South, a school for African boys with a practical agricultural focus, where he saw harsh racial segregation.
Angered by segregation, he joined the ZAPU Youth League.
He began secondary education at a school that may be Harare Secondary School.
He took part in a student protest against oppressive laws and was expelled from school.
He crossed into Zambia to join the liberation struggle and was one of ten cadres selected for military training in North Korea.
He returned to Rhodesia after training and was deployed as an intelligence operative in Salisbury, gathering information on the colonial forces and helping youths leave for military training.
He was arrested and held at Gonakudzingwa, Gwelo and Whawha prisons for twelve years.
He was released from detention, and later that year married his long-time sweetheart Esther Dumba.
He crossed into Zambia again to resume duties in the armed struggle, having used his prison years to finish secondary education.
A sentence cut by the column break appears to say he was selected to study for an honours degree at Exeter University in the United Kingdom.
He returned to Zimbabwe and joined the civil service as Secretary (Legal Affairs) in the Ministry of Transport.
He was later made Deputy Secretary for Home Affairs.
He was appointed Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs, holding the post until 2004.
He took up a post connected to Mines and Mining Development (details unclear) and then served as Governor of Manicaland Province until his retirement in 2008.
He retired from public office; he also served ZANU PF as Manicaland Provincial Chairman and later consulted for the UNDP on structuring South Sudan's Ministry of Interior.
He died at home in Harare after a long battle with cancer, aged 82.

summary: Victor Rungani, who fought under the names Nyoka, Victor Chikudo and Jackson Moyo, was born in Bikita and became a youth organiser in Highfield before crossing into Mozambique in 1975. He rose in ZANLA from workshop head and transport director to sabotage and advance-detachment commander, ending the war at an assembly point in Matabeleland South. After independence he served in the Zimbabwe National Army, retiring as a Brigadier General in 1998 with several service medals and the Grand Officer of the Zimbabwe Order of Merit, and then joined the War Veterans ministry. He died in April 2025 and the Politburo accorded him national hero status.

timeline.text: He began primary school at Mashingaidze Primary School in Zaka, later moving through Mutimwi and Zimuto Central primary schools.
He started Forms One and Two at Zimuto Secondary School, then moved to Luveve Secondary School in Bulawayo in 1969.
He moved to Salisbury and lived in Highfield, a hotbed of nationalism, where colonial oppression pushed him into politics.
He was elected Organising Secretary of the Highfield Youth Branch during the Pearce Commission and later of Highfield District.
He crossed into Mozambique, passed through Machaze, Chibawawa and Nyadzonia bases, and received military training at Mapinduzi Camp in Chimoio.
After training he was deployed to ZANLA's transport department as head of its workshops.
He was appointed to the ZANLA General Staff and then made Provincial Transport Director for Manica Province, moving to Gaza Province in June.
He was deployed on the Sector Two operational front in Gaza Province.
He was appointed Commander of Sabotage Operations for Gaza Province Sector Three.
He joined the advance detachment covering Filabusi, Gwatemba and Fort Rixon, scouting and securing routes ahead of the main ZANLA force.
He opened the Gwanda and Matonjeni/Matopos detachments, and at the ceasefire went to Juliet Assembly Point (Zezani) in Matabeleland South.
He was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army (starting rank partly illegible) and became Commanding Officer of 43 Infantry Battalion in Gutu.
He was appointed Colonel.
He retired from the Zimbabwe National Army and joined the Ministry of War Veterans of the Liberation Struggle.
He died at Mbuya Dorcas Hospital in Harare, aged 76, and was afterwards accorded national hero status.

summary: Luke Mushore, nom de guerre Dick Joboringo, was expelled from Bernard Mzeki College in 1966 for leading protests, later joined early guerrilla activity around Chiweshe and Muzarabani and trained in Tanzania in 1971. As a ZANLA commander in Mashonaland Central he fought battles at Mauswa and Chahwanda and captured the Grey Scout Douglas Hawksworth, rising to detachment commander and General Staff member. After independence he worked briefly in the police and public service, then served as a ZANU PF official and Member of Parliament for Muzarabani, and farmed successfully. He died in June 2025 and the Politburo conferred national hero status on him.

timeline.text: He began secondary education at the Anglican-run Bernard Mzeki College.
He organised violent protests against discriminatory practices at the school, was caned and then expelled.
He lived with his grandmother in Chiweshe, worked as a bar attendant and joined youths mobilised by Chief Chiweshe Mukorekore to sabotage white-owned tobacco farms.
Hounded by authorities, he returned to Muzarabani and married Mavis Bizeni, then linked up with a unit of early freedom fighters led by Rex Nhongo.
He and other youths travelled to Chifombo Base in Zambia, helping carry the spirit medium of Mbuya Nehanda on a makeshift stretcher.
He was selected for military training at Mgagao in Tanzania, in a group of pioneer ZANLA fighters who also fought alongside FRELIMO.
His trained group re-entered Rhodesia through Chadereka in Mashonaland Central to join pioneering fighters, his operational zone covering Centenary, Guruve and Mt Darwin.
In his first clash with the Rhodesian Army at Mauswa his group forced the enemy to retreat with heavy casualties, at the same time as an attack on Altena Farm by another group.
He was appointed Section Commander with Cde Mazivisa as deputy, and led his unit to victory in the Chahwanda Battle against the mounted Rhodesian Grey Scouts.

He captured Grey Scout Douglas Hawksworth, who was posing as a land development officer, and sent him to Mozambique, an event that drew international attention to ZANLA's respect for the Geneva Convention.
He was promoted Detachment Commander for his exploits, which included opening the Chesa front in Mt Darwin and fronts in Mutoko, Mutare and Nyanga.
He became a member of the General Staff while still serving at the front; in 1975 and 1976 he operated in Manica Province.
He briefly joined the new police force, was posted to Mutoko, and later seconded to the Ministry of Sports and Culture and deployed to Chinhoyi.
He resigned from the public service to serve ZANU PF full time and retired to Muzarabani.
He was elected Member of Parliament for Muzarabani and assigned to the Security Cluster portfolio committee.
He was re-elected MP for Muzarabani North; he was also part of the national steering committee of war veterans during land reform and became a noted farmer.
He died after a long illness, aged 76, and was conferred national hero status.

summary: Sydney Gata was born in Marandellas, became politically active at school under Ndabaningi Sithole, fled to Botswana and went on to study chemical and aeronautical engineering abroad, earning a PhD in solar energy engineering. After independence he lectured at the University of Zimbabwe, helped build technical training institutions and became the first African General Manager and later CEO of ZESA, helping found the Southern African Power Pool. He later held senior international energy roles and worked on major power-project consultancies before returning to lead ZESA Holdings again in 2019. He died in July 2025 and was accorded national hero status.

timeline.text: He began primary school at Nyamure and Mutema in Chipinge, moving to Chikore Mission in 1954, where he met Rev Ndabaningi Sithole.
With Sithole he formed a group of schoolboys that opposed Smith's government, took part in protests and was suspended from school for resisting forced relocations from Chipinge to Bikita and Gokwe.
After O-level at Hartzel and A-level at Fletcher High, he fled to Botswana to escape political persecution.
He graduated in chemical engineering from Windsor University in Ontario, after first studying science at the University of Guelph in Canada.

Unable to find suitable work in Rhodesia, he taught for six months at Swaneng High School in Botswana, then moved to the UK to lecture at the University of London while completing a Master's degree, the first Zimbabwean to do so in that field, and a PhD in solar energy engineering.
He moved to a university department of mechanical engineering and aeronautics in London, while also helping stateless Zimbabwean refugees seeking asylum in the UK.

He returned to Zimbabwe and lectured in the University of Zimbabwe's Faculty of Engineering, later becoming Deputy Secretary in the manpower planning ministry, where he led construction of polytechnics and a national training centre.
He became General Manager of the Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Company, the first African to hold the post, and drove the merger of separate electricity bodies into ZESA.
He was selected to the board of the Central African Power Corporation.

He was appointed Chief Executive Officer of the Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority, overseeing Hwange Power Station stages, the main 330kV transmission system, interconnectors and rural and urban electrification, and helping found the Southern African Power Pool.
He resigned as ZESA general manager and moved to the UK, taking on senior roles with the World Energy Council and its committees.
He served as a peer review adviser to the African Development Bank and reviewed energy programmes of 47 Sub-Saharan African countries.
He was appointed a director of Integrated Energy Systems Ltd in the UK and seconded to a Zimbabwean investment bank as senior adviser on project finance.

As Executive Chairman of ZESA Holdings he led the restructuring that split ZESA into six successor companies and, at the Rural Electrification Agency, oversaw Hwange and Kariba South upgrades and irrigation rehabilitation projects.
He became Managing Partner of EMC Continental, advising on power projects in the SADC region.
He advised Rockingham Business Holdings on moving the Marsden B power station from New Zealand to Newcastle, South Africa.
He was appointed co-principal privatisation transaction adviser for NetOne Cellular during a process involving MTN.
He advised on feasibility and the power purchase agreement tender for a 250MW independent power producer for Eskom in South Africa.
He was reappointed Chairman and CEO of ZESA Holdings and advanced renewable-energy and Mozambican gas-power projects.
He died in Harare after a short illness, aged 79, and was accorded national hero status.

summary: Jairos Dambga Jiri was born in Bikita in 1921 and had his schooling cut short by unpaid fees. After walking to Bulawayo for work and serving as a cook at a barracks that rehabilitated wounded soldiers, he began feeding and housing destitute and disabled people in the 1940s. This grew from a foster home and garden project into a registered society and then the nationwide Jairos Jiri Association, with 16 centres by 1982, and brought him many local and international honours. He died in Harare in 1982 and was posthumously declared a national hero in September 2024.

timeline.text: Born at Mazvimba Village in Bikita District, the youngest of four children.
Started school but was sent back home because the family could not pay the fees, ending his formal education early.
Took work in Masvingo with a white employer who treated him badly, then walked to Bulawayo with his brother Mazviyo looking for a job.
Joined a military unit at Llewellin Barracks as a cook; seeing wounded soldiers being rehabilitated sparked his desire to help disabled and disadvantaged people.
Married Sophia in 1943, then in 1945 began feeding and clothing destitute people on the streets of Bulawayo out of his own small earnings.

While working as a shop assistant, converted his four-roomed Mzilikazi house into a foster home for beggars and disabled people; the city's African Affairs director, Dr E. H. Ashton, gave land for a gardening project.
After colonial refusals, registered the Bulawayo and Bikita Physically Defective Society, and on 15 October the city council let him use a Makokoba building to train disabled people.
Set up a management committee chaired by Dr Ashton to run the Society; it later secured government grants that began flowing in 1956.
Separated from Sophia and married Betty; the Bulawayo City Council gave land in Nguboyenja and the Society moved there.
Awarded the MBE by the Queen of the United Kingdom.
Toured Britain, America, Ghana and Nigeria seeking donations (meeting President Kennedy), then joined other charity operators to form the Jairos Jiri Association.
Granted the Freedom of the City of Bulawayo.

The Society took the name Jairos Jiri; Nguboyenja Centre was caring for 110 physically challenged, 72 blind and 18 deaf persons, and further centres were opened in Luveve, Fort Victoria, Gwelo, Salisbury, Silobela and Umtali.
Widened the charity's work to training entrepreneurs and musicians; the Association produced artists such as Fanyana Dube and Paul Matavire.
Attended the International Symposium on Rehabilitation in Kampala and had an audience with Pope Paul VI, receiving a blessing and a Holy Year medal.
Received an honorary Master of Arts from the University of Rhodesia, a humanitarian award from the Salisbury Union of Jewish Women and a Lions International service award.
Honoured with the Freedom of the City of Angeles, the Goodwill Industries International Award and the Rotary International Year of Disabled Persons Award.
Died of hypertension at Dzidzo House in Harare aged 61; by then the number of Jiri centres had grown from one in 1950 to 16.
The Politburo, led by President Mnangagwa, posthumously accorded him national hero status.

summary: Enos David Malandu, known in the struggle as Cde Teacher, was a first-born child from Insiza who went on to study in South Africa and earned a Master's in Public Administration in the United States. On returning to Rhodesia he joined the ZIPRA nationalist movement, trained in Tanzania, and became ZAPU's Chief Commissar and an ideological instructor in Zambia. He later joined the Lancaster House delegation, served on ZAPU's National Executive Council, managed the Zimtraco company, and helped negotiate the 1987 Unity Accord. He died in 1990 and was buried in Bulawayo; he was declared a national hero in August 2025.

Won a scholarship to study Public Administration at Messiah College in South Africa and taught briefly there after graduating.
Secured another bursary to take a Master's in Public Administration at the University of Pittsburgh in the United States.
Returned to Rhodesia after his degree and became involved with the ZIPRA movement, marking the start of his formal role in the nationalist struggle.

Selected for military training at Morogoro in Tanzania, where he stood out as a leading intellectual and ideological figure; with Cde Ambrose Mutinhiri he helped shape the camp's structures and the dual military-political training model.
After training went to Zambia and joined ZAPU, where he was appointed Chief Commissar for his intellectual leadership and organisational ability.
Posted to Nampundwe Camp in Zambia, where he taught Marxism-Leninism to cadres.
Was part of the delegation to the Lancaster House Conference in London.
Returned home and was appointed to the ZAPU National Executive Council; also served in the Commissariat Department as an ideological educator and strategist.
Moved into economic administration as General Manager of Zimtraco, ZAPU's commercial arm set up to create jobs and stability for returning ZIPRA cadres.
Took part in the negotiations that led to the Unity Accord, then continued in the ZANU-PF Commissariat Department until his death.
Died in Filabusi after a short illness.
Posthumously declared a national hero.

summary: Joseph Zethi Dube, known as Cde Zwangami, was born in Matobo in 1935 and studied in Johannesburg, where he joined the ANC Youth League before recruiting youths for ZAPU. After a 1961 arrest he fled to Zambia and trained in Egypt and Cuba, later acting as ZAPU's representative in Latin America and serving in the Joint Military Command delegation and the ZIPRA High Command. At independence he joined the national army as a Colonel and became Commandant at Inkomo Barracks, retiring in 1986 to work at Blue Ribbon Foods and the University of Zimbabwe. He died in February 1996 and was later declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Matobo District, one of only two sons of the family.
Enrolled at St Joseph Primary School; finished in 1950 and went on to Empandeni Secondary School.
After the Junior Certificate taught briefly at Sontala Primary School, then went to Johannesburg to matriculate at Damelin College, joined the ANC Youth League and worked as a dispatch clerk.
Arrested at Kezi by the District Commissioner while recruiting youths for ZAPU, held for three months, then jumped bail and fled to Lusaka, Zambia.
Went for military training in Egypt, gaining skills in organisation, infiltration, weapons handling and intelligence coordination.
Trained in Cuba and attained the rank of Captain; from 1966 to 1969 served as ZAPU's representative in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Deployed to Zambia, where he took part in operational planning and field assignments.
Named to the ZAPU delegation to the Joint Military Command, contributing to coordination, training oversight and strategy.
During the formation of ZIPA was appointed advisor to the ZIPRA command element.
Posted again to Havana, Cuba as ZAPU's official representative for Latin America and the Caribbean.
Appointed to the ZIPRA High Command, serving in the Commissariat Department on logistics, supplies and personnel welfare.
At Independence was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a Colonel and became Commandant at Inkomo Barracks until 1985.
Selected to serve on the Joint High Command overseeing force integration, conventional training and demobilisation.
Retired from the army and moved to the private sector as Senior Personnel Manager at Blue Ribbon Foods.
After leaving active politics took an academic post at the University of Zimbabwe, where he served until his death.
Died of heart failure at United Bulawayo Hospitals aged 60 and was buried at Lady Stanley Cemetery.
Posthumously declared a national hero for his contribution to the liberation struggle and the nation.

summary: Petros Khumalo, known as Cde Mpondo, was born in Lupane in 1940 and left for Zambia after primary school, where he worked as a council clerk. Returning to Rhodesia in 1964 he had to flee arrest and joined ZAPU in Lusaka, then trained in Tanzania and later received medical training in the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom. He served as a medical officer at Nampundwe Camp and as ZIPRA's logistics officer for medical supplies, and after Independence became a Major in the national army, including a posting guarding the Beira Corridor. He died in Bulawayo of tuberculosis.

timeline.text: Born in Lupane as the youngest of four children.
Started primary school at Fatima Mission in Lupane, and after Standard Six went to live with a cousin in Northern Rhodesia (now Zambia).
Found work as a clerk with the Livingstone City Council.

Returned to Rhodesia during rising repression; security forces sought to arrest him on suspicion of passing intelligence, so he fled to Livingstone and then Lusaka, where he joined ZAPU and worked with nationalists such as Robson Manyika and Stephen Nkomo.
Underwent military training in Tanzania and was deployed to the Hwange-Binga operational sector.
Recalled and sent with a medical team to the Soviet Union for advanced medical training, in recognition of his aptitude and earlier administrative experience.

Chosen for further professional training in the United Kingdom, then posted to Nampundwe Transit Camp in Zambia as Medical Officer, running clinical services, medical staff and drug supplies and introducing preventive health measures.
Recalled and raised to the ZIPRA High Command in Zambia as Logistics Command Officer for medical supplies.
After the ceasefire returned to Zimbabwe among senior cadres led by Lookout Masuku and was deployed to the Romeo Assembly Point in Chinhoyi.
Transferred to Harare under Operation Sovereign Independence Exercise Plan (OPSEEP), working with the British Military Advisory and Training Team on integrating the armed forces.
At Independence was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as a Major and posted to Harare District as a Staff Officer Grade II.
Redeployed to an infantry battalion in Mutare tasked with safeguarding the Beira Corridor in a volatile environment marked by incursions and sabotage.
Died at Hillside Health Centre in Bulawayo after battling tuberculosis.

summary: Victor Kuretu was a Manicaland teacher who became a ZAPU youth leader in Sakubva and was jailed, detained at Wha Wha and restricted at Sakubva for his nationalist activism under the Rhodesian regime. After release in 1970 he moved to Harare, stayed active in politics, and after Independence worked at Dairibord while holding ZAPU and later ZANU-PF leadership posts. He helped lead the ex-political prisoners' association ZEPPDRA, serving as National Chairperson from 2005 until his death. The Politburo agreed to accord him national hero status after he died.

First arrested in connection with his political activities, and was repeatedly targeted by the Rhodesian authorities afterwards.

Held for six months at Mutare Central Prison before being detained at the Wha Wha detention centre, created after the Rhodesian justice minister issued mass restriction and detention orders against nationalists.
Released from Sakubva Restriction Camp after a period of restriction.
Moved to Harare, worked as a salesman and stayed politically active, being elected to local party and ward-level positions including for Ward 35 in Mufakose.

After Independence worked for Dairibord Zimbabwe while serving as ZAPU District Chairperson.
After the Unity Accord took leadership roles in ZANU-PF, rising from district to provincial level.

Elected National Chairperson of the Zimbabwe Ex-Political Prisoners, Detainees and Restrictees Association (ZEPPDRA), after earlier serving as its Deputy Secretary for Information and Publicity.

After a revelation in 1957 he founded the African Apostolic Church in 1959 and served as its Bishop and later Archbishop, building a movement that spread across Zimbabwe and abroad. timeline.text: Born near Mvuma during a deadly influenza outbreak and named Mamvura (child of water) by his mother.
Presumed dead as a sick infant, he was taken to a German priest at Holy Cross Mission, who baptised him Paul when the child revived and cried out.
After his father died, the family moved from Chirumanzu to Kwenda Village in Njanja, Chikomba District.
Began learning Catholic catechism under his maternal uncle and started a daily habit of prayer despite being illiterate.
Started primary school at Masvaure Methodist School in Chikomba, where he often withdrew into the bush to pray.
Sold a cow inherited from his father to pay fees at Kwenda Mission, where he stayed with an evangelist and topped his class.
Sold cattle from his sister's bride price to raise fees and joined Howard Institute at Chiweshe for Standards Five to Seven.
Won the Beit Trust Scholarship that paid for his teacher training at Howard Institute.
Completed teacher training.
Posted as the only teacher at Gweshe Primary School and grew enrolment from 25 pupils through a door-to-door campaign.
Experienced several visions that strengthened his faith and drew him to bring others closer to Christ.
Moved to Chideme Primary School, continuing his teaching and spiritual work.
Transferred to Sadza Primary School as head and evangelist, preaching, healing and performing miracles.
Moved to Chirasauta to help his younger brother in a general dealer shop while continuing evangelism.
On the way back from Easter prayers at Mudanda in Buhera he received a revelation to found a new church called The African Apostolic Church.
The African Apostolic Church was officially founded with him as Bishop, and it spread quickly across Rhodesia.
Ran four retail businesses and supported freedom fighters with prayer, clothing and foodstuffs.
Sold his businesses to devote himself fully to leading the church.
Died aged 107 of natural causes and was accorded national hero status by the Politburo.

Spent three months at Selibe Phikwe Prison with relatives and comrades, then was airlifted to Nampundwe in Zambia for another three months.
Began basic military training at Mulungushi Dam under the Zambian Army with ZIPRA attachments.
Selected for advanced military training in Odessa in the Soviet Union.
Completed the Soviet course, returned and became an instructor at Solwezi, then was deployed to Siyavonga on the Zambezi.

Commanded 41 Infantry Battalion.
Served as Defence Attache to the Republic of Zambia.
Posted to the Adjutants' Generals Pool before retiring.
Died at Gwanda General Hospital after a long illness, aged 69, and was accorded national hero status.

summary: Mupamaonde grew up in Bikita District, attended Silveira Mission and left for Botswana and Zambia in 1972 to join the liberation war. He trained in commando skills in Tanzania and in artillery and weapons systems in the Soviet Union, becoming an expert in missile technology. He opened new fronts around Kariba, fought the 1977 Kariba battle, rose to Commander of Northern Front Two in 1979 and led the downing of Air Rhodesia Flight 827. After Independence he settled into farming, died in March 2026 and was declared a national hero.

timeline.text: Born in Bikita District, second in a family of 16 children.
Began primary school at Mupamaonde Primary School.
Went on to Silveira Mission School for secondary education.
Crossed into Botswana, stayed briefly in Francistown, and travelled to Mwembeshi in Zambia to enlist for military training.
Sent to Morogoro, Tanzania, for six months of commando instruction alongside later ZDF commander Philip Valerio Sibanda.
Nominated for specialised artillery training in the Soviet Union, including Advanced Weapons Systems, where he excelled.
Under Cde Nikita Mangena he was again selected for specialised training involving a Russian-made missile system.
After finishing training he was deployed to a Gaza Province command under Cde Makasha.
With fellow commander Barbatone Sibhona he opened new fronts in the Kariba region, attacking Kariba Airport and Rhodesian bases.
Led an artillery battery at a Kariba battle that lasted nearly an hour and blocked enemy reinforcements without any freedom fighter lost.
His sabotage units destroyed the Nyawodza and Tsororo bridges and mined routes, wrecking over thirty Rhodesian military vehicles.
Elevated to Commander of Northern Front Two with at least 350 fighters, covering the area from the Chewore River to Binga.
Led Operation Disrupt Tourism, in which his team shot down Air Rhodesia Flight 827 at Kariba.
His supply-line ambushes made parts of Mashonaland West such as Nyimo, Chenjiri and Makonde effectively no-go zones for Rhodesian forces.
Deployed to Romeo Assembly Point near Makonde Primary School until Independence.
Returned to quiet civilian life and farming in Mashonaland.
Died after a long illness at St Albert's Mission Hospital and was accorded national hero status.

He fought in Chitepo Sector, was wounded in the Honde Valley in 1977, and was later sent to Romania for training and instruction. After Independence he served as an artillery and infantry officer, commanded 2 Infantry Brigade during the DRC operation and led the Staff College and National Defence University before a secondment to the lands ministry. He earned several degrees up to a doctorate and was declared a national hero by the Politburo.

timeline.text: Born in Rukweza Village, Makoni District, the eldest of 13 children of Jacob Tichaona Chingono and Winnie Chingono.

As head boy at Nyazura Adventist Mission he organised a strike against colonial segregation that damaged school property; police arrested him and fellow students, he was held at Rusape and later released to sit his O-Levels with a trial pending.
After O-Levels he and a friend, Wilbert Moyo, joined ZANLA and crossed into Mozambique; he chose front-line training over a refugee camp.
Operated for almost nine months in the Nyanga and Gandanzara areas of Chitepo Sector under commanders Lameck Temba and Etherton Shungu.
Seriously wounded when his group was bombed from the air in the Honde Valley and was evacuated to Mozambique to recover.
While recuperating he organised logistics and liaison with Mozambican authorities for an attack on Ruda Camp led by Solomon Mujuru and Josiah Tungamirai, then returned with the force to Chimoio.
Chosen for his bravery to join a group of twenty cadres led by Etherton Shungu for specialised military training in Romania.
Remained in Romania as an instructor and came home at Independence.
Completed the Standardisation Course at the Zimbabwe Military Academy and was posted to the Field Artillery Regiment as a battery commander, helping to establish 2 Field Artillery Regiment.

His newly integrated artillery unit served in Mozambique in an infantry role; he later led the Presidential Guard Battalion and wrote its brigade's first training exercise in the Nyanga Training Area.
Took part in Operation Sovereign Legitimacy in the DRC, first handling logistics at Army Headquarters and then commanding 2 Infantry Brigade on the Eastern Front during the ceasefire.
Held senior staff and training posts including Commandant of the Zimbabwe Staff College, Inspector at Army Headquarters, Senior Directing Staff and Dean at the Zimbabwe National Defence University.
Seconded to the Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Water and Rural Resettlement as Chief Director in the office of Minister Air Chief Marshal Shiri, helping drive reforms in agriculture.
Rose from Lieutenant to the rank of Major General (promotion year garbled in the text).
After his death the Politburo under President Mnangagwa accorded him national hero status.

timeline.text: Born in Kampaundi Village near Empress Mine, Gokwe, the last of eight children of Hubert and Maria Matemadanda.

Joined ZANLA as a young teenager.
Trained at Chifombo Camp and was then assigned to movement work between Zambia and Mozambique.
Crossed into Mozambique via Feira, spent four months near the Zambia-Malawi border, then returned to Zambia to help Patrick Kombayi and others supply fighters and refugees.
Sent back to Mozambique for further training at Tembwe Camp, then deployed to Takawira Sector, Detachment A, under Hillary Mudhuri.
Wounded in combat in August 1979 and evacuated to Mozambique for treatment; he returned to the front in October and resumed duties in Area C of Takawira Sector.
Joined former fighters at Dendera Assembly Point and was made a Political Commissar who educated communities on the coming first general elections.

summary: Born in Makoni District in 1962 to a family dispossessed of its ancestral land, he was shaped by colonial racial discrimination at work and a beating by Rhodesian soldiers. He joined the liberation struggle alone in 1978, trained at a Chitepo Sector base in Mozambique and adopted the name Kid Mawrongwrong. After Independence he rose in the Zimbabwe National Army from Officer to Major General (2017), serving in procurement, finance and personnel directorates. timeline.text: Born in Nyadongo Village in Tandi area, Makoni District, the first of eight children of Enos Dzihwema and Stella Kajokoto.
His family lost its ancestral land in Dombo to a white settler, was denied resettlement and was moved by the Makoni District Commissioner to Tanda in Headlands Communal Lands.
Attended Chapwanya and then Tsikada primary schools, finishing in 1972 after skipping a grade.
Attended St John's Secondary School in Chikwaka and completed Ordinary Level in 1977.
Worked briefly as a clerk at Pearl Assurance and was refused a salary review on grounds of age while a white colleague of the same age earned more, deepening his awareness of colonial injustice.
Was beaten by Rhodesian soldiers who suspected him of spying for ZANLA while he returned from obtaining a juvenile registration certificate.
Left home alone to join the liberation struggle after two companions backed out; crossed the Nyangombe River into Nyanga where he stayed a month with fighters before being moved toward Mozambique.
With a group that had grown to fifteen he crossed the Gairezi River into Mozambique and reached the forward operational base of Chitepo Sector, where he was told to train at the front.
Underwent military training at the base under several instructors; as platoon commissar of about thirty-five trainees he took the nom de guerre Kid Mawrongwrong.
Fought bravely in operations in Chitepo Sector and at the ceasefire gathered with his detachment at an assembly point in Nyanga.
After Independence on 18 April 1980 he was attested into the Zimbabwe National Army as an Officer on 9 October 1980.
Promoted to Lieutenant (1981), Captain (1984) and Major (1986).
Held procurement posts and served as General Manager of the Army Clothing Factory (dates approximate).
Promoted to Lieutenant Colonel (1992) and Colonel (1998).
Director Finance at ZDF Headquarters, followed by other procurement and personnel directorates (dates approximate).
Promoted to Brigadier General.
Served as Director General Services Personnel at ZDF Headquarters.
Reached the rank of Major General on retirement and later held ministry and board posts, including Chief Director roles in two ministries.
Died in India after septic shock aged 64; the Politburo under President Mnangagwa accorded him national hero status.

summary: Richard Ruwodo, known in the war as Moshe Pwititi, was born in Mutare District and worked at Bata Shoe Company before joining ZANLA in 1975. After training in Mozambique he handled finance at ZANU headquarters in Maputo, and after Independence he built a career in the army's pay and finance branches, becoming its first Black Director of Pay and Records and eventually a Major General. He earned several campaign, service and liberation medals as well as the Grand Officer of the Zimbabwe Order of Merit. After his death the Politburo accorded him national hero status, and he was survived by his wife and children.

timeline.text: Started primary school at Mutasa Primary School in Mutare District and finished there in 1968.
Entered Highfields Secondary School in Harare, where he completed Ordinary Level in 1972.
Took a job as a salesman at Bata Shoe Company and was later promoted to Relief Manager, staying until 1975.
Left his job and home to join the liberation struggle in the ranks of ZANLA, motivated by political discussions with peers and a wish to free the country.
Underwent military training at Chimoio in Mozambique as part of the third group of recruits, alongside Shaw Matemachani and Thomas Byuma.
After training, was posted to ZANU Headquarters in Maputo as Director of Finance, working under Ernest Kadungure, who later became a national hero.
Committed himself to building and professionalising the Zimbabwe National Army and was appointed Deputy Chief Paymaster under the acting Chief Paymaster, Colonel Bratton.
Listed in his promotion history as reaching the rank of Lieutenant (rank and date partly legible).
Attended the Intermediate Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Attended the Senior Officers' Signals Course.
Became the first Black Director of Zimbabwe Army Pay and Records, leading reforms of pay and records systems and the integration of new staff into a corps that had been mostly white.
Attended the Command and Staff Course at the Zimbabwe Staff College.
Promoted to Major General according to the promotion list.
Held senior finance posts including Chief Paymaster and Director Finance Branch at Army Headquarters and Brigadier Finance at Defence Forces Headquarters.
Died at Avenues Clinic, aged 69 according to the text.
After his death the Politburo, led by President Mnangagwa, unanimously conferred national hero status on him for his contributions to the liberation struggle, unity and development.
